authors.name: Abbo of Fleury
authors.identity: hagiographer, grammarian, computist; Latin prose writer
authors.biography: Born c. 945 near Orléans, oblate of Fleury, and trained there in grammar, dialectic, and computus. At the invitation of Oswald of Worcester he taught at Ramsey Abbey in the Fenland from 985 to 987, where he wrote the Passio Sancti Eadmundi at the request of the Ramsey monks and dedicated it to Dunstan. Returning to Fleury, he became abbot in 988 and defended his monastery against episcopal encroachment; he died in 1004 in a brawl at La Réole while attempting to reform the priory of La Réole.
authors.profile: One of the leading scholars of tenth-century Europe. At Ramsey he composed the Passio Sancti Eadmundi (985-987), the earliest Latin life of King Edmund of East Anglia and the basis of Ælfric's Old English life; his other works include the Quaestiones grammaticales (dedicated to his English students), computistical treatises, and the Collectio canonum.
authors.style: Clear, correct Latin prose with the polish of the Fleury school; the Passio builds its narrative through dramatic dialogue and carefully staged scenes of Edmund's martyrdom and the discovery of his incorrupt body.
authors.concerns: The union of grammar, computus, and exegesis in monastic learning; royal sanctity and the cult of St Edmund; the reform of monastic discipline.
authors.significance: The principal conduit of continental monastic learning into the English Benedictine Reform; his teaching at Ramsey raised the standard of Latin scholarship in England, and his Passio Eadmundi founded the literary cult of St Edmund, patron saint of the English kingdom.
authors.uncertainty: None significant for the works recorded here; the Passio's dedication to Dunstan and composition at Ramsey (985-987) are established.
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography

authors.name: Alcuin of York
authors.biography: Pupil and then master of the school of York under Ælberht; visited Rome in 781 and joined the court of Charlemagne, becoming the leading intellectual of the Carolingian Renaissance; abbot of Tours from 796 until his death.
authors.profile: A large corpus of letters (including the famous letter of 793 on the sack of Lindisfarne), poems (notably on York and its library), educational dialogues on grammar, rhetoric, and dialectic, biblical commentaries, and liturgical and polemical writings against adoptionism.
authors.style: Elegant, courtly Latin; epistolary warmth and learning; verse of wide metrical range.
authors.concerns: The reform of learning and the correction of texts; pastoral care of rulers; orthodoxy; the preservation of the Northumbrian scholarly tradition abroad.
authors.significance: The chief transmitter of Anglo-Saxon learning to the Continent; architect of the educational program of Charlemagne's court.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate (c. 735, sometimes given 732–735).
themes: The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
sources: The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition

authors.name: Aldhelm
authors.biography: West Saxon nobleman educated at Canterbury under the archbishop Theodore and the abbot Hadrian; abbot of Malmesbury and, from c. 705, first bishop of Sherborne. The first major Anglo-Latin author, he composed in an elaborate 'hermeneutic' style that set the standard for insular Latinity for centuries.
authors.profile: Principal works: the prose and verse De virginitate (in praise of virginity, with a catalogue of exemplars), the Epistola ad Acircium (a treatise on Latin metre addressed to King Aldfrith of Northumbria), the Aenigmata (one hundred Latin riddles), the Carmen rhythmicum, and a small corpus of letters.
authors.style: Learned, allusive 'hermeneutic' Latin rich in Grecisms, archaisms, and rare vocabulary; metrical virtuosity in both hexameters and rhythmic verse.
authors.concerns: Monastic virtue, especially virginity; Latin learning and prosody; the unity of the English church.
authors.significance: Founder of the Anglo-Latin literary tradition; his works were models for Bede, Boniface, Alcuin, and the tenth-century Benedictine reformers.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate (from later sources, principally William of Malmesbury).
movements: Early Anglo-Latin Learning and the Northumbrian Golden Age
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Old English Literature, 2nd edition

authors.name: Alexander Barclay
authors.nationality: English (writing in England); Scottish by birth
authors.biography: Born about 1484, probably in Scotland; educated perhaps at Oxford, he became a priest, chaplain at the college of St Mary Ottery in Devon, then a Benedictine monk of Ely and finally rector of All Hallows, Lombard Street. He died at Croydon in June 1552. His Ship of Fools (1509) adapted Sebastian Brant's Narrenschiff through Locher's Latin, and his five Eclogues (c. 1514) introduced pastoral to England.
authors.profile: The first English pastoralist and the translator of the most widely read satire of the age. The Ship of Fools is a comprehensive estates satire — a gallery of fools from the scholar to the bishop — written in fluent rhyme royal and five-line stanzas, and the Eclogues, based on Mantuan, moralize the shepherd's life and the corruption of courts and clergy.
authors.style: Smooth, competent stanzaic verse; moral satire without Skeltonic fury; a translator's fidelity to his Latin sources over originality.
authors.concerns: The folly of the estates; clerical reform; the moral uses of pastoral; the dignity of English as a literary language.
authors.significance: Introduced both the estates satire of the continental Renaissance and the pastoral eclogue into English; a principal channel by which humanist satire reached the Tudor reading public.
authors.uncertainty: Birthplace and early life uncertain; the date of the Eclogues is approximate.

authors.name: Alfred the Great
authors.identity: king; translator; lawgiver; patron of letters
authors.biography: King of Wessex 871–899. After the near-collapse of his kingdom before the Viking army, his victory at Edington (878) and the treaty with Guthrum secured a period of reconstruction in which he pursued a deliberate program of educational revival, gathering scholars at his court and translating into English the books 'most necessary for all men to know'. Died 26 October 899.
authors.profile: Personally translated (or directed the translation of) Gregory's Pastoral Care with his famous Preface (c. 890), Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, Augustine's Soliloquies, and the first fifty prose Psalms; commissioned the Old English Orosius, the Old English Bede, Werferth's translation of Gregory's Dialogues, his own law code (the Domboc), and the Common Stock of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (c. 892).
authors.style: Clear, idiomatic prose that adapts rather than slavishly renders its Latin sources; the Preface to the Pastoral Care is a classic statement of vernacular purpose.
authors.concerns: The restoration of wisdom and literacy as the foundation of just rule; the defense of the kingdom and the Christian people.
authors.significance: Founder of the English prose tradition; his translations preserved classical and patristic texts in the vernacular and set the model for all later Old English prose.
authors.uncertainty: The extent of his personal authorship is debated: the Preface is certainly his, but the translations were produced by his circle under his direction.

works.title: Old English Boethius (with the Meters of Boethius)
Old English Pastoral Care (with Alfred's Preface)

sources: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle: A Revised Translation

authors.name: Andrew Boorde
authors.biography: Born about 1490 in Sussex; educated at Oxford and a Carthusian monk before leaving the order to practise medicine. He travelled widely in Europe and the Mediterranean, and his books — The Dyetary of Health (1542) and The First Book of the Introduction of Knowledge (1547) — made him the first English writer of popular medicine and travel. He died in the Fleet prison in April 1549.
authors.profile: The first English popular medical writer and the father of the English travel book. The Dyetary prescribes diet and regimen in plain English for the common reader, and The Introduction of Knowledge — the first English book of travels written from personal observation — describes the peoples of Europe in prose and verse, with specimens of their languages.
authors.style: Homely, practical prose; the physician's plain advice; travellers' tales told with a journalist's eye for the odd and useful.
authors.concerns: Popular health and regimen; the description of foreign nations; the usefulness of knowledge to the commonwealth.
authors.significance: Founded the English traditions of popular medicine and of the travel book; his writings document the widening world of the Tudor reader.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; parts of the biography rest on late testimony.

authors.name: Anne Askew
authors.biography: Born about 1521 into a Lincolnshire gentry family; married against her will to Thomas Kyme. Her refusal to accept the doctrine of transubstantiation brought her before the authorities in 1545 and 1546; racked in the Tower — reportedly by the Lord Chancellor himself — she was burned at Smithfield on 16 July 1546. Her accounts of her two examinations were printed with John Bale's commentary in 1546–47.
authors.profile: Author of the first English autobiography of a Protestant martyr and the most important woman's voice of the Henrician Reformation. The Examinations record her interrogations in her own words — scriptural, witty, and unyielding — and made her the exemplary female witness of the English church, read and reprinted through the sixteenth century and canonized by Foxe.
authors.style: First-person testimony in the plain style; scriptural riposte reported as dialogue; a cool exactness under the shadow of the stake.
authors.concerns: The right of the laity, and of women, to read and interpret scripture; the sacrament debated as doctrine; the witness of the body against the bishops.
authors.significance: The founding text of English women's religious autobiography and a landmark of the martyrological tradition; her voice resounds in Foxe and in the later women writers of the Reformation.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; details of the racking rest on Foxe and Bale.

authors.name: Asser
authors.nationality: Welsh (writing in Latin for the West Saxon court)
authors.biography: Monk of St David's in Wales, recruited by Alfred c. 885 as one of the scholars of his court; bishop of Sherborne from c. 895. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records his death in 909 (or 908).
authors.profile: Author of the Life of King Alfred (893), the principal contemporary biography of an English king: a vivid, partly annalistic portrait of Alfred's wars, piety, illnesses, and program of learning.
authors.style: Latin biography blending Welsh and Carolingian conventions (Einhard's Charlemagne is a model) with annals of the years 849–887.
authors.concerns: The justification and celebration of Alfred's kingship; the union of learning with rule.
authors.significance: The main primary source for Alfred's reign and character.
authors.uncertainty: The Life's authenticity was long debated (the 'Leofric interpolation' question); modern scholarship accepts it as substantially genuine. Dates approximate.
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry

authors.name: Bede
authors.biography: Entered the monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow as a child and remained there all his life, becoming priest and teacher; he never travelled beyond Northumbria yet became the most learned man of his age in western Europe. Died on Ascension Day, 26 May 735, dictating his last work.
authors.profile: Author of the Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum (completed 731), the foundational history of the English people; De temporum ratione (725), which fixed the practice of dating from the Incarnation (AD); biblical commentaries on nearly every book of scripture; the metrical and prose lives of St Cuthbert; De natura rerum; the letter to Egbert (734); and school texts on orthography and metre.
authors.style: Clear, economical, carefully sourced Latin; narrative skill in the miracle stories of the Historia; scholarly exactitude in computus and chronology.
authors.concerns: The unity and orthodoxy of the English church; chronology and computus; the transmission of patristic exegesis; the moral formation of clergy.
authors.significance: 'The father of English history'; the Historia preserves the Cædmon story, the earliest extended Old English verse, and much else besides; his computus standardized European chronology.
authors.uncertainty: Little uncertainty: the Historia's autobiographical colophon and Cuthbert's account of his death are reliable; birth year inferred from his own statements.

works.title: Vita Sancti Cuthberti (metrical and prose lives)

sources: A Guide to Old English, 8th edition

authors.name: Blind Hary
authors.biography: A blind poet or minstrel ('Blind Hary') who composed the Wallace c. 1477, reciting it before James IV for payment; royal treasury records note payments to him in the 1470s and 1490s. Almost nothing else is known of his life.
authors.profile: Author of The Wallace (c. 1477), an epic verse life of William Wallace in heroic couplets, drawing on the lost biography by John Blair and on oral tradition.
authors.style: Robust, declamatory couplets; fierce anti-English sentiment and graphic battle scenes; the folk-heroic exaggeration of Wallace's deeds.
authors.concerns: Scottish freedom and the cult of Wallace; loyalty and betrayal; national memory.
authors.significance: The Wallace was for centuries the most popular book in Scotland after the Bible (Burns acknowledged its inspiration) and fixed the popular image of Wallace for posterity.
authors.uncertainty: Nearly everything about him is conjectural; dates approximate.

authors.name: Boniface
authors.biography: Monk of Nursling (Hampshire); missionary to Frisia and Germany from 716, organizing the church in Hesse and Thuringia; archbishop of Mainz from c. 745; reformed the Frankish church in councils; martyred with his companions at Dokkum in Frisia on 5 June 754.
authors.profile: His correspondence — with popes, kings, and English correspondents such as Eadburga, Bugga, and Egbert of York — is the richest epistolary record of the eighth century; he also wrote an Ars grammatica, an Ars metrica, and a collection of Latin riddles and poems.
authors.style: Plain, forceful epistolary Latin; pedagogic clarity in the grammatical works.
authors.concerns: Mission; church discipline and reform; the pastoral and intellectual nurture of his English network.
authors.significance: The greatest of the Anglo-Saxon missionaries; his letters document the cultural links between England and the Carolingian world.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the Crediton birthplace rests on late tradition.
sources: The Blackwell Encyclopaedia of Anglo-Saxon England, 2nd edition

authors.name: Byrhtferth of Ramsey
authors.biography: Monk of Ramsey Abbey, pupil of Abbo of Fleury during Abbo's stay there (985–987); the most learned English computist of his generation.
authors.profile: Author of the Enchiridion (c. 1011), a bilingual manual of computus and related sciences in Latin and Old English; probably the author of the Life of St Oswald and possibly of annals in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for the late tenth century.
authors.style: Learned, allusive Latin (in the hermeneutic tradition) alternating with clear expository Old English.
authors.concerns: Computus, number symbolism, and the sciences of the quadrivium as handmaids of the liturgical year.
authors.significance: The chief witness to the scientific culture of the Benedictine Reform in England.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; attributions partly conjectural.
sources: British Library Digitised Manuscripts

authors.name: Catherine Parr
authors.biography: Born about 1512; the sixth wife of Henry VIII, whom she married in 1543. A learned woman of reformist sympathies, she narrowly escaped arrest for heresy in 1546. Her Prayers or Meditations appeared in 1545, the first book printed under the name of an English queen, and The Lamentation of a Sinner in 1547 after the king's death. She died on 5 September 1548, shortly after marrying Thomas Seymour.
authors.profile: The first English queen in print. Prayers or Meditations (1545) adapts the Imitatio Christi into a personal devotional idiom, and The Lamentation of a Sinner (1547) is a conversion narrative and confession in the new evangelical mode, declaring the futility of works and the sufficiency of faith in Christ.
authors.style: Warm, first-person devotion; the language of interiority and the afflicted conscience; scriptural quotation woven into prayer.
authors.concerns: Personal faith and justification; the education of women (she oversaw the schooling of the young Elizabeth); the reform of devotion from within the court.
authors.significance: A pioneer of English women's devotional writing and a patron of the reformed cause; her example licensed the religious authorship of later English women.
authors.uncertainty: Birth year approximate (1512); the extent of her direct influence on Elizabeth's education is documented but partly inferential.

authors.name: Cynewulf
authors.biography: Nothing is known of Cynewulf beyond his name, which he wove as a runic acrostic into the epilogues of four Old English poems: The Fates of the Apostles, Elene, Juliana, and Christ II. Candidates proposed for identification include a Cynewulf bishop of Lindisfarne (d. 783), but the question remains open.
authors.profile: The four signed poems form a coherent body of religious narrative and meditation; scholars have also attributed other poems (notably in the Exeter and Vercelli books) to his 'school' without consensus.
authors.style: Ornate, reflective religious narrative; typological reading of scripture and legend; runic signature passages that meditate on judgment and the last things.
authors.concerns: Salvation, judgment, and the vanity of the world; the apostolic and imperial foundations of the Church; the poet's own sinfulness.
authors.significance: The only named author of a substantial Old English poetic corpus besides Cædmon, and the first English poet to sign his work.
authors.uncertainty: Identity and dates entirely unknown; dating proposals range from the late eighth to the tenth century.
movements: The AB Language Group (West Midlands Devotional Prose)
sources: English Historical Documents, Volume I: c. 500–1042

authors.name: Cædmon
authors.biography: The first named English poet. According to Bede's account (Historia ecclesiastica IV.24), Cædmon was an illiterate cowherd at the monastery of Whitby under Abbess Hild who received the gift of song in a dream; thereafter he turned biblical narrative into vernacular verse, becoming a monk and composing a large body of religious poetry, of which only the nine-line 'Hymn' survives in Old English.
authors.profile: Cædmon's Hymn, a praise of God the Creator, survives in Northumbrian and West Saxon versions copied into manuscripts of Bede's Historia. It is the earliest datable poem in Old English and the foundation of the English vernacular religious tradition.
authors.style: Alliterative verse in the traditional Germanic style applied to Christian subject matter; simple, dignified praise of creation.
authors.concerns: The rendering of scripture into the vernacular; creation as the work of God.
authors.significance: As narrated by Bede, Cædmon exemplifies the consecration of native poetic form to Christian content; his Hymn is the starting point of the English poetic record.
authors.uncertainty: Known only from Bede's account, which has legendary elements; dates approximate; no poetry beyond the Hymn is securely attributed to him.
sources: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume A: The Middle Ages

authors.name: Dan Michel of Northgate
authors.biography: A Benedictine monk of St Augustine's Abbey, Canterbury, who in 1340 completed the Ayenbite of Inwyt (Remorse of Conscience), a Kentish translation of the French Somme le Roi of Frère Lorens. He is the first known translator of that influential manual of vices and virtues into English.
authors.profile: Translator of the Ayenbite of Inwyt (1340), the most extensive surviving Kentish prose text and a mine of early fourteenth-century English vocabulary.
authors.style: Faithful, word-for-word translation preserving the structure of the French original; conservative Kentish dialect with extensive learned vocabulary.
authors.concerns: The moral instruction of the laity through the doctrine of vices, virtues, and the sacrament of penance.
authors.significance: The Ayenbite is a unique record of the Kentish dialect and a major document of lay religious instruction on the eve of the Black Death.
authors.uncertainty: Known only from the colophon of his translation.
sources: The King's Reformation: Henry VIII and the Remaking of the English Church

authors.name: Edward Hall
authors.biography: Born in London about 1497; educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge, and at Gray's Inn. A lawyer and MP, he compiled his great chronicle of the Wars of the Roses, The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York, which Richard Grafton printed in 1548, the year after Hall's death.
authors.profile: Author of the chronicle that made the Tudor interpretation of history — the Wars of the Roses as God's judgement on rebellion, culminating in the providential union under the Tudors — the official story of England. Shakespeare drew the material of his English history plays, often nearly phrase by phrase, from Hall's Union through Holinshed.
authors.style: Ample, oratorical prose; set speeches composed for the great men of the action; the providential scheme applied to the narrative of faction and battle.
authors.concerns: The horror of civil war; the legitimacy and providence of the Tudor dynasty; history as the school of princes.
authors.significance: The principal historiographical source of Shakespeare's histories and of the Elizabethan understanding of the fifteenth century; his set speeches shaped the English historical imagination.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

works.title: The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York

authors.name: Felix of Crowland
authors.biography: Monk and hagiographer of the first half of the eighth century, associated by later tradition with the monastery of Crowland in the Fens; he wrote at the request of King Ælfwald of East Anglia (r. c. 713–749).
authors.profile: Author of the Vita Sancti Guthlaci (c. 730–740), the Latin life of the Mercian hermit Guthlac of Crowland, which became the source of the Old English poems Guthlac A and B and of later vernacular lives.
authors.style: Clear, careful Latin prose modeled on Evagrius's Life of Antony and Sulpicius Severus's Life of Martin; vivid accounts of Guthlac's battles with demons in the fens.
authors.concerns: The eremitic ideal; spiritual warfare; the sanctity of the Anglo-Saxon royal and monastic world.
authors.significance: His Life is among the earliest Latin hagiography composed in England and the starting point of a long vernacular tradition devoted to Guthlac.
authors.uncertainty: Almost nothing known of his life; the Crowland association is late.
sources: The Riverside Chaucer, 3rd edition

authors.name: Gavin Douglas
authors.biography: Born about 1474, third son of the Earl of Angus; educated at St Andrews and provost of St Giles, Edinburgh. His Palice of Honour (c. 1501) and the allegories King Hart and Conscience followed; his Eneados, the translation of Virgil's Aeneid completed on 22 July 1513, is the first complete rendering of the poem in any British language. Bishop of Dunkeld from 1515, he died in London of the plague in September 1522.
authors.profile: The last great poet of the Scottish Chaucerians and the first British translator of the Aeneid. The Palice of Honour is a courtly dream vision of dazzling learning; King Hart an allegory of the heart's court; and the Eneados — in vigorous Scots couplets, with a prologue to each book describing the Scottish seasons — ranks with Surrey's as one of the two great Tudor translations of Virgil.
authors.style: Aureate Chaucerians diction in the allegories; in the Eneados, a plain, energetic Scots that renders Virgil's gravitas in northern idiom; the seasonal prologues are the finest nature poetry in Scots.
authors.concerns: The translation of classical epic into the vernacular; honour, fame, and the education of princes; the defence of poetry against its detractors.
authors.significance: Author of the first complete Aeneid in any form of English and the summit of the Scottish Chaucerians; his Eneados passed the classical inheritance to the northern Renaissance.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the dating of King Hart is editorial.

authors.name: Geoffrey Chaucer
authors.biography: Son of a London vintner; page in the household of the Countess of Ulster, soldier in France (captured 1359–60), and thereafter a royal servant — esquire of the king's household, controller of customs and of the wool subsidy, justice of the peace for Kent, clerk of the king's works, and member of parliament. His diplomatic missions took him to France and Italy (1372–73, 1378), where he encountered the poetry of Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio. He died on 25 October 1400 and was buried in Westminster Abbey, founding what became Poets' Corner.
authors.profile: Author of the Book of the Duchess (c. 1368–72), the House of Fame (c. 1378–80), the Parliament of Fowls (c. 1380–82), Troilus and Criseyde (c. 1382–86), the Legend of Good Women (c. 1386–88), the Treatise on the Astrolabe (1391), and the unfinished Canterbury Tales (c. 1387–1400), together with Boece, the Romaunt of the Rose (disputed), and the short poems.
authors.style: The perfection of the decasyllabic line and rhyme royal in English; mastery of frame narrative, ironic personae, and dramatic monologue; the synthesis of French courtly forms, Italian narrative, and native English comedy into a new poetic language.
authors.concerns: Love in its courtly, comic, and philosophical dimensions; the ethics of storytelling; fortune, free will, and providence; the estates of society in pilgrimage and satire.
authors.significance: Universally regarded as the father of English poetry: he fixed the London dialect as the literary standard, naturalized the decasyllabic line, and created a body of work — above all the Canterbury Tales and Troilus — of the first European rank.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the canon and chronology of some minor works are debated; the Romaunt of the Rose attribution is disputed.
themes: Reformation faith and the authority of scripture

authors.name: Geoffrey of Monmouth
authors.biography: Of Welsh or Breton descent and educated probably at Oxford, he spent most of his career as a canon of St George's chapel, Oxford; in 1152 he was consecrated bishop of St Asaph in Wales, a see he may never have visited, and he died c. 1155. His Historia Regum Britanniae made him one of the most influential writers of the European Middle Ages.
authors.profile: Author of the Historia Regum Britanniae (c. 1136–38), the Prophetiae Merlini (c. 1135), and the Vita Merlini (c. 1150), which together created the Matter of Britain.
authors.style: Elegant, deliberately classicizing Latin prose; the fabrication of a continuous British history from Trojan Brutus to the Saxon conquest; the vivid set-pieces of Arthur's reign and the prophecies of Merlin.
authors.concerns: The antiquity and dignity of the British (Welsh) past; the legitimation of Norman rule through Trojan descent; prophecy as political instrument.
authors.significance: The Historia created the Arthurian legend as a European literary possession and shaped British historiography for four centuries; without it there is no Brut, no Grail cycle, no Malory.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; the sources of his 'British book' remain the central problem of Arthurian scholarship.

authors.name: George Cavendish
authors.identity: biographer; gentleman usher to Cardinal Wolsey
authors.biography: Born in Suffolk about 1497; entered the service of Cardinal Wolsey as gentleman usher about 1522 and attended him through his fall and death in 1530. Retiring to Suffolk, he wrote The Life and Death of Cardinal Wolsey between about 1554 and 1558 from his intimate knowledge of the Cardinal's household. The work circulated in manuscript and was first printed in 1641. He died about 1562.
authors.profile: Author, with Roper's Life of More, of the twin masterpiece of Tudor biography. The Life and Death of Cardinal Wolsey — the rise, magnificence, and fall of the butcher's son who ruled England — is the classic of Tudor life-writing: eyewitness, circumstantial, and tragic, with the great scenes (Wolsey's fall at Cawood, his death at Leicester) rendered as drama. Shakespeare drew on it for Henry VIII.
authors.style: Ample, plain narrative prose; the usher's exact memory for gesture, word, and scene; tragic structure imposed on recent history.
authors.concerns: The fall of princes as moral example; the memory of Wolsey against his detractors; loyalty to the great house he had served.
authors.significance: With Roper, founded English secular biography; his portrait of Wolsey — and through it of Henry VIII's court — shaped the English historical imagination from Shakespeare onward.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate.

works.title: The Life and Death of Cardinal Wolsey

authors.name: Gerald of Wales
authors.biography: Grandson of Nest, the Welsh princess, and of a Norman baron; educated at Paris, he became archdeacon of Brecon and courtier of Henry II, accompanying Prince John to Ireland in 1185 and preaching the crusade through Wales with Archbishop Baldwin in 1188. He twice sought the see of St Davids and was twice refused; retired to Lincoln, he died c. 1223, still writing.
authors.profile: Author of the Topographia Hibernica (1188), Expugnatio Hibernica (1189), Itinerarium Cambriae (1191), Descriptio Cambriae (1194), and the autobiographical De Rebus a Se Gestis, among much else.
authors.style: Vivid, gossipy, self-promoting Latin; ethnography seasoned with marvel and prejudice; the love of a good story over strict accuracy; an unflagging attention to his own career.
authors.concerns: The Welsh church's independence; the conquest and description of Ireland; the character and customs of the Welsh and Irish peoples.
authors.significance: The Itinerarium and Descriptio are the classic medieval accounts of Wales, and the Expugnatio the principal narrative of the English conquest of Ireland; his works are foundational for both national historiographies.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; his own writings, though copious, are self-serving.

authors.name: Gildas
authors.biography: British cleric of the sixth century, traditionally associated with the north of Britain and later with Brittany; revered as 'Gildas the Wise' by the Anglo-Saxons, who drew on his work.
authors.profile: Author of De excidio et conquestu Britanniae (c. 540s), a fierce sermon-polemic against the sins of the British kings and clergy which opens with the only near-contemporary narrative of the Saxon settlement of Britain, including the battle of Mount Badon.
authors.style: Rhetorical Latin saturated with biblical allusion, in the tradition of the Old Testament prophets; denunciatory and elegiac by turns.
authors.concerns: Divine punishment and national sin; the ruin of Britain as a moral catastrophe.
authors.significance: The principal source for post-Roman Britain; heavily used by Bede, who made Gildas's providential scheme the backbone of early English history.
authors.uncertainty: Dates and career largely conjectural, reconstructed from later Welsh and Breton tradition and internal evidence.
sources: A Book of Middle English, 4th edition

authors.name: Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey
authors.biography: Born at Hunsdon about 1516, eldest son of the Duke of Norfolk; brought up with the Duke of Richmond (Henry VIII's illegitimate son) and educated in the humanist manner. A soldier and courtier — he served in the French wars of the 1540s and was wounded at the siege of Montreuil — he was arrested in December 1546 on largely fabricated charges of quartering the royal arms, and beheaded on Tower Hill on 19 January 1547, the last victim of Henry VIII's reign. His poems circulated in manuscript and were printed in Tottel's Miscellany (1557); his translation of Aeneid II and IV was published in 1554 and 1557.
authors.profile: The refiner of the English sonnet: he gave the form the rhyme scheme (abab cdcd efef gg) that became the 'English' or Shakespearean sonnet, and his smooth decasyllabic line pointed the way to the Elizabethan style. His translation of Virgil's Aeneid, Books II and IV — the first English blank verse — created the unrhymed iambic pentameter that Marlowe and Shakespeare made the language of English drama.
authors.style: Regular, musical decasyllables; elegant management of the Petrarchan materials; a grave, chivalric sensibility; in the Aeneid translation, a new plainness of diction answering Virgil's.
authors.concerns: Nobility and honour under tyranny; love, constancy, and the ruin of Troy as an image of English court politics; the translation of classical epic into English verse.
authors.significance: Inventor (with Wyatt) of the English sonnet form and of blank verse — the two technical foundations of Elizabethan poetry and drama; his life and death dramatized the fate of the old nobility under the Tudors.
authors.uncertainty: Birth year given as 1516 or 1517 in the records; some lyrics attributed to him in Tottel are of uncertain authorship.

works.title: Aeneid, Books II and IV (Surrey's translation)

authors.name: Henry Medwall
authors.biography: Born about 1462; educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge, and employed as chaplain and notary to Cardinal John Morton, Archbishop of Canterbury. His Fulgens and Lucrece, played at Morton's household at Lambeth about 1497, is the earliest surviving secular English play, printed by John Rastell about 1512–16. He died about 1502.
authors.profile: Author of the first secular English drama. Fulgens and Lucrece dramatizes a humanist debate — whether nobility lies in birth or in virtue — as a Roman comedy of courtship, complete with a subplot in which two servants, A and B, compete for the audience's employment; his Nature is a full-scale morality play of man's fall and amendment. Both were played in Morton's great hall, the seedbed of the Tudor interlude.
authors.style: Debate framed as drama; the interweaving of serious argument and servant comedy; the morality convention put to secular and humanist use.
authors.concerns: True nobility and the claims of virtue over birth; the reform of manners; the education of the great household through play.
authors.significance: Bridging medieval morality and humanist comedy, Fulgens and Lucrece begins the secular English stage tradition that runs to the Elizabethan theatre.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate.

authors.name: Henry of Huntingdon
authors.biography: Son of a Norman clerk and an English mother, and archdeacon of Huntingdon from c. 1110, he was commissioned by Alexander, bishop of Lincoln, to write a history of England; he travelled with the court, visited Rome (1139), and continued revising his Historia Anglorum until his death c. 1157.
authors.profile: Author of the Historia Anglorum (first version 1129, continued to 1154), the most widely read English chronicle of the twelfth century, and of verse epigrams including the satirical De contemptu mundi.
authors.style: Clear, vivid narrative with a moralist's relish for battles, plagues, and the falls of great men; the ubi sunt meditation and the contemptus mundi theme; patriotic celebration of the English past.
authors.concerns: The providential shape of English history; the transience of earthly power; the continuity of the English people through conquest.
authors.significance: The Historia Anglorum is a principal source for the Norman and Angevin periods and the classic expression of twelfth-century historical moralism.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; details of his career rest on his own book.

authors.name: Hugh Latimer
authors.biography: Born of a yeoman family at Thurcaston about 1485; educated at Cambridge, where he was converted from conservative orthodoxy to the reformed faith in the 1520s. A preacher of extraordinary popular power, he became bishop of Worcester in 1535, resigned in 1539 over the Six Articles, and preached through the Edwardian years, notably the Sermon of the Plough (1548) and the Lent sermons before Edward VI (1549). Under Mary he was imprisoned with Ridley and Cranmer and burned at Oxford on 16 October 1555, urging Ridley: 'we shall this day light such a candle, by God's grace, in England, as I trust shall never be put out.'
authors.profile: The greatest English preacher of the Reformation. His printed sermons — above all the Sermon of the Plough and the Sermons before King Edward VI — are the classics of Tudor homiletics: plain, concrete, homely in metaphor, and fearless in their attack on landlords, enclosers, and corrupt clergy.
authors.style: The plain style made dramatic: rural simile, proverb, anecdote, and direct address; a yeoman's concreteness yoked to scriptural authority.
authors.concerns: Preaching as the cure of the commonwealth; social justice against enclosure and greed; the duty of bishops and landlords; the Word before ceremony.
authors.significance: The model of English preaching for a century and a principal voice of the Reformation's social conscience; his sermons document the moral crisis of mid-Tudor England.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

works.title: The Sermons before King Edward VI

authors.name: Hwætberht
authors.biography: A monk of Wearmouth-Jarrow from boyhood who studied in Ireland in his youth and took the religious name Eusebius. He succeeded Ceolfrith as abbot of Wearmouth-Jarrow c. 716 and remained abbot until his death c. 747. He was a friend and correspondent of Boniface and a close associate of Bede, who dedicated works to him.
authors.profile: Author of the Aenigmata Eusebii, forty Latin riddles on encyclopedic subjects ranging from the alphabet and the liberal arts to the natural world, composed in the tradition of Symphosius and Aldhelm.
authors.style: Hexameter riddles marked by learned wordplay and allusive density, modelled closely on Aldhelm; the subjects move from grammatical abstraction to cosmology and natural history.
authors.concerns: The encyclopedic ordering of knowledge; the riddling description of creation; the transmission of Aldhelmian learning in Northumbria.
authors.significance: His riddles, together with Tatwine's, carried the Aldhelmian riddle tradition into the Northumbrian Renaissance and stand behind the vernacular riddle collection of the Exeter Book.
authors.uncertainty: Death date approximate (c. 747); the riddles are securely attributed by manuscript tradition.
sources: The Oxford Handbook of Tudor Literature, 1485–1603

authors.name: James I of Scotland
authors.biography: Captured at sea by the English in 1406 at the age of eleven, he spent eighteen years as a prisoner at the English court, where he received a full education in the company of Henry V's courtiers and poets. Released in 1424, he returned to rule Scotland with reforming vigour until his murder by conspirators at Perth on 21 February 1437.
authors.profile: Traditionally credited with The Kingis Quair (c. 1424), the dream vision in which the captive narrator sees his beloved and is consoled by the goddesses of love and fortune; the attribution rests on the poem's own claims and manuscript tradition.
authors.style: Graceful Chaucerian rhyme royal with an autobiographical frame; the fusion of Boethian consolation with courtly love vision; precociously Renaissance delight in nature and architecture.
authors.concerns: Love, fortune, and providence; the education and duties of a prince; captivity and deliverance.
authors.significance: The Kingis Quair is the fountainhead of the Scottish Chaucerian tradition and one of the great prison poems of European literature.
authors.uncertainty: The attribution of the Quair to James I is traditional and widely accepted but not absolutely certain.

authors.name: John Bale
authors.identity: playwright; polemicist; antiquary; bishop of Ossory
authors.biography: Born at Cove, Suffolk, on 21 November 1495; entered the Carmelite order at Norwich, then converted to the Reformation in the 1530s. He wrote King Johan (c. 1538), the first English history play and a weapon of Henrician propaganda; The Image of Both Churches (c. 1545), a running commentary on Revelation; and the Illustrium Maioris Britanniae Scriptorum Summarium (1548), the first bio-bibliography of British writers. Bishop of Ossory in Ireland in 1553, he fled abroad under Mary and returned under Elizabeth, dying at Canterbury in November 1563.
authors.profile: The founder of English literary history and of the Protestant history play. King Johan turned the chronicle matter of England into stage polemic, and the Summarium — enlarged at Basel in 1557–59 as the Scriptorum Illustrium Maioris Brytanniae Catalogus — preserved the names and titles on which later literary history rests.
authors.style: Furious polemical energy; the apocalyptic scheme of the two churches applied to history; catalogue and inventory as instruments of scholarship and propaganda alike.
authors.concerns: The identification of the pope with Antichrist; the English church and nation as God's elect; the record of British writers as proof of national dignity.
authors.significance: Inventor of the English history play and of English literary bibliography; his catalogues transmitted knowledge of the medieval English canon to the Renaissance.
authors.uncertainty: None significant.

works.title: The Chief Promises of God unto Man

authors.name: John Barbour
authors.biography: Archdeacon of Aberdeen and a clerk in the service of Robert II; he travelled repeatedly to England and France for study (Oxford and Paris) and royal business. His Brus, completed c. 1375, earned him a royal pension, and he died on 13 March 1395.
authors.profile: Author of The Brus (c. 1375), a verse chronicle of the wars of independence celebrating Robert Bruce and James Douglas; other works attributed to him (including a Troy book) are lost.
authors.style: Energetic octosyllabic couplets; vivid battle narrative and stirring speeches; the celebration of freedom ('A! Fredome is a noble thing!') within a providential frame.
authors.concerns: Scottish independence and national identity; the virtue of freedom against tyranny; chivalric loyalty.
authors.significance: The father of Scottish poetry and of Scottish national historical literature; the Brus is the first great work in Older Scots.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; his other works are lost, so the canon rests on the Brus alone.

authors.name: John Capgrave
authors.biography: Born at Lynn on 21 April 1393, he studied at Cambridge, joined the Augustinian friars, and became prior of their house at Lynn; he travelled to Rome in 1450 and died on 12 August 1464. The most learned English writer of his generation, he composed in both Latin and English.
authors.profile: Author of the Life of St Katharine (c. 1445), the Life of St Norbert, the Abbreuiacion of Cronicles, the chronicle of England to 1417, the pilgrimage guide Ye Solace of Pilgrimes, and numerous Latin commentaries and lives.
authors.style: Learned, well-ordered prose and Lydgatean verse; the devout scholar's care for accuracy and orthodoxy; the blending of chronicle and hagiography.
authors.concerns: The cult of St Katharine and the defence of learning; English history in the Lancastrian interest; orthodox devotion against Lollardy.
authors.significance: The leading East Anglian man of letters of the mid-fifteenth century; his Katharine is a classic of the learned saint's life.
authors.uncertainty: Little uncertain: his own works and the Lynn records document his career closely.

authors.name: John Clanvowe
authors.biography: A knight of Richard II's household and lifelong companion of Sir William Neville, with whom he is buried at Constantinople, where both died in October 1391; their joint tomb, with its crossed swords, survives in Istanbul. A member of the 'Lollard knights' circle, he wrote both courtly and reforming works.
authors.profile: Author of The Two Ways (c. 1391), a Lollard-leaning devotional prose tract, and of The Boke of Cupide (The Cuckoo and the Nightingale, c. 1386), a Chaucerian dream poem long attributed to Chaucer.
authors.style: Graceful Chaucerian verse in the dream poem; plain, scriptural prose in the devotional tract.
authors.concerns: The two ways of life and death; the reform of the church; courtly love within a Christian frame.
authors.significance: The Two Ways is a principal document of the Lollard sensibility among the courtly elite, and the Boke of Cupide testifies to the immediate diffusion of Chaucerian poetry.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the extent of his personal Lollardy is debated.

authors.name: John Colet
authors.identity: humanist; dean of St Paul's; founder of St Paul's School
authors.biography: Born in London in 1467, son of a Lord Mayor; studied at Oxford and in Italy. His Oxford lectures on the epistles of St Paul (c. 1497–1505) broke with scholastic method and made him the father of English humanism; he became dean of St Paul's in 1505 and founded St Paul's School in 1509, appointing William Lily its first master. He died on 16 September 1519. His grammatical treatise, the Aeditio, was printed in 1527.
authors.profile: The founder of the Oxford reform that produced English humanism. His Paul's lectures, teaching scripture from the plain text rather than the glosses, converted a generation — including Erasmus, who called him the ideal of the Christian humanist — and his Aeditio contributed the English accidence to the standard school grammar.
authors.style: Expository clarity aimed at the unlearned; plain-text biblical exposition; the reformer's impatience with ceremonial and gloss.
authors.concerns: The primitive church as model; education as the reform of Christendom; the layman's access to scripture.
authors.significance: The inspirer of Erasmus and More and the founder of the English humanist movement; his school and his lectures set the intellectual course of the Tudor century.
authors.uncertainty: None significant; the Aeditio's precise date of composition is approximate.

authors.name: John Duns Scotus
authors.biography: The subtlest of the scholastic philosophers: he entered the Franciscans c. 1280, studied and taught at Oxford and Paris, and lectured on the Sentences at Oxford c. 1300–02 and Paris 1302–05; transferred to Cologne in 1307, he died there on 8 November 1308. His thought defined one of the two great schools of late medieval theology.
authors.profile: Author of the Ordinatio (his revision of the Oxford Sentences lectures, c. 1300–08), the Quaestiones Quodlibetales, and treatises on metaphysics, logic, and natural theology, including his famous proof of God's existence.
authors.style: Rigorous, compressed, terminologically innovative argument; the 'formal distinction' and the univocity of being; a dialectical subtlety that earned him the title Doctor Subtilis.
authors.concerns: The univocity of being and the nature of metaphysics; the freedom of God and of the will; the Immaculate Conception; individuation (haecceitas).
authors.significance: Founder of Scotism, which rivalled Thomism for centuries and shaped theology into the Reformation; among the most influential British philosophers of all time.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and early life approximate; the authenticity of parts of the corpus remains disputed.

authors.name: John Fisher
authors.identity: bishop of Rochester; theologian; cardinal; martyr and saint
authors.biography: Born at Beverley in 1469; educated at Cambridge, where he became Master of Michaelhouse and chancellor of the university, and the patron of Erasmus and of Greek studies. Bishop of Rochester from 1504, he was the confessor of Lady Margaret Beaufort and the most respected preacher of his age. Refusing the oath of supremacy, he was made a cardinal by Paul III and executed on 22 June 1535; canonized in 1935.
authors.profile: The great conservative preacher of the early Reformation. His sermons — against Luther (1521) and on the penitential psalms — are the classic statements of the old orthodoxy in the new age of print, and his commentary on the seven penitential psalms (1505, enlarged 1508) was the devotional bestseller of the early Tudor period.
authors.style: Scholastic learning in a plain, forceful pulpit style; the expository sermon built on the literal text; pastoral warmth under doctrinal rigour.
authors.concerns: The defence of the old faith; penance and the sacrament; the reform of the clergy from within; the university as the church's school.
authors.significance: The intellectual leader of English Catholicism in the crisis of the 1520s and 1530s; his life and death defined the conservative alternative to the Henrician settlement.
authors.uncertainty: None significant.

authors.name: John Gower
authors.biography: A London poet of Kentish or Yorkshire gentry stock, connected with the court of Richard II and later a supporter of Henry IV; friend of Chaucer, who dedicated Troilus and Criseyde to him. He composed in three languages — French (Mirour de l'Omme, c. 1376–79), Latin (Vox Clamantis, c. 1377–81), and English (Confessio Amantis, c. 1386–90) — and spent his last years blind at St Mary Overey priory, Southwark, where his tomb with its effigy of the three books remains.
authors.profile: The Confessio Amantis, a collection of some 140 exemplary tales framed by the confession of the lover Amans to Genius, the priest of Venus, is the most substantial English poem of the century after Chaucer's; the Vox Clamantis allegorizes the Peasants' Revolt and the corruption of the estates.
authors.style: Smooth, correct octosyllabic couplets; a 'middle style' of plain moral discourse; the frame-narrative and exemplary tale as instruments of ethical teaching.
authors.concerns: Love as a school of virtue and self-knowledge; the corruption of the estates; good kingship and the common good.
authors.significance: With Chaucer and Langland, one of the three great English poets of the Ricardian age; the Confessio is a principal monument of late medieval narrative art.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and family origins conjectural; the chronology of his three major poems is partly inferred.
themes: Humanist education and the ideal commonwealth

authors.name: John Heywood
authors.biography: Born about 1497, probably in London; a singer, musician, and entertainer at the court of Henry VIII and the household of Princess Mary. He married Joan Rastell, the niece of Thomas More, and remained a Catholic: in 1564 he left England for Mechelen, where he died about 1580. His interludes were played at court and in the great households, and his collections of proverbs and epigrams were bestsellers for a century.
authors.profile: The master of the Tudor interlude. The Four PP, The Play of the Weather, and A Play of Love turn the debate form into comedy of ideas — the palmer, pardoner, pothecary, and pedlar disputing who can tell the greatest lie; Jupiter taking petitions on the weather. His A Dialogue Conteynyng the Nomber in Effect of All the Prouerbes in the Englishe Tongue (1546) collected the proverb wisdom of England, and The Spider and the Fly (1556) is the great allegorical poem of the Marian reaction.
authors.style: Deadpan comic logic, punning debate, and the proverb as structural unit; a style that teaches while it jokes, and jokes while it teaches.
authors.concerns: The comedy of opinion and authority; religious satire from within orthodoxy; the wisdom of proverb lore; the politics of the Reformation seen from the losing side.
authors.significance: The first English comic dramatist of the print era and the conduit by which the interlude became the comedy of the Elizabethan stage; his proverb collections fixed the common sayings of the language.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; the dating of the interludes is largely inferential.

authors.name: John Leland
authors.biography: Born in London about 1503; educated at St Paul's School under William Lily and at Cambridge, Oxford, and Paris. Commissioned in 1533 as King's Antiquary, he travelled England and Wales in the 1530s and 1540s recording libraries, monuments, and topography, planning a vast description of Britain he never completed. He went mad in the late 1540s and died on 18 April 1552. His Itinerary remained in manuscript until the eighteenth century.
authors.profile: The father of English antiquarianism. His Itinerary notes preserve the record of monastic libraries on the eve of the Dissolution and remain a primary source for English topography; his Cygnea Cantio (1545), a Latin poem on the Thames, and his other Latin verse earned him a European reputation in his lifetime.
authors.style: The note-taking style of the field antiquary: inventories, measurements, and reports jotted on the road, without literary finish.
authors.concerns: The recovery of British antiquity; the description of the realm; the preservation of manuscripts and monuments against the destruction of the Dissolution.
authors.significance: Founded the study of British antiquities and preserved irreplaceable evidence of medieval England; his collections were quarried by every later antiquary from Bale to Camden.
authors.uncertainty: None significant; the Itinerary's exact itinerary chronology is editorial.

authors.name: John Lydgate
authors.biography: Benedictine monk of the abbey of Bury St Edmunds, ordained priest in 1397, and educated (perhaps at Gloucester College, Oxford) before a career as the most prolific English poet of the fifteenth century. He enjoyed the patronage of Henry V, Humphrey Duke of Gloucester, and the London civic elite; late in life he received a royal pension, and he died c. 1449, buried at Bury.
authors.profile: Author of the Troy Book (1412–20), the Siege of Thebes (c. 1420–22), the Fall of Princes (1431–38), the Temple of Glas (c. 1400–05), the Life of Our Lady, and an immense output of mummings, pageants, saints' lives, and devotional and occasional verse — over 140,000 lines attributed to him.
authors.style: Chaucerian forms (rhyme royal, couplets) with aureate diction and rhetorical amplification; copious moralizing; the 'Lydgate line' (often headless pentameter) that became the standard of mid-century verse.
authors.concerns: The moral exemplarity of history (the falls of princes); the honour of England and its rulers; devotional and civic piety.
authors.significance: The dominant English poet between Chaucer and Skelton, read and imitated throughout the fifteenth century (and printed by Caxton and de Worde); his Fall of Princes shaped the Tudor mirror-for-magistrates tradition.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; the canon is so large that attributions remain in flux.
themes: Tyranny and the abuse of power

authors.name: John Mirk
authors.biography: An Augustinian canon and prior of Lilleshall Abbey, Shropshire, active in the 1380s and 1390s; he compiled the Festial, a cycle of English sermons for the feasts of the church year, with a companion instructional work for parish priests (Instructions for Parish Priests).
authors.profile: Author of the Festial (c. 1380s) and Instructions for Parish Priests, among the most widely copied English sermon collections of the later Middle Ages.
authors.style: Plain, lively English sermons built on exempla, miracles, and verse tags; the vivid storytelling of popular piety adapted for parish preaching.
authors.concerns: The instruction of the laity in the feasts, sacraments, and moral duties of the church year.
authors.significance: The Festial is the classic collection of the English late medieval sermon and a principal witness to orthodox vernacular preaching in the age of Lollardy.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; details come almost entirely from his own prefaces.

authors.name: John of Salisbury
authors.biography: Educated at Paris under the greatest masters of the twelfth-century schools — Abelard, William of Conches, Gilbert of Poitiers — he returned to England as secretary to Archbishop Theobald and then to Thomas Becket, whose exile he shared and whose murder he witnessed (1170). He became bishop of Chartres in 1176 and died there on 25 October 1180.
authors.profile: Author of the Policraticus (1159), the first great medieval treatise on political theory; the Metalogicon (1159), a defence of the trivium; the Historia Pontificalis; and a celebrated correspondence.
authors.style: Classical learning worn lightly and worn for moral ends; the organic metaphor of the body politic; satiric portraits of courtiers; the first medieval theory of tyrannicide.
authors.concerns: The limits of royal power; the education of the prince and the clerk; the relation of church and state; the value of humane letters.
authors.significance: The Policraticus is the most important political treatise between Augustine and Aquinas and the fountainhead of medieval constitutionalism; its organic state theory shaped political thought for centuries.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the chronology of his Paris studies is reconstructed from the Metalogicon.

authors.name: John Rastell
authors.biography: Born in London about 1475; a lawyer of the Middle Temple and the brother-in-law of Thomas More, whose circle he printed. His press issued More's early works and his own plays — The Four Elements (c. 1520) and the translation Calisto and Melebea (c. 1530) — and his chronicle The Pastime of People (c. 1529). His opposition to the clergy's exactions brought him imprisonment, and he died in prison in June or July 1536.
authors.profile: The first English printer-playwright. The Four Elements is a didactic interlude teaching cosmology and geography through drama, and The Pastime of People compresses the history of Britain into a popular chronicle; his press was the vehicle of the More circle and of the earliest English humanist drama.
authors.style: Instruction through entertainment; the interlude as lecture hall and theatre at once; plain prose and functional verse.
authors.concerns: Popular education in the new learning; the reform of clerical exactions; law, printing, and the spread of knowledge.
authors.significance: A founder of the English printing trade in its humanist phase; his interludes and chronicles made the new learning available to a popular audience.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the date of his death (1536) is established by legal records.

authors.name: John Redford
authors.identity: playwright; composer; master of the choristers at St Paul's
authors.biography: Born about 1486; almoner and master of the choristers at St Paul's Cathedral, where he trained the boys who performed his play Wit and Science (c. 1539). He was a noted composer and organist — John Heywood married his daughter — and died in 1547.
authors.profile: Author of Wit and Science, the most accomplished of the school moralities: the allegory of Wit's wooing of Lady Science, with the giant Tediousness, the Vice Idleness, and the comic conversion of the booby Ingnorance, written for boy actors with songs and dances. The play survives in a single manuscript with its music cues.
authors.style: The morality convention refreshed with music, dance, and schoolroom comedy; allegorical personification handled with theatrical tact.
authors.concerns: The marriage of wit and learning; the discipline of the school; the education of boys through play and music.
authors.significance: The finest of the school interludes and a direct ancestor of the academic drama and the court masque; his St Paul's boys became one of the great Elizabethan playing companies.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the play's date (c. 1539) is editorial.

authors.name: John Skelton
authors.identity: poet; satirist; orator regius; tutor to Prince Henry
authors.biography: Educated at Cambridge and Oxford, where he was laureated (1488), and at Louvain (1492); he styled himself 'poet laureate'. Tutor to Prince Henry (the future Henry VIII) from about 1496 to 1502, he became rector of Diss in Norfolk (c. 1504) and 'orator regius' at court. His later career was a running satirical war with Cardinal Wolsey, whom he attacked in verse so freely that he took sanctuary at Westminster in 1523, where he died on 21 June 1529.
authors.profile: The dominant English poet of the early Tudor period and the inventor of the 'Skeltonic' line — short, breathless, rhymed couplets of irregular length. His canon runs from the dream-satire The Bowge of Courte (c. 1499) through the mock-elegy Philip Sparrow (c. 1505), the low-life tour de force The Tunning of Elinour Rumming (c. 1517), the morality play Magnificence (c. 1515–23), and the great anti-Wolsey satires Speke Parrot (1521), Colin Clout (c. 1522), and Why Come Ye Nat to Courte? (c. 1522–23), to the self-crowning dream vision The Garland of Laurel (1523).
authors.style: The Skeltonic: tumbling short lines, obsessive rhyme, macaronic Latin, colloquial diction, and a satirical voice that moves between learned allusion and street abuse; also a master of the aureate, 'laureate' high style.
authors.concerns: The corruption of the clergy and the court; the duties of kingship; the poet's laureate authority; the defence of the English language against Latinate pretension.
authors.significance: The first great English satirist of the print era and the bridge between the medieval and Renaissance poetries; his Skeltonics were imitated for a century and admired by the Elizabethans, who read him as the scourge of Wolsey.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and birthplace uncertain; some Skeltonic attributions among minor poems remain debated.

works.title: Why Come Ye Nat to Courte?

authors.name: John Trevisa
authors.biography: Cornish-born scholar of Exeter College and Queen's College, Oxford, fellow of Queen's and later vicar of Berkeley, Gloucestershire, in the household of Thomas, Lord Berkeley, for whom he translated major Latin works into English prose.
authors.profile: Translator of Ranulf Higden's Polychronicon (completed 1387, with his famous Dialogue on Translation between a Lord and a Clerk) and of Bartholomaeus Anglicus's De proprietatibus rerum (1398); also translated works of religious instruction and political theory.
authors.style: Vigorous, expansive English prose; the confident handling of learned Latin vocabulary and its rendering into idiomatic English; a stated program of translation for the benefit of English readers.
authors.concerns: The provision of learning in English; the dignity of the vernacular; the duties of lordship and clergy.
authors.significance: With the Wycliffite translators, Trevisa helped create the learned English prose of the late fourteenth century; his Dialogue on Translation is a classic statement of vernacular self-consciousness.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the extent of his role in the Wycliffite Bible translation is debated.
sources: Poetry and Politics in the English Renaissance, revised edition

authors.name: John Wyclif
authors.biography: Fellow and master of Balliol College, Oxford, and the dominant figure in the university's theological debates from the 1360s; doctor of theology c. 1372. From c. 1376 he developed the doctrines — dominion founded on grace, the primacy of scripture, and the rejection of transubstantiation — that were condemned by the Blackfriars council of 1382. Retired to his living at Lutterworth, Leicestershire, where he died on 31 December 1384; his remains were exhumed and burned as a heretic in 1428.
authors.profile: Author of an immense Latin corpus — De Civili Dominio (1375–76), De Veritate Sacrae Scripturae, De Officio Regis, the Trialogus, the Postilla, and many sermons — and traditionally credited (though modern scholarship dissents) with inspiring the English Wycliffite Bible.
authors.style: Relentlessly logical scholastic argument deployed for radical ends; a plain, urgent English style in the sermons attributed to him.
authors.concerns: The poverty of the church and the renunciation of temporal lordship; scripture as sole authority; the eucharist; the rights of kings against the papacy.
authors.significance: The intellectual founder of Lollardy and the most consequential English heretic: his movement produced the first English Bible and permanently altered the terms of English religious debate.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the extent of his personal role in the English Bible translation is disputed.

authors.name: Julian of Norwich
authors.biography: An anchoress of St Julian's church, Norwich, who at the age of thirty and a half, during a grave illness in May 1373, received sixteen revelations ('showings') of Christ's Passion; she spent the following decades meditating on their meaning and composed two versions of her account — the Short Text and the Long Text (the latter c. 1393). Her actual name is unknown; she is called Julian from her church.
authors.profile: Author of Revelations of Divine Love (the Book of Showings), the first surviving book in English known to have been written by a woman and one of the great theological works of the Middle Ages.
authors.style: A plain, meditative prose of extraordinary depth; the famous image of the hazelnut and of the world's littleness held in God's hand; paradoxical, affirmative theology expressed with homely simplicity.
authors.concerns: The love of God shown in the Passion; the motherhood of God ('Jesus as mother'); sin, suffering, and the final 'all shall be well'.
authors.significance: The first woman author in English whose major work survives; her theology of divine love and of the motherhood of Christ has made her a central figure in both medieval studies and modern spirituality.
authors.uncertainty: Almost everything about her life is conjectural; her name, family, and education are unknown.

authors.name: Layamon
authors.biography: A priest of Areley Kings (Ernleye) on the Severn in Worcestershire, as he names himself in the prologue to the Brut; he flourished c. 1200. Nothing else is known of him, but his Brut — an English verse adaptation of Wace's Roman de Brut with additions from Welsh tradition — is the first great treatment of Arthurian history in English.
authors.profile: Author of the Brut (c. 1190–1215), some 16,000 lines of alliterative-influenced verse chronicling British history from Brutus to Cadwalader; its Arthur section is the fullest early English account of the king.
authors.style: A conservative poetic idiom blending the old alliterative line with rhyme; archaic vocabulary and formulaic diction; simple, dignified narrative movement.
authors.concerns: The translation of British history into English; the continuity of the English people and language.
authors.significance: The first named poet of the post-Conquest English tradition and a principal conduit by which Arthurian history entered English literature.
authors.uncertainty: Known only from his own prologue; dates conjectural.
sources: Sir Thomas Wyatt: The Complete Poems

authors.name: Margery Kempe
authors.biography: Daughter of John Brunham, mayor of Lynn, and wife of the merchant John Kempe, with whom she had fourteen children. After a post-natal crisis and a vision of Christ, she adopted a life of intense devotion — weeping uncontrollably at the thought of the Passion, wearing white, and travelling as a pilgrim to Jerusalem, Rome, Santiago de Compostela, and through northern Europe — while repeatedly examined for heresy and vindicated. She dictated her Book to scribes in the late 1430s.
authors.profile: The Book of Margery Kempe (c. 1436–38), commonly called the first autobiography in English, records her spiritual life, pilgrimages, and trials in vigorous third-person prose.
authors.style: Direct, colloquial, vivid narrative; the blending of mystical experience with the detail of everyday mercantile and domestic life; a startling frankness about body, tears, and social conflict.
authors.concerns: The imitation of Christ's Passion; the legitimacy of lay, female, married spirituality; the discernment of her own calling against clerical suspicion.
authors.significance: Her Book is a unique document of female lay piety and of the social world of fifteenth-century East Anglia, and a foundational text of women's writing in English.
authors.uncertainty: Known almost entirely from her Book; dates approximate; the scribe's mediation complicates the text's authorship.

authors.name: Matthew Paris
authors.biography: A monk of St Albans from 1217, he succeeded Roger Wendover as the abbey's chronicler in 1236 and made St Albans the foremost centre of English historical writing; friend and correspondent of Henry III, he travelled to Norway (1248) and died in 1259. He wrote, copied, and illuminated his own manuscripts with maps and drawings of exceptional skill.
authors.profile: Author of the Chronica Majora (begun c. 1240, continued to 1259), the greatest English chronicle of the thirteenth century; also the Historia Anglorum (abbreviation), the lives of the two Offas and of St Alban, and the Gesta Abbatum.
authors.style: Vivid, opinionated, encyclopedic narrative; fierce criticism of the king, the papacy, and the friars; the integration of maps, itineraries, and marginal drawings into the historical record.
authors.concerns: The liberties of the English church and kingdom against papal and royal encroachment; the moral judgement of rulers; the recording of contemporary events from documents and eyewitnesses.
authors.significance: The Chronica Majora is the indispensable narrative source for the reign of Henry III and a landmark of medieval book art as well as of historiography.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and parentage unknown; his surname may reflect continental training.

authors.name: Miles Coverdale
authors.biography: Born about 1488 in the North Riding of Yorkshire; educated at Cambridge and an Augustinian friar before converting to the Reformation. Working in Antwerp, he produced the first complete printed English Bible in 1535, and he edited the Great Bible of 1539, which was ordered to be read in every parish church. Bishop of Exeter in 1551, he went into exile under Mary and returned under Elizabeth, dying on 20 January 1569.
authors.profile: The translator of the first complete printed English Bible. The Coverdale Bible (1535), translating chiefly from German and Latin versions, gave the English church its Psalter — still sung as Coverdale's version in the Book of Common Prayer — and the Great Bible (1539) put an English Bible in every parish church, its wording (largely Tyndale's) forming the base of the Authorized Version.
authors.style: A flowing, musical prose less angular than Tyndale's; mastery of the cadence of the Psalms; the dignity of liturgical English.
authors.concerns: The complete vernacular Bible; the Psalter in English worship; the reform of the church through the Word.
authors.significance: Completed the English Bible and fixed the English Psalter; the Coverdale Psalms remain in liturgical use into the twenty-first century.
authors.uncertainty: Birth year approximate; the exact place of printing of the 1535 Bible (Antwerp or Cologne) is debated.

authors.name: Nennius
authors.biography: Welsh scholar of the early ninth century, traditionally identified as the compiler of the Historia Brittonum; otherwise unknown.
authors.profile: The Historia Brittonum (c. 829/30) assembles genealogies, origin legends (including the Trojan foundation story of the Britons), the lives of St Patrick and St Germanus, and the earliest datable Arthur material — the list of Arthur's twelve battles culminating at Mount Badon.
authors.style: Composite, compilatory Latin prose of varied quality, drawing on earlier written and oral sources.
authors.concerns: The antiquity and identity of the Britons; the deeds of their heroes against the Saxons.
authors.significance: The earliest extended Arthurian text in insular literature and a major witness to British historical tradition.
authors.uncertainty: The prologue's attribution to Nennius is not found in all manuscripts; the work is composite and its authorship disputed.
sources: Middle English Dictionary

authors.name: Nicholas Love
authors.biography: Prior of the Carthusian house of Mount Grace in Yorkshire (1410–21), where he oversaw the translation of the Meditationes Vitae Christi into English as the Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ (c. 1410), the most widely circulated devotional work in fifteenth-century England and one explicitly approved by Archbishop Arundel against Lollard translation.
authors.profile: Translator and adapter of the pseudo-Bonaventuran Meditationes Vitae Christi as the Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ, with extensive original additions.
authors.style: Affective, meditative prose designed to make the life of Christ present to the reader; conservative theology and smooth, accessible English.
authors.concerns: The orthodox channeling of lay devotion to the humanity of Christ; the containment of vernacular heresy.
authors.significance: The Mirror was the great bestseller of fifteenth-century English devotional prose, surviving in more manuscripts than any other Middle English text of its kind and shaping lay piety to the Reformation.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and early career unknown; death date approximate.

works.title: The Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ

authors.name: Nicholas Udall
authors.biography: Born at Southampton in 1504; educated at Winchester and Corpus Christi College, Oxford. Headmaster of Eton from 1534 (dismissed in 1541) and later of Westminster, he was a reformer who prospered under Edward VI and Mary alike. His Ralph Roister Doister, written about 1552, was printed about 1566. He died on 23 December 1556.
authors.profile: Author of the first English comedy. Ralph Roister Doister — five acts of Roman comedy built on Plautus's Miles Gloriosus, with the braggart soldier, the parasitic Merrygreek, and the London widow Dame Christian Custance — transplanted classical comic structure into English life and English verse, establishing the pattern the Elizabethan comedians followed.
authors.style: Doggerel couplets of deliberate comic roughness; the miles gloriosus and the cunning servant in English dress; songs and jigs built into the action.
authors.concerns: The imitation of Roman comedy; school drama as moral and rhetorical training; the comic punishment of vanity and presumption.
authors.significance: Wrote the first English comedy on the classical model, the direct ancestor of the Elizabethan stage comedy; his school drama linked the interlude tradition to the professional theatre.
authors.uncertainty: The precise date and first printing of Roister Doister are uncertain (c. 1552–53, printed c. 1566).

authors.name: Orm
authors.biography: An Augustinian canon, probably of Elsham Priory in north Lincolnshire, who composed the Ormulum, a vast collection of verse homilies on the gospels, c. 1180; his brother Walter is named in the dedication. Nothing else is recorded of his life.
authors.profile: Author of the Ormulum (c. 1180), some 20,000 short lines of gospel paraphrase and exegesis in the East Midland dialect; only about an eighth survives (Bodleian Library, MS Junius 1).
authors.style: A strictly regular unrhymed septenarius metre; a unique, systematic orthography (double consonants marking vowel length) of great value to historical linguists; plain homiletic exposition.
authors.concerns: The teaching of the gospels to the English laity in the vernacular; the reform of preaching after the Lateran emphasis on pastoral care.
authors.significance: The Ormulum is the most ambitious early Middle English religious work and a landmark in the history of English orthography and phonology.
authors.uncertainty: Known only from the dedication; dates approximate (c. 1150–1200).
themes: The Virgin Mary and Marian devotion
sources: The Book of Common Prayer: The Texts of 1549, 1559, and 1662

authors.name: Osbern Bokenham
authors.biography: An Augustinian friar of Stoke by Clare, Suffolk, and doctor of divinity (Cambridge), who composed his Legends of Holy Women between 1443 and 1447 at the request of East Anglian patrons, several of them women. He died c. 1464.
authors.profile: Author of the Legends of Holy Women (1443–47), a collection of thirteen verse saints' lives — including those of Margaret, Anne, Katherine, Cecilia, and Mary Magdalene — with a substantial autobiographical prologue; also a prose treatise on the Mappula Angliae (a translation of Higden).
authors.style: Lydgatean verse with aureate diction; the female saint's life treated with tenderness and dramatic force; an unusually self-revealing authorial voice.
authors.concerns: The cult of female sanctity and its patronage by devout women; the legitimacy of vernacular hagiography.
authors.significance: The Legends are the principal fifteenth-century English monument of the female saints' lives and a major document of literary patronage by women.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; his career before the 1440s is unknown.

authors.name: Ranulf Higden
authors.biography: A Benedictine monk of St Werburgh's abbey, Chester, where he spent his whole career, dying on 12 March 1364; his Polychronicon, a universal history and geography compiled from earlier writers, became the standard history of England, translated into English by John Trevisa in 1387 and printed by Caxton in 1482.
authors.profile: Author of the Polychronicon (completed c. 1327, continued to 1352), with its celebrated first book describing the geography of the world and of Britain, and of the Ars Componendi Sermones and other didactic works.
authors.style: The industrious compiler's art: orderly encyclopedic arrangement, clear Latin, and a moralizing attention to the marvellous; the Polychronicon's world-description was a favourite of later chroniclers and cartographers.
authors.concerns: The unity of sacred and secular history; the description of the world and of Britain; the moral instruction of the clergy.
authors.significance: The Polychronicon dominated English historical writing for two centuries and, in Trevisa's translation, became one of the great monuments of fourteenth-century English prose.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; his continuations of the Polychronicon are hard to separate from those of his successors.

authors.name: Reginald Pecock
authors.biography: Fellow of Oriel College, Oxford, and successively bishop of St Asaph (1444) and Chichester (1450).
