The outstanding orthodox theologian of fifteenth-century England, he wrote in English to answer Lollardy by reason rather than force; his rejection of the church's reliance on authority and his defence of preaching earned him trial for heresy in 1457, public abjuration, and imprisonment at Thorney Abbey, where he died c. 1461.
authors.profile: Author of the Repressor of Over Much Blaming of the Clergy (c. 1449–55), The Book of Faith (1456), the Donet, the Folewer to the Donet, and other works of vernacular theology, most of them condemned and burned with him.
authors.style: A remarkable plain English of argument, invented vocabulary (e.g., 'unbileve' for infidelity), and dialectical method applied to vernacular controversy.
authors.concerns: The rational defence of orthodoxy; the 'doom of reason' against mere authority; the instruction of the laity.
authors.significance: The most original English theologian between Wyclif and the Reformation and a pioneer of philosophical prose in English; his condemnation dramatizes the fifteenth-century church's fear of vernacular theology.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; much of his corpus survives only in fragments or in his own summaries.

works.title: The Repressor of Over Much Blaming of the Clergy

authors.name: Richard de Bury
authors.biography: Born on 24 January 1287, he became tutor to the future Edward III, and thereafter the king's trusted servant: keeper of the privy seal, chancellor (1334–35), and bishop of Durham from 1333. An insatiable collector, he assembled one of the greatest libraries in England, and his household probably produced the Philobiblon, completed shortly before his death on 14 April 1345.
authors.profile: Author (or patron-author) of the Philobiblon (1344), the celebrated Latin treatise on the love of books, their care, and their lending — the first bibliophilic classic in English literature.
authors.style: Elegant, allusive Latin prose; the book personified as the companion of wisdom; practical rules for the custody of manuscripts enlivened by satire on careless clerks and students.
authors.concerns: The preservation and circulation of learning; the duties of clergy and princes to books; the reform of the universities.
authors.significance: The Philobiblon is the foundational text of English bibliophilia and a precious record of fourteenth-century book culture; de Bury's library fed Durham's later collections.
authors.uncertainty: The precise authorship of the Philobiblon (de Bury or his chaplain Robert Holcot) is debated.

authors.name: Richard Holland
authors.biography: A priest and secretary or chaplain to Archibald Douglas, Earl of Moray, for whom he composed the Buke of the Howlat (c. 1448); he later joined the exiled Douglases in England, was forfeited with them, and died c. 1483, perhaps in Orkney.
authors.profile: Author of the Buke of the Howlat (c. 1448), an alliterative beast-allegory in which the owl, ashamed of his ugliness, appeals through the birds to the pope and emperor, a satire on pride, flattery, and the Douglas family's enemies.
authors.style: The northern alliterative long line in intricate thirteen-line stanzas; the beast parliament as political allegory; a blend of heraldic pageantry and moral satire.
authors.concerns: Pride and humility; the flattery of courts; the honour of the Douglas family.
authors.significance: The Howlat is the last major alliterative poem of the Scottish tradition and a key document of Douglas politics and northern heraldry.
authors.uncertainty: Little is known of him; dates approximate and career reconstructed from Douglas records.

authors.name: Richard Rolle
authors.biography: Studied briefly at Oxford, then withdrew c. 1321 to become a hermit, finally settling near the Cistercian nunnery of Hampole in south Yorkshire, where he died in the Black Death (1349). The most widely read English spiritual writer of the fourteenth century, he was venerated as a saint, though never canonized.
authors.profile: Author of Latin treatises (Incendium Amoris, Emendatio Vitae, Melos Amoris) and English epistles (Ego Dormio, The Commandment, The Form of Living, addressed to the anchoress Margaret Kirkby) and of English psalm commentaries; his writings survive in hundreds of manuscripts.
authors.style: A highly personal, affective style built on the experience of 'fire, sweetness, and song' (calor, dulcor, canor); rhythmic prose with alliterative cadence; scriptural commentary fused with autobiography.
authors.concerns: The love of God as experienced warmth and song; the solitary life; the guidance of contemplatives, especially women recluses.
authors.significance: The father of the English mystical tradition: his affective spirituality shaped Rolle-influenced devotional prose for two centuries, and his English epistles are the earliest surviving writings of their kind.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the chronology of his writings is debated; the medieval cult attributed miracles to him.

authors.name: Robert Fabyan
authors.biography: A London draper, alderman, and sheriff (1493–94), Fabyan retired from civic life about 1502 and compiled his chronicle of England and France, which he finished by 1504 (with continuations to 1509). He died in London in 1513, and the work was printed by Richard Pynson in 1516 as The New Chronicles of England and France.
authors.profile: Author of the standard London chronicle of the early Tudor period. Organized annalistically around the mayors and sheriffs of London, Fabyan's chronicle supplied Shakespeare and the Tudor historians with the matter of English history from Brutus to Henry VII, and its verse interjections ('L'envoy') give it a distinctly civic literary character.
authors.style: The annalist's plain record, organized by civic year; occasional moralizing verse; a Londoner's eye for pageant, execution, and civic ceremony.
authors.concerns: The history of England and France as moral example; the dignity and record of the city of London.
authors.significance: The principal vernacular chronicle between the Brut tradition and Hall; a chief source of Tudor historical consciousness and of Shakespeare's history plays at second hand.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date unknown.

works.title: The New Chronicles of England and France

authors.name: Robert Henryson
authors.biography: A university graduate ('Master') who served as schoolmaster of the grammar school of Dunfermline and as a notary public; his name appears in the records of Dunfermline Abbey in 1478. He died c. 1500. The finest of the fifteenth-century makars, he is grouped by Dunbar among the dead poets of the Lament for the Makaris.
authors.profile: Author of the Morall Fabillis of Esope (c. 1480s), the Testament of Cresseid (c. 1475–90), Orpheus and Eurydice, Robene and Makyne, and a body of shorter moral poems.
authors.style: Chaucerian forms infused with northern speech; rueful, compassionate irony; the beast fable raised to satiric and philosophical art; mastery of the 'ballat royal' stanza.
authors.concerns: Justice, prudence, and the social order; the tragedy of Cresseid as a drama of sin, punishment, and late repentance; mortality and consolation.
authors.significance: Universally ranked with Dunbar as the greatest of the makars; his Testament of Cresseid is the most powerful continuation of Chaucer ever written, and his Fabillis the summit of the European fable tradition in the vernacular.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; almost nothing is known of his life beyond the Dunfermline records.

works.title: The Morall Fabillis of Esope the Phrygian

authors.name: Robert Mannyng
authors.biography: A Gilbertine canon of Sempringham Priory, Lincolnshire, who spent part of his career at Sixhills. He translated the Anglo-Norman Manuel des péchés of William of Wadington as Handlyng Synne (begun 1303), the classic English manual of penance, and later composed the Chronicle (completed 1338), a verse history of England from Noah to Edward I based on Wace and Peter Langtoft.
authors.profile: Handlyng Synne (1303) made the casuistry of confession vivid through exemplary tales; the Chronicle (1338) is a principal vernacular history of England in the earlier fourteenth century.
authors.style: Plain, fluent couplets; the telling anecdote and moralized exemplum; skilful adaptation of French sources for a provincial English audience.
authors.concerns: Pastoral instruction of the laity; the moral meaning of English history.
authors.significance: Handlyng Synne is a cornerstone of Middle English penitential literature and a major source for the exemplum tradition; the Chronicle bridges the Brut tradition and the verse histories of the fourteenth century.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; details of his life come from his own prefaces.
sources: Tudor Drama before Shakespeare, 1485–1590: New Directions for Research, Criticism, and Pedagogy

authors.name: Robert Whittington
authors.biography: Born at Lichfield about 1480; studied at Oxford, where he was laureated for grammar. He taught in London and wrote a series of grammatical and rhetorical textbooks, of which the Vulgaria (1520) — model sentences in Latin and English for schoolboys — is the most famous. He died about 1553.
authors.profile: The most successful school grammarian of the generation before Lily's Grammar was standardized. The Vulgaria's paired Latin and English sentences, drawn from everyday school and city life, are at once a textbook and a vivid picture of early Tudor London, and its jibes at Lily made it a document of the grammar wars of the 1520s.
authors.style: The schoolmaster's sentence-builder; colloquial English paired with schoolboy Latin; combative prefaces addressed to rival grammarians.
authors.concerns: The teaching of Latin through the vernacular; the rivalries of the grammar schools; the manners and language of London boys.
authors.significance: A principal maker of the Tudor school curriculum; the Vulgaria is a unique record of the spoken English of the early sixteenth century.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate.

authors.name: Roger Ascham
authors.identity: humanist; tutor to Elizabeth I; Latin secretary
authors.biography: Born at Kirby Wiske about 1515; educated at St John's College, Cambridge, where he taught Greek and reformed the pronunciation of it. Tutor to Princess Elizabeth from 1548 to 1550, he served as Latin secretary under Mary and Elizabeth. His Toxophilus (1545), a dialogue in praise of archery, won him a royal pension, and The Schoolmaster, begun about 1563, was published posthumously in 1570 by his widow. He died on 30 December 1568.
authors.profile: The most readable of the English humanist educators. Toxophilus is the first English treatise on a sport and a model of the plain style; The Schoolmaster — built around the instruction of the young Elizabeth — attacks Italianate corruption, prescribes the double translation of Latin, and records the educational practice of the age in the finest English prose between More and Hooker.
authors.style: The plain style refined into art: concrete, anecdotal, sinewy English that he explicitly opposed to the inkhorn inflation of his contemporaries.
authors.concerns: The education of the English governing class; the discipline of imitation and translation; the morality of travel; archery and bodily training as parts of the curriculum.
authors.significance: Tutor and intellectual model of Elizabeth I; The Schoolmaster governed English pedagogical theory for two centuries and remains the classic defence of the vernacular for learning.
authors.uncertainty: Birth year approximate (1514 or 1515).

authors.name: Roger Bacon
authors.biography: Educated at Oxford and Paris, where he lectured on Aristotle, he joined the Franciscans c. 1257 and, frustrated by the neglect of experimental science, sought the patronage of Pope Clement IV, for whom he composed the Opus Maius, Opus Minus, and Opus Tertium in 1267–68. He was condemned by his order c. 1278 and imprisoned, and died c. 1292.
authors.profile: Author of the Opus Maius (1267), a programmatic encyclopedia of the sciences — mathematics, optics, experimental science, moral philosophy, and the reform of learning — together with works on grammar, astronomy, alchemy, and the calendar.
authors.style: Urgent, polemical, encyclopedic prose; the advocacy of mathematics and experiment ('scientia experimentalis') as the foundation of knowledge; prophetic visions of technology (ships, cars, flying machines).
authors.concerns: The reform of the universities and of the church through science; the study of languages and texts; the practical power of knowledge.
authors.significance: The greatest scientific mind of the medieval West before the fourteenth-century natural philosophers; his experimental program made him the patron figure of early modern science in England (and the hero of Victorian legend).
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and the chronology of his Oxford years approximate; the circumstances of his condemnation are unclear.

authors.name: Sir David Lindsay
altNames: Sir David Lindsay of the Mount
authors.identity: poet; playwright; herald; Lyon King of Arms
authors.biography: Born about 1486 at the Mount in Fife; attached to the court of James IV and the companion and usher of the young James V, whom he exhorted in The Dreme (1528). Lyon King of Arms from 1542 and a lord of session, he was the leading advocate of the reformed cause in Scottish letters. His Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis was played at Linlithgow in 1540 and enlarged at Cupar in 1552. He died about April 1555.
authors.profile: The major Scottish poet of the Reformation. The Dreme (1528) instructs the young king in a dream vision; The Testament of the Papyngo (1530) is a dying parrot's satire of court and clergy; and Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis — the great morality of the Scottish Reformation — stages the trial of the estates before King Humanitie, with John the Common-Weill the plaintiff and the vices of the church in the dock.
authors.style: Direct satirical address in fluent Scots; the dream vision and the testament turned to political use; the morality play expanded to a national parliament.
authors.concerns: The reformation of the Scottish church; the education of the king; the common weal against the estates; justice for the poor.
authors.significance: The poet of the Scottish Reformation and the author of its greatest dramatic work; the Satyre is the summit of Scots drama and was played and reprinted for generations.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the exact date of his death (1555) is uncertain within the year.

works.title: Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis

authors.name: Sir Thomas Elyot
authors.biography: Born about 1490 into a family of west-country lawyers; he served Wolsey as clerk and became a diplomat and clerk of the king's council. Falling from favour in the 1530s, he devoted himself to letters: The Boke Named the Governour (1531), dedicated to Henry VIII, The Castle of Health (1534), and the first Latin–English dictionary (1538). He died on 26 March 1546.
authors.profile: The principal English theorist of humanist education and the gentleman magistrate. The Governour — drawing on Castiglione, Erasmus, and the Italian humanists — defined the curriculum, the virtues, and the physical training of the ruling class, and it introduced scores of classical commonplaces into English prose. His Dictionary (1538) founded English lexicography.
authors.style: Earnest, copious Ciceronian prose; the deliberate enrichment of English vocabulary from Latin; a moralist's directness beneath the classical apparatus.
authors.concerns: The education of princes and magistrates; the union of learning and virtue in the ruling class; the health of body and commonwealth; the capacities of the English language.
authors.significance: Author of the classic statement of the Tudor educational ideal, read by every Elizabethan schoolmaster, and of the dictionary that began the English lexicographical tradition.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

authors.name: Sir Thomas More
authors.identity: humanist; lawyer; statesman; Lord Chancellor; martyr and saint
authors.biography: Born in Milk Street, London, on 7 February 1478, the son of a judge; page to Cardinal Morton; studied at Oxford and the Inns of Court. A friend of Erasmus from 1499, he translated Lucian with him, wrote the Latin epigrams, and published Utopia at Louvain in 1516. Entered royal service in 1517; undersheriff of London, speaker of the Commons (1523), chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, and Lord Chancellor (1529–32). Refusing the oath of supremacy, he was imprisoned in the Tower in April 1534 and beheaded on 6 July 1535; canonized in 1935.
authors.profile: The presiding genius of English humanism. Utopia (1516) invented the fictional commonwealth; The History of King Richard III (c. 1513–18), written in both Latin and English, is the first great work of English historical prose and the source of Shakespeare's Richard III; the controversial dialogues of 1529–33 (A Dialogue Concerning Heresies, The Supplication of Souls, The Confutation of Tyndale's Answer) are the summit of Reformation polemic; and A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation (1534), written in the Tower, is a masterpiece of devotional prose.
authors.style: Irony, wit, and the dramatic management of dialogue; the plain English style of the later controversial works; Latinity of European standard in the epigrams and Utopia.
authors.concerns: The reform of Christendom and the commonwealth; the claims of conscience against the state; property, enclosure, and social justice; the defence of the old church against the new theology.
authors.significance: Author of the founding text of utopian fiction, the first classic of English historiography, and one of the great prose styles of the language; his life and death made him the exemplary conscience of the English Reformation.
authors.uncertainty: None significant; the dating of Richard III's composition remains approximate.

works.title: A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation
The History of King Richard III

authors.name: Sir Thomas Wyatt
authors.biography: Born at Allington Castle, Kent, in 1503; educated at St John's College, Cambridge. A courtier and diplomat for Henry VIII — he was esquire of the body, ambassador in France, Italy, and Spain, and knighted in 1535 — he was twice imprisoned in the Tower: in 1536, during the fall of Anne Boleyn, and in 1541 on charges of treasonable correspondence. Released through the influence of Catherine Howard, he died of fever at Sherborne, Dorset, on 11 October 1542. His poems circulated in manuscript during his life; 96 were printed posthumously in Tottel's Miscellany (1557).
authors.profile: The founder of the English lyric tradition. He introduced the Petrarchan sonnet into English (translating and imitating the Rime sparse with rugged, deliberate roughness), wrote the great courtly lyrics ('They flee from me', 'Whoso list to hunt', 'My galley charged with forgetfulness'), the three verse epistles known as the Satires (c. 1536), and a paraphrase of the seven penitential psalms composed after his 1536 imprisonment.
authors.style: A difficult, compressed, colloquial style — enjambment against the rhyme, metrical irregularity used for dramatic emphasis, and the plain speech of the courtier set against Petrarchan convention.
authors.concerns: The dangers of court life under an absolute prince; the claims of truth against flattery; love, honour, and the unstable self; the psalmist's repentance as a model for the Tudor subject.
authors.significance: With Surrey, he established the sonnet, the courtly lyric, and the verse satire in English, providing the formal foundations of the Elizabethan poetic achievement; Tottel's printing of his verse made him the first modern English poet of the anthologies.
authors.uncertainty: The canon rests on manuscript attributions (principally the Egerton MS); the extent of his relationship with Anne Boleyn is conjectural.

authors.name: Stephen Hawes
authors.biography: Born about 1474, probably in Suffolk; educated perhaps at Oxford, he became groom of the chamber to Henry VII. His Pastime of Pleasure was printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1509 and The Example of Virtue about 1504; he died about 1523, the last significant poet of the Chaucerian-Lydgatian school.
authors.profile: The last of the medieval allegorists and a favourite of the early Tudor court. The Pastime of Pleasure recounts the education, courtship, and knightly career of the hero Graunde Amoure in rhyme royal and couplets, an allegorical summa of chivalric and learned ideals; The Example of Virtue traces the soul's progress through Youth to Age and Eternity.
authors.style: Aureate diction in the Lydgatian manner; rhyme royal handled with fluency; allegorical machinery of pilgrimage, tower, and tournament.
authors.concerns: The seven liberal arts; chivalric education and courtly love; the soul's moral progress; the poet's role as teacher of princes.
authors.significance: The bridge between the medieval allegorical tradition and Tudor court poetry; Spenser read him, and The Pastime of Pleasure kept the dream-allegory alive into the Renaissance.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; little is known of his life beyond his court service.

authors.name: Stephen of Ripon
authors.biography: A priest of Ripon and member of Bishop Wilfrid's household, conventionally identified with the Æddi Stephanus whom Bede says Wilfrid brought back from Kent as a singing-master (fl. c. 670-720). He accompanied Wilfrid on his journeys and wrote the Vita Sancti Wilfridi (c. 712-714) at the request of Acca of Hexham and Tatberht of Ripon. Nothing else is known of his life, and even his identification with Bede's 'Æddi' rests on a plausible but unproven equation.
authors.profile: The earliest identifiable Anglo-Latin biographer after the anonymous Lindisfarne life of Cuthbert. His Vita Wilfridi is a partisan defence of his hero against the charges of Wilfrid's enemies, cast in the conventions of late-antique hagiography.
authors.style: Vigorous, episodic narrative with a strong authorial voice; vivid set-piece scenes (Wilfrid's shipwreck, his Roman appeals, his deathbed); simpler and more direct Latin than Aldhelm's, with a notable absence of the hermeneutic manner.
authors.concerns: Episcopal authority and the primacy of Rome; the sanctity of a controversial political bishop; the deeds of the apostolic missionary as evidence of holiness.
authors.significance: His Vita Wilfridi is the earliest surviving biography written in England about a contemporary English churchman, and a principal source for the history of the seventh-century Northumbrian church and Wilfrid's career.
authors.uncertainty: Identification with Bede's Æddi Stephanus is traditional, not proven. Birth and death dates unknown; floruit c. 670-720.
sources: English Historical Documents, Volume III: 1189–1327

authors.name: Tatwine
authors.biography: A Mercian by birth who became a monk at Breedon-on-the-Hill in Leicestershire, a house with Northumbrian connections. He was consecrated archbishop of Canterbury in 731, succeeding Berhtwald, and died in office in 734. Bede records his consecration in the Historia ecclesiastica.
authors.profile: Author of the Aenigmata, forty Latin riddles with a preface, on theological, philosophical, and grammatical subjects, and of a Latin grammar (Ars Tatuini) based on Donatus. His riddles are the first Latin riddle collection composed in England to survive complete.
authors.style: Compact hexameter riddles in the manner of Symphosius and Aldhelm, but with doctrine rather than natural history as their usual subject; the verse is plain and schoolmasterly rather than hermeneutic.
authors.concerns: The union of grammatical learning with theology; the encyclopedic description of creation through the riddle form; Christian teaching for the schoolroom.
authors.significance: With Aldhelm and Hwætberht he established the Anglo-Latin riddle tradition that fed into the vernacular Exeter Book Riddles; his grammar helped transmit the Insular grammatical tradition.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and place uncertain (Mercia by tradition); the attribution of the riddles and grammar to him is secure.
sources: English Literature in the Sixteenth Century, Excluding Drama

authors.name: Theodore of Tarsus
authors.identity: exegete, canonist, and teacher; Latin prose writer
authors.biography: Born in Tarsus in 602 and educated in the Greek East (probably at Antioch and Constantinople), he was living as a monk in Rome when Pope Vitalian consecrated him archbishop of Canterbury in 668, with Hadrian the African as his companion and adviser. Together they toured England, reformed the English church, and founded the school of Canterbury, where Greek and Latin learning, canon law, and biblical exegesis were taught. He died on 19 September 690.
authors.profile: The Laterculus Malalianus, a Latin exegetical and chronographical treatise on the life of Christ, is attributed to him (written at Canterbury in the 670s); the biblical commentaries from the Canterbury school preserve his and Hadrian's teaching; the penitential that circulates under his name is traditionally attributed to him. His school produced Aldhelm and the earliest English manuscript culture.
authors.style: In the Laterculus Malalianus, dense and sometimes idiosyncratic Latin shaped by Syriac and Greek exegetical sources, with a chronological apparatus; the Canterbury commentaries preserve an unusual blend of Greek and Latin patristic learning.
authors.concerns: The chronology and exegesis of the life of Christ; the union of Greek and Latin Christian learning; church order and penance; the education of an English clergy.
authors.significance: As organizer of the Canterbury school he is the founder of Anglo-Saxon Latin learning; his church reforms and synods (Hertford 672, Hatfield 679) unified the English church, and his teaching reached Bede's Northumbria through his pupils.
authors.uncertainty: The attribution of the Laterculus Malalianus and the Penitential to him is traditional and widely accepted, but not beyond dispute. Birth and death dates are recorded by Bede.
sources: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume B: The Sixteenth Century and the Early Seventeenth Century

authors.name: Thomas Chestre
authors.biography: A late fourteenth-century English poet known only from his works, which name him 'Thomas Chestre' in their final lines; he flourished c. 1380–1400. Nothing else is recorded of his life.
authors.profile: Author of Sir Launfal (an English adaptation of Marie de France's Lanval), the romance Libeaus Desconus (from Renaud de Beaujeu's Le Bel Inconnu), and the romance Octavian; some scholarship also attributes The Isle of Ladies to him.
authors.style: Energetic tail-rhyme stanzas; brisk narrative compression of French sources; a fondness for the supernatural generosity of fairy mistresses and the rewards of loyalty.
authors.concerns: The adaptation of French courtly romance for English popular audiences; the claims of loyalty, love, and largesse.
authors.significance: A representative figure of the late Middle English tail-rhyme romance; his Sir Launfal is the fullest English treatment of the Lanval story and a staple of the Breton lay tradition in England.
authors.uncertainty: Dates and circumstances wholly unknown; the attributions rest on the poems' self-naming.

authors.name: Thomas Cranmer
authors.identity: archbishop of Canterbury; liturgist; theologian; martyr
authors.biography: Born at Aslockton on 2 July 1489; fellow of Jesus College, Cambridge. His suggestion that the universities should judge the validity of Henry VIII's marriage brought him to the king's notice; he became Archbishop of Canterbury in 1533 and presided over the annulment, the royal supremacy, and the dissolution. Under Edward VI he produced the two Books of Common Prayer (1549, 1552), the Book of Homilies (1547), and the Forty-Two Articles (1553). Under Mary he was tried, degraded, and — after recanting and then withdrawing his recantations — burned at Oxford on 21 March 1556, thrusting the hand that had signed the recantations first into the fire.
authors.profile: The architect of the English liturgy. The Book of Common Prayer is his monument: collects, services, and the prose of worship that fixed the devotional language of English for four centuries ('ashes to ashes, dust to dust'). He was the principal author of the first Book of Homilies (1547) and of the doctrinal statement of the Edwardian church.
authors.style: Ritual prose of unmatched gravity and compression: parallel phrasing, scriptural cadence, and the direct address of congregation by priest; a style built for the voice.
authors.concerns: Worship in the vernacular; the simplification of the liturgy on scriptural principles; royal supremacy and the reform of doctrine; the unity of the English church.
authors.significance: Author of the defining text of Anglican worship, still in daily use; the Prayer Book's prose ranks with Tyndale's Bible as the foundation of modern English devotional language.
authors.uncertainty: None significant; the division of authorship within the 1547 Homilies is partly editorial.

works.title: A Defence of the True and Catholic Doctrine of the Sacrament

authors.name: Thomas Hoccleve
authors.biography: A clerk of the Privy Seal office in Westminster from c. 1387 for some thirty-five years, he knew Chaucer personally and called himself his disciple; his poems — above all the autobiographical passages of the Series — record his anxiety, his 'maladie' of 1416, and the precarious life of a married office-holder. He died in 1426.
authors.profile: Author of the Regiment of Princes (1411), the classic English mirror-for-princes addressed to the future Henry V; the Series (c. 1419–21), a linked set of tales and complaints containing the first English poetic autobiography; and shorter poems including the Male Regle.
authors.style: Correct Chaucerian verse with a plain, personal voice; rueful self-portraiture; the adaptation of courtly and didactic forms to the experience of bureaucracy and illness.
authors.concerns: Good governance and the duties of princes; poverty, patronage, and the ethics of office; his own mental suffering and its consolation.
authors.significance: The first English poet to write extensively about his own life and illness; the Regiment is a principal document of Lancastrian political literature and of the Chaucerian inheritance.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the cause of his 1416 'maladie' remains debated.
themes: The English vernacular and national letters

authors.name: Thomas Linacre
authors.identity: physician; humanist; founder of the Royal College of Physicians
authors.biography: Born about 1460, probably at Canterbury; studied at Oxford and in Italy, where he learned Greek from Politian and took a medical degree at Padua. Physician to Henry VIII, tutor of the young Thomas More, and founder of the Royal College of Physicians (1518), he translated Galen into Latin with unprecedented accuracy and wrote De Emendata Structura Latini Sermonis (1524), the first scientific Latin grammar by an Englishman. He died on 20 October 1524.
authors.profile: The English pioneer of Greek medicine and philology. His Galen translations (1517–23) restored the texts of ancient medicine to the West, and his Latin grammar, applying the new philology to the classical language, is a landmark of English humanism.
authors.style: The philologist's precision; translation as recovery of the original; grammar as science rather than schoolroom drill.
authors.concerns: The restoration of Greek learning; the reform of medicine on Galenic foundations; the accurate use of Latin among physicians and scholars.
authors.significance: Founded the scientific study of medicine in England and the College of Physicians; his translations and grammar made him, with Colet and Grocyn, one of the three pillars of the Oxford reform.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and birthplace approximate.

authors.name: Thomas Malory
authors.biography: Commonly identified with Sir Thomas Malory of Newbold Revel, Warwickshire, a War of the Roses knight with a long record of violence and imprisonment, who describes himself in the colophon of his book as 'knight prisoner' and prays for his deliverance. He completed Le Morte Darthur in prison in the ninth year of Edward IV (1469–70) and died on 14 March 1471; Caxton printed the work in 1485.
authors.profile: Author of Le Morte Darthur, the great prose compilation of the Arthurian legend in English, from the sword in the stone through the Grail quest to the death of Arthur and the ruin of the Round Table.
authors.style: A spare, rhythmic prose of paratactic clauses and ritual dialogue; the reduction of the French prose cycles to a single tragic arc; scenes of chivalry, combat, and pathos of enduring power.
authors.concerns: The ideals and contradictions of chivalry — loyalty, love, and treason; the costs of the Grail quest; the fall of a fellowship through sin.
authors.significance: Le Morte Darthur is the definitive English Arthurian book and the first great prose romance in the language; through Caxton's edition it fixed the Arthurian story for all subsequent English literature.
authors.uncertainty: The identification of the author with the Warwickshire knight is probable but not certain; the circumstances of composition are known only from the colophon.

authors.name: Thomas Usk
authors.biography: A London scrivener and clerk who attached himself first to the party of John of Northampton and then betrayed it to Nicholas Brembre and the royalist faction, serving as under-sheriff of Middlesex. Imprisoned after the Merciless Parliament of 1388, he wrote the Testament of Love in the Tower and was executed at Tyburn on 4 March 1388.
authors.profile: Author of the Testament of Love (c. 1384–88), an allegorical prose apologia in the Boethian and Chaucerian manner — for centuries printed as Chaucer's — in which Love consoles the imprisoned author and vindicates his political life.
authors.style: Elaborate allegorical prose with Chaucerian echoes; the fusion of love allegory with political self-defence; Boethian consolation adapted to a treason trial.
authors.concerns: The justice of his political career; fortune, free will, and the consolations of love and philosophy.
authors.significance: The Testament is the first major prose work in the Chaucerian line and a unique document of Ricardian factional politics; its false attribution to Chaucer long shaped the poet's canon.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; details of his political career come from hostile records.

authors.name: Walter Hilton
authors.biography: Probably educated at Cambridge and trained in canon law before becoming an Augustinian canon of Thurgarton Priory, Nottinghamshire; he died on 24 March 1396. His writings circulated widely and were printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1494.
authors.profile: Author of the Scale of Perfection (Book I c. 1380s, addressed to an anchoress; Book II c. 1390s), the most influential English treatise on contemplation; of the Epistle on the Mixed Life, addressed to a devout layman; and of other works including Of Angels' Song and the translation of the Stimulus Amoris attributed to him.
authors.style: Measured, theologically precise prose; the famous image of the spiritual life as a ladder or scale; cautious discrimination between true and false mystical experience; clarity and pastoral warmth.
authors.concerns: The reformation of the soul in the image of God; the relation of active and contemplative lives; the discernment of spirits.
authors.significance: The classic systematizer of English mysticism; the Scale of Perfection remained a standard of English devotional reading into the seventeenth century (used by Augustine Baker and his circle).
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and early career conjectural; some works attributed to him are disputed.

authors.name: Walter Map
authors.biography: A Herefordshire-born clerk of Welsh descent who studied at Paris and served Henry II as a royal justice and travelling ambassador; he attended the Lateran Council of 1179 and became a canon of St Paul's and archdeacon of Oxford. The archsatirist of the Angevin court, he died c. 1210.
authors.profile: Author of De Nugis Curialium (Courtiers' Trifles, c. 1181–92), a miscellany of satire, gossip, marvels, and history that preserves some of the earliest Arthurian and fairy material in Latin; the Goliardic poems once attributed to him are not his.
authors.style: Biting, allusive, deliberately disordered satire of the court and the religious orders; the anecdote raised to moral fable; a proto-Renaissance pessimism about the world he served.
authors.concerns: The vices of courts and monasteries; the vanity of worldly service; the relations of the sexes; the marvels of Wales and the Celtic past.
authors.significance: De Nugis is the supreme literary monument of the twelfth-century courtier's disenchantment and a key source for the early Arthurian and Herla/fairy traditions.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; the De Nugis survives in a single manuscript and its text is unstable.

authors.name: Werferth
authors.biography: Bishop of Worcester from c. 872 to his death (c. 915); one of the scholars of King Alfred's court circle named by Asser.
authors.profile: Translator of Gregory the Great's Dialogues into Old English (c. 890s), a work commissioned by Alfred and prefaced by him; the earliest extensive Old English translation of a major patristic text.
authors.style: Faithful, competent Mercian-flavoured prose, somewhat more literal than the other Alfredian translations.
authors.concerns: The transmission of Gregory's hagiographical and pastoral teaching to a vernacular audience.
authors.significance: A key figure of the Alfredian translation program; his Dialogues preserve a major stage in the development of Old English prose.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; the attribution of the translation rests on Asser's Life of Alfred and Alfred's own Preface.
sources: English Historical Documents, Volume II: 1042–1189

authors.name: William Baldwin
authors.biography: Born about 1515; a scholar of Oxford who became corrector of the king's printing under Edward VI and a prolific editor and compiler. His Treatise of Moral Philosophy appeared in 1547; his prose satire Beware the Cat, written in 1552–53, was printed in 1561. He planned and partly compiled A Mirror for Magistrates, printed in 1559 after his death. He died about 1563.
authors.profile: The author of the first English work of sustained prose fiction and the begetter of A Mirror for Magistrates. Beware the Cat — a night-long exchange of stories about cats, set in a London printing house and framed as a fantastic listening experiment — is the first English novel in embryo, and its anti-Catholic satire made it dangerous enough to be suppressed. The Mirror, which he edited and contributed to, became one of the most influential books of the Elizabethan age.
authors.style: Framed narrative in the plain style; printer's-shop realism; satirical fable with a serious theological edge.
authors.concerns: Protestant polemic against the old religion; the uses of fiction for truth-telling; the moral instruction of magistrates through the falls of great men.
authors.significance: A founding figure of English prose fiction and of the complaint tradition; his Mirror for Magistrates supplied subjects and rhetoric to Spenser, Shakespeare, and the whole Elizabethan tragic imagination.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; the division of authorship within the Mirror is editorial.

authors.name: William Caxton
authors.biography: A Kentish mercer who spent three decades in the Low Countries, rising to governor of the English merchants at Bruges, where he learned printing at Cologne and produced the first book printed in English, his own Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (Bruges, c. 1473–74). In 1476 he set up the first English press at Westminster, printing some hundred books — Chaucer, Malory, Gower, Lydgate, the Golden Legend, and his own translations — before his death c. 1491.
authors.profile: Printer and translator: the Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (c. 1473–74), The Game and Playe of the Chesse (1474), the History of Reynard the Fox (1481), the Golden Legend (1483), and numerous prologues and epilogues that constitute a body of critical prose.
authors.style: Lucid, idiomatic translation from French sources; a merchant's plain style enriched by courtly vocabulary; the prologues' genial self-presentation as servant of the 'comyn wele'.
authors.concerns: The provision of good books in English; the standardization of the language ('ouer rude termes' and the dialect of Kent); the moral and chivalric education of the nobility and gentry.
authors.significance: The introducer of printing to England: his press fixed the form of the English classics, began the standardization of written English, and made the fifteenth century's literature the sixteenth century's inheritance.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; the exact site and date of his first printing remain debated.
themes: The education of princes and magistrates

works.title: Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye

authors.name: William Dunbar
authors.biography: A graduate of St Andrews (MA 1479) and a Franciscan novice in his youth, he served from c. 1500 as a clerk and poet at the court of James IV, for whom he wrote the celebratory poems of the marriage to Margaret Tudor (1503); he received a royal pension from 1500. He disappears from record after the battle of Flodden (1513), and died c. 1520.
authors.profile: Author of some eighty poems preserved chiefly in the Bannatyne and Maitland manuscripts: the Lament for the Makaris (c. 1505), The Goldyn Targe, The Tretis of the Tua Mariit Wemen and the Wedo (c. 1500–07), the flying with Kennedy, the dream allegories, and the great occasional verse of the court.
authors.style: The most technically virtuosic of the makars: aureate magnificence (The Goldyn Targe) alternating with scabrous colloquial satire (the Tretis); the refrain, the flying, the alliterative line, and the French formes fixes all mastered; a voice by turns celebratory, venomous, elegiac, and devout.
authors.concerns: The vanity of life and the power of death (Timor mortis conturbat me); the hypocrisies of court and clergy; the duties and pleasures of the royal court.
authors.significance: With Henryson, the greatest poet of medieval Scotland; the Lament for the Makaris is one of the supreme elegies in the language and gave the Scottish tradition its name.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; his clerical status and career details are conjectural.

works.title: The Tretis of the Tua Mariit Wemen and the Wedo

authors.name: William Langland
authors.birthplace: probably Cleobury Mortimer, Shropshire, or the Malvern Hills area
authors.biography: Almost everything known of him is inferred from Piers Plowman, whose dreamer 'Will' is a long-clothed clerk of the Malvern country, married, and living in London in poverty among the Cornhill folk; the poem's A-text (c. 1367–70), B-text (c. 1377–79), and C-text (c. 1386–88) show a career of continuous revision. He is commonly identified with the William Langland recorded at Oxford and in London in the 1390s, though the identification is uncertain.
authors.profile: Author of Piers Plowman, the greatest English allegorical poem: a sequence of dream visions in which Will searches for Truth, Dowel, Dobet, and Dobest amid the estates of fourteenth-century England.
authors.style: Unrhymed alliterative long lines of extraordinary range — satiric, homiletic, apocalyptic, tender; the allegorical dream vision fused with estates satire and biblical exegesis; the personification of abstract virtues with concrete social observation.
authors.concerns: The reform of society and church through penance and truth; the theology of grace and merit; poverty, labour, and the social order.
authors.significance: With Chaucer and Gower, the third summit of Ricardian poetry; Piers Plowman became the rallying text of reformist and radical traditions (it was read by the rebels of 1381 and printed by the Tudor reformers) and one of the most studied poems in English.
authors.uncertainty: Biography almost entirely conjectural; the attribution of the poem rests on manuscript rubrics and internal evidence.

authors.name: William Lily
authors.identity: grammarian; first High Master of St Paul's School
authors.biography: Born at Odiham about 1468; studied at Oxford and in Italy, where he learned Greek. Appointed by John Colet as the first High Master of St Paul's School in 1512, he wrote the Latin grammar that, revised by Colet and Erasmus, became the standard school grammar of England. He died in February 1522 (new style 1523).
authors.profile: Author of the grammar that schooled England for three centuries. The Short Introduction of Grammar ('Lily's Grammar'), with its English accidence and its Latin Brevissima Institutio, was prescribed by royal proclamation under Henry VIII and Edward VI and memorized by every grammar-school boy from Shakespeare to Johnson — who quotes it, and its misquotations, throughout the literature of the period.
authors.style: The schoolmaster's clarity: paradigms, rules in English for boys, Latin examples; a grammar written to be memorized.
authors.concerns: The reform of Latin teaching on humanist principles; the founding of a public grammar school; the union of Greek learning with Christian education.
authors.significance: The author of the most widely used textbook in English history; Lily's Grammar structured the linguistic formation of the entire literate class of early modern England.
authors.uncertainty: The exact division of the grammar's authorship among Lily, Colet, and Erasmus is editorial.

authors.name: William of Malmesbury
authors.biography: A monk and librarian of Malmesbury Abbey, where he spent his whole career, becoming precentor and, late in life, refusing the abbacy; he died c. 1143. The greatest English historian since Bede, he gathered his materials from libraries across England and corresponded with the learned of his day.
authors.profile: Author of the Gesta Regum Anglorum (first version 1125, revised to c. 1135), the Gesta Pontificum Anglorum (1125), the Historia Novella (c. 1140–43), and saints' lives including those of Wulfstan, Dunstan, and Aldhelm.
authors.style: Polished, allusive Latin modelled on classical historians; critical assessment of sources; a gift for anecdote and character; patriotic pride in English history tempered by Norman loyalties.
authors.concerns: The continuity of the English kingdom from the Anglo-Saxons to his own day; the moral exemplarity of history; the recovery of the English past after the Conquest.
authors.significance: The founder of critical English historiography after Bede; his Gesta Regum is the principal narrative source for Anglo-Norman history and the model for the century's chroniclers.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; his Anglo-Saxon sources were largely lost in the Reformation.

authors.name: William of Ockham
authors.identity: philosopher; logician; political theorist; Franciscan friar
authors.biography: A Franciscan who studied and taught at Oxford, where his teaching was denounced to the papal court at Avignon (1324); while awaiting judgement he became embroiled in the Franciscan poverty controversy, fled Avignon with Michael of Cesena in 1328, and spent the rest of his life under the protection of the emperor Louis of Bavaria at Munich, writing political works against the papacy until his death in 1347.
authors.profile: Author of the Summa Logicae (c. 1323), the Ordinationes on the Sentences, the Quodlibeta, and a series of political treatises on poverty and papal power.
authors.style: The 'razor' of terminist logic: relentless elimination of superfluous entities and distinctions; a new theory of signs and mental language; clear, devastating polemic in the political works.
authors.concerns: The foundations of logic and knowledge; universals and nominalism; the limits of papal power; apostolic poverty.
authors.significance: The most consequential English philosopher of the Middle Ages: his nominalism reshaped European philosophy and theology (via Buridan, the via moderna, and Luther), and his political theory laid groundwork for conciliarism and modern notions of sovereignty.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the chronology of his early works rests on internal evidence.

authors.name: William Roper
authors.biography: Born about 1496; a lawyer of Lincoln's Inn who married Margaret, Thomas More's eldest daughter, in 1521, and lived in More's household at Chelsea for sixteen years. He wrote The Life of Sir Thomas More between about 1553 and 1558 from intimate memory; it circulated in manuscript and was first printed in 1626. He died on 4 January 1578.
authors.profile: Author of the first great English biography of a private man. The Life of Sir Thomas More — the portrait of the Chancellor at Chelsea: his prayers, his jests, his relations with his family, and his final refusal of the oath — is the classic of Tudor life-writing and the foundation of the More legend that Shakespeare's play and the later tradition inherited.
authors.style: Plain, affectionate, anecdotal prose; the vivid recalled dialogue of the Chelsea household; a son-in-law's reverence without hagiographical inflation.
authors.concerns: The memory and example of More; conscience against the state; the sanctity of the family and the household.
authors.significance: Established the English biographical tradition and supplied the human More to every later age; a primary source of the first importance for the English Reformation.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

works.title: The Life of Sir Thomas More

authors.name: William Tyndale
authors.biography: Born in Gloucestershire about 1494; educated at Oxford (BA 1512, MA 1515) and Cambridge. Denied episcopal patronage for an English Bible, he left England in 1524 and worked in Germany and the Low Countries: his New Testament was printed at Worms in 1526 and smuggled into England; the Pentateuch followed in 1530 and a revised New Testament in 1534. Betrayed at Antwerp in 1535, he was strangled and burned at Vilvoorde on 6 October 1536.
authors.profile: The father of the English Bible. His translations — made from the Greek of Erasmus and the Hebrew — gave English scripture its enduring shape: the Authorized Version of 1611 retains perhaps ninety per cent of his New Testament phrasing. As a polemicist he wrote the most effective Reformation tracts in English: The Obedience of a Christian Man (1528), The Parable of the Wicked Mammon (1528), The Practice of Prelates (1530), and An Answer unto Sir Thomas More's Dialogue (1531).
authors.style: The plain style at its greatest: short sentences, monosyllabic Saxon diction, and rhythms tuned for reading aloud; learned argument made colloquial and urgent.
authors.concerns: The authority of scripture over church and prince; justification by faith; the translation of the Word into every ploughboy's language; the duty of obedience and its limits.
authors.significance: The principal architect of English biblical prose and of the language of English devotion; his translation work shaped the King James Bible and, through it, the speech of the English-speaking world.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; details of his early Gloucestershire life rest on Foxe's Acts and Monuments.

works.title: An Answer unto Sir Thomas More's Dialogue
The Obedience of a Christian Man
The Parable of the Wicked Mammon

authors.name: Wulfstan
authors.biography: Bishop of London 996–1002, bishop of Worcester 1002–1016, and archbishop of York 1002–1023; the principal counselor and draftsman of law under kings Æthelred II and Cnut.
authors.profile: Author of the Sermo Lupi ad Anglos (1014), the most famous Old English sermon, preached in the crisis of the Danish invasions; the Institutes of Polity (a treatise on the orders of Christian society); the Canons of Edgar; the law codes of Æthelred and Cnut; and a series of eschatological homilies (De Antichristo, De falsis deis) warning of the approaching end.
authors.style: A distinctive, urgent rhythm built on two-stress phrases, alliteration, intensifying repetition, and cumulative word-pairs; the most recognizable idiolect in Old English prose.
authors.concerns: National repentance; social order and the duties of each estate; the coming of Antichrist; the law of God as the foundation of earthly law.
authors.significance: With Ælfric, the last great writer of Old English prose; his homilies and law codes shaped the response of the English church and state to the conquest of 1016.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and early career unknown; the canon of his writings rests on stylistic analysis.

works.title: Wulfstan's Eschatological Homilies (De Antichristo, De falsis deis, and related sermons)

sources: Dictionary of Old English: A to I online

authors.name: Wulfstan the Cantor
authors.biography: Monk and precentor of the Old Minster, Winchester, active in the 990s; a leading figure of the literary culture of the Benedictine Reform.
authors.profile: Author of the Narratio metrica de Sancto Swithuno (c. 996), a verse life of St Swithun with an important prose preface describing the rebuilding of the Old Minster; also credited with the Life of St Æthelwold.
authors.style: Accomplished Latin hexameters in the classical revival manner of the tenth-century reform; encomiastic tone.
authors.concerns: The cult of the saints as the glory of the reformed church; the commemoration of Winchester's patrons and builders.
authors.significance: The principal Latin poet of the late Old English period; his Narratio is a major source for the architecture and liturgy of the Old Minster.
authors.uncertainty: Little biographical detail known; attributions of the Æthelwold life debated.
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Medieval English Literature 1100–1500

authors.name: Ælfric Bata
authors.biography: A pupil of Ælfric of Eynsham who identifies himself by the nickname 'Bata' and addresses his master with affectionate humour in the colloquies. He probably taught at a monastic school in the first quarter of the eleventh century (fl. c. 1005-1025). His life is otherwise unknown.
authors.profile: Author of the Colloquia and the Colloquia difficiliora, Latin conversation manuals modelled on Ælfric's Colloquy but far more expansive and boisterous: they dramatize daily life in the monastic school with dialogue about food, drink, beatings, and petty theft.
authors.style: Colloquial, hyperbolic Latin with a taste for comic exaggeration and insult; the texts deliberately enlarge the vocabulary of daily life beyond the classroom classics.
authors.concerns: The teaching of spoken Latin; the discipline and everyday realities of the monastic school; the relationship between master and pupil.
authors.significance: His colloquies preserve a uniquely vivid picture of eleventh-century English school life and document the vitality of the vernacular-Latin classroom tradition founded by Ælfric.
authors.uncertainty: Known only from his texts; floruit approximate (c. 1005-1025); birth and death dates unknown.
sources: The Cambridge History of Early Modern English Literature

authors.name: Ælfric of Eynsham
authors.biography: Educated at Winchester under Bishop Æthelwold, the leading figure of the Benedictine Reform; monk and mass-priest at Cerne Abbas (c. 987–1005); first abbot of Eynsham (1005–c. 1010). The greatest and most prolific writer of Old English prose.
authors.profile: Author of the two series of Catholic Homilies (c. 989–995), the Lives of Saints (c. 993–998), the Grammar and Glossary (the first Latin grammar in a European vernacular), the Colloquy, translations of Genesis and other Old Testament books (the Old English Hexateuch), De temporibus anni, pastoral letters, and numerous shorter homilies and treatises.
authors.style: Rhythmical, alliterative prose of extraordinary clarity and control — a deliberately plain style designed to be read aloud and understood; careful avoidance of apocryphal excess.
authors.concerns: Orthodox teaching for clergy and laity; the dignity and capacity of the English language; the education of the young; resistance to superstition and error.
authors.significance: The culmination of the Old English prose tradition; his works circulated more widely than any other vernacular prose of the period and influenced English religious writing for centuries.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; several works are attributed to him on stylistic grounds.
sources: Beowulf: A Verse Translation

authors.name: Æthelweard
authors.biography: Ealdorman of the western provinces and descendant of King Æthelred I; patron of Ælfric of Eynsham; died c. 998.
authors.profile: Author of the Chronicon (c. 980), a Latin version of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle down to 973, written for his kinswoman Matilda, abbess of Essen, with a famous prologue praising King Alfred.
authors.style: Dense, hermeneutic Latin of the sort parodied by his contemporary William of Malmesbury's sources; learned vocabulary and Grecisms.
authors.concerns: The antiquity and dignity of the West Saxon royal line; the cultivation of Latin learning among the secular aristocracy.
authors.significance: An important witness to the text of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and to lay Latin literacy in late Anglo-Saxon England.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; identification with the ealdorman Æthelweard of the charters is standard but rests on prosopography.
sources: The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

authors.name: Æthelwold of Winchester
authors.identity: monastic reformer; Latin and Old English prose writer; translator
authors.biography: Born into a noble Winchester family c. 904-909, brought up at the court of King Æthelstan, and ordained with Dunstan. He became a monk at Glastonbury under Dunstan, was made abbot of the derelict monastery of Abingdon (c. 954), and in 963 was appointed bishop of Winchester, where he expelled the secular clerics of the Old and New Minsters and installed monks. He was the most radical and effective leader of the Benedictine Reform, a teacher of Ælfric, and a patron of manuscript production and the arts. He died on 1 August 984.
authors.profile: Author of the Regularis Concordia (c. 970), the customary that unified English monastic observance under royal patronage; traditionally credited with the Old English translation of the Rule of St Benedict (c. 960s) and associated with the Old English New Minster Charter (966) and possibly the Benedictine Office. His school at Winchester created the standardized literary language ('Winchester words') used by Ælfric.
authors.style: In the Regularis Concordia, clear expository Latin organized for practical liturgical use, with vivid prescriptions for ceremony (the Visitatio Sepulchri, the 'tropes'); in the vernacular Rule, plain idiomatic Old English translating Benedict's Latin closely.
authors.concerns: Uniformity of observance; the king as protector of reformed monasticism; the education of monks in Latin and the vernacular; the liturgy as the centre of the religious life.
authors.significance: The architect of the English Benedictine Reform and of the alliance between the crown and the reformed monasteries; his Winchester school and standardized Old English shaped the literary language of the late tenth century and of Ælfric's and Wulfstan's prose.
authors.uncertainty: Birth year approximate (c. 904-909). The attribution of the Old English Benedictine Rule and Benedictine Office to him is traditional and widely but not universally accepted.
themes: Women's experience and the feminine voice

works.title: The Old English Rule of St Benedict

sources: TEAMS Middle English Texts Series

works.title: A Defence of the True and Catholic Doctrine of the Sacrament
altTitles: The Defence of the True and Catholike Doctrine of the Sacrament of the Body and Bloud of Our Saviour Christ
works.description: Cranmer's principal theological work, published in 1550, defining the eucharist against both transubstantiation and mere memorialism; the fullest statement of the Reformed doctrine of the sacrament in English.
works.plot: The book argues from scripture and the fathers that Christ is truly but spiritually present in the eucharist, received by faith; it refutes the Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation (against Stephen Gardiner) and the Zwinglian reduction of the sacrament to a bare sign, distinguishing 'sacramentally' from 'corporally', and it defends the vernacular liturgy and communion in both kinds.
works.significance: The classic English statement of the Reformed eucharist and Cranmer's most sustained piece of theological prose; it fixed the middle course of Anglican sacramental doctrine for centuries.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1550 during Cranmer's ascendancy under Edward VI, in the controversy with Bishop Stephen Gardiner (imprisoned for his opposition); the doctrine of the Defence shaped the communion rite of the 1552 Prayer Book, and Cranmer recanted it under Mary before renouncing his recantations at the stake in 1556.
works.structure: Five books of doctrinal argument with patristic citation, cast as a reply to Gardiner's defence of the corporal presence.

works.title: A Dialogue Concerning Heresies
altTitles: A Dialogue of Sir Thomas More, Knight
works.description: More's first and longest English polemical work against the Lutheran heresy, cast as a four-book dialogue between More and a young 'messenger' sent by a friend who is tempted by the reformers.
works.plot: In Book I More defends the veneration of images, pilgrimages, and miracles; Book II discusses the authority of the Church and the corruption of Tyndale's New Testament translation; Book III refutes Luther's and Tyndale's views on faith and works; Book IV defends the clergy and the burning of heretics, arguing that Luther's doctrine leads to sedition and the destruction of the sacraments.
works.significance: The major English Catholic response to the early Reformation, documenting the doctrinal battle over scripture and tradition, and one of the fullest exhibits of More's prose — combative, witty, and colloquial — outside the Latin works.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written 1528–29 after More had read Tyndale's New Testament and his Obedience of a Christian Man; part of the print war between More (with Bishop John Fisher) and the English reformers conducted under Bishop Tunstall's licence to read heretical books.
works.characters: Thomas More (as speaker); The Messenger
works.structure: Four books of continuous dialogue; the anonymous messenger relays objections while More answers at length with authorities, anecdotes, and comic deflation of the reformers.

works.title: A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation
works.description: More's last and greatest English work, written in the Tower of London while awaiting execution, a dialogue in which an elderly Hungarian uncle instructs his nephew on bearing tribulation, especially the fear of death under persecution.
works.plot: Set in Hungary on the eve of a Turkish invasion, the dialogue moves from the general consolation of tribulation, through the temptations of fear, scruple, and despair, to the specific comfort of martyrdom, culminating in the uncle's meditation on the passion of Christ as the pattern of all suffering.
works.significance: The masterpiece of English devotional prose of its age, and one of the great prison writings in the language; its controlled serenity under sentence of death has made it the most widely read of More's English works.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in the Tower between More's arrest (April 1534) and execution (6 July 1535), after his refusal of the Oath of Succession; the manuscript was smuggled abroad and first printed in London by Richard Tottel in 1553, under Mary I.
works.characters: Anthony (the uncle); Vincent (the nephew)
works.structure: Three books of dialogue between the aged Anthony and his nephew Vincent, with inset parables and a famous treatment of the temptation to suicide; the fictional frame thinly veils More's own imprisonment.

editions.title: A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation (The Yale Edition of the Complete Works of St. Thomas More, vol. 12)
editions.editor: Louis L. Martz and Frank Manley

works.title: A Play of Love
works.description: John Heywood's debate interlude on the pains and pleasures of love, printed by William Rastell in 1534; the first English play devoted wholly to the analysis of courtship.
works.plot: A man loved but not loving pleads his case against a man loving but not loved, each claiming the sharper pain; their debate is referred to a woman neither loving nor loved, who judges between them; the argument moves through the paradoxes of desire to a reconciliation in which the four parties pair off, demonstrating that love's pleasures and pains are inseparable.
works.significance: The first sustained dramatic treatment of love in English and the purest example of the debate-interlude form; it links medieval love-casuistry to the Renaissance comedy of courtship.
works.meter: Couplets with stanzaic lyric interludes
works.context: Printed in 1534, the year of the Act of Supremacy; the play belongs to the courtly debate tradition of the early Tudor household, drawing on the amatory casuistry of the medieval demande d'amour and anticipating the love-debates of Elizabethan drama.
works.characters: Lover Not Loved; Loved Not Loving; Neither Lover Nor Loved; Both Lover and Loved
works.structure: A formal disputation in two parts, with the Vice 'Neither-lover-nor-loved' as referee and a concluding judgement that resolves the debate into mutual pairing.

works.title: A Summons to Prayer
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201 (eleventh century)
works.description: A short poem calling the faithful to prayer at the ringing of the church bell, celebrating the power of the Lord's Prayer to guard the soul and summoning all creation to join in worship.
works.plot: At the sound of the bell the poet summons the congregation to prayer: the Lord's Prayer is a shield against the devil, and prayer joins earth to heaven; the poem closes by calling on all beings to praise the Lord.
works.significance: A rare Old English poem tied to the actual practice of the daily office, and a small masterpiece of liturgical verse.
works.meter: Alliterative long line, brief and incantatory, suited to its liturgical occasion.
works.context: The poem belongs to the CCCC 201 group and reflects the Benedictine Reform's emphasis on the daily offices and the sanctification of time through prayer.
works.structure: A liturgical summons organized around the bell, the prayer, and the assembly of creation in praise.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: A Treatise of Moral Philosophy
altTitles: A Treatise of Morall Phylosophie, Contaynyng the Sayinges of the Wyse
works.description: William Baldwin's popular compilation of moral sayings and exemplary lives of philosophers, first published by Edward Whitchurch in 1547 and enlarged by Thomas Palfreyman; one of the most frequently reprinted English books of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
works.plot: The book arranges the sayings of the ancient philosophers under topical heads — of God, of wisdom, of justice, of friendship — and follows them with brief lives of the philosophers, ending each section with moral application for Christian readers.
works.significance: The most widely read English wisdom-book of the early modern period and a key channel by which classical moral philosophy reached vernacular readers; it established Baldwin's reputation before his editorship of A Mirror for Magistrates.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Compiled in the 1540s by Baldwin, then a corrector in Edward Whitchurch's printing house, during the flood of popular moral and sententious literature under Edward VI; Palfreyman's enlarged version (1555 onwards) carried it through dozens of editions to 1651.
works.structure: A compendium in four books: sayings of the philosophers, their lives, answers and apophthegms, and parables, with a running apparatus of moralization.

works.title: Aeditio
works.description: The elementary Latin grammar composed for St Paul's School, traditionally attributed to John Colet with the collaboration of William Lily and Erasmus; the English 'Accidence' later incorporated into the authorized Lily's Grammar.
works.plot: A short accidence of the eight parts of speech with English rules and Latin examples, designed for beginners at St Paul's, prefaced by Colet's school statutes and the 'Carmen de Moribus'.
works.significance: The germ of the national school grammar and a document of the Erasmian educational reform at its English source, St Paul's School.
works.meter: Prose with Latin verse
works.context: Composed c. 1509–18 for the school Colet founded in 1509 and refounded in 1512 with Mercers' Company endowment; the English Accidence printed as Aeditio in 1527 became the basis of the royal grammar of 1540.
works.structure: Pedagogical manual with rules and paradigms.
works.attributionNotes: The grammar is a collaborative production of the St Paul's circle; the traditional ascription to Colet as founder reflects the school's origin rather than sole authorship, and Erasmus revised the text.

works.title: Aeneid, Books II and IV (Surrey's translation)
works.description: Surrey's translation of Virgil's Aeneid, Books II and IV — the fall of Troy and the tragedy of Dido — in unrhymed iambic pentameter, the first English blank verse. Book IV was printed by John Day in 1554 and both books in Tottel's 1557 edition; the translation fixed the metre that Marlowe and Shakespeare made the language of English drama.
works.plot: Book II: Aeneas recounts Troy's last night — the horse, the burning, Priam's death, the loss of Creusa. Book IV: Dido's passion for Aeneas, their union in the cave, his departure, and her suicide on the pyre.
works.significance: The invention of blank verse, the metre of English tragedy and epic from Marlowe to Milton; alongside Douglas's Scots Eneados, the founding translation of Virgil into English.
works.meter: Blank verse — unrhymed iambic pentameter — used for the first time in English; the line Surrey invented from the Italian versi sciolti and Virgil's hexameter.
works.context: Translated in Surrey's last years, when he stood near the throne; the fall of Troy and the ruin of Dido's court read as parables of Henrician politics.
works.characters: Aeneas; Dido; Priam; Sinon; Anna; Mercury
works.structure: Two books of the epic, chosen for their pathos; the translation follows Virgil book by book without prologue apparatus.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Aeneid of Henry Howard Earl of Surrey

works.title: Aenigmata
works.description: Aldhelm's collection of one hundred Latin riddles in hexameters, enclosed as the final part of the Epistola ad Acircium (addressed to King Aldfrith of Northumbria). The first riddle collection of medieval England and the direct model for the vernacular Exeter Book riddles.
works.plot: Each riddle speaks in the first person, obliquely describing its subject — the elements, creatures, household objects, tools of learning — with the last line of each revealing or hinting the solution (water, the wind, the raven, the pen, the alembic, and so on).
works.significance: The model and quarry of the entire insular riddle tradition, Latin and vernacular.
works.meter: Dactylic hexameters, technically virtuosic.
works.context: Written c. 686-700 as part of the Epistola ad Acircium, a treatise on Latin metre for King Aldfrith; imitated by Tatwine, Eusebius, and Boniface, and translated into Old English in the Exeter Book tradition.
works.characters: the speaking objects of the riddles
works.structure: A numbered sequence of one hundred enigmas, framed by the prefatory acrostic poem on Aldhelm's own name.
works.attributionNotes: Aldhelm's authorship is certain.
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography

works.title: Aenigmata (Hwætberht's Riddles)
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Royal 12.C.xxiii (tenth century), with the riddles of Tatwine
works.description: Forty Latin riddles composed by Hwætberht (Eusebius), abbot of Wearmouth-Jarrow (c. 716-c. 747) and associate of Bede, in the tradition of Symphosius and Aldhelm. The riddles range over the natural world, the cosmos, and the tools of learning — the sun and moon, the winds, the sea, the alphabet, and the liberal arts.
works.plot: The riddles personify their subjects, from celestial bodies and elemental forces to letters and numbers, each speaking obliquely of its nature and powers; the collection moves from the macrocosm of heaven and earth to the microcosm of human learning.
works.significance: The Northumbrian counterpart to Aldhelm's and Tatwine's riddle cycles, completing the Anglo-Latin riddle corpus that inspired the vernacular riddles of the Exeter Book.
works.meter: Latin hexameters modelled closely on Aldhelm, with his alliteration and ornamental diction; the verse is learned and allusive, written for readers trained in the monastic school.
works.context: Composed at Wearmouth-Jarrow in the age of Bede, when the twin monastery was the richest centre of learning in western Europe; the riddles show Aldhelm's influence carried into Northumbria and the riddle form serving the encyclopedic ambitions of the Northumbrian Renaissance.
works.structure: Forty self-contained hexameter riddles in an encyclopedic sequence, deliberately continuing and answering the tradition of Aldhelm's century of riddles; the arrangement suggests a curriculum of knowledge from cosmology to grammar.
works.attributionNotes: Securely attributed to Hwætberht (Eusebius), abbot of Wearmouth-Jarrow, by manuscript tradition.

works.title: Aenigmata (Tatwine's Riddles)
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Royal 12.C.xxiii (tenth century), with the riddles of Hwætberht
works.description: Forty Latin riddles with a verse preface composed by Tatwine, monk of Breedon-on-the-Hill and archbishop of Canterbury (731-734). The riddles treat theological, philosophical, and grammatical subjects — faith, hope, charity, the five senses, the letters of the alphabet, the books of the Bible — in the manner of Symphosius and Aldhelm.
works.plot: Each riddle speaks in the first person about its own nature, requiring the reader to identify abstractions (the virtues, the liberal arts, grammatical categories) and objects (the pen, the sword, the book) from oblique descriptions built on learning rather than natural history.
works.significance: With Aldhelm's and Hwætberht's collections, Tatwine's riddles define the Anglo-Latin riddle tradition that stands behind the Exeter Book Riddles; they document the teaching of abstract theology through the schoolroom genre.
works.meter: Latin hexameters of schoolmasterly correctness, plainer than Aldhelm's hermeneutic verse; the riddles average six to eight lines and often begin with a paradoxical self-description.
works.context: Composed in the learned milieu of Breedon and Canterbury in the generation after Aldhelm, the riddles show the classroom union of grammar, theology, and verse composition that characterized early Anglo-Latin culture and fed the vernacular riddle tradition.
works.structure: A preface followed by forty self-contained riddles arranged in a deliberate sequence from theological virtues through philosophical abstractions to grammatical and physical subjects; the collection is the earliest complete Latin riddle cycle composed in England.
works.attributionNotes: Securely attributed to Tatwine by manuscript tradition and internal evidence; the riddles are contemporary with his Canterbury years or earlier.

works.title: Alcuin's Letters
works.description: The surviving correspondence of Alcuin of York — over 280 letters to kings, bishops, and friends, from Charlemagne and his court to the monks of Lindisfarne and the school of York: the richest epistolary record of the Carolingian Renaissance and of the network that carried Anglo-Saxon learning to the Continent.
works.plot: The letters range from affairs of state and church (the condemnation of adoptionism, the imperial coronation, the Danish raids) to friendship, consolation, and literary patronage; the most famous is the letter of 793 to the community of Lindisfarne after the Viking sack, interpreting the disaster as divine correction and urging repentance.
works.significance: The principal documentary source for the intellectual life of the Carolingian age and its English foundations.
works.meter: Latin prose, with verse epistles among the corpus.
works.context: Written 780-804 from York and the Frankish court; edited by E. Dümmler in MGH Epistolae IV (1895).
works.characters: Charlemagne; Arno of Salzburg; the monks of Lindisfarne; Æthelhard of Canterbury; Eanbald of York
works.structure: A chronologically arranged correspondence of over 280 items.
works.attributionNotes: Alcuin's authorship is certain.

works.title: Alfred's Domboc
works.form: law code in Old English prose
works.description: King Alfred's law book: an introduction translating the Ten Commandments and Mosaic law into English, followed by Alfred's own code and an appendix of Ine's laws. A founding document of the idea of English law as the law of a Christian people, consciously modelled on the Old Testament.
works.plot: The prologue renders Exodus 20-23 — the commandments, the laws of injury, slavery, and property — as the ancient foundation of law; Alfred's own clauses then regulate oaths, treachery against lords, sanctuary, the church, marriage, wounds, theft, and the ordeal, closing with the principle of compensation where no earlier provision exists.
works.significance: The classic statement of Anglo-Saxon kingship as Christian legislation; the foundation text of the later English common law tradition.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Issued in the later years of Alfred's reign, c. 893; preserved in Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 173 (with the Chronicle).
works.characters: Alfred (legislator); Moses (prologue)
works.structure: Tripartite: Mosaic introduction, Alfred's code, and the appended code of Ine.
works.attributionNotes: Alfred's authorship of the prologue and code is certain.

works.title: Alliterative Morte Arthure
works.description: The great alliterative tragedy of King Arthur: some 4,300 lines recounting Arthur's continental conquests, his war against the emperor Lucius, and his fall through Mordred's treason and his own pride, culminating in his dream of Fortune's wheel and his death. A poem of imperial ambition and Christian judgement, preserved in the Thornton manuscript, and a principal source of Malory's Morte Darthur.
