works.plot: Arthur, refusing tribute to Rome, leads his army across the Channel, defeats the giant of Mont St Michel, and conquers the emperor Lucius; at the height of his power the dream of Fortune's wheel warns him of the fall to come, and the news of Mordred's rebellion and Guinevere's adultery brings him home to the final battle, where Gawain dies and Arthur, mortally wounded, is buried at Glastonbury.
works.significance: The most powerful Arthurian poem of the alliterative tradition and the classic English statement of Arthur's tragedy; its influence on Malory and on the modern Arthurian revival (Tennyson read it in Malory's shadow) is profound.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line at its most heroic, with formulaic battle diction.
works.context: Composed c. 1400 in the north of England, blending chronicle history with romance matter and the tragedy of Fortune; preserved in the Thornton manuscript (Lincoln Cathedral MS 91, c. 1440) and used by Malory in his tale of Arthur and Lucius.
works.characters: Arthur; Gawain; Mordred; Guinevere; Lucius; the giant of Mont St Michel; Fortune
works.structure: A two-movement tragedy of rise and fall, with the dream of Fortune as its pivot and the battles as its set-pieces.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Alms-Giving
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A nine-line homiletic poem urging the giving of alms while one still lives, since after death no gift can avail the soul. It is the briefest complete poem in the Exeter Book.
works.plot: The poet exhorts his audience to clothe the naked and feed the hungry now, in life, because the opportunity ends at death, when the soul must face judgment with only what it has given away.
works.significance: A miniature of the Old English homiletic tradition in verse, showing the poets' capacity for lapidary moral statement.
works.meter: Nine alliterative long lines; compressed formulaic phrasing typical of the Exeter gnomic-homiletic manner.
works.context: Almsgiving was a central obligation of Anglo-Saxon Christianity, legislated in the law codes and urged in the homilies of Ælfric and Wulfstan; the poem distils that teaching into a single memorable exhortation.
works.structure: A single compact exhortation built on the antithesis between the living body's power to give and the corpse's helplessness.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Amis and Amiloun
works.description: A romance of sworn brotherhood and sacrifice, adapted from the widespread European legend of the two friends: Amis and Amiloun, identical in appearance, exchange places in trial by combat and marriage, and Amis slays his own children to cure his friend's leprosy — before a miraculous restoration rewards their loyalty. One of the most powerful of the Auchinleck romances.
works.plot: The sworn brothers part; Amiloun takes Amis's place in a judicial combat over a false accusation, and later, when Amiloun is struck with leprosy for the deception, Amis learns in a vision that his children's blood will cure him — and the sacrifice, made in secret, is rewarded by the children's resurrection.
works.significance: The classic English treatment of the friendship-and-sacrifice legend, and a favourite test case for the romance's religious and ethical codes.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets in the Auchinleck manner.
works.context: Composed c. 1300 from an Anglo-Norman source (Ami et Amile), in the East Midlands; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript (c. 1330) and three later copies.
works.characters: Amis; Amiloun; Belisaunt; the steward (villain); Amiloun's wife
works.structure: A double-plot of symmetrical substitution (combat; wedding-night; sacrifice), resolved by miracle and final reunion.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: An Answer unto Sir Thomas More's Dialogue
altTitles: An Answere unto Sir Thomas Mores Dialoge
works.description: Tyndale's reply to More's Dialogue Concerning Heresies, published in 1531; the central exchange of the great English print war between the two men.
works.plot: The book answers More point by point: Tyndale defends his translation of the New Testament against More's charges of corruption, argues that the church is the congregation of believers known by scripture, not the pope's institution, denies that he teaches rebellion, and attacks More's church of ceremonies with the full battery of scriptural citation, closing with a devastating personal address to 'Master More'.
works.significance: One half of the greatest controversy in early English prose: the Tyndale–More exchange fixed the rhetorical terms of the Reformation debate, and the Answer remains the fullest statement of Tyndale's ecclesiology and translation theory.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1531 as the direct reply to More's Dialogue Concerning Heresies (1529); More answered with the Confutation of Tyndale's Answer (1532–33), completing the most sustained intellectual duel of the English Reformation, conducted from exile and the chancellorship respectively.
works.structure: A point-by-point refutation following the order of More's Dialogue, in Tyndale's plain and urgent prose; the first major English controversy conducted wholly in print.

works.title: An Exhortation to Christian Living
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201 (eleventh century)
works.description: A homiletic poem of ninety-two lines urging its audience to keep God's commandments, resist the devil, and live in readiness for death and judgment. The poem is direct, urgent, and practical in its moral teaching.
works.plot: The poet exhorts the faithful to love God, keep his commands, avoid sin and the devil's snares, and remember the brevity of life and the certainty of judgment; wealth and pleasure are fleeting, but the soul's fate is eternal.
works.significance: A representative of the reform movement's verse catechesis, showing the homiletic mode of late Old English poetry at its most direct.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with the homiletic formulas of late Old English preaching; the verse is plain and expository rather than ornamental.
works.context: The poem belongs to the late Old English group of CCCC 201 (with Judgement Day II, A Summons to Prayer, and the Menologium), texts associated with the Benedictine Reform's devotional and catechetical programme.
works.structure: A sequence of direct exhortations in the second person, each grounded in the antithesis between this world's brevity and the soul's eternity, closing with the promise of heavenly reward.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Ancrene Wisse
works.form: rule and devotional treatise in prose
works.description: A rule of life for three anchoresses, written in the West Midlands 'AB language' c. 1225–40: eight parts treating the devotional routine, the custody of the senses, temptation, confession, penance, love, and the inner life. It is the greatest prose work of early Middle English, celebrated for its psychological acuity, its homely and exact imagery, and its humane severity.
works.plot: Addressing the anchoresses as a loving director, the author regulates their prayers and reading, anatomizes the temptations of the solitary life (with the famous allegory of the royal wooing of the soul), teaches the art of confession, and unfolds the degrees of love culminating in union with Christ.
works.significance: The masterpiece of early Middle English prose and the supreme English contribution to the literature of the solitary life; its influence reaches the Cloud-author and beyond.
works.meter: Rhythmical, alliterative prose of great art; concrete domestic metaphor (the anchorhold as house, the heart as its lady).
works.context: Written in Herefordshire or the Welsh Marches for three sisters enclosed near a church, in the milieu that produced the Katherine Group; revised and translated into French and Latin, and copied into the sixteenth century.
works.characters: the three anchoresses (addressees); Christ as lover-king (allegorical)
works.structure: Eight books moving from outer rule (devotions, senses) to inner rule (heart, conscience) and love; interlaced with exemplary tales and allegories.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; authorship_status reflects scholarly consensus (the author is sometimes speculatively identified with a Dominican or Augustinian director).

editions.title: Ancrene Wisse: A Corrected Edition of the Text in Cambridge, Corpus Christi College, MS 402

works.title: Andreas
works.form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 1,722 lines on the apocryphal Acts of Andrew and Matthias: the apostle Andrew, sailing incognito with Christ himself as his helmsman, voyages to the cannibal city of Mermedonia to rescue his fellow apostle Matthew. The poem recasts the apostle as a heroic seafarer in the manner of Beowulf, with some of the corpus's most vivid voyage imagery.
works.plot: Christ, disguised as a ship's captain, ferries the reluctant Andrew over the stormy sea, hearing his preaching on the way; in Mermedonia, Andrew is seized, tortured, and imprisoned, but a flood released from a stone pillar drowns his tormentors and revives them, converting the city; Andrew establishes a church and departs, leaving the poem's didactic epilogue.
works.significance: The fullest Old English saint's life in verse and a celebrated example of the heroic adaptation of hagiography.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre in the classical heroic manner.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 29v-52v); based on a Latin version of the apocryphal Acts, itself known in Old English prose from the Blickling manuscript.
works.characters: Andrew; Christ (the helmsman); Matthew; the Mermedonians
works.structure: A sea-voyage frame enclosing the martyrdom-and-conversion narrative, with speeches, miracles, and a flood scene modelled on Exodus; the poem borrows formulaic lines directly from Beowulf.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the Beowulf borrowings are stylistic, not evidence of authorship.

works.title: Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis
altTitles: The Satire of the Three Estates
works.description: Lindsay's great morality drama of the Scottish Reformation: King Humanitie, seduced by Sensualitie and the vices, is recalled to virtue by Divine Correction, and summons a parliament of the three estates — Spirituality, Temporalitie, Merchant — where John the Common-Weill indicts the church's abuses and the vices are tried and hanged. Played at Linlithgow in 1540 and enlarged at Cupar in 1552.
works.plot: Rex Humanitas falls under the rule of Wantonness, Placebo, and Solace; Divine Correction reforms him; the estates meet in parliament, hear John the Common-Weill's complaint, and pass the acts of reform, the play closing with the sermon of Folly.
works.significance: The greatest Scottish play and the dramatic summa of the northern Reformation; its parliament scene made drama an instrument of national reform and remained a living text into the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Scots couplets of great stage energy; songs, interludes, and the sermon of Folly closing the action.
works.context: First played before James V at Linlithgow in 1540; the enlarged Cupar performance (1552) addressed the eve of the Scottish Reformation, and the play remained in performance for a century.
works.characters: Rex Humanitas; Divine Correction; Sensualitie; Flatterie; Falset; Dissait; John the Common-Weill; Spirituality; Temporalitie; Merchant
works.structure: A two-part morality expanded to a national parliament: the king's moral fall and recovery (Part I) and the public trial and reformation of the estates (Part II).
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: Sir David Lindsay: Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis

works.title: Apollonius of Tyre
works.form: prose romance in Old English prose
works.description: The Old English prose translation of the Historia Apollonii regis Tyri — the story of the shipwrecked prince Apollonius, his lost wife and daughter, and their final reunion: the first prose romance in English and the ancestor of Shakespeare's Pericles and of the Apollonius tradition that runs through Gower and the Middle Ages.
works.plot: Apollonius of Tyre, having solved the riddle of the incestuous king Antiochus, flees by sea; shipwrecked at Pentapolis, he wins the king's daughter in marriage; at sea their daughter is born and the queen, apparently dead, is cast overboard in a sealed coffin; the daughter, raised at Mytilene, is sold to a brothel-keeper but preserves her honour by her wisdom; the story ends in the great recognition scene, when the family is reunited at Ephesus and Mytilene.
works.significance: The first English prose romance; the bridge between the classical romance tradition and the Middle English romances and Shakespeare's Pericles.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Translated c. 1000-1050 from the Latin Historia Apollonii (a late antique romance); the unique manuscript is Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201, which also contains Wulfstan's homilies.
works.characters: Apollonius; Antiochus; Arcestrates of Pentapolis; the queen; the daughter (Thasia); Athenagoras of Mytilene
works.structure: A continuous romance narrative of adventure, loss, and recognition, in the incest-riddle frame of the Latin source.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translator.

editions.title: The Old English Apollonius of Tyre

works.title: Athelston
works.description: A dark romance of kingship and treason, unique in the canon: the king Athelston, swayed by the traitor Wymond, puts his sworn brother and his family to the ordeal of fire, and is saved from tyranny only by the intervention of the archbishop and the test of the fire itself. Its grim political realism makes it unlike any other English romance.
works.plot: Four messengers become sworn brothers; Athelston becomes king, and the envious Wymond persuades him that Earl Egeland plots treason; Athelston's violence against the earl's pregnant wife and children is halted when the archbishop curses him and the ordeal of fire acquits the innocent, exposing Wymond and restoring the fellowship.
works.significance: The most politically serious of the English romances — a study of tyranny, sanctuary, and the ordeal — and a favourite text for the romance's engagement with law and kingship.
works.meter: Twelve-line tail-rhyme stanzas, often grimly emphatic.
works.context: Composed c. 1355–80 in the East Midlands, drawing on the legend of St Edmund and on baronial and ecclesiastical politics; preserved uniquely in Cambridge, Gonville and Caius College, MS 175.
works.characters: Athelston; Wymond; Egeland; Edyff; the archbishop
works.structure: A compact tragedy of misrule in three movements (oath, slander, ordeal), with the archbishop's excommunication as its pivot.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Azarias
altTitles: The Canticle of the Three Youths
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.form: religious narrative poem with embedded canticle
works.description: A poem on the ordeal of the three youths — Azarias, Ananias, and Misael — in Nebuchadnezzar's fiery furnace, based on Daniel 3 and on the canticle of praise they sing from the flames. The poem shares a substantial passage with the Junius manuscript poem Daniel.
works.plot: The three youths refuse to worship Nebuchadnezzar's golden image and are cast into the furnace; protected by the angel of God, they walk unharmed amid the flames and sing a canticle of praise in which all creation is summoned to bless the Lord, from the heavens and waters to the beasts and the sons of men.
works.significance: Together with Daniel it shows how Old English poets rendered the canticles of the liturgy in the native heroic idiom, turning scriptural praise into alliterative poetry.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the canticle's catalogues of creation are carried by parallel alliterative phrases in the liturgical style.
works.context: The story of the three youths was read typologically in Anglo-Saxon England: the furnace prefigured both the Incarnation (the fire that does not burn) and the Church's endurance under persecution. The poem is closely related to Daniel in the Junius manuscript.
works.characters: Azarias, Ananias, Misael, Nebuchadnezzar
works.structure: A bipartite structure: a brief narrative of the ordeal followed by the long canticle of praise, a liturgical catalogue of creation in the manner of the Benedicite.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The relationship with Daniel (shared lines) is a standing crux of Old English scholarship; the two poems may derive from a common source or one from the other.

works.title: Bald's Leechbook
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Royal 12.D.xvii (mid-tenth century, Winchester)
works.description: The most ambitious medical work in any early medieval vernacular: a systematic Old English leechbook in three books, compiled at Winchester in the mid-tenth century and named for Bald and Cild, the physicians named in its metrical colophon. It organizes hundreds of remedies for ailments from head to foot, drawing on Latin medical learning translated into English.
works.plot: Book I treats external ailments (head to toe), Book II internal diseases, and Book III a miscellany of surgical procedures, with remedies drawn from Greek, Latin, and native traditions; the work instructs the physician in diagnosis, pharmacy, bloodletting, and surgery, and includes charms as well as herbal and mineral preparations.
works.significance: The earliest substantial medical treatise in any western European vernacular, invaluable for the history of medicine and of Old English scientific prose, and a demonstration of the vernacular's capacity for technical writing.
works.context: Compiled in the Winchester milieu on the eve of the Benedictine Reform, the Leechbook shows the court's patronage of practical learning and the translation of Mediterranean medicine into English; it is the ancestor of the Middle English medical manuscript tradition.
works.structure: A systematic reference work organized by ailment and body-part (a capite ad calcem), with numbered remedies under each heading; the third book is looser, mixing surgery, obstetrics, and charms.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous compilation; the colophon names Bald as owner and Cild as writer, not as authors of the medical content.

editions.title: Leechdoms, Wortcunning, and Starcraft of Early England

works.title: Bede's Death Song
works.manuscriptDate: St Gallen, Stiftsbibliothek 254 (ninth century or earlier); Northumbrian version in Cambridge, University Library Kk.5.16 (the Moore Bede, c. 737)
works.description: A five-line alliterative poem, the last words of the dying Bede, recorded in the Epistola Cuthberti de obitu Bedae. The poet meditates on the soul's necessary journey out of the body and the judgment each man must face for his deeds. It is the earliest datable Old English poem.
works.plot: Bede, near death, reflects that no man's wisdom can outrun his need to consider, before departing, what judgment his soul will receive for the good and evil he has done.
works.significance: The earliest datable poem in English, and a uniquely documented case of vernacular verse preserved with its author, date, and occasion of composition.
works.meter: Five lines of classic alliterative verse in the Northumbrian dialect, preserved with Latin paraphrase; the earliest securely datable example of English poetry.
works.context: Recorded by Bede's pupil Cuthbert in the letter describing the master's death on 26 May 735; the poem circulated in two dialect versions and in many manuscripts of the Historia ecclesiastica, often with a Latin translation.
works.characters: Bede (speaker)
works.structure: Five alliterative long lines in two movements: the inevitability of the soul's departure, and the reckoning of deeds before the judge.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Bede in the Epistola Cuthberti, composed, according to the letter, on his deathbed; the attribution is accepted by modern scholarship, though the poem circulated anonymously in some manuscripts.

works.title: Beowulf
works.description: The greatest surviving poem in Old English: a heroic epic of 3,182 alliterative lines recounting the deeds of the Geatish hero Beowulf against the monster Grendel, Grendel's mother, and, fifty years later, a dragon. It combines the legendary history of Scandinavia with a profound Christian meditation on heroism, mortality, and the limits of earthly glory.
works.plot: The young hero Beowulf sails from Geatland to Denmark to rid King Hrothgar's hall Heorot of the man-eating monster Grendel, whom he defeats in a night combat; he then tracks Grendel's mother to her underwater lair and slays her. Rewarded and honoured, he returns home and eventually rules the Geats for fifty years, until a dragon, enraged by the theft of a cup from its hoard, ravages his kingdom; the aged king kills the dragon but dies of his wounds, and the poem ends with his funeral pyre and the foreboding of his people's doom.
works.significance: The foundational epic of English literature; the first extended poetic masterpiece in any Germanic vernacular; a touchstone for subsequent English poetry (Tolkien, Auden, Heaney) and for the study of Germanic legend.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre: four stresses per line divided by a caesura; formulaic diction, kennings, and variation throughout.
works.context: Composed somewhere between the age of Bede and the eve of the Conquest, and copied c. 1000 in the Nowell Codex (British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv); its heroes belong to sixth-century Scandinavia (Hygelac's raid on Frisia, c. 521, is historical), while its audience was Christian Anglo-Saxon England.
works.characters: Beowulf, Hrothgar, Grendel, Grendel's mother, the dragon, Wiglaf, Hygelac, Unferth, Wealhtheow, Scyld Scefing
works.structure: A bipartite structure (youthful Danish adventures; old age and the dragon) framed by the funerals of Scyld Scefing and Beowulf; interlaced with digressions — the Finnsburh episode, the Sigmund lay, the Swedish-Geatish wars, and the 'Lay of the Last Survivor' — that mirror and darken the main action.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; authorship_status reflects scholarly consensus. Ascribed to no known poet.

editions.title: Klaeber's Beowulf and The Fight at Finnsburg
editions.editor: R. D. Fulk, Robert E. Bjork, and John D. Niles (eds.)

sources: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume A: The Middle Ages

works.title: Bevis of Hampton
works.description: One of the most popular of all Middle English romances: the adventures of Bevis of Southampton, sold into heathen lands by his mother's treachery, who wins the Saracen princess Josian, fights dragons and giants, and at last reclaims his English inheritance. Its vigorous, episodic narrative survived in verse, prose, and print into the seventeenth century.
works.plot: Bevis's mother plots his father's murder and marries the murderer; the boy is sold overseas, but wins fame and the love of Josian; after adventures in Armenia, Cologne, and England — including his defeat of the dragon of Cologne and his final siege of Southampton — he regains his lands and ends his days as a monk with Josian.
works.significance: The archetypal popular romance: its immense circulation (Chaucer's Sir Thopas parodies its tail-rhyme form) makes it central to the history of English popular reading.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets, later rewritten in tail-rhyme in some manuscripts.
works.context: Composed c. 1300 from an Anglo-Norman original (Boeve de Haumtoun); preserved in six manuscripts, the Auchinleck (c. 1330) foremost, and repeatedly printed from c. 1500 to the seventeenth century.
works.characters: Bevis; Josian; Ascopard the giant; Saber; the dragon of Cologne; King Ermin
works.structure: A sprawling episodic quest in the Auchinleck manner, with exile, conversion, combat, and restoration as its repeating units.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Beware the Cat
altTitles: Beware the Cat: The First English Novel
works.description: William Baldwin's anti-Catholic prose satire of 1552–53, in which a company of men swap stories proving that cats can speak and understand; printed posthumously in 1561 and often claimed as the first English novel.
works.plot: The narrator, Master Streamer, overhears a conversation among the household of John Young while lodged at the printing house; the talk turns to cats, and Gregory Streamer relates how, having eaten a cat, he gained the power to understand animal speech, recounting the trial of Mouse-slayer before the cat parliament and the bawdy doings of cats and priests — a satire on Catholic superstition, oral tradition, and the credulity of tale-collectors.
works.significance: Claimed as the first English novel for its sustained prose fiction and self-conscious narrative framing; it is also a sophisticated satire on storytelling, tradition, and the authority of print, anticipating the narrative experiments of the Elizabethan period.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in 1552–53 at the press of John Day, where Baldwin worked; its satire of Catholic ritual (the cat's mass) fitted the Edwardian Reformation moment, and by its printing in 1561 (with a prefatory epistle to John Young) the political climate had changed again.
works.characters: Master Streamer (narrator); Gregory Streamer; Mouse-slayer; Grimalkin; John Young (the printer)
works.structure: A framed narrative in three orations, with inset stories (the cat's life of Grimalkin, the trial of Mouse-slayer) and a self-conscious apparatus of marginal glosses and running commentary on the reliability of oral report.
works.attributionNotes: Printed anonymously in 1561 with initials 'G. B.'; the attribution to William Baldwin rests on the prefatory matter and the internal evidence of the printing-house setting, and is accepted by modern scholarship.

editions.title: Beware the Cat: The First English Novel
editions.editor: William A. Ringler, Jr., and Michael Flachmann

works.title: Blickling Homilies
works.description: A collection of eighteen anonymous Old English homilies for the church year, preserved in the Princeton Blickling manuscript: the earliest substantial vernacular sermon collection, contemporary with the first series of Ælfric's Catholic Homilies but plainer and more popular in style. Contains the famous vision of hell and of the places of the souls ('the three utterances of the soul').
works.plot: The homilies treat the major feasts — Annunciation, Palm Sunday, Easter (with the harrowing of hell), Rogationtide, Ascension, Pentecost, the Assumption, and the feasts of the apostles — expounding the gospel readings with vivid narrative expansions: the descent into hell, the soul's journey after death, and the architecture of the otherworld.
works.significance: The principal witness to the pre-Ælfrician homiletic tradition and to vernacular eschatological imagery.
works.meter: Old English prose; occasional rhythmical passages.
works.context: Copied c. 971, probably in Mercia or East Anglia; the manuscript (Princeton, Scheide Library, MS 71) is closely contemporary with the Beowulf manuscript's milieu.
works.characters: the evangelists' figures (Christ, the apostles, Mary, the blessed and the damned)
works.structure: Eighteen independent homilies in calendar order, each built on a gospel pericope with exegetical and exemplary digressions.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Boece
works.description: Chaucer's prose translation of Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, the work that above all others shaped his thought: the dialogue between the imprisoned Boethius and Lady Philosophy on fortune, free will, providence, and the sovereign good. Made c. 1380–86 with the aid of the commentary tradition, it is the foundation of the Boethian strain that runs through all his poetry.
works.plot: Boethius, imprisoned and awaiting death, laments his fall until Lady Philosophy appears and, through a graduated argument in prose and verse (the metres), cures him: showing that fortune is mutable by nature, that true happiness lies in God, that evil men are punished by their own wickedness, and that providence and free will are compatible.
works.significance: The most consequential translation Chaucer made: through it, the Consolation became English literature's native philosophical idiom, from Chaucer to Elizabeth I's translation and beyond.
works.meter: Prose translation of the whole, metres included, dense with the philosophical vocabulary Chaucer coined or naturalized.
works.context: Composed c. 1380–86, drawing on the Latin text and the commentary of Nicholas Trevet; its influence pervades Chaucer's mature poems (Troilus, the Knight's Tale, the ballades) and the whole English Boethian tradition.
works.characters: Boethius; Lady Philosophy
works.structure: Five books of alternating prose and metrical sections, in the Menippean form of the original; Chaucer renders the metres in prose, with explanatory glosses from the commentaries.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure (named in the Retraction).

works.title: Boniface's Letters
works.description: The correspondence of the missionary Boniface and his circle — some 150 letters exchanged with popes, kings, and above all the English friends and pupils who sustained his mission (Eadburga, Bugga, Leoba, Lull, Egbert of York): the most vivid documentary record of the Anglo-Saxon missions to the Continent.
works.plot: The letters carry the whole business of the German mission: requests for books and prayers, reports of synods and conversions, the felling of the sacred oak at Geismar, appeals for English nuns and scholars, consolations, and the last letters before the martyrdom at Dokkum (754); several are verse epistles with riddles for the nuns of Wessex.
works.significance: The richest source for the Anglo-Saxon missionary movement and for the literary culture of its female religious correspondents.
works.meter: Latin prose with verse epistles.
works.context: Written 716-754 from the mission field in Frisia and Germany; edited by M. Tangl, MGH Epistolae Selectae I (1916).
works.characters: Boniface; Lull; Leoba; Eadburga of Minster-in-Thanet; Bugga; Egbert of York; Daniel of Winchester; Pope Gregory II and III
works.structure: A correspondence of c. 150 letters, including letters addressed to Boniface.
works.attributionNotes: The core letters are Boniface's own; the collection includes his correspondents.

works.title: Calisto and Melebea
altTitles: A New Comedy in English in Manner of an Interlude
works.description: An anonymous English adaptation of the first four acts of Fernando de Rojas's Celestina, printed by John Rastell c. 1525–30; the first English version of the Spanish classic.
works.plot: Calisto, rejected by Melibea, seeks the help of the old bawd Celestina, who wins the lady for him by her arts; the fragment (the play survives incomplete) follows the first movement of Rojas's tragicomedy through the lovers' meeting, ending before the deaths that close the original.
works.significance: The first English adaptation of the Celestina and an early witness to Anglo-Spanish literary exchange; it extends the range of the interlude to tragicomic romance and anticipates the Elizabethan stage's use of continental fiction.
works.meter: Couplets with stanzaic songs
works.context: Printed c. 1525–30, probably by John Rastell, whose press had connections to the Spanish trade through the More circle (More's daughter married into the Rastell family, and Vives was in England); the Celestina, the great Spanish masterpiece of 1499, was thus introduced to English readers a generation before Mabbe's full translation.
works.characters: Calisto; Melibea; Celestina; Sempronio; Parmeno
works.structure: A scene-by-scene dramatization of the opening of the Celestina, compressed into interlude form, with the bawd's character preserved in translation.
works.attributionNotes: No author is named; the play has been attributed to John Rastell on the evidence of the press and the More circle's Spanish connections, but the attribution is conjectural.

works.title: Catholic Homilies
altTitles: Ælfric's Catholic Homilies, First and Second Series
works.description: Ælfric's two series of forty sermons for the church year (c. 989-995), the masterpiece of Old English prose: orthodox, elegantly plain expositions of the gospel readings, written in the rhythmical alliterative style and prefaced by a Latin preface deploring the doctrinal errors of the anonymous homiletic tradition. The most widely copied vernacular preaching text of the Anglo-Saxon period.
works.plot: Each homily expounds the pericope of the day with patristic learning made lucid for the laity — the feasts of Christ and the saints, the parables, the miracles — carefully distinguishing orthodox doctrine from apocryphal excess; the two series together provide a complete homiletic cycle for the year in the order of the liturgical calendar.
works.significance: The summit of the Old English homiletic tradition and the foundation of standard literary Old English.
works.meter: Rhythmical, alliterative prose of Ælfric's mature 'plain style'.
works.context: Composed at Cerne Abbas c. 989-995 at the request of the ealdorman Æthelweard and his son Æthelmær; over thirty manuscripts and fragments survive.
works.characters: Christ; the saints of the calendar
works.structure: Two series of forty homilies each, organized by the church year; each homily opens with the gospel text in English and proceeds by exegesis, exemplum, and exhortation.
works.attributionNotes: Ælfric's authorship is certain.
themes: Reformation faith and the authority of scripture

editions.title: Ælfric's Catholic Homilies: The First Series (EETS SS 17)

works.title: Cely Letters
works.description: The business correspondence of the Cely family, London wool merchants of the Staple of Calais, 1472–88: some 250 letters and papers recording the wool trade, shipping, politics, and daily life of a merchant family in the age of Edward IV and Richard III. The most vivid surviving record of English commercial life in the fifteenth century.
works.plot: The letters pass between the brothers Robert, Richard, and George Cely in London and Calais and their factors, recording the buying and shipping of wool, prices and freights, news of the wars in France and at home (including the fall of Richard III), and the family's hunting, hawking, and domestic affairs.
works.significance: The classic document of fifteenth-century English commerce and the merchant's English, complementing the Paston archive's gentry perspective.
works.meter: Prose: brisk, practical mercantile English, of great linguistic value.
works.context: Written 1472–88, when the Celys' Calais staple stood at the centre of England's wool economy; discovered in 1860 among the family's papers and edited by H. E. Malden (1900).
works.characters: George Cely; Richard Cely the elder and younger; William Maryon; the Calais factors
works.structure: A documentary archive of business correspondence, chronological in arrangement, spanning sixteen years.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative (family and factors); authorship_status reflects the archive's collective character.

works.title: Chaucer's Short Poems
altTitles: The Minor Poems of Geoffrey Chaucer
works.description: The corpus of Chaucer's shorter poems: the philosophical ballades (Fortune, Truth, Gentilesse, Lak of Stedfastnesse), the complaints (Anelida and Arcite, the Complaint of Mars, the Complaint unto Pity, A Complaint to his Lady), the envoy to Scogan, the ABC to the Virgin, and the love lyrics. Together they show the courtly poet at work across every register, from the rueful 'Flee fro the prees' to the burlesque of Sir Thopas's kin.
works.plot: The poems range from the lover's complaints of Mars and Anelida (with its paired verse of great formal ambition) through the moral ballades on truth and steadfastness — 'Flee fro the prees, and dwelle with sothfastnesse' — to the devotional ABC and the comic self-portraits of the envoys.
works.significance: The ballade of Truth and its kin made Chaucer the English master of the short moral poem; the corpus preserves the courtly occasions and formal experiments of his art.
works.meter: Ballades, roundels, rhyme royal, and experimental stanzas; the ABC is an alphabetical acrostic in translation from Deguileville.
works.context: Composed across Chaucer's career (c. 1370–1400), many for courtly occasions and patrons (John of Gaunt, the king's circle); preserved in the manuscript anthologies of the fifteenth century and collected by Thynne (1532).
works.characters: the speakers of the complaints and ballades; Mars; Venus; Anelida; Arcite
works.structure: A corpus of independent lyrics and complaints, several (Anelida and Arcite, the Complaint of Mars) with substantial narrative frames.
works.attributionNotes: The core canon is secure; a few attributions remain debated.

works.title: Chester Mystery Plays
works.description: The Chester cycle of twenty-four plays, from the fall of Lucifer to the Last Judgement, performed at Whitsun by the guilds of Chester from the early fifteenth century (with later tradition dating its origin to the fourteenth) until 1575, the last of the great cycles to be suppressed. Its eight-line stanza, its Expositor figure, and its homiletic restraint give it a distinctive ceremonial gravity.
works.plot: The cycle dramatizes salvation history in twenty-four pageants — the Creation and fall, Noah's flood (with the famous drinking-song of Noah's wife), Abraham and Isaac, the Prophets, the Nativity, the ministry, the Passion, the Harrowing of Hell, and the Last Judgement — with the Expositor commenting on the action's prophetic meaning.
works.significance: The last surviving performance tradition of the English cycles (revived at Chester from 1951), and a classic of English civic theatre.
works.meter: The characteristic Chester stanza (aaabcccb, with internal rhyme) and the Expositor's couplets.
works.context: Performed at Whitsun in Chester from at least the early fifteenth century (a fourteenth-century origin is traditional), revised in the early sixteenth century, and performed until 1575; preserved in five manuscripts and printed in 1607.
works.characters: God; Lucifer; Adam and Eve; Noah and his wife; Abraham and Isaac; the Virgin Mary; Christ; Antichrist; the Expositor
works.structure: Twenty-four pageants on the Corpus Christi model, with the Expositor's speeches linking the Old Testament type to its New Testament fulfilment.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative; the tradition attributing the cycle's origin to the monk Ranulph Higden is legendary.

editions.title: The Chester Mystery Cycle
editions.editor: R. M. Lumiansky and David Mills (eds.)

works.title: Christ and Satan
works.form: religious narrative poetry in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 729 lines in three parts, closing the Junius manuscript: the lament of the fallen angels in hell, the harrowing of hell and the Resurrection, and the temptation of Christ in the wilderness. Its long speeches of Satan and the fallen host are the most extended 'infernal' passages in Old English.
works.plot: Part I: Satan and his angels bewail their fall and their exile from the light of heaven, in a series of remorseful laments. Part II: the harrowing of hell — Christ's descent to liberate the patriarchs — is narrated together with the Resurrection and Ascension. Part III: the devil tempts the fasting Christ in the desert, and is answered and routed; the poem ends with the Last Judgment.
works.significance: The fullest English treatment of the fallen angels before Milton; its harrowing-of-hell narrative is the classic vernacular statement of the theme.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the style varies sharply between sections, suggesting composite authorship.
works.context: Preserved in the Junius manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11, pp. 213-229); the three parts may be independent poems of different dates gathered by the compiler.
works.characters: Satan; the fallen angels; Christ; the devils of the temptation; Eve (in retrospect)
works.structure: Three loosely joined narrative sections on a cosmic theme — fall, redemption, and the final victory — unified by the figure of Satan's defeat.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; possibly composite.

works.title: Christ I (The Advent Lyrics)
works.description: The first part of the Exeter Book 'Christ' trilogy: twelve Advent lyrics (439 lines) elaborating the 'O' antiphons of the Christmas liturgy, hailing Christ under his liturgical titles — key of David, cornerstone, dayspring, Emmanuel. The eleventh lyric's 'Eala Earendel' inspired Tolkien's mythology of Eärendil.
works.plot: The lyrics, addressed to Christ or spoken in his voice, celebrate the mystery of the Incarnation: the closed door of the Virgin, the cornerstone rejected by builders, the light rising in darkness, the bridegroom come to Zion. Each lyric meditates on a title or antiphonal image and prays for the coming of the Lord.
works.significance: The great Advent poetry of the period; source of the 'Earendel' passage that founded Tolkien's legendarium.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; lyric intensity rather than narrative continuity.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book as the opening of the composite poem 'Christ' (fols. 8a-14a); the antiphons are those sung at vespers in the week before Christmas.
works.characters: Christ; Mary; the faithful of Zion
works.structure: A lyric sequence of twelve meditations on the antiphons, framed by the liturgical season of Advent.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; once attributed to Cynewulf with the rest of the trilogy, but the Advent lyrics are now regarded as separate and unsigned.

works.title: Christ II (The Ascension)
works.description: The middle section of the Exeter Book 'Christ' (427 lines), signed by Cynewulf: a meditation on the Ascension based on Gregory the Great's homily, celebrating Christ's 'leaps' — from heaven to earth, into the womb, onto the cross, into the tomb and hell, and back to the throne of glory.
works.plot: The poet meditates on the Ascension as the climax of Christ's career of 'leaps' (from the Song of Songs image of the beloved leaping upon the mountains), recounts the apostles' grief and the angel's promise of return, interprets the 'gifts of men' of Psalm 67 (the talents of wisdom and craft distributed to mankind), and closes with a vision of the Last Judgment and Cynewulf's runic signature and prayer.
works.significance: The classic Old English treatment of the Ascension; its gifts-of-men passage inspired The Gifts of Men and Fortunes of Men.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the signature passage is elaborately wrought.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 14a-20b) between the Advent lyrics and Christ III; based on Gregory the Great's Homily 29 on the Gospels.
works.characters: Christ; the apostles; the angel
works.structure: A homiletic meditation in verse: Gregory's leaps, the ascension narrative, the catalogue of gifts, eschatological conclusion, and runic signature.
works.attributionNotes: Signed by Cynewulf in runes.

works.title: Christ III (The Judgment)
works.form: religious narrative (eschatological vision) in alliterative verse
works.description: The final section of the Exeter Book 'Christ' (798 lines): the grandest poetic vision of the Last Judgment in Old English, in which Christ appears on the cross at doomsday, the elements dissolve, the sinners and the blessed speak their laments and thanks, and the poem closes on the joys of heaven.
works.plot: The poem opens with the sudden coming of the Judge, the blast of trumpets, and the conflagration of the world — the sea, the stars, the mountains consumed; Christ, still bearing the wounds and the cross, separates the blessed and the damned, who speak in antiphonal choruses (the damned reproaching their sins, the blessed thanking Christ for the 'thirst on the cross'); the poem ends with the blessed entering the heavenly city.
works.significance: The summit of Old English eschatological poetry; a major source for later medieval judgment literature.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of sustained grandeur; celebrated descriptions of the dissolving cosmos.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 20b-32a); the judgment scenes draw on patristic and homiletic eschatology.
works.characters: Christ the Judge; the blessed; the damned
works.structure: A visionary sequence: theophany, cosmic dissolution, the dialogue of blessed and damned, and the entry into heaven; the speeches are organized in paired laments and thanksgivings.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; formerly assigned to Cynewulf with the rest of the trilogy.

works.title: Chronica Majora
works.description: Matthew Paris's universal and English chronicle, revised and expanded from Roger of Wendover's Flores Historiarum and continued by Matthew with his own annals down to 1259; the greatest historical work of thirteenth-century England, illustrated with Matthew's own marginal drawings.
works.summary: Beginning with the creation, the Chronica Majora concentrates on English and European affairs from the Norman Conquest onward, becoming a detailed contemporary record for the reign of Henry III: the conflicts with the barons, the campaigns in Wales and Gascony, the affairs of the friars and the universities, and the author's outspoken criticisms of king and pope.
works.significance: The fullest and most vivid narrative source for thirteenth-century England, and a landmark of English book production through its author's maps and marginal illustrations.

works.title: Chronicon
works.form: history and chronicle in Latin prose
works.description: The Latin chronicle of Ealdorman Æthelweard, descendant of King Æthelred I and patron of Ælfric: a translation and adaptation of a lost version of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle down to 973, dedicated to his kinswoman Matilda, abbess of Essen. Its prologue contains the celebrated eulogy of King Alfred.
works.plot: The chronicle retells the annals from the creation and the Saxon settlement through the West Saxon and English kings to Edgar's death (975), in four books of deliberately archaic, 'hermeneutic' Latin studded with Grecisms; the prologue to Matilda praises Alfred — 'the unshakeable pillar of the western people' — and explains the work's purpose.
works.significance: A major witness to the text of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and to lay Latin culture among the late Anglo-Saxon aristocracy.
works.meter: Dense hermeneutic Latin prose.
works.context: Composed c. 978-988 by the ealdorman Æthelweard, 'the historian' of the Æthelweard-Ælfric circle; the unique manuscript (Cotton MS Otho A.x) was destroyed in the Cotton fire of 1731, and the text rests on Savile's 1596 edition.
works.characters: Matilda of Essen (addressee); Alfred; the West Saxon kings
works.structure: Four books of annals in translation, with a dedicatory prologue.
works.attributionNotes: Æthelweard's authorship is stated in the prologue.

works.title: Cleanness
works.description: The Gawain-poet's homiletic poem of 1,812 alliterative lines on purity ('clannesse'): expanding the gospel parable of the wedding feast, it retells the Flood, the destruction of Sodom, and Belshazzar's feast as three great exemplary narratives of God's vengeance on filth and pride, culminating in the writing on the wall. The most rhetorically powerful of the Cotton Nero poems.
works.plot: From the parable of the guest without a wedding garment, the poet unfolds the doctrine of the clean heart; Noah's Flood shows God's cleansing of the world's filth; the destruction of Sodom his vengeance on unnatural lust; and Belshazzar's feast — with its vessels stolen from the Temple, its drunken blasphemy, and the mysterious hand writing Mene, Tekel, Peres — his judgement on sacrilege and pride.
works.significance: The most powerful homiletic poem of the alliterative revival; its Belshazzar episode is among the greatest descriptive set-pieces in Middle English poetry.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line at its most sumptuous, with elaborate descriptive passages (the Flood, the feast, the Temple vessels).
works.context: Composed c. 1375–1400 by the Gawain-poet; preserved uniquely in Cotton Nero A.x. The poem's courtly castigation of 'fylþe of þe flesch' speaks to the Ricardian culture of courtly and clerical reform.
works.characters: Noah; Abraham; Lot; Belshazzar; Daniel; the Queen; God
works.structure: A homiletic frame (the beatitude 'blessed are the clean of heart' and the wedding parable) enclosing three parallel biblical exempla of increasing elaboration, each a set-piece of alliterative description.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; assigned to the Gawain-poet on grounds of style and shared manuscript.

works.title: Colin Clout
works.description: Skelton's longest satire: the plain countryman Colin Clout — a persona borrowed from the shepherd-poets, which Spenser later took up — reports what the commons say of the clergy: their pomp, their ignorance, their neglect of preaching, and the corruption of the bishops, all in the voice of 'the people's' plain truth.
works.plot: Colin sets out to speak 'of the spiritual estate'; the poem catalogues the clergy's abuses through the reported speech of the commons, answers the expected objections of the bishops, and ends with an appeal to the lay powers for reform.
works.significance: The great English anticlerical satire of its age and the direct ancestor of Spenser's Colin Clout; its plain-man persona became a convention of English satire.
works.meter: Sustained Skeltonics over 1,200 lines; the metre's repetitiveness enacts the commons' insistent complaint.
works.context: Written as the Reformation crisis gathered, about 1522; the poem voices the anticlericalism of the laity without committing itself to the Lutheran programme.
works.characters: Colin Clout; the clergy (collectively)
works.structure: A long single-voiced complaint organized as report ('the commons say...') with interposed answers to clerical objections; the plain man's persona licenses the satire.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Colloquia (Ælfric Bata)
works.manuscriptDate: Oxford, St John's College MS 154 (eleventh century), alongside Ælfric's Colloquy
works.description: A pair of Latin conversation manuals by Ælfric Bata, a pupil of Ælfric of Eynsham: the Colloquia and the harder Colloquia difficiliora. Modelled on Ælfric's Colloquy, they dramatize the daily life of the monastic school with boisterous, hyperbolic dialogues about food, drink, beatings, theft, and the relations of master and pupil.
works.plot: The dialogues stage conversations among schoolboys and between pupils and master: bargaining for food, complaining of hunger, confessing petty theft, enduring (and threatening) beatings, and practising the vocabulary of daily life in the monastery — shoes, clothes, bedding, the refectory, the infirmary, and the latrine.
works.significance: The most vivid surviving picture of eleventh-century English school life, and evidence of the living tradition of spoken Latin that the Benedictine Reform established in English monasteries.
works.context: Composed in the generation after Ælfric's Colloquy (c. 998), the dialogues show the continuity of the reform's vernacular-Latin classroom tradition into the eleventh century, and their earthy realism is a deliberate antidote to the classicizing curriculum.
works.characters: Ælfric Bata (speaker), his pupils, stock schoolboys and masters
works.structure: A loose sequence of dramatic dialogues without sustained plot, each built to drill vocabulary through exchange; the speakers are stock schoolboys and masters, and the humour is deliberately exaggerated.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ælfric Bata, who names himself in the texts and addresses Ælfric of Eynsham as his master; the attribution is conventional and generally accepted, though the texts are transmitted anonymously in their manuscript.

works.title: Colloquy
works.form: grammar and didactic prose (dialogue) in Latin with Old English gloss
works.description: A school dialogue between a master and his pupils who impersonate the trades — ploughman, shepherd, oxherd, hunter, fisherman, merchant, shoemaker, smith, cook — composed by Ælfric for the teaching of Latin conversation, with an Old English interlinear gloss added later by a teacher (Ælfric Bata). The liveliest classroom text of the Anglo-Saxon period.
works.plot: The master questions each boy about his craft: the ploughman feeds the oxen, the hunter takes deer and boar for the king, the fisherman risks the sea for his catch, the merchant crosses the sea to sell and buy; each defends the dignity of his work, and the dialogue ends with the master's advice on industry and good counsel.
works.significance: The most vivid picture of Anglo-Saxon daily life and trades in the period's literature.
works.meter: Latin prose with interlinear Old English gloss.
works.context: Composed c. 998-1005 at Cerne Abbas or Eynsham; the unique manuscript is British Library, Cotton MS Tiberius A.iii (mid-eleventh century).
works.characters: the Master; the pupils (ploughman, shepherd, hunter, fisherman, fowler, merchant, shoemaker, salter, baker, cook, and others)
works.structure: A question-and-answer dialogue of some 75 exchanges, each trade a set piece.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ælfric on stylistic grounds; the Old English gloss is by another hand (Ælfric Bata).
themes: The English vernacular and national letters

works.title: Confessio Amantis
works.description: John Gower's English masterpiece: a collection of some 140 exemplary tales, mostly from Ovid, framed by the confession of the aging lover Amans to Genius, priest of Venus, who anatomizes the seven deadly sins as they corrupt love. Over 33,000 lines of octosyllabic couplets, with a Latin apparatus, it is the most substantial English poem of the century after the Canterbury Tales.
works.plot: Amans, sick with unrequited love, prays to Venus and Cupid, who assign him Genius as confessor; book by book, Genius examines him on the sins of love, illustrating each with exemplary narratives — Florent and the loathly lady, Constance, Apollonius of Tyre, the tale of the Three Questions, and the story of Nebuchadnezzar's dream that closes the poem with a mirror for kings — until Venus cures him, shows him his aged face, and dismisses him 'John Gower' from love's service.
works.significance: The classic English poem of the seven sins and the great 'mirror' collection of the Ricardian age; its tales (Apollonius, Florent) entered Shakespeare and the English narrative tradition.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets of great smoothness — the 'middle style' Gower made his own.
works.context: Composed c. 1386–90 at the request of Richard II (first recension) and revised for Henry of Lancaster (c. 1392–93), in the period of the Peasants' Revolt and the king's fall; preserved in some fifty manuscripts and printed by Caxton (1483).
works.characters: Amans (John Gower); Genius; Venus; Cupid; the exemplary figures of the tales
works.structure: An eight-book confessional frame (prologue, seven sins, epilogue) enclosing the exemplary tales, with the lover's cure as the poem's comic-pathetic resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Gower's authorship secure; the poem's Latin verses name him throughout.

editions.title: The English Works of John Gower

works.title: Croxton Play of the Sacrament
works.description: An East Anglian miracle play of c. 1461 on the host: the Jewish merchant Jonathas and his fellows buy the consecrated wafer from the Christian merchant Aristorius, subject it to their tests — and when they stab it, it bleeds, and the image of Christ appears, converting them all. Its staging directions (the cauldron, the severed hand, the miraculous oven) make it the most spectacular of the English miracle plays.
works.plot: Aristorius, tempted by gold, sells the host to Jonathas, who with his companions proves it in their own body of tests: boiling, oven, and dagger; the host bleeds, sticks to Jonathas's hand, and the image of Christ as a child reproves them; their conversion follows, the church is reconciled, and the play ends with the doctor's epilogue and the procession.
works.significance: The fullest English miracle play and the most spectacular document of the late medieval eucharistic cult; its staging is central to the history of English theatre.
works.meter: Couplets and stanza forms, with stage directions prescribing spectacular effects.
works.context: Composed c. 1461 at Croxton, Norfolk (the banns name the village), when the cult of the host and the Corpus Christi confraternities flourished; its treatment of Jews reflects the period's anti-Judaism, and its conversion plot the theology of eucharistic miracle; preserved in Trinity College, Dublin, MS F.4.20.
works.characters: Jonathas; Aristorius the merchant; the priest Isoder; the Jews Jason, Jasdon, Masphat, Malchus; the Bishop; the Image of Christ
works.structure: A two-part miracle (the bargain and the testing; the miracle and conversion), framed by the banns and the closing sermon.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Cursor Mundi
works.description: A vast northern verse history of the world, some 24,000 lines, 'running' (cursor) through sacred history from Creation to Doomsday: Old Testament narrative, the life of Christ, the Virgin, the apostles, and the finding of the cross. The most comprehensive biblical paraphrase in Middle English, designed to rival secular romance in the affections of its audience.
works.plot: The poem retells the Old and New Testament story in chronological sequence — Creation, the patriarchs, Christ's life and Passion, the early church — with moralizations and legends (including the harrowing of hell) woven into the biblical narrative.
works.significance: The largest Middle English biblical poem and the principal popular scriptural compendium before the Wycliffite Bible; a major witness to lay biblical culture.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets (with some septenary sections) in the northern dialect.
works.context: Composed c. 1300 in the north of England (Durham or Yorkshire), in the tradition of the Historia Scholastica and vernacular biblical paraphrase; preserved in nine manuscripts, with a southern version made c. 1400.
works.characters: Christ; the Virgin Mary; the patriarchs, apostles, and saints
works.structure: A seven-part chronicle following the ages of the world, with prologue and epilogue framing the narrative as a book for 'lewed' men.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Cygnea Cantio
works.description: Leland's Latin poem in praise of the Thames, in which a swan sings as it glides down the river from Oxford to London, celebrating the towns, palaces, and worthies along its banks; published with a long commentary by the author in 1545.
works.plot: The swan's song follows the Thames from its source past Oxford, Windsor, and Hampton Court to Westminster and London, praising each place and the Tudor dynasty; the commentary supplies the antiquarian and topographical learning that the verse compresses.
works.significance: The earliest sustained literary celebration of the Thames and the model for the river-poems of Spenser (the Thames–Medway marriage) and Denham's Cooper's Hill; a key monument of Tudor antiquarian humanism.
works.meter: Latin hexameters
works.context: Published 1545 during Leland's final productive years, as part of his programme of celebrating the antiquities of Britain in Latin verse (the unpublished Genethliacon and the unfinished De uiris illustribus).
works.characters: The Swan (speaker)
works.structure: A single long Latin poem with Leland's own prose commentary, a form modelled on the Renaissance edition of a classical text.

works.title: Cædmon's Hymn
works.manuscriptDate: margins of eighth-century manuscripts of Bede
works.description: A nine-line praise poem to God the Creator, composed, according to Bede's Historia ecclesiastica (IV.24), by the illiterate cowherd Cædmon after a dream in which he was commanded to sing of the beginning of created things. It is the earliest datable poem in Old English.
works.plot: The poem praises the heavenly Father, the measurer of fate, who established the beginning of every wonder: first he created heaven as a roof for the children of men, then the middle-earth, the guardian of mankind made the earth for men. (This is the traditional five-line paraphrase; the text runs to nine lines with epithets varying by version.)
works.significance: The earliest surviving English poem and the foundation of the English religious poetic tradition.
works.meter: Nine lines of alliterative accentual metre, with formulaic epithets ('heofonrices weard', 'moncynnes weard').
works.context: Composed c. 657–680 at Whitby under Abbess Hild; Bede gives a Latin paraphrase and says the vernacular text was preserved; it survives in Old English in the margins and endleaves of some twenty-one manuscripts of the Historia, the earliest (the 'Moore Bede') datable to 737.
works.characters: God the Creator
works.structure: A single doxological period: address, epithets of God, and the two works of creation (heaven, earth).
works.attributionNotes: Traditionally attributed to Cædmon on Bede's authority; the extant Old English texts are translations back from oral memory of the original, which Bede knew only in paraphrase.

editions.title: The Anglo-Saxon Minor Poems (Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records, vol. VI)

sources: A Book of Middle English, 4th edition

works.title: Dame Sirith
altTitles: The Interlude of the Clerk and the Girl
works.description: The earliest English fabliau: a comic tale of 450 lines in which the clerk Wilekin, failing to seduce Margery, buys the services of the old bawd Dame Sirith, whose trick with a weeping dog convinces Margery to yield. The poem may have been designed for performance by one or two speakers.
works.plot: The lovesick clerk Wilekin woos Margery without success; Dame Sirith, hired for a fee, persuades Margery that her weeping bitch is a transformed woman punished for refusing a clerk — and Margery consents rather than share that fate.
works.significance: The first English fabliau and a landmark in the history of English comedy and secular drama; the bawd-and-trickster plot anticipates Chaucer's fabliaux.
works.meter: Irregular rhyming couplets with dialogue assignable to speakers (semi-dramatic form).
works.context: Composed c. 1275 in the East Midlands; preserved in Bodleian Library, Digby MS 86 (c. 1300).
works.characters: Wilekin the clerk; Margery; Dame Sirith
works.structure: A short fabliau of courtship, trickery, and capitulation, largely in dialogue, with explicit staging cues.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Daniel
works.form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 764 lines on the book of Daniel, from the Junius manuscript: the three youths in Nebuchadnezzar's fiery furnace, the king's dream of the tree and his madness, and the fall of Babylon to the Medes and Persians under the writing on the wall — with the liturgical Canticles of the three youths (the 'Azarias' material) expanded into songs of praise.
works.plot: The poem follows Daniel and his companions at the Babylonian court; Nebuchadnezzar's idol and the furnace; the king's dream of the great tree, interpreted by Daniel as his own pride and coming fall; his seven years of bestial madness and restoration; Belshazzar's feast, the writing on the wall, and the city's fall to Cyrus. The youths' prayers and songs in the furnace (the Canticum trium puerorum) are rendered as extended lyric passages.
works.significance: A sustained meditation on pride and the fall of kings, central to the Junius manuscript's providential scheme.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the canticle passages show a more ornate, lyrical style.
works.context: Preserved in the Junius manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11); related to the Exeter Book poem Azarias, which preserves a version of the first canticle.
works.characters: Daniel; Nebuchadnezzar; Belshazzar; Azarias, Ananias, and Misael (the three youths); Cyrus
works.structure: Episodic biblical narrative punctuated by lyric set-pieces (the canticles), with an admonitory frame on pride and the fall of kings.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: De Civili Dominio
works.description: John Wyclif's most explosive treatise (1375–76), expounding his doctrine of dominion: lordship is founded on grace, so that the sinful clergy — the pope included — forfeit their right to temporal possessions, and kings may and must strip the church of its wealth. The book that made Wyclif the theorist of disendowment and the target of papal condemnation.
works.plot: Wyclif argues that all dominion derives from God and is held only by the righteous; the reprobate hold possessions unjustly; the clergy's endowment was conditional on their holiness and may be revoked by lay lords; and the English king, as God's vicar in his realm, is bound to reform and disendow the delinquent church.
works.significance: The theoretical charter of Lollardy's attack on ecclesiastical wealth and the most consequential political theology written in medieval England.
works.meter: Latin prose in the Oxford scholastic manner, relentlessly syllogistic.
works.context: Composed at Oxford and Lutterworth in 1375–76, when the papal-imperial politics of the Great Schism's prelude and the English crown's anti-papal statutes (Provisors, Praemunire) gave Wyclif's theories immediate political force; nineteen propositions from it were condemned by Gregory XI in 1377.
works.characters: none (theological treatise)
works.structure: Three books of scholastic argument, from the metaphysics of dominion through its application to the church to the duties of the king.
works.attributionNotes: Wyclif's authorship secure.

works.title: De Emendata Structura Latini Sermonis
altTitles: On the Correct Structure of Latin Prose
works.description: Thomas Linacre's treatise on Latin syntax, published in London by Richard Pynson in 1524; the first systematic Latin grammar composed by an Englishman and a landmark of the humanist reform of grammar.
works.plot: The work analyses Latin construction in six books, replacing the medieval speculative grammars with a descriptive account of syntax based on the usage of Cicero and the best classical authors, illustrated with abundant quotations.
works.significance: A founding document of English classical scholarship; its descriptive method influenced the whole European tradition of Latin grammar, and it secured Linacre's European reputation among humanists.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Linacre, physician to Henry VIII and the foremost English Greek scholar of his generation, composed the work over 1512–24 after his return from Italy; it was printed by Pynson and used in the schools alongside the authorized grammar.
works.structure: Six books of systematic grammatical exposition with a preface to Prince Arthur's tutor and a dedication to the grammar-school masters.

works.title: De excidio et conquestu Britanniae
altTitles: On the Ruin and Conquest of Britain
works.description: Gildas's jeremiad against the sins of the British kings and clergy, opening with the only near-contemporary narrative of the Saxon settlement of Britain, including the battle of Mount Badon. The principal source for post-Roman Britain and the foundation of the providential reading of British history that Bede adopted.
works.plot: Part I narrates the Roman occupation, the coming of the proud Saxons as mercenaries, their revolt, and the British resistance culminating in Ambrosius Aurelianus and the victory at Mount Badon. Parts II and III denounce the five tyrant kings (Constantine, Aurelius Caninus, Vortipor, Cuneglas, and Maglocunus) and the corrupt British clergy in the manner of the Old Testament prophets.
works.significance: The indispensable (if tendentious) source for the adventus Saxonum and for the moral theology of national disaster.
works.meter: Rhetorical Latin prose saturated with biblical allusion.
works.context: Composed in Britain, traditionally c. 540s, a generation after Mount Badon; the earliest surviving extended insular text after the Roman period.
works.characters: Ambrosius Aurelianus; the five tyrant kings; the Saxon mercenaries
works.structure: A tripartite sermon-polemic: historical prologue, royal denunciations, clerical denunciations — history entirely subordinated to moral exhortation.
works.attributionNotes: Gildas's authorship is traditional and generally accepted; the dating rests on inference.
sources: English Literature in the Sixteenth Century, Excluding Drama

works.title: De Nugis Curialium
works.description: Walter Map's miscellany of court gossip, satire, Welsh legend, ghost story, and moral anecdote, assembled piecemeal during his service at the court of Henry II; 'a jest book and a jest at the same time', as one editor put it, and the only certain work by one of the wittiest Latin writers of the age.
works.summary: Five distinctiones gather tales of the court of Henry II, satirical portraits of monks and courtiers, the legend of Sadius and Galo, the story of the Welsh king Herla and the fairy bride, and the earliest surviving connected account of the birth of Lancelot; Map's dissuasio to his friend Ruffinus against marriage closes the work.
works.significance: A unique window onto the oral culture and court life of Henry II's England, an early witness to Arthurian material, and a masterpiece of twelfth-century Latin satire and narrative.

works.title: De temporum ratione
works.form: didactic and scientific prose (computus) in Latin
works.description: Bede's treatise on time and its reckoning, the standard medieval textbook of computus: the calculation of Easter, the solar and lunar cycles, the ages of the world, and — decisively — the practice of dating years from the Incarnation of Christ (annus Domini), which the work made universal in western Europe.
works.plot: The treatise proceeds from the smallest units of time (moments, hours, days) through the calendar, the lunar cycles, and the Easter tables to the great divisions of world history — the six ages of the world and the seventh age of rest — closing with a chronicle of the world's six ages down to 725.
works.significance: The most influential computistical work of the Middle Ages; the origin of the BC/AD dating convention in general use.
works.meter: Latin prose.
works.context: Composed at Jarrow in 725 for the monks' instruction; a revision and expansion of Bede's earlier De temporibus (703).
works.characters: none
works.structure: A systematic didactic treatise in 71 chapters, concluding with the world chronicle (chapter 66) as the practical demonstration of its chronology.
works.attributionNotes: Bede's authorship is certain.
sources: English Historical Documents, Volume II: 1042–1189

works.title: De virginitate (prose and verse)
works.form: didactic treatise in Latin prose and hexameter verse
works.description: Aldhelm's double treatise in praise of virginity, composed in both prose and verse: a celebration of chastity sustained by a vast catalogue of exemplars — biblical heroes, virgin martyrs, and ascetics — in the ornate 'hermeneutic' Latin that made Aldhelm the model of insular style.
works.plot: The prose treatise (addressed to the nuns of Barking, headed by Hildelith) argues the superiority of virginity over marriage and the other states of life, adducing the patriarchs, prophets, martyrs, and virgins as witnesses; the accompanying Carmen de virginitate recasts the argument in hexameters with a culminating allegorical battle of the vices and virtues.
works.significance: The founding text of the Anglo-Latin literary tradition and of its characteristic learned style.
works.meter: Ornate hermeneutic Latin prose; the Carmen is in dactylic hexameters.
works.context: Composed for the double monastery of Barking, probably c. 675-705; the prose was praised by Bede and widely imitated.
works.characters: Hildelith and the nuns of Barking (addressees); the exemplars: Elijah, Daniel, the Maccabees, Agnes, Cecilia, and others
works.structure: A thematic treatise built from scriptural and hagiographical exempla, concluded by the allegorical psychomachia of the verse version.
works.attributionNotes: Aldhelm's authorship is certain.
themes: Women's experience and the feminine voice
sources: TEAMS Middle English Texts Series

works.title: Deor
works.description: A poem of 42 lines spoken by a displaced court poet, Deor, who consoles himself with a catalogue of legendary woes — Weland's captivity, Beadohild's pregnancy, Mæðhild's grief, Theodoric's exile, Eormanric's tyranny — each closed by the refrain 'Þæs ofereode, þisses swa mæg' ('That passed over, so may this').
works.plot: Deor, supplanted in his lord's favour by a rival scop named Heorrenda, lists the legendary sorrows that came to an end and applies the refrain to his own case, ending with a brief, ambiguous self-identification as the once-favoured poet of the Heodenings.
works.significance: A rare glimpse of the court poet's self-consciousness and of the consolation-structure that underlies the Old English elegies.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre with a six-part strophic structure marked by the refrain.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; its allusions are the earliest English witnesses to the legends of Weland the smith and Eormanric the Goth.
works.characters: Deor (speaker); Weland; Beadohild; Mæðhild; Theodoric; Eormanric; Heorrenda
works.structure: Five legendary exempla framed by the refrain, followed by the poet's personal application; the refrain is the earliest in English poetry.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the speaker's name is part of the fiction.
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry

works.title: Digby Mary Magdalene
altTitles: The Digby Play of Mary Magdalene
works.description: The most ambitious of the English saints' plays (c. 1480–1500, 2,139 lines): the life of Mary Magdalene from her worldly grandeur and conversion through her apostolate in Marseilles to her thirty years as a desert hermit fed by angels. Its multiple locations, ship voyages, and spectacular effects make it the fullest surviving English drama of a female saint.
works.plot: Mary, the proud lady of Magdalene castle, falls into lechery; Christ's grace converts her, and after the Passion she sails to Marseilles, converts the king and queen, raises the queen from death, and converts the pagan priest; retiring to the wilderness, she is fed by angels, receives the last rites, and her soul is borne to heaven.
works.significance: The fullest English female saint's play and the most elaborately staged of the East Anglian dramas; its conversion and travel plot is a summit of the miracle play tradition.
works.meter: Couplets and stanza forms, with macaronic Latin in the liturgical scenes.
works.context: Composed c. 1480–1500 in East Anglia, in the flourishing of the Mary Magdalene cult; preserved in Bodleian Library, Digby MS 133 (c. 1512), with The Conversion of St Paul and the morality Wisdom.
works.characters: Mary Magdalene; Christ; the King and Queen of Marseilles; the pagan priest; the angels; the devils
works.structure: A multi-location saint's play in the continental manner, moving between Jerusalem, Marseilles, and the wilderness, with ships, temple, and heaven's scaffolds.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

editions.title: The Late Medieval Religious Plays of Bodleian MSS Digby 133 and E Museo 160
editions.editor: Donald C. Baker, John L. Murphy, and Louis B. Hall Jr (eds.)

works.title: Dives and Pauper
works.description: An anonymous prose treatise of c. 1405–10 in dialogue form on the Ten Commandments, in which the rich man Dives asks and the poor man Pauper answers — a vast compendium of moral theology, canon law, and social commentary, notable for its defence of poverty, its discussion of images and tithes, and its sympathy with reformist positions short of heresy. The great popular summa of fifteenth-century English orthodoxy.
works.plot: Dives, the wealthy layman, poses the hard questions of Christian practice — the worship of images, oaths, tithes, usury, the duties of the rich to the poor — and Pauper, the poor and learned clerk, answers each with doctrine, law, and exemplum, through all ten commandments.
works.significance: The most comprehensive vernacular treatment of the Decalogue in medieval England and a central witness to the social teaching of the late medieval church on wealth, poverty, and images.
works.meter: Plain, copious prose with Latin quotations translated for the lay reader.
works.context: Composed c. 1405–10, in the aftermath of Arundel's Constitutions (1409), by a learned clerk conversant with both orthodox and reformist positions; printed by Pynson (1493) and read into the Reformation.
works.characters: Dives; Pauper
works.structure: A sustained catechetical dialogue in ten commandments, with the social argument between rich and poor as its dramatic engine.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; a Franciscan authorship has been conjectured.

works.title: Ego Dormio
altTitles: Ego Dormio et Cor Meum Vigilat
works.description: Richard Rolle's English epistle on the three degrees of love, written c. 1340 for a nun of Yedingham (or a recluse of his circle): a lyrical meditation, interspersed with the lyric 'My king that water grette', on the ascent from the love of God's creatures through the love of Christ's humanity to the highest love, which he describes as 'wonderful' — the experience he had felt at Hampole.
works.plot: Taking its text from the Song of Songs ('I sleep and my heart wakes'), the epistle teaches the recipient the three degrees of love — insuperable, inseparable, singular — describes Rolle's own experience of heavenly song, and closes with the Passion meditation and the lyric of Christ's weeping for man's sin.
works.significance: The classic statement of Rolle's three degrees of love and a key text of the early English mystical epistles.
works.meter: Rhythmical, alliterative prose with the lyric 'My king' in rhymed stanzas.
works.context: Composed c. 1340 in Yorkshire, among Rolle's earliest English writings, for the guidance of a woman religious; preserved in numerous manuscripts, often with the other English epistles.
works.characters: Rolle (writer); the nun of Yedingham (addressee)
works.structure: A single epistle in three movements, with the inset lyric as its devotional climax.
works.attributionNotes: Rolle's authorship secure.

works.title: Elene
altTitles: The Finding of the True Cross
works.form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: Cynewulf's longest signed poem (1,321 lines), on the legend of the Finding of the True Cross: the empress Helena, mother of Constantine, journeys to Jerusalem, compels the Jews to reveal the site of the Crucifixion, and recovers the cross. The poem is a masterpiece of typological narrative, casting Helena as a heroic queen and the cross as the sign of victory.
