works.plot: Constantine, granted a vision of the cross before battle, sends his mother Helena to Jerusalem; her search, the interrogation of the Jew Judas (who resists, is imprisoned, converted by a sign, and baptized as Cyriacus), the miraculous finding of the three crosses, the proof by resurrection of a dead youth, the conversion of the Jews, and Helena's building of churches; the epilogue carries Cynewulf's runic signature and his meditation on judgment and poetry.
works.significance: The richest treatment in early English poetry of the cross as sign of victory; the locus classicus of Cynewulf's typological art.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the signature passage is among the most ornate in the corpus.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 121v-133v); based on the Latin Acta Cyriaci tradition of the Inventio crucis legend.
works.characters: Elene (Helena); Constantine; Judas/Cyriacus; Satan (in the debate with Judas)
works.structure: A conversion narrative in the heroic manner, organized around three debates (Constantine's vision, Helena's interrogations, Judas's conversion) and closing on the runic signature.
works.attributionNotes: Signed by Cynewulf in runes.

works.title: Emaré
works.description: A Breton lay on the Constance legend: the princess Emaré, cast out by her incestuous father, drifts across the sea in a boat with her child, and through the marvellous cloth she weaves and the recognitions it brings, is restored to her husband and kingdom. The legend Chaucer used for the Man of Law's Tale, told as a fairy-tale of patient suffering.
works.plot: Emaré, given a magic cloth by the emperor, refuses her father's marriage proposal and is set adrift; she marries the king of Galys, is slandered by her wicked mother-in-law and cast out again with her son Segramour; after years in Rome, her husband finds her and all are reconciled.
works.significance: The most artful English version of the Constance story and a central text for the romance's treatment of incest, exile, and female patience.
works.meter: Twelve-line tail-rhyme stanzas.
works.context: Composed c. 1400, probably in the north-east Midlands, from the Constance legend (ultimately Trivet's chronicle, as in Chaucer); preserved uniquely in BL Cotton MS Caligula A.ii.
works.characters: Emaré; her father the emperor; the king of Galys; the wicked mother-in-law; Segramour
works.structure: A double exile-and-return plot organized by the magic cloth and the repeated sea voyages, in the Constance tradition.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Enchiridion
works.form: didactic and scientific prose (computus) in Latin and Old English
works.description: Byrhtferth of Ramsey's bilingual manual of computus and the related sciences (c. 1011), written in alternating Latin and English: the fullest surviving treatise on the Anglo-Saxon science of time — the calendar, the lunar cycles, number symbolism, and the harmony of the cosmos — composed for the instruction of the young monks of Ramsey.
works.plot: The manual explains the computation of Easter, the course of the sun and moon through the zodiac, the elements, the ages of the world and of man, the symbolic meanings of numbers, and the figures of grammar and rhetoric, all ordered to the liturgical year and the contemplation of the world's design.
works.significance: The richest surviving witness to the scientific culture of the Benedictine Reform.
works.meter: Bilingual prose with verse passages.
works.context: Composed 1011 at Ramsey Abbey by Byrhtferth, pupil of Abbo of Fleury; unique manuscript: Oxford, Bodleian Library, Ashmole 328.
works.characters: the young monks of Ramsey (addressees)
works.structure: Four books of didactic exposition, alternating between Latin and English, with diagrams and tables.
works.attributionNotes: Byrhtferth's authorship is certain (he names himself).

works.title: Eneados
works.description: Douglas's complete translation of Virgil's Aeneid into Scots couplets, completed on 22 July 1513 — the first full translation of the poem in any British language — with a thirteenth book from Mapheus Vegius, and a prologue to each book in which the translator speaks of the Scottish seasons, his art, and his critics. Printed at London in 1553.
works.plot: Virgil's epic entire: Aeneas's flight from Troy, the wanderings, the tragedy of Dido, the descent to the underworld, and the wars in Italy — with Vegius's supplement completing the hero's apotheosis.
works.significance: The first complete British Aeneid and the summit of Scots humanist translation; its prologues are the finest nature poetry in Scots, and the translation passed Virgil to the northern Renaissance.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in vigorous Scots; the prologues alternate aureate and plain registers with seasonal description.
works.context: Completed in the year of Flodden (1513), when the Scottish court and much of its nobility were destroyed; Douglas's translation of the epic of exile and foundation speaks to a nation in crisis.
works.characters: Aeneas; Dido; Turnus; Anchises; Venus; Juno
works.structure: Twelve books of the Aeneid plus the thirteenth book of Vegius; each book preceded by a prologue, of which the seasonal prologues (VII, XII, XIII) are the most celebrated.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: Virgil's Aeneid Translated into Scottish Verse by Gavin Douglas

works.title: Epigrammata
altTitles: Epigrammata clarissimi disertissimique viri Thomae Mori
works.description: More's collected Latin epigrams, printed together with his Utopia in 1518, including translations from the Greek Anthology, satirical and courtly verse, and the poems on his own fortune and on kingship.
works.plot: The collection has no single argument; it ranges from verse translations of Greek epigrams made with William Lily, through witty satires on astrologers and courtiers, to the programmatic 'Progymnasmata' and poems celebrating the accession of Henry VIII.
works.significance: The finest Latin verse written by an Englishman of the early Renaissance and a showcase of the Erasmian revival of classical epigram; the coronation poems mark the beginnings of English Renaissance panegyric.
works.meter: Elegiac couplets, hendecasyllables, and other classical metres
works.context: Composed across More's humanist career from the late 1490s; the Progymnasmata with Lily (an exercise translating Greek epigrams) dates from c. 1503–04; the collection was printed by Froben at Basel in 1518 together with the third edition of Utopia.
works.structure: A printed miscellany grouped by type: translations from the Greek Anthology, original epigrams, and the coronation poems of 1509.

works.title: Epistle on the Mixed Life
works.description: Walter Hilton's epistle addressed to a wealthy layman, probably a lord, teaching the 'mixed life' — the life that joins the active works of mercy and the duties of estate with the inner practice of contemplation. It is the classic English statement that contemplation is not the preserve of monks: lay people in the world may and should live the contemplative life in their degree.
works.plot: Hilton distinguishes three lives — active, contemplative, and mixed — and argues that the mixed life, combining works of charity and governance with prayer and meditation, is the life of prelates and devout lay lords; he then teaches his addressee the practice of this life in his daily affairs.
works.significance: The founding text of the 'mixed life' tradition that legitimized lay contemplation and shaped the spirituality of the fifteenth-century gentry.
works.meter: Plain, authoritative prose of the Hilton school.
works.context: Composed c. 1385, when the growth of lay piety and the demand for vernacular guidance was transforming English religious life; preserved in numerous manuscripts, often with the Scale of Perfection.
works.characters: Hilton (writer); the devout layman (addressee)
works.structure: A single epistle in two movements: the doctrine of the three lives, and its application to the recipient's estate.
works.attributionNotes: Hilton's authorship secure.

works.title: Everyman
works.description: The most famous of the English moralities, translated from the Dutch Elckerlijc (c. 1495) around 1500: Everyman, summoned by Death to render his account, finds that Fellowship, Kindred, Goods, and even his own Strength and Beauty desert him, and that only Good Deeds — and Knowledge, Confession, and the priesthood — go with him into the grave. Its stark allegory of death has kept it on the stage for five centuries.
works.plot: God, seeing mankind sunk in worldly love, sends Death to Everyman with the summons to his reckoning; one by one his companions refuse the journey — Fellowship, Kindred, Cousin, Goods — until Good Deeds, weakened by his neglect, sends him to Knowledge, who leads him through Confession and penance to the sacraments; at the grave, Strength, Discretion, Beauty, and the Five Wits desert him in turn, and only Good Deeds descends with him, as the angels receive his soul.
works.significance: The classic English play of death and the reckoning: its allegory has made it the most performed medieval English drama in the modern world.
works.meter: Couplets and stanza forms, plain and weighty, with the Dutch original's structure faithfully kept.
works.context: Translated from the Dutch Elckerlijc (c. 1495) c. 1500 and printed by Richard Pynson and John Skot c. 1510–1535; continuously performed since, including modern productions (Hofmannsthal's Jedermann at Salzburg descends from it).
works.characters: Everyman; Death; God; Fellowship; Kindred; Cousin; Goods; Good Deeds; Knowledge; Confession; Strength; Discretion; Beauty; the Five Wits; the Angel; the Doctor
works.structure: A single-movement morality of the final journey, with the successive desertions of the companions as its pitiless rhythm and the doctrine of the reckoning as its frame.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; translated from the Dutch, whose authorship is likewise disputed.

works.title: Exodus
works.form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 590 lines on the Israelites' crossing of the Red Sea, from the Junius manuscript: a bravura reworking of Exodus 13-14 in which Moses becomes a heroic leader and the crossing a nautical epic, prefiguring the Christian's passage through the waters of baptism and the harrowing of hell.
works.plot: After a prologue on Moses and the law, the poem narrates the pursuit of the Israelites by Pharaoh's host, the pillar of cloud and fire, the parting of the waters, the drowning of the Egyptians, and the Israelites' division of spoils on the far shore; it closes with an allegorical exegesis of the crossing (the 'keys of the deep', the 'spiritual meanings') and allusions to Noah, Abraham, Solomon's temple, and the end of the world.
works.significance: The most stylistically daring of the Old Testament poems; its sea imagery is a high point of Old English diction.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of unusual density; famous kennings for the sea ('the whale's road', 'the swan's riding-place').
works.context: Preserved in the Junius manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11, pp. 143-171); the poem is often linked with the Cædmonian school of biblical paraphrase mentioned by Bede.
works.characters: Moses; Pharaoh; the Israelites; Abraham; Noah
works.structure: Narrative epic with an extended typological epilogue; the abrupt shifts of scene (Noah, Abraham, the temple) have prompted theories of textual disruption.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the Cædmonian attribution is traditional only.

works.title: Expugnatio Hibernica
works.description: Gerald of Wales's history of the Anglo-Norman invasion and conquest of Ireland (1169–85), framed as a panegyric of Henry II and of Gerald's own relatives among the conquerors, the Geraldines; composed from 1188 and read publicly at Oxford in 1188 or 1189.
works.summary: Gerald recounts the coming of the Normans under Strongbow and the campaigns that established English lordship in Ireland, devoting special attention to the deeds of the FitzGeralds, to the character of the Irish, and to the prophecies and prodigies attending the conquest.
works.significance: The foundational narrative of the English presence in Ireland, shaped by family partisanship but indispensable as the earliest extended account of the conquest; a model of twelfth-century historical rhetoric.

works.title: Fall of Princes
works.description: John Lydgate's monumental translation (over 36,000 lines) of Boccaccio's De Casibus Virorum Illustrium, commissioned by Humphrey Duke of Gloucester and completed in 1438: a procession of the falls of princes from Adam to King John of France, moralized by the ghostly narrator Boccaccio himself. The encyclopedic English 'tragedy' of fortune, and the ancestor of the Mirror for Magistrates.
works.plot: The poet, in a Boethian frame, receives the sorrowing Boccaccio, who recounts example after example of greatness overthrown — Nimrod, Saul, Priam, Alexander, Caesar, Nero, Arthur, and the modern princes — each tale closing with the moral of fortune's wheel; the work ends with the falls of the French and English kings and a defense of poetry itself.
works.significance: The great English poem of the falls of princes and the conduit by which Boccaccio's tragic vision became the Tudor theory of tragedy; its influence on the Elizabethan stage is direct.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas with prose links, aureate and copious.
works.context: Commissioned by Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, in 1431 and completed in 1438, during the wars in France and the king's minority; printed by Pynson (1494) and continuously read; the Mirror for Magistrates (1559) descends directly from it.
works.characters: Lydgate (dreamer); Boccaccio (narrator); the fallen princes of history
works.structure: Nine books of exemplary falls within the dream-vision frame, with the envoy to Duke Humphrey as its patronage climax.
works.attributionNotes: Lydgate's authorship secure.

works.title: Festial
works.description: John Mirk's cycle of English sermons for the feasts of the church year, composed c. 1380s at Lilleshall Abbey: lively, exemplum-rich homilies designed for parish priests to read to their congregations, from Advent through the temporale and sanctorale to the dedication of the church. The most popular sermon collection of late medieval England.
works.plot: Each sermon expounds the day's feast — its history, its scripture, and its moral — with the miracle stories and exempla that made the Festial famous: the monk and the birds, the usurer's bees, the proud lady's punishment — and closes with practical instruction for the parish.
works.significance: The classic of the English late medieval sermon and the principal record of orthodox parish preaching in the age of Lollardy; its exempla are a treasury of popular piety.
works.meter: Plain, animated prose with verse tags and exemplary narrative.
works.context: Composed by the Augustinian canon John Mirk, prior of Lilleshall, in the 1380s, for the 'ignorant' parish clergy; it spread across England in some forty manuscripts and was printed by Caxton (1483) and repeatedly thereafter.
works.characters: the exemplary figures of the tales
works.structure: A cycle of seventy-four (or more) sermons following the church year, in the homiletic-exemplary manner.
works.attributionNotes: Mirk's authorship secure (he names himself in the preface).

works.title: Floris and Blancheflour
works.description: An idyllic romance of young love, adapted from the Old French Floire et Blancheflor: the Saracen prince Floris and the Christian captive Blancheflour, brought up together, are parted by his parents, and Floris pursues her to the emir's tower in Babylon, where love and loyalty overcome jealousy and force. The gentlest of the early English romances.
works.plot: Floris's parents sell Blancheflour to merchants to end the match; she is taken to the emir of Babylon's harem tower; Floris follows, bribes his way in, is discovered in the maidens' tower, and is saved from death when the lovers' mutual devotion moves the emir to mercy and their marriage.
works.significance: The classic English romance of young love and constancy, and a key witness to the transmission of the sentimental romance from France to England.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets, gently lyrical in tone.
works.context: Composed c. 1250 in the south-east from the French Floire et Blancheflor (c. 1150), one of the most widely translated romances of the Middle Ages; preserved in four English manuscripts from c. 1300 onward.
works.characters: Floris; Blancheflour; the emir of Babylon; Clarice; Darys the porter
works.structure: A quest-romance in two movements (parting; pursuit and rescue), with the tower and the garden as symbolic settings.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Fulgens and Lucrece
works.description: Henry Medwall's interlude of the wooing of Lucrece, performed at the household of Cardinal Morton; the earliest surviving secular English play, printed by John Rastell c. 1512–16.
works.plot: The Roman senator Fulgens promises his daughter Lucrece to the suitor of greater nobility, Publius Cornelius or Gaius Flaminius; the debate on true nobility (virtue versus birth) is interwoven with a subplot in which two serving-men, A and B, woo Lucrece's maid and re-enact the contest in comic parallel. The play breaks off in the unique surviving copy before the conclusion.
works.significance: The first surviving secular English play and a landmark in the transition from medieval moral drama to Renaissance comedy; its debate on true nobility and its pairing of serious and comic plots anticipate the structure of Elizabethan drama.
works.meter: Rhyme royal and couplets, with prose dialogue in the comic scenes
works.context: Written for performance at a feast given by Cardinal John Morton (probably Christmas 1497), in whose household Medwall was chaplain; the play adapts Buonaccorso da Montemagno's De vera nobilitate (translated by John Tiptoft c. 1460), and Rastell's printing (c. 1512–16) preserved it for the sixteenth-century stage tradition.
works.characters: Fulgens; Lucrece; Publius Cornelius; Gaius Flaminius; A (servant); B (servant); Joan (Lucrece's maid)
works.structure: Two-part interlude alternating the serious debate of the senators with the comic subplot of the servants, with direct addresses to the banqueting audience.

works.title: Gammer Gurton's Needle
altTitles: A Ryght Pithy, Pleasaunt and Merie Comedie: Intytuled Gammer Gurtons Nedle
works.description: The classic English village farce of the lost needle, composed c. 1552–53, probably at Christ's College, Cambridge, and printed in 1575; the second of the two earliest English comedies (with Ralph Roister Doister).
works.plot: Gammer Gurton's precious needle is lost while mending the breeches of her servant Hodge; the whole household turns out to search, suspicion falls on the neighbour Dame Chat, and the village curate Doctor Rat is beaten in a confusion of break-ins and brawls; the needle is at last discovered — in the seat of Hodge's breeches — with a resounding yell, and the company shares the ale in reconciliation.
works.significance: One of the two founding comedies of the English stage: its picture of village life, its rich dialect comedy, and its plot of the lost needle set the pattern for English farce from Shakespeare's Merry Wives to the twentieth century.
works.meter: Rhyming couplets ('rhyming fourteeners'), with the famous drinking song 'Back and side go bare'
works.context: Composed c. 1552–53, with the title-page attribution of the 1575 edition to 'Mr. S. Master of Art' generally identified as William Stevenson of Christ's College, Cambridge, where the play was probably acted; it belongs to the university revival of classical comedy in the 1550s.
works.characters: Gammer Gurton; Hodge; Diccon the Bedlam; Dame Chat; Doctor Rat; Master Bayly; Tib; Cock
works.structure: Five acts in a single village setting, modelled on Roman comedy but filled with native farce: the plot turns on the lost object, the false accusation, and the comic discovery.
works.attributionNotes: The 1575 title page ascribes the play to 'Mr. S. Master of Art', identified by modern scholarship (most fully by Charles W. Whitworth) as William Stevenson of Christ's College, Cambridge; the attribution is probable rather than certain.

works.title: Genesis A
works.form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 2,935 lines paraphrasing Genesis 1-22, from the creation and the fall of the angels to the sacrifice of Isaac. The longest of the Junius manuscript poems, it is the foundational Old Testament epic of the period, composed in the plain style of the 'Cædmonian' school.
works.plot: The poem recounts the fall of the rebel angels, the six days of creation, the fall of Adam and Eve and their expulsion, Cain and Abel, the generations to Noah, the Flood and the covenant, the tower of Babel, and the story of Abraham to the near-sacrifice of Isaac, concluding with the promise of the seed.
works.significance: The earliest sustained biblical epic in English; a primary witness to the vernacular reception of scripture.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre in a relatively plain, narrative style.
works.context: Preserved in the Junius manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11); its opening lines were long known as 'Cædmon's Genesis' from the early editor Junius's attribution.
works.characters: God; Adam; Eve; Satan; Cain; Abel; Noah; Abraham; Sarah; Isaac; Lot
works.structure: Continuous biblical paraphrase in epic form, with an interpolated passage (Genesis B, lines 235-851) translated from Old Saxon treating the fall in greater detail.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; attribution to Cædmon is traditional and no longer accepted.

works.title: Genesis B
works.form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 617 lines, interpolated into Genesis A (lines 235-851), translated from an Old Saxon original and containing the most celebrated scenes of the fall in Old English: Satan's proud rebellion ('better for me to be a king in hell'), the temptation of Adam by the disguised tempter, and the grief of Eve.
works.plot: The poem opens with Satan's boast against God and his binding in hell; an envoy demon journeys to Eden and, taking the form of a serpent, tempts first Adam (unsuccessfully) and then Eve, deceiving her with the promise of a vision of heaven; Eve eats and persuades Adam; the poem closes on their shame and the beginning of repentance, with the original ending lost in the transition back to Genesis A.
works.significance: Contains the finest dramatic treatment of the fall in early English poetry; its Satan anticipates Milton's in power and pathos, a connection first argued by Sievers in 1875.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre, with occasional hypermetric lines betraying the Old Saxon original.
works.context: Translated into Old English from an Old Saxon poem (possibly connected with the ninth-century Heliand milieu) and interpolated into Genesis A in the Junius manuscript; the Old Saxon original survives only in a few Vatican fragments.
works.characters: Satan; the Tempter (demon); Adam; Eve
works.structure: A dramatic expansion of the fall narrative built on lengthy speeches — Satan's monologue, the tempter's persuasions, Eve's lament — unique in the corpus for its psychological interest.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the interpolation was first detected by Eduard Sievers (1875).

works.title: Gentleness and Nobility
works.description: A debate interlude on the nature of true nobility, printed by John Rastell c. 1529 and attributed to Rastell (or, by some, to John Heywood); an early dramatic statement of the humanist case that virtue, not birth, makes the gentleman.
works.plot: A Knight, a Merchant, and a Ploughman dispute whether gentleness resides in ancestry or in virtue; the Ploughman, arguing that nobility of birth without worth is empty, is supported against the Knight's hereditary claims, and the debate — refereed by the Philosopher — concludes with the definition of true gentleness as virtuous living, with a sharp satire of idle gentlemen who live off others' labour.
works.significance: The first English play devoted wholly to the question of true nobility, and a rare dramatic voice for the commonwealth critique of hereditary privilege; it anticipates the social debates of Elizabethan drama.
works.meter: Couplets
works.context: Printed c. 1529, in the year of the Reformation Parliament; the play's defence of labour and its satire of idle gentry voice the social criticism of the humanist commonwealth tradition (More's Utopia, Starkey's Dialogue), and its attribution to Rastell connects it to the More circle.
works.characters: The Knight; The Merchant; The Ploughman; The Philosopher
works.structure: A formal disputation in two parts, with the Philosopher as moderator and the three estates as speakers; the debate is enlivened by comic abuse between the Knight and the Ploughman.
works.attributionNotes: Printed without author's name; the play is traditionally attributed to John Rastell (whose press produced it), with John Heywood also proposed; modern scholarship accepts Rastell as the likeliest author without certainty.

works.title: Gesta Regum Anglorum
altTitles: Deeds of the Kings of the English
works.description: William of Malmesbury's history of the English kings from the arrival of the Anglo-Saxons (449) to the twenty-eighth year of Henry I (1127–28), the most learned English history of the twelfth century, deliberately modelled on Bede and written with a polished Latinity that set a new standard for English historiography.
works.summary: Five books carry the narrative from the adventus Saxonum through the kings of Wessex and the Norman Conquest to Henry I; the work combines narrative history with biography, anecdote, and documentary research, drawing on a library of sources now partly lost and on William's own travels and enquiries.
works.significance: The outstanding English historical work between Bede and the later twelfth century; a model of critical method and style, cited and pillaged by later chroniclers, and a primary witness to Anglo-Saxon history after the Conquest.

editions.title: Gesta Regum Anglorum
editions.editor: R. A. B. Mynors, R. M. Thomson, and M. Winterbottom (eds.)

works.title: Gloria I and II
altTitles: The Greater and Lesser Doxology Poems
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.form: religious lyric (liturgical paraphrase) in alliterative verse
works.description: Two short Old English versifications of the liturgical Gloria: Gloria I (57 lines) paraphrases the Greater Doxology sung at Mass, praising the Trinity and Christ the Lamb of God; Gloria II (20 lines) is a brief rendering of the doxology of praise to Father, Son, and Spirit.
works.plot: Gloria I moves from the angels' song of praise through the attributes of the persons of the Trinity to Christ the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, ending with a prayer for mercy. Gloria II offers a compact doxology in verse.
works.significance: Evidence of the Old English church's project of rendering the central texts of the liturgy into the vernacular poetic idiom.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with the balanced parallelism appropriate to liturgical praise; the shorter poem is notably compact.
works.context: The Benedictine Reform's devotion to the liturgy gave new prominence to the sung ordinary of the Mass; vernacular paraphrases like these made its texts accessible to those whose Latin was limited.
works.structure: Both poems are direct liturgical paraphrases; Gloria I is organized by the successive clauses of the Gloria in excelsis, closing with the Agnus Dei petitions.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The two poems are separate compositions.

works.title: Godly Queen Hester
altTitles: A New Interlude Drawn out of the Holy Scripture of Godly Queen Hester
works.description: An anonymous interlude on the biblical story of Esther, printed in 1561 but composed c. 1525–29; a political allegory in which the virtuous queen and her wise counsellor save the realm from the wicked minister.
works.plot: King Ahasuerus, misled by the proud Aman, signs a decree against the Jews; Queen Hester, advised by the wise Mardocheus, intercedes with the king at the risk of her life, exposes Aman's malice, and obtains his overthrow and the deliverance of her people — with the collop-eating scene of Aman's gluttony played as comic Vice-business.
works.significance: The first surviving English dramatization of the Esther story and a striking example of the interlude as political counsel; it shows biblical drama absorbing the new humanist debate on counsel and tyranny.
works.meter: Couplets with stanzaic passages
works.context: Composed c. 1525–29, almost certainly for a noble household: the story of Esther had long served as an allegory of good counsel and royal deliverance, and the play has been read (by Greg Walker and others) as a veiled commentary on the fall of Wolsey, in which the virtuous queen intercedes against an overmighty minister.
works.characters: King Ahasuerus; Queen Hester; Mardocheus; Aman; Ardion (Aman's servant); Hardydardy; Pride; Adulation; Ambition
works.structure: A continuous interlude alternating the counsel scenes of Hester and Mardocheus with the comic scenes of Aman and his servants, ending in judgement and the elevation of Mardocheus.

works.title: Goostly Psalmes and Spirituall Songes
works.description: Miles Coverdale's collection of metrical psalms, hymns, and carols translated from the German (chiefly Luther), printed c. 1535; the first English hymn book, intended for congregational singing.
works.plot: Forty-one pieces — metrical versions of the psalms, Luther's hymns (including 'Ein feste Burg' as 'Our God is a defence and tower'), the Creed, the Lord's Prayer, and canticles — each with its tune indicated, prefaced by an epistle on the right use of psalmody in church and home.
works.significance: The first English hymn book and the beginning of English congregational song; its psalms anticipate the metrical psalters of Sternhold and Hopkins, and its translation of 'Ein feste Burg' entered the English hymnic tradition.
works.meter: Metrical stanzas in ballad and hymn metres, set to German tunes
works.context: Printed c. 1535 during Coverdale's continental exile, drawing on the Wittenberg hymn books; Henry VIII's 1546 proclamation against 'ballads, rhymes, and lewd songs' included it among the books to be burned, and only one complete copy survives (Queen's College, Oxford).
works.structure: A hymn book arranged by liturgical use, with a preface on singing and notes of the tunes to which the pieces are set.

works.title: Grammar and Glossary
works.form: grammar and didactic prose in Old English
works.description: Ælfric's Latin grammar written in English — the first grammar of Latin composed in any European vernacular — with its companion glossary of Latin words arranged by subject. A landmark in the history of education and of the vernacular as an instrument of learning.
works.plot: The Grammar adapts the Excerptiones de Prisciano to teach the parts of speech, declensions, and conjugations entirely through the medium of English, explaining Latin forms with English equivalents; the Glossary lists vocabulary by topics (the body, kinship, the church, tools, birds, beasts) in Latin with English glosses.
works.significance: The first vernacular Latin grammar in Europe; a milestone in the history of English education.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Composed c. 998, when Ælfric was at Cerne Abbas or Eynsham; at least fifteen manuscripts survive, evidence of its use in schools into the twelfth century.
works.characters: the schoolboys of Eynsham (addressees)
works.structure: A systematic school grammar in sections on the eight parts of speech, followed by the thematic glossary.
works.attributionNotes: Ælfric's authorship is certain.
themes: Tyranny and the abuse of power

works.title: Guthlac A
works.form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 818 lines on the Mercian hermit Guthlac of Crowland: his arrival in the fenland retreat, his battles with the demons who tempt and torment him, and his vindication by the apostle Bartholomew. Based on Felix's Latin Vita, the poem turns the saint's spiritual warfare into heroic combat in the native manner.
works.plot: The young Mercian warrior Guthlac, renouncing war, takes up the solitary life in the fens of Crowland; demons assault his cell, carry him to the gates of hell, and accuse him of pride; the apostle Bartholomew commands his release and the devils obey; Guthlac returns victorious, and the poem closes with his death and the angels' reception of his soul.
works.significance: The classic vernacular treatment of the hermit-warrior and of the fenland as spiritual battlefield.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre, with the diction of heroic combat applied to spiritual warfare.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 32b-44b); source: Felix of Crowland's Vita Sancti Guthlaci (c. 730-740).
works.characters: Guthlac; the demons; Bartholomew; the angels
works.structure: A hagiographical epic in the heroic mode: renunciation, the demonic wars (a psychomachia in narrative form), heavenly vindication, and death; speeches dominate the central combat scenes.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Guthlac B
works.description: A poem of 561 lines on the death of St Guthlac of Crowland, from the Exeter Book: the saint's illness, his last conversation with his servant Beccel, and the ascent of his soul, which flies like a bird to heaven. Distinct from Guthlac A in style and emphasis, it is one of the most tender poems in the corpus.
works.plot: Stricken with his final illness, Guthlac instructs his disciple Beccel, foretelling his own death on the seventh day; his soul departs like a bird to the heavenly home, and a light shines over the fen; Beccel, instructed to tell his sister Pega, buries him and the poem closes with a prayer. The poet's meditation on death — 'death is no man's friend' — frames the narrative.
works.significance: The finest Old English poem on the death of a saint; its bird-image for the soul's flight is among the period's most memorable figures.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; gentler and more meditative than Guthlac A.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 44b-52b); source: Felix's Vita Sancti Guthlaci.
works.characters: Guthlac; Beccel; Pega; the angels
works.structure: A single, intimate deathbed narrative: prophecy, farewell dialogue, and the ascent of the soul, framed by prologue and prayer.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; distinct authorship from Guthlac A is generally accepted.

works.title: Guy of Warwick
altTitles: The Romance of Guy of Warwick
works.form: romance in couplets and tail-rhyme stanzas
works.description: The longest and one of the most widely read of the English romances, in couplets and tail-rhyme stanzas: the career of Guy, earl of Warwick, who wins the lady Felice by feats of arms, then renounces the world to fight as God's champion and die as a hermit. Its hero was England's favourite romance champion for three centuries.
works.plot: Guy, a steward's son, wins Felice through tournaments and foreign wars; struck by remorse, he leaves her to do penance as a pilgrim, returning in disguise to defend England against the giant Colbrond at Winchester; recognized only at his death, he is buried by Felice, who follows him in holiness.
works.significance: The romance of Guy fixed the image of the penitent knight in English culture and remained a bestseller until the Civil War; it is central to the study of romance readership.
works.meter: Couplets in the Auchinleck version; tail-rhyme stanzas in later copies.
works.context: Composed c. 1300 from Anglo-Norman sources, drawing on Warwick legend and the cult of Guy; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript and many later copies and prints, into the seventeenth century.
works.characters: Guy; Felice; Colbrond the giant; Reinbrun (their son); Herhaud
works.structure: A two-part structure — chivalric career, then penitential career — with the Colbrond episode and the deathbed recognition as climaxes.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Hali Meiðhad
works.description: An alliterative prose epistle in praise of virginity, addressed to young women contemplating the religious life, in the AB language of the Katherine Group. It contrasts the blessedness of the virgin bride of Christ with the miseries of married life, in a rhetorical tradition going back to patristic treatises on virginity.
works.plot: The author extols virginity as the highest estate, describes the joys of the heavenly bridegroom, and — in famously vivid passages — details the pains and humiliations of marriage and childbearing to urge his readers to choose the better part.
works.significance: The classic Middle English statement of the virginity ideal, and a prime exhibit of the period's energetic anti-matrimonial rhetoric (the counterpart of the Wife of Bath's prologue).
works.meter: Rhythmical, heavily alliterative prose of the AB language group.
works.context: Composed in the early thirteenth-century West Midlands, in the circle of Ancrene Wisse; preserved in Bodleian MS Bodley 34 and BL Cotton MS Titus D.xviii.
works.characters: the virgin reader (addressee); Christ as bridegroom
works.structure: A single sustained exhortation moving from praise of virginity through satiric anatomy of marriage to the rewards of the heavenly marriage.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Handlyng Synne
works.description: Robert Mannyng of Brunne's English verse adaptation (begun 1303) of the Anglo-Norman Manuel des péchés of William of Wadington: a manual of penance in some 12,000 lines expounding the commandments, the deadly sins, the sacraments, and the art of confession, illustrated with scores of exemplary tales. It is the classic Middle English penitential handbook.
works.plot: The poem moves systematically through the commandments and sins, each doctrine illustrated by cautionary exempla — the dancing carolers cursed by a priest, the usurer, the witch of Ely — and concludes with instruction on confession, contrition, and satisfaction.
works.significance: The principal English treatment of penance between the thirteenth-century homilies and Chaucer's Parson's Tale (which draws on related material), and a treasury of the exemplum tradition.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets of plain, efficient didactic verse in the Lincolnshire dialect.
works.context: Begun in 1303 by the Gilbertine canon Robert Mannyng at Sempringham Priory, Lincolnshire, translating Wadington's manual for an English lay audience; preserved in the Vernon and Bodleian Digby manuscripts among others.
works.characters: the exemplary sinners and saints of the tales
works.structure: A didactic sequence organized by commandment, sin, and sacrament, with narrative exempla inset throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed by the author's own preface to 'Robert of Brunne'.

works.title: Havelok the Dane
altTitles: The Lay of Havelok the Dane
works.description: A Lincolnshire romance of some 3,000 lines on the dispossessed prince Havelok, brought up as a kitchen-boy at Grimsby, whose royal birthmark, strength, and marriage to the princess Goldeboru lead to the recovery of the thrones of Denmark and England. Its sympathetic depiction of labouring life and its Lincolnshire topography make it unique among the romances.
works.plot: The orphaned Havelok is saved from the usurper Godard by the fisherman Grim, who flees with him to England; in disguise he serves as a kitchen hand at Lincoln, where the usurper Godrich marries the princess Goldeboru to him in mockery; Havelok's revealed royalty, his defeat of the usurpers, and his double coronation conclude the poem.
works.significance: One of the finest English romances: its realism about work and poverty, and its fusion of folk-tale, dynastic, and hagiographical elements, make it a classic of the genre.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with marked northern (East Midland/Lincolnshire) dialect features.
works.context: Composed c. 1280–90 in Lincolnshire, drawing on local legend (Grimsby's foundation) and Anglo-Norman sources (Lai d'Haveloc, Gaimar); preserved uniquely in Bodleian Library, Laud Misc. 108.
works.characters: Havelok; Goldeboru; Grim the fisherman; Godard; Godrich; Ubbe
works.structure: A double exile-and-restoration plot (Havelok and Goldeboru in parallel), with an interpolated miracle episode and a long climactic battle.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Hickscorner
works.description: An anonymous early morality interlude of the conversion of three rogues — Freewill, Imagination, and the Vice Hickscorner — printed by Wynkyn de Worde c. 1513–15.
works.plot: Freewill and Imagination, fallen into idleness and vice, meet the hardened rogue Hickscorner, who boasts of his crimes and rails at virtue; Pity and Contemplation reprove them, and the three rogues are brought to repentance, confess their sins, and set out on pilgrimage, with the play ending in a vision of the joys of heaven.
works.significance: One of the earliest printed English moralities and the first to centre on the conversion of rogues; its Vice, Hickscorner, is a landmark in the development of the stage devil's comic heir, and its tavern realism anticipates the rogue literature of the Elizabethans.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic passages
works.context: Printed c. 1513–15 by Wynkyn de Worde, in the generation after Everyman; the play's tavern scenes and rogue-cant document the underworld of early Tudor London, and its popularity carried it through editions to the 1560s.
works.characters: Freewill; Imagination; Hickscorner; Pity; Contemplation; Perseverance
works.structure: A continuous morality play in two movements — the rogues' boasting fellowship and their conversion — with the Vice Hickscorner as the play's comic engine.

works.title: Historia Anglorum
works.description: Henry of Huntingdon's history of England from the earliest times to the accession of Henry II in 1154, notable for its vivid battle narratives, its interest in the English past as national history, and the substantial body of original verse — including the political poems addressed to Henry I — embedded in the prose.
works.summary: Ten books (the latest recension) move from Roman and Anglo-Saxon Britain through the Norman kings to the anarchy of Stephen's reign; the work incorporates earlier sources (Bede, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle) while supplying independent contemporary witness for the twelfth century, including the famous account of the Battle of Lincoln.
works.significance: A principal narrative source for the reign of Stephen, and a central text of twelfth-century English national historiography; its verse makes it a bridge between Anglo-Latin and vernacular literary traditions.

editions.title: Historia Anglorum: The History of the English People

works.title: Historia Brittonum
works.form: history and chronicle (composite) in Latin prose
works.description: A composite history of the Britons compiled in Wales in 829/30 and traditionally attributed to Nennius: genealogies, origin legends (the Trojan descent of the Britons), the lives of St Patrick and St Germanus, and the earliest datable Arthur material — the list of Arthur's twelve battles culminating at Mount Badon.
works.plot: The work assembles disparate materials on the age of the world, the Trojan origins of the Britons, the Roman occupation, Vortigern and the coming of the Saxons, the boy-prophet Ambrosius, the wars of Arthur ('dux bellorum'), the genealogies of the Saxon and Welsh kings, and the 'wonders of Britain' — an anthology of British historical memory rather than a continuous history.
works.significance: The earliest extended Arthurian text in insular literature; the principal quarry of later Welsh and English Arthurian history (Geoffrey of Monmouth).
works.meter: Latin prose of varying registers.
works.context: Compiled in Gwynedd c. 829/30 during the Mercian ascendancy in Wales; preserved in some forty manuscripts in Welsh, English, and continental recensions.
works.characters: Vortigern; Ambrosius; Arthur; Patrick; Germanus; Hengist and Horsa
works.structure: Compilatory: a sequence of heterogeneous sections of varying provenance, several marked as the work of 'Nennius the disciple of Elvodugus'.
works.attributionNotes: The prologue attributes the compilation to Nennius, but not all manuscripts carry it; the work is demonstrably composite.
sources: The Oxford Handbook of Tudor Literature, 1485–1603

works.title: Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum
altTitles: Ecclesiastical History of the English People
works.form: history and chronicle (ecclesiastical history) in Latin prose
works.description: Bede's masterpiece, completed in 731: the history of the English church and people from Caesar's invasions to 731, in five books. It is the primary narrative source for early Anglo-Saxon history, the origin of the AD dating system's general use, and the conduit through which Cædmon's Hymn and much else survives.
works.plot: The five books trace the conversion of the English kingdoms — the mission of Augustine to Kent (597), the Northumbrian mission of Paulinus and Aidan, the Synod of Whitby (664) — interspersed with saints' lives (Cuthbert, Æthelthryth), miracles, letters, and the famous account of the poet Cædmon; the work closes with a summary of Britain's ecclesiastical state and Bede's autobiographical colophon.
works.significance: 'The father of English history'; the indispensable source for the first three centuries of English Christianity and for the early vernacular poetic record.
works.meter: Latin prose of classical clarity; contains the earliest recorded English verse (Cædmon's Hymn) in paraphrase.
works.context: Composed at the twin monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow from earlier annals, lives, and documents; dedicated to King Ceolwulf of Northumbria.
works.characters: Augustine of Canterbury; Æthelberht; Edwin; Oswald; Aidan; Hild; Cuthbert; Cædmon; Theodore; Wilfrid
works.structure: Annalistic-chronological within each book, organized by kingdom and diocese; documentary (letters, synods) and hagiographical materials are woven into the narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Bede's authorship is certain (his own colophon).

editions.title: Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English People
editions.editor: Bertram Colgrave and R. A. B. Mynors (eds.)

sources: The Riverside Chaucer, 3rd edition

works.title: Historia Regum Britanniae
altTitles: The History of the Kings of Britain
works.description: Pseudohistorical chronicle tracing the kings of Britain from the legendary Brutus of Troy to the Saxon conquest, the principal source of the Arthurian legend in England. Geoffrey claims to translate 'a certain very ancient book in the British tongue' given him by Walter, archdeacon of Oxford; its authority was attacked by William of Newburgh and Gerald of Wales but it decisively shaped medieval British historiography.
works.summary: Geoffrey of Monmouth narrates the foundation of Britain by Brutus, a descendant of Aeneas, and proceeds through the reigns of the legendary kings — Lear, Cymbeline, and above all Arthur, whose conquests extend over much of Europe — to the Saxon domination and the prophecies of Merlin (the Prophetiae Merlini, later incorporated as Book VII). The work made Arthur a pan-European figure and provided the framework for Wace, Layamon, and the later chronicle tradition.
works.significance: The single most influential piece of British historical writing of the Middle Ages: over 200 manuscripts survive, and it furnished the matter of Britain for romance, chronicle, and national myth from Wace's Roman de Brut to Malory and beyond.

editions.title: The History of the Kings of Britain

works.title: Homiletic Fragment I and II
works.manuscriptDate: Vercelli Book (Vercelli, Biblioteca Capitolare CXVII), late tenth century
works.description: Two homiletic poems in the Vercelli Book. Homiletic Fragment I (47 lines) is a meditation on deceitful friendship, comparing the false friend to the bee whose honey is sweet but whose sting is deadly. Homiletic Fragment II (20 lines) laments man's hardness of heart amid the world's sorrows.
works.plot: Fragment I warns against the friend who speaks fair but plots evil, elaborating the image of the bee through biblical and proverbial wisdom. Fragment II meditates on grief and the human failure to heed the truth, in a fragmentary surviving text.
works.significance: Witnesses to the close relationship between Old English homiletic prose and verse, and to the moral psychology of the late Anglo-Saxon church.
works.meter: Alliterative long line in the homiletic manner of the Vercelli Book's prose sermons; both texts are imperfectly preserved.
works.context: The Vercelli Book pairs these poems with its collection of doomsday homilies and with The Dream of the Rood, Elene, and Andreas; the fragments belong to the same culture of vernacular preaching and moral verse.
works.structure: Fragment I develops a single governing simile (the treacherous friend as bee) with proverbial expansions; Fragment II is a broken meditation on sorrow and heedlessness.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The two fragments are distinct poems.

works.title: Incendium Amoris
works.description: Richard Rolle's principal Latin treatise (c. 1340–43), an autobiographical and doctrinal account of the contemplative life as he himself had experienced it: the warmth of divine love (calor), its sweetness (dulcor), and its song (canor), with instruction on prayer, meditation, and the discernment of spirits. The founding text of the English mystical tradition.
works.plot: Rolle recounts his own conversion and his experience of the three degrees of love — fire, sweetness, and heavenly song — defends the contemplative life against its critics, and teaches the reader to progress from reading through prayer to the 'fire of love' that unites the soul to God.
works.significance: The first major work of the English mystical tradition and the fountainhead of its characteristic language of warmth, sweetness, and song.
works.meter: Latin prose, rhetorical and warm, with the psalm commentary woven in.
works.context: Composed c. 1340–43 in the north of England, early in Rolle's hermit career, and later translated into Middle English (the Fire of Love); among the most widely read Latin spiritual works of the English fourteenth century.
works.characters: Rolle (as witness and teacher)
works.structure: A prologue and forty-two chapters mixing autobiography, doctrine, and scriptural commentary, with the author's own experience as the organizing proof.
works.attributionNotes: Rolle's authorship secure.

works.title: Institutes of Polity
altTitles: Institutes of Polity, Civil and Ecclesiastical
works.form: didactic treatise (political theology) in Old English prose
works.description: Wulfstan's treatise on the orders of Christian society: the duties of the king, the bishops, the clergy, the nobles, and the people in a rightly ordered realm — 'eight columns that support the kingdom'. The clearest statement of Anglo-Saxon political theology and the seedbed of Wulfstan's law codes.
works.plot: The treatise defines each estate's office: the king shall protect the church and rule justly; bishops shall teach and judge; the clergy shall keep chastity and learning; ealdormen shall give righteous judgments; the people shall labour and obey — all bound by the law of God, whose breach brings ruin on the land.
works.significance: The fullest Anglo-Saxon statement of the theory of the Christian commonwealth.
works.meter: Wulfstan's rhythmical two-stress prose.
works.context: Composed c. 1008-1020 in the crisis of Æthelred's reign and revised under Cnut; preserved in later eleventh-century manuscripts, chiefly Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201.
works.characters: the Christian king; the bishops; the estates of the realm
works.structure: A systematic treatise in chapters on the estates of the realm, from the heavenly king down through the earthly orders.
works.attributionNotes: Wulfstan's authorship is established on stylistic grounds.

works.title: Interlude of Youth
works.description: An anonymous morality interlude of the fall and repentance of Youth, composed c. 1513–14 and printed c. 1530–35; a compact dramatization of the prodigal's return.
works.plot: Youth, flattered by Riot, Pride, and Lechery, abandons Charity and Humility for the tavern and the stews; Charity and Humility lament and warn him, and Youth, brought low, repents and returns to virtue, ending with a prayer for the king and the audience's amendment.
works.significance: A compact and influential example of the early Tudor morality, dramatizing the prodigal theme that would run through the century to the Elizabethan stage; it survives as a witness to the interlude's household origins.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic songs
works.context: Composed c. 1513–14, probably for a noble household (the prayer for the king suggests courtly performance), and printed c. 1530–35; it belongs to the same early Tudor wave as Hickscorner and Magnificence, in which the morality play becomes a vehicle for aristocratic moral counsel.
works.characters: Youth; Charity; Humility; Riot; Pride; Lechery
works.structure: A short two-part morality play of temptation and return, with the Vices' songs and taunts alternating with Charity's warnings.

works.title: Itinerarium Cambriae
works.description: Gerald of Wales's account of the preaching tour of Wales undertaken in 1188 with Archbishop Baldwin of Canterbury to recruit for the Third Crusade, combining topographical description, ethnography of the Welsh, anecdote, and vigorous self-promotion; the companion work to the Descriptio Cambriae (1194).
works.summary: Gerald narrates the itinerary of Baldwin's mission through south and north Wales, recording the sermons, the reception of the party, local marvels and legends, the character and customs of the Welsh, and his own prominent role in the enterprise; the two books culminate in the preaching of the cross.
works.significance: One of the finest works of twelfth-century travel and ethnographic writing, a primary source for medieval Wales, and a major witness to the Latin literary culture of the Welsh marches.

works.title: Jacob and Esau
altTitles: A New Mery and Wittie Comedie or Enterlude, Newely Imprinted, Treating upon the Historie of Jacob and Esau
works.description: An anonymous Protestant biblical interlude on the story of Jacob and Esau from Genesis, printed in 1568; one of the liveliest mid-century dramatizations of the doctrine of election.
works.plot: The play follows Genesis 25–27: the differing natures of the twins Jacob and Esau, the sale of the birthright for a pottage, Isaac's blessing of Jacob obtained through Rebecca's counsel, and Esau's rage and reconciliation; the serious matter of election is framed by the comic servants of the household (Ragan, Mido, and the boy Abra) whose tricks and misadventures mirror the plot.
works.significance: The most accomplished of the mid-century biblical interludes and an important document of Protestant dramatic theory; its comic subplot anticipates the structure of Elizabethan biblical and history plays.
works.meter: Couplets and 'rhyming fourteeners'
works.context: Composed c. 1550–58 in the Edwardian and Marian years, when the doctrine of predestination was at the centre of English religious debate; the play's prologue makes the case for the godly theatre, and it was printed in 1568 for the Elizabethan market.
works.characters: Isaac; Rebecca; Jacob; Esau; Ragan; Mido; Abra; Deborah; Hanan
works.structure: Five acts with act and scene divisions, alternating the biblical action with a fully developed comic subplot, and a prologue arguing that election is the play's theme.

works.title: Johan Johan
altTitles: A Mery Play between Johan Johan the Husbande, Tyb his Wyfe, and Syr Jhan the Preest
works.description: John Heywood's one-act farce of a cuckolded husband sent on errands by his wife and her lover the priest; printed by William Rastell in 1533.
works.plot: Johan Johan, suspecting his wife Tyb of entertaining Sir John the priest, is dispatched by her on a series of errands — to mend a pail, to fetch wax — while she dines with the priest; returning to find them feasting on a pie he was sent away from, Johan at last drives the priest out with blows, and the play ends with the husband's triumphant threat to beat Tyb too.
works.significance: The first English farce on the theme of the cuckolded husband and the anticlerical triangle that would recur through the century; its rapid domestic action makes it the most theatrically economical of Heywood's plays.
works.meter: Couplets
works.context: Printed in 1533 by Rastell, the year that saw the first parliamentary attacks on clerical marriage jurisdiction and mortuary fees; the play's satire of the lecherous parish priest draws on the fabliau tradition of Chaucer's Miller's Tale and the popular anticlerical jest.
works.characters: Johan Johan; Tyb (his wife); Sir John (the priest)
works.structure: A single-scene farce of errands and discovery, ending in a cudgel-fight; the play is a dramatization of the anti-clerical fabliau of the priest, the wife, and the credulous husband.

works.title: Judith
works.form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A fragmentary poem of 349 lines (the opening is lost) retelling the apocryphal Book of Judith: the Hebrew heroine beheads the Assyrian general Holofernes in his tent and rouses her people to victory. The poem recasts the biblical heroine as a figure of the heroic tradition — a maiden of God wielding the sword against the enemies of her people.
works.plot: Judith, beautiful and wise, is brought to the drunken Holofernes's tent; praying for aid, she seizes his sword and strikes off his head in two blows, then carries the head back to Bethulia in a food-bag. At dawn she shows the head to her people and delivers a speech of triumph; the Hebrews attack the leaderless Assyrians, who flee; Judith receives the spoils of Holofernes as her reward, and the poem ends with praise of God.
works.significance: The finest Old English poem on a female biblical hero; a masterly fusion of heroic style and devotional purpose.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre, with vigorous battle diction.
works.context: Preserved in the Nowell Codex (British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv) immediately after Beowulf; the biblical book of Judith was known to the Anglo-Saxons through the Vulgate and Ælfric's later prose homily on the same subject.
works.characters: Judith; Holofernes; the Bethulians
works.structure: Dramatic narrative in the heroic manner: the tent scene, the return, the battle, and the distribution of spoils; the heroine's speeches drive the action.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Juliana
works.form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: Cynewulf's signed poem of 731 lines on the passion of St Juliana of Nicomedia: the virgin martyr who withstands her pagan suitor, defeats a demon sent to tempt her, and endures torture and death. The poem contains the most extended debate between saint and demon in Old English.
works.plot: Juliana refuses to marry the prefect Eleusius unless he converts; denounced by her father, she is beaten, hung by the hair, and thrown in prison, where a demon disguised as an angel urges her to yield; she seizes him and forces him to confess his works, then is subjected to fire and a boiling cauldron, and finally beheaded — her soul received into heaven, her persecutors drowned at sea. The epilogue carries Cynewulf's runic signature.
works.significance: The classic Old English virgin-martyr poem and the fullest statement of the saint-demon debate.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 65b-76v); based on a Latin passio of Juliana.
works.characters: Juliana; Eleusius; Africanus (her father); the demon; the angel
works.structure: A debate-driven passio: successive confrontations (suitor, father, demon, judge) leading to martyrdom, framed by the demon's confession of the history of evil and the poet's runic prayer.
works.attributionNotes: Signed by Cynewulf in runes.

works.title: King Hart
works.description: Douglas's allegory of the life of man: King Hart rules his castle of the body with the five senses as his servants until Dame Pleasance and her court — Youthheid, Fresche Delyte, Wantonness — enter and corrupt him; age, sickness, and death storm the castle, and the soul departs. The great Scots allegory of the body politic and the body natural.
works.plot: King Hart, counselled by Ressoun, admits Dame Pleasance and her court; the castle falls into riot; Conscience, Ressoun, and Wisdome are driven out; Age besieges and takes the castle, and Hart dies, leaving his soul to God's judgement.
works.significance: The finest Scots allegory of the body's rule and a bridge between the moralities and the Renaissance anatomy of the self; admired by the later Scots poets.
works.meter: Stanzaic verse in the Chaucerian tradition; vigorous personification allegory.
works.context: Written in Douglas's maturity, perhaps after the death of James IV at Flodden (1513); the castle's fall shadows the fall of the king's court.
works.characters: King Hart; Dame Pleasance; Youthheid; Fresche Delyte; Ressoun; Conscience; Age; Decrepitness
works.structure: A sustained allegory of the besieged castle in the morality tradition, moving from the entrance of pleasure through riot to death and judgement.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Douglas on manuscript authority; the attribution is generally accepted.

works.title: King Horn
works.description: The earliest surviving Middle English romance, some 1,500 short couplet lines telling the exile, adventures, and restoration of Horn, son of the murdered king of Suddene, who wins the love of Rymenhild, defeats the Saracen invaders, and regains his kingdom. Its spare, ballad-like narrative makes it the classic of the 'ancestral romance' of exile and return.
works.plot: Horn, cast adrift by the invaders who killed his father, grows up at the court of King Aylmar, where Rymenhild loves him; exiled through the envy of Fikenhild, he proves himself in Ireland, rescues Rymenhild from a forced marriage in disguise as a beggar, and returns to avenge his father and reclaim Suddene.
works.significance: The fountainhead of the English romance tradition and the earliest witness to the exile-and-return plot that governs the genre.
works.meter: Short rhyming couplets, often of three stresses, with formulaic diction.
works.context: Composed c. 1225 in the south of England from an Anglo-Norman source (the Romance of Horn of Thomas); preserved in Cambridge University Library MS Gg.4.27 (c. 1300) and two later manuscripts.
works.characters: Horn; Rymenhild; Fikenhild; King Aylmar; Athulf; the Saracen invaders
works.structure: A tripartite exile-and-return plot with disguise, recognition, and wedding scenes; narrated in terse couplets with abrupt transitions.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

editions.title: King Horn: An Edition Based on Cambridge University Library MS Gg.4.27(2)

works.title: King Johan
works.description: John Bale's historical morality play of King John, composed c. 1538 and surviving in a single manuscript revised in the 1550s; regarded as the first English history play.
works.plot: King John, the champion of England's ancient liberties against the papal usurpation, is beset by the allegorical forces of Rome — Sedition, Dissimulation, Usurped Power, Private Wealth — and the clergy, who stir rebellion and bring about his poisoning by Dissimulation disguised as a monk; Widow England and her allies Verity and Imperial Majesty restore the true succession, and the play ends with John vindicated as a proto-Protestant martyr and the papal power expelled.
works.significance: The first English history play: its fusion of the morality tradition with national history and its anti-papal reading of King John set the pattern for the Elizabethan history play, directly anticipating Shakespeare's King John.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic passages
works.context: Composed c. 1538 during Bale's Protestant exile/activity under Cromwell's patronage, at the moment when Henry VIII's break with Rome made King John a usable hero; Bale revised the play for Elizabeth (the manuscript addresses her), aligning it with the Elizabethan settlement's anti-papal politics.
works.characters: King John; Widow England; Sedition; Dissimulation; Usurped Power; Private Wealth; Verity; Imperial Majesty; Nobility; Clergy; Civil Order; Stephen Langton; Pope Innocent III
works.structure: A two-part play mixing historical persons (John, Stephen Langton, the Pope) with morality personifications, revised by Bale to address Elizabeth I; the structure alternates the king's historical action with the Vices' comic plotting.

editions.title: The Complete Plays of John Bale, vol. 1

works.title: Lacnunga
works.form: medical manual and charm collection (Old English prose and verse)
works.description: A less orderly but more eclectic collection of remedies, charms, and prayers than Bald's Leechbook, compiled in the early eleventh century. It is best known for preserving the pagan-tinged metrical charms — above all the Nine Herbs Charm — alongside Christian prayers and learned Latin-derived recipes.
works.plot: The collection gathers remedies for wounds, fevers, eye and ear complaints, and childbirth, mixing herbal preparations with spoken charms and ritual instructions; its metrical charms invoke Woden and the herbs' powers while concluding with Christian formulas, in a characteristic fusion of traditions.
works.significance: The richest source of Old English charms, including the great Nine Herbs Charm, and a unique window onto the interface of learned medicine, popular healing, and pagan survival in late Anglo-Saxon England.
works.meter: The embedded charms are in alliterative verse (the Nine Herbs Charm, the Journey Charm); the surrounding recipes are plain instructional prose.
works.context: The manuscript belongs to the late Old English period's flourishing of vernacular medicine, when remedies circulated in monastic and lay households; the charms preserve elements of Germanic pre-Christian ritual under a Christian surface, a central document of the 'Christian-pagan synthesis'.
works.structure: A compilation in no strict order, grouping remedies by source rather than ailment; the metrical charms stand out from the surrounding prose as the collection's literary high points.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous compilation; the name 'Lacnunga' ('Remedies') is editorial, from the first remedy's heading.

editions.title: Anglo-Saxon Remedies, Charms, and Prayers from British Library MS Harley 585: The Lacnunga

works.title: Lament for the Makaris
works.description: William Dunbar's elegy on the poets ('makaris') of Scotland and the world (c. 1505, 100 lines): a procession of the dead — Chaucer, Lydgate, Gower, Henryson, and the court poets of the Stewart kings — each stanza closed by the refrain 'Timor mortis conturbat me' (the fear of death troubles me). The greatest short elegy of the Scottish tradition, and the poem that gave the makars their name.
works.plot: The poet, reflecting that all things must die, calls the roll of the dead poets: first the great English trio of Chaucer, Gower, and Lydgate, then the Scottish makers — Barbour, Hary, Holland, and above all 'the noble rhetor' Henryson — and finally the court poets of his own youth, closing with the fear of death and the petition that God provide for the poet before he joins them.
works.significance: One of the great elegies in the language: its roll-call fixed the canon of the makars and its refrain became the proverbial voice of late medieval mortality.
works.meter: Four-line stanzas with the Latin refrain, austere and musical.
works.context: Composed c. 1505 at the court of James IV, when Dunbar's generation was passing and the print era beginning; printed by Chepman and Myllar (1508); it names the Scottish tradition 'makaris' for all later criticism.
works.characters: Dunbar (speaker); the dead poets (Chaucer, Gower, Lydgate, Barbour, Hary, Henryson, and others)
works.structure: Twenty-five stanzas of single-movement elegy, the refrain tolling each catalogue entry, in the ubi sunt tradition.
works.attributionNotes: Dunbar's authorship secure.

works.title: Lancelot of the Laik
works.description: A Scottish romance of some 3,500 lines adapting the French prose Lancelot: Arthur's war with Galiot, Lancelot's secret love for Guinevere, and the dream-vision in which the lover's conscience anatomizes his state. The only Scottish Arthurian romance, composed in the age of the makars for a court that read both Chaucer and the French cycles.
works.plot: Arthur, weakened by tyranny and war with the rebel Galiot, is saved by Lancelot, who fights incognito and compels Galiot's submission; the second half turns inward, as a dream allegory of love's joys and pains lays bare Lancelot's adulterous devotion to the queen.
works.significance: The sole Scottish Arthurian romance and a significant witness to the reception of French Arthurian prose in the Stewart court.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets in Older Scots, with aureate ornament.
works.context: Composed c. 1460–79 in Scotland, adapting the French prose Lancelot and the amatory allegory tradition; preserved uniquely in Cambridge University Library MS Kk.1.5 (c. 1500).
works.characters: Lancelot; Arthur; Guinevere; Galiot
works.structure: A two-part structure — chivalric war, then amatory dream vision — that joins the French romance of arms to the Chaucerian allegory of love.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Laterculus Malalianus
altTitles: The Laterculus Malalianus of Theodore of Tarsus
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 139 (twelfth century)
works.description: A Latin exegetical and chronographical treatise on the life of Christ, attributed to Theodore of Tarsus, archbishop of Canterbury, and written at Canterbury in the 670s. Based on the Greek chronography of John Malalas, it expounds the gospel account of Christ's life in the light of eastern exegesis and computes the ages of the world; it is the principal surviving witness to the school of Theodore.
works.plot: The treatise moves through the life of Christ from the Incarnation to the Passion, glossing each episode with eastern exegetical traditions (on the Virgin, the baptism, the temptations, the crucifixion) and interweaving chronographical calculations of the world's ages drawn from Malalas's chronicle, concluding with eschatological reflection on the last things.
works.significance: The earliest theological work composed in England, and the founding document of the Canterbury school that made England a centre of Greek-influenced Latin learning; a unique witness to the eastern roots of Anglo-Saxon exegesis.
works.context: Written when Theodore and Hadrian were building the school of Canterbury, the treatise shows the direct importation of Greek and Syriac learning into England; the same exegetical traditions appear in the Canterbury biblical commentaries preserved in Milan, and Theodore's pupils carried them into the Northumbrian Renaissance of Bede.
works.structure: A continuous exegetical treatise organized by the gospel narrative, with digressions into chronology and typology; the style is dense and allusive, marked by the Greek learning of its source.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Theodore of Tarsus on the basis of its Greek sources, its Canterbury origin, and its consistent transmission with Theodore's school texts; the attribution is widely accepted but rests on inference rather than explicit ascription.

works.title: Layamon's Brut
works.description: Layamon's verse chronicle of Britain, some 16,000 lines adapting Wace's Roman de Brut with additions from Welsh and English tradition, from the Trojan Brutus to the Saxon conquest, including the fullest early English account of King Arthur. It is the first major treatment of the Arthurian legend in English.
works.plot: Following the Trojan Brutus's settlement of Britain, the poem recounts the line of British kings — Lear, Cymbeline, and above all Arthur, whose conquests, Round Table, and death it narrates at length — down to the Saxon victory and Arthur's prophesied return.
works.significance: The first Arthurian epic in English and the bridge from the alliterative tradition to Middle English romance; its Arthur material influenced the entire subsequent Arthurian tradition in England.
works.meter: A hybrid line blending the native alliterative half-line with loose rhyme and French-derived couplets; formulaic and archaic diction.
works.context: Composed by the priest Layamon of Areley Kings, Worcestershire, c. 1190–1215, in the generation after the loss of Normandy, when English was re-emerging as a literary language; preserved in BL Cotton MS Caligula A.ix (earlier, longer) and Cotton MS Otho C.xiii (later, shortened, fire-damaged).
works.characters: Brutus; King Lear; Arthur; Guinevere; Merlin; Vortigern; Hengest; Cadwalader
works.structure: A continuous regnal chronicle organized by successive kings, with Arthur as its structural and emotional centre.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship secured by the prologue's self-naming of Layamon, priest of Ernleye (Areley Kings).

editions.title: Layamon's Brut, or Hystoria Brutonum
editions.editor: W. R. J. Barron and S. C. Weinberg (eds.)

works.title: Le Morte Darthur
altTitles: The Whole Book of King Arthur and of His Noble Knights of the Round Table
works.description: Sir Thomas Malory's great prose compilation of the Arthurian legend, completed in prison in 1469–70 and printed by Caxton in 1485: from the sword in the stone and the winning of Guinevere, through the adventures of Lancelot, Tristram, and the Grail quest, to the breaking of the Round Table, the last battle, and Arthur's passing to Avalon. The definitive English Arthurian book.
works.plot: Malory weaves the French prose cycles and English alliterative poems into a single tragic narrative: Arthur's accession and marriage, the founding of the Round Table, the quests and loves of its knights, the Grail quest that divides the fellowship, the adultery of Lancelot and Guinevere, and the final war against Mordred in which Arthur falls — his body borne to Avalon, his epitaph 'Rex quondam Rexque futurus'.
works.significance: The summit of English Arthurian literature and the conduit of the Arthurian story to Spenser, Tennyson, and the modern novel; its vision of chivalry — at once idealized and doomed — is the period's most enduring legacy.
works.meter: Prose: paratactic, ritual, and rhythmic, with the famous Malorian cadence of balanced clauses and repeated key words.
works.context: Completed by the 'knight prisoner' Thomas Malory in the ninth year of Edward IV (1469–70), during the Wars of the Roses; Caxton's 1485 print fixed the text for three centuries until the discovery of the Winchester manuscript (1934) revealed the pre-print version.
works.characters: Arthur; Lancelot; Guinevere; Gawain; Tristram; Isolde; Galahad; Merlin; Morgan le Fay; Mordred
works.structure: Eight books (Caxton's twenty-one divisions) of interlaced adventure compressed into linear narrative, with the Grail and the Lancelot-Guinevere tragedy as the arcs that break the fellowship.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Sir Thomas Malory of Newbold Revel (d. 1471) on the evidence of the colophons; the identification is widely though not universally accepted.

editions.title: The Works of Sir Thomas Malory
editions.editor: Eugène Vinaver (ed.); rev. P. J. C. Field

works.title: Legends of Holy Women
works.description: Osbern Bokenham's collection of thirteen verse lives of female saints, written 1443–47 at the request of a circle of East Anglian patrons, several of them women: Margaret, Anne, Christine, the Eleven Thousand Virgins, Faith, Agnes, Dorothy, Mary Magdalene, Katherine, Cecilia, Agatha, Lucy, and Elizabeth of Hungary. The major fifteenth-century English legendary of women's sanctity.
works.plot: Each life narrates the saint's birth, conversion, and martyrdom (or holy death), with the debates, torments, and miracles of the genre; the framing prologues record the patrons who commissioned each legend, making the work a document of literary patronage as much as of hagiography.
works.significance: The principal fifteenth-century English collection of female saints' lives and a uniquely documented instance of women's literary patronage in the period.
works.meter: Couplets and rhyme royal in the Lydgatean style, aureate but warm.
works.context: Composed 1443–47 by the Augustinian friar Osbern Bokenham of Stoke by Clare, Suffolk, for Lady Katherine Denston, Isabel Hunt, and other East Anglian gentry women; preserved in BL Arundel MS 327 (the author's own manuscript).
works.characters: St Margaret; St Anne; St Katherine; St Mary Magdalene; St Cecilia; and the other saints; Bokenham (narrator)
works.structure: A sequence of independent verse legends, each with its own prologue naming the patron, in the Chaucerian-Lydgatean manner.
works.attributionNotes: Bokenham's authorship secure; he names himself and his patrons throughout.

works.title: Life of King Alfred
works.description: Asser's biography of King Alfred, written in 893 by the Welsh bishop of Sherborne: the principal contemporary portrait of the king — his childhood, illnesses, wars against the Vikings, piety, and program of learning — and the main source for the Alfredian Renaissance.
works.plot: The life follows Alfred from birth (849) through his education and accession (871), the Viking wars culminating in Edington (878) and the treaty with Guthrum, the rebuilding of London and the kingdom's defences, and the gathering of scholars — Werferth, Plegmund, Æthelstan, Grimbald, John the Old Saxon — for the translation program; an annalistic section covers the years to 887, and the work ends with Alfred's daily round of prayer, judgment, and study.
works.significance: The primary source for Alfred's reign and the only near-contemporary biography of an Anglo-Saxon king.
works.meter: Latin prose of the ninth-century insular school.
works.context: Composed 893 at the West Saxon court; the unique manuscript (British Library, Cotton MS Otho A.xii) was largely destroyed in 1731, and the text rests on the 1574 edition and sixteenth-century transcripts.
works.characters: Alfred; Asser (narrator); Guthrum; Werferth; Plegmund; Ealhswith
works.structure: Biography modelled on Einhard's Charlemagne, with an embedded chronicle of the years 849-887 and anecdotal set-pieces (the story of the cakes is a later interpolation).
works.attributionNotes: Asser's authorship is stated in the text and generally accepted after long debate.
