sources: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume B: The Sixteenth Century and the Early Seventeenth Century

works.title: Lily's Grammar
works.description: The authorized Latin grammar of the English schools, compiled from the grammars of William Lily and John Colet, edited and revised by Erasmus, and imposed by royal proclamation of Henry VIII in 1540 as the single grammar to be used in all schools.
works.plot: A textbook in two parts: the English 'Introduction of the Eight Parts of Speech' (the Accidence) and the Latin 'Brevissima Institutio' (syntax and prosody), with the famous prefatory poem 'Carmen de Moribus' on schoolboy manners.
works.significance: The most influential textbook in the history of English education: in use (as the 'Eton Grammar') for three centuries, it shaped the Latinity of every educated English writer from Shakespeare to Johnson, and its jingling rules became proverbial.
works.meter: Prose with Latin verse paradigms
works.context: The grammar grew out of Colet's statutes for St Paul's School (c. 1509), Lily's part in its composition, and Erasmus's revisions; after Lily's death (1522) it was printed in various forms until the royal proclamation of 1540 and the authorized edition of 1549 standardized it, making it the one book every grammar-school boy knew.
works.structure: Two-part pedagogical manual, with rules, paradigms, and examples arranged for memorization.
works.attributionNotes: A collaborative compilation traditionally credited to William Lily as first high master of St Paul's; Colet and Erasmus contributed substantially, and the standard attribution to Lily is conventional rather than strictly authorial.

works.title: Linacre's Galen translations
altTitles: The Galen Translations of Thomas Linacre
works.description: Thomas Linacre's Latin translations of six treatises of Galen, printed by Richard Pynson between 1521 and 1523, which restored the Greek Galen to European medicine and established Linacre as the founder of the English school of medical humanism.
works.plot: The translations cover Galen's De sanitate tuenda, Methodus medendi, De temperamentis, De naturalibus facultatibus, De pulsuum usu, and De symptomatum differentiis, rendered into a purified humanist Latin from the Greek texts Linacre collated.
works.significance: The founding texts of English medical humanism: by purging the medieval Latin Galen of Arabist corruption, Linacre transformed European medical education and helped found the Royal College of Physicians (1518), of which he was first president.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Translated c. 1517–23 after Linacre's Greek studies under Chalcondyles and Politian in Italy; Pynson printed the treatises in 1521–23, and they were reprinted on the continent, remaining the standard Latin Galen for over a century.
works.structure: Six separate treatises translated and printed with prefaces to Henry VIII and to Linacre's medical colleagues.

works.title: Lives of Saints
works.form: hagiography (saints' lives) in Old English prose
works.description: Ælfric's collection of saints' lives, passions, and legends (c. 993-998), composed for his patron Æthelweard: the largest vernacular hagiographical collection of the Anglo-Saxon period — virgins, martyrs, kings, and hermits of the universal church, told in Ælfric's rhythmical prose with his characteristic doctrinal care.
works.plot: The lives recount the passions of the early martyrs (Agnes, Alban, Lucy, the Forty Soldiers), the deeds of the virgin saints (Æthelthryth, Agatha, Cecilia), the kings and missionaries of England (Edmund, Oswald, Swithun, Cuthbert), and the great ascetics (Antony, Basil, Martin, Benedict) — each life framed by Ælfric's homiletic introductions and conclusions drawing out the moral for his audience.
works.significance: The fullest vernacular hagiography of the period; the principal vehicle of the saints' cults in late Anglo-Saxon England.
works.meter: Rhythmical, alliterative prose.
works.context: Composed at Cerne Abbas c. 993-998; the principal manuscript is British Library, Cotton MS Julius E.vii.
works.characters: the saints of the collection; Æthelweard and Æthelmær (patrons)
works.structure: A collection of over thirty independent lives, each a self-contained narrative homily.
works.attributionNotes: Ælfric's authorship is certain.

works.title: Lusty Juventus
works.description: A Protestant morality interlude of the youth Juventus, tempted by Hypocrisy and the devil but restored by Good Counsel and God's Merciful Promises; printed c. 1550 with the author's name given as R. Wever.
works.plot: Juventus (Youth), fresh from his conversion, is tempted by the devil's instruments — Hypocrisy, Fellowship, and Abominable Living — who draw him into sin and despair; Good Counsel and Knowledge recall him, God's Merciful Promises assures him of forgiveness through Christ, and the play ends with Juventus's restoration and a call to the audience to follow his example.
works.significance: The most explicitly doctrinal of the Edwardian moralities and a prime example of the interlude as Reformation propaganda; its title character became the proverbial type of the reformed youth.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic passages
works.context: Composed in the early years of the Edwardian Reformation (c. 1547–53) and printed c. 1550; its polemic against hypocrisy and works-righteousness and its emphasis on justification by faith make it a direct dramatic expression of Protestant doctrine for a young audience.
works.characters: Juventus; Good Counsel; Knowledge; God's Merciful Promises; The Devil; Hypocrisy; Fellowship; Abominable Living
works.structure: A continuous morality play of temptation, fall, and restoration, with the devil and Hypocrisy as the comic Vices and a concluding address to the young.
works.attributionNotes: The title page names 'R. Wever' as author; nothing further is known of him, and the ascription cannot be independently confirmed.

works.title: Magnificence
works.description: Skelton's morality play: Prince Magnificence, a figure of the good ruler (and transparently of Henry VIII), is seduced by the courtly vices — Fansy, Counterfeit Countenance, Cloaked Collusion, Courtly Abusion — into riot and misrule, stripped of his wealth and driven to despair, and finally restored by Good Hope, Perseverance, and Measure.
works.plot: Liberty and Measure advise the Prince against Fansy; Magnificence follows the vices, is robbed and reduced to suicidal despair by Adversity, and is rescued by Good Hope, Redress, and Perseverance, who restore him to the rule of Measure.
works.significance: The first English morality play with a political programme and the bridge between the medieval moralities and the Tudor interludes; it established the genre of the king-as-everyman that Bale and the Elizabethans inherited.
works.meter: Couplets and short stanzas of functional verse, with Skeltonic flourishes in the Vice speeches.
works.context: Written in the years of Wolsey's ascendancy, when Skelton watched the young king's government with alarm; the play reads as a warning to Henry VIII against misrule and extravagance.
works.characters: Magnificence; Fansy; Counterfeit Countenance; Cloaked Collusion; Courtly Abusion; Adversity; Good Hope; Perseverance; Measure
works.structure: A full-scale morality in the tradition of Everyman, with a political allegory of the prince's fall and amendment; the Vice roles carry the comic weight.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: John Skelton: The Complete English Poems

works.title: Mandeville's Travels
altTitles: The Voyage and Travels of Sir John Mandeville
works.description: The Book of Sir John Mandeville, the most popular travel book of the Middle Ages: a compilation, originally in French (c. 1357), of pilgrimage routes to Jerusalem, the marvels of Asia, the lands of Prester John, and the wonders of the East, framed by the persona of an English knight of St Albans whose travels are largely fictive. Its Middle English versions (from c. 1375) circulated more widely than any other travel narrative.
works.plot: The narrator describes the way to Jerusalem and the holy places, then the farther East — Egypt, India, Cathay, the isles of the East — collecting marvels (the vegetable lamb, the phoenix, the fountain of youth), the palace of Prester John, and the customs of strange peoples, in a geography poised between pilgrimage, wonder, and imperial fantasy.
works.significance: The great medieval bestseller of travel and wonder, and a foundational text of the European imagination of the East — read by explorers into the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Prose: plain, fluent, and endlessly translatable; the English versions descend from the French via Latin.
works.context: Composed in French c. 1357, probably by a clerk in Liège or northern France using genuine itineraries and encyclopedias; translated into English from c. 1375 in several versions (the 'Defective' version foremost); printed by Wynkyn de Worde (1496); Columbus and Raleigh read it.
works.characters: Sir John Mandeville (persona); Prester John; the Great Khan
works.structure: An itinerary organized by regions and routes, with the pilgrimage to Jerusalem as its centre and the marvels of the East as its circumference.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the 'Sir John Mandeville' persona is generally regarded as fictional.

works.title: Mankind
works.description: The liveliest of the English moralities (c. 1465–70): the comedy of Mankind, the East Anglian farmer, tempted from his spade and his beads by Mischief, New Guise, Nowadays, and Nought, and the devil Titivillus, whose whispered discouragements drive him to despair — until Mercy reclaims him. Famous for its scatological comedy and its collection of money from the audience, it shows the morality in its most theatrical form.
works.plot: Mercy instructs Mankind in labour and prayer; the vice-companions tempt him to idleness and lechery; the devil Titivillus, appearing under the stage, whispers despair and steals his devotion; Mankind falls, is saved from suicide by Mercy's return, and repents, beating off the vices with his spade.
works.significance: The most theatrical of the moralities and a key witness to professional playing in the fifteenth century; its Titivillus and audience games bridge medieval and Tudor comedy.
works.meter: Couplets, stanza forms, and the macaronic dog-Latin of the vices, with remarkable metrical variety.
works.context: Composed c. 1465–70 in East Anglia (Cambridgeshire/Norfolk), for performance by a travelling company; preserved in the Macro manuscript (Folger MS V.a.354).
works.characters: Mankind; Mercy; Mischief; New Guise; Nowadays; Nought; Titivillus
works.structure: A compact morality of temptation, fall, and mercy, in the alternating mode of sermon and farce, with direct address and the audience collection ('Now gostly to our purpose') as its signature.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Maxims I and II
works.form: wisdom poetry (gnomic verse) in alliterative verse
works.description: Two collections of gnomic verse — Maxims I in the Exeter Book (204 lines, in three sections) and Maxims II in British Library Cotton Tiberius B.i (66 lines) — assembling traditional wisdom about the order of the world: what befits a king, a warrior, a woman, a tree, frost, the sea, and the road; 'wyrd goes as it shall'.
works.plot: The maxims proceed by association through the natural and social orders: the king belongs in the hall, the sword in battle, the hawk on the glove, the frost to the earth, the mind to wisdom; each thing is 'in its place' — a poetic articulation of the period's sense of a world arranged by custom and providence.
works.significance: The fullest repository of Old English gnomic wisdom and of the period's sense of natural and social order.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre in short, proverb-like units.
works.context: Maxims I: Exeter Book (fols. 88b-92b); Maxims II: London, British Library, Cotton MS Tiberius B.i (with the Menologium, c. 1050).
works.characters: none
works.structure: Catalogue structure: strings of 'X shall be / belongs to' gnomes, organized by loose association rather than narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Middle English Religious Lyrics
works.description: The devotional strand of the Middle English lyric corpus: meditations on the Passion ('I syng of a myden', 'Lullay, myn lykyng'), laments of the Virgin at the cross (the planctus Mariae), prayers to Christ and the saints, and poems on death and judgement. These lyrics carry the affective piety of the period into verse of great formal variety and emotional power.
works.plot: The poems stage the central scenes of late medieval devotion — the Annunciation, the Nativity, the Crucifixion as witnessed by Mary, the soul's dialogue with the crucified Christ, the memento mori — in first-person, lyric form.
works.significance: The most intimate record of late medieval English piety; together with the mystery plays, the religious lyrics are the principal vernacular vehicle of Passion and Marian devotion.
works.meter: Carol form, tail-rhyme, rhyme royal, and macaronic verse, often with musical settings implied by burdens and refrains.
works.context: The lyrics were copied into preaching and devotional manuscripts (the Vernon manuscript, Digby 102, Sloane 2593) and printed in early sixteenth-century carol collections; many served Franciscan and parochial devotion.
works.characters: Christ; the Virgin Mary; the soul (speaker)
works.structure: A corpus of independent lyrics; the characteristic movements are invocation, meditation, and petition.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous as a corpus; a few poems are attributed to known devotional writers.

works.title: N-Town Plays
works.description: A cycle of forty-two plays compiled in East Anglia in the second half of the fifteenth century, so called because its banns announce performance 'in N-town' — the name to be supplied by whatever town staged it. Its distinctive compilation includes a Passion play of great elaboration (the Mary Play tradition), the Parliament of Heaven, and the trial of Joseph and Mary, with a strong Marian and doctrinal emphasis.
works.plot: From the Parliament of Heaven and the fall of Lucifer, the cycle moves through the Old Testament, the life of the Virgin (her conception, presentation, and betrothal, the trial of Joseph and Mary), the Nativity, the ministry and Passion — with its long two-part Passion sequence — to the Resurrection, the Assumption, and the Last Judgement.
works.significance: The most learned and Mariological of the cycles, and the principal witness to the East Anglian Passion play tradition; its compilation shows the cycle form in the making.
works.meter: Thirteen-line and eight-line stanza forms, with the rime couée of the incorporated plays.
works.context: Compiled c. 1468–1500 in East Anglia (perhaps at Bury St Edmunds or Thetford), in the devotional culture that produced Bokenham and Capgrave; preserved in BL Cotton MS Vespasian D.viii.
works.characters: God; the Virgin Mary; Joseph; Christ; Pilate; Satan; the Prolocutor
works.structure: A compilation cycle: some pageants written for the cycle, others (the Mary Play, the Passion Play) incorporated from self-standing East Anglian dramas, under a general prologue claiming the N-town staging.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative (compilational); authorship_status reflects the cycle's collective making.

works.title: Narratio metrica de Sancto Swithuno
altTitles: The Metrical Life of St Swithun
works.form: hagiography (saint's life) in Latin hexameter verse
works.description: Wulfstan the Cantor's verse life of St Swithun, bishop of Winchester (d. 862), composed c. 996 for the translation of the saint's relics into the rebuilt Old Minster: a Latin epic in the classical revival manner of the Benedictine Reform, with a prose preface (a letter to Bishop Ælfheah) describing the rebuilding of the cathedral and its monuments.
works.plot: The poem narrates Swithun's life and episcopate, his humility, his miracles (the broken eggs restored, the bridge-mending saint), and the translation of 971, when the reluctant saint consented at last to be moved indoors; the preface details the new tower, crypt, organ, and bells of Æthelwold's Old Minster — a unique architectural record.
works.significance: The principal Latin poem of the late Old English period and a major source for Winchester's architecture and liturgy.
works.meter: Dactylic hexameters in the tenth-century classical manner.
works.context: Composed c. 996 at the Old Minster, Winchester, following the translation of Swithun's relics (971) and Æthelwold's building campaign; unique manuscript: British Library, Royal MS 15 C.vii.
works.characters: Swithun; Æthelwold; Ælfheah (dedicatee); Edgar
works.structure: A verse vita in two books framed by the prose dedicatory epistle.
works.attributionNotes: Wulfstan the Cantor's authorship is certain (he names himself in the prose preface).

works.title: Nature
altTitles: Nature, a goodly interlude of Nature
works.description: Henry Medwall's morality play of the fall and reformation of Man, the earliest surviving full-scale English morality written for a noble household; printed c. 1530–34 by William Rastell.
works.plot: Nature creates Man and sets Reason and Sensuality over him; Man follows Sensuality into the tavern and the arms of Pride, and the seven deadly sins strip him of his goods; Age and Shamefacedness bring him to repentance, and Reason restores him to grace. The play dramatizes the cycle of innocence, sin, and penitential return.
works.significance: The earliest surviving English morality play composed for a secular household audience and the first full example of the genre after Everyman; it documents the adaptation of the morality tradition to Renaissance taste and anticipates the moral interludes of the 1560s.
works.meter: Rhyme royal and couplets
works.context: Written in the late 1490s, probably for Morton's household like Fulgens and Lucrece; it draws on the tradition of The Castle of Perseverance and Everyman while giving new prominence to worldly temptation, and William Rastell's printing (c. 1530–34) secured its influence on the mid-century interludes.
works.characters: Nature; Man; Reason; Sensuality; Pride; World; Age; Shamefacedness; Innocence
works.structure: Two-part morality play with allegorical personifications, alternating processional scenes of the sins with debate between Reason and Sensuality.

works.title: Nice Wanton
altTitles: A Preaty Interlude Called Nice Wanton
works.description: An anonymous Protestant morality interlude of the divergent fates of three children, printed in 1560; a dramatization of godly education and its neglect.
works.plot: Xantippe's three children grow up under her indulgence: Ishmael and Dalila fall into idleness, gambling, and prostitution, and come to the gallows; the godly Barnabas, who studies scripture, is spared and comforts his repentant mother and sister; the Vice Iniquity frames the action, and the epilogue draws the moral of education and the rod.
works.significance: A representative Protestant morality whose twin plots of the saved and the damned child dramatize the educational programme of the Reformation; it marks the absorption of humanist pedagogy into the morality tradition.
works.meter: Couplets
works.context: Composed c. 1547–53, in the years of the Edwardian Reformation, when the godly education of children became a central Protestant theme; printed in 1560 for the Elizabethan market, with a title-page woodcut of the flogging schoolmaster.
works.characters: Xantippe; Barnabas; Ishmael; Dalila; Iniquity; Eulalia; The Worldly Shame
works.structure: A continuous morality play of two contrasted life-paths, with Iniquity as the linking Vice, songs, and a concluding moral address.

works.title: Old English Bede
works.form: translation (ecclesiastical history) in Old English prose
works.description: The anonymous Old English translation of Bede's Historia ecclesiastica, produced in the Alfredian circle: the earliest vernacular rendering of a major historical work in England and a primary witness to the text of Bede. It preserves the Old English text of Cædmon's Hymn in the West Saxon dialect.
works.plot: The translation follows Bede's five books closely, rendering the history of the conversion and the saints of the early English church into fluent West Saxon prose, with the Hymn of Cædmon given in a West Saxon verse translation rather than in the original Northumbrian form.
works.significance: The standard vernacular text of Bede in late Anglo-Saxon England and a monument of the Alfredian translation program.
works.meter: Old English prose; contains alliterative verse (Cædmon's Hymn) in translation.
works.context: Translated c. 890-930, probably in Mercia within the Alfredian orbit; principal manuscripts: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 41, and Oxford, Bodleian Library, Tanner 10.
works.characters: Bede (author); the saints and kings of the Historia
works.structure: Five books of translated ecclesiastical history.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; no evidence for the older attribution to Alfred himself.
sources: Poetry and Politics in the English Renaissance, revised edition

works.title: Old English Boethius (with the Meters of Boethius)
altTitles: The Old English Consolation of Philosophy
works.form: translation (philosophical dialogue) in Old English prose and verse
works.description: The Alfredian translation of Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, the most important philosophical work of the period in English: Boethius's dialogue with Lady Philosophy on fortune, free will, and providence, transformed by the translator into the idiom of the Germanic heroic world (Wyrd becomes a goddess of fate under God's governance). An alliterative verse rendering of the work's songs, the Meters of Boethius, accompanies the prose.
works.plot: The imprisoned Boethius, lamenting his fall, is visited by Philosophy (Wisdom), who teaches him that true happiness lies not in wealth, power, or fame but in God; the dialogue moves through the problem of evil to the reconciliation of divine foreknowledge with human freedom — the translator's expansions turning Philosophy's arguments into vivid vernacular images (the wheel of fate, the tyrant's empty power, the 'tool' of kingship).
works.significance: The first English philosophical classic; the Meters are the largest surviving corpus of Alfredian verse.
works.meter: Old English prose; the Meters of Boethius are in alliterative verse.
works.context: Translated in Alfred's circle c. 890-899 from the Latin of Boethius with the help of a commentary tradition; preserved in Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Bodley 180 (prose, mid-tenth century) and British Library, Cotton MS Otho A.vi (meters, burned 1731, transcript).
works.characters: Boethius (the Mind); Wisdom (Philosophy); Wyrd (Fate)
works.structure: Five books of alternating prose and verse (the metra), the prose translated freely, the verse rendered both in prose and, in a separate version, in alliterative verse.
works.attributionNotes: Traditionally attributed to Alfred himself; modern scholarship sees his close direction with the possibility of personal composition.
themes: The Virgin Mary and Marian devotion
sources: The Book of Common Prayer: The Texts of 1549, 1559, and 1662

works.title: Old English Dialogues of Gregory
works.form: translation (hagiographical dialogue) in Old English prose
works.description: Bishop Werferth of Worcester's translation of Gregory the Great's Dialogues, the collection of Italian saints' lives and miracle stories that was among the most popular books of the Middle Ages, including the life of St Benedict. Commissioned by King Alfred, it is the only Alfredian translation securely assigned to a named scholar other than the king.
works.plot: Gregory, in dialogue with his deacon Peter, recounts the lives and miracles of the holy men of Italy in four books: Benedict and his monks, the visionary saints, the raising of the dead, and the fate of souls after death — the work that fixed Benedict's cult in the west and fed the homiletic imagination of Anglo-Saxon England (its 'Vision of Fursey' and soul-journey stories echo through the Blickling and Vercelli homilies).
works.significance: The earliest extensive Old English translation of a major patristic work and the conduit of Gregory's hagiography into the vernacular.
works.meter: Old English prose, close and literal in style.
works.context: Translated by Werferth, bishop of Worcester (c. 872-915), at Alfred's request c. 890s; principal manuscripts: British Library, Cotton MS Otho C.i (fragmentary) and Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 322.
works.characters: Gregory the Great; Peter the deacon; Benedict of Nursia; the Italian saints
works.structure: Four books of dialogue, each a collection of miracle narratives framed by Gregory's conversation with Peter.
works.attributionNotes: Werferth's authorship rests on Asser's Life of Alfred and Alfred's own Preface.

works.title: Old English Hexateuch
works.description: The Old English translation of the first six books of the Bible (Genesis through Joshua), composed principally by Ælfric (who translated Genesis with his own preface) and completed by an anonymous translator: the earliest substantial rendering of the Bible into English and the most lavishly illustrated vernacular manuscript of the Anglo-Saxon period.
works.plot: The Hexateuch renders Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Joshua into English — the patriarchal narratives, the exodus and the law, the conquest of Canaan — in Ælfric's lucid prose for the first portion and a more literal style thereafter; the preface explains Ælfric's reluctance to translate scripture, lest the unlearned mistake its plain sense.
works.significance: The first English Bible translation of scale and a monument of late Anglo-Saxon book art.
works.meter: Old English prose; rhythmical in the Ælfrician portions.
works.context: Ælfric's Genesis and preface c. 1000; the whole compiled with the remaining books by the mid-eleventh century; principal manuscript: British Library, Cotton MS Claudius B.iv, with over 390 illustrations.
works.characters: Adam, Abraham, Joseph, Moses, Joshua, and the biblical patriarchs
works.structure: Six biblical books in translation, prefaced by Ælfric's preface to Genesis.
works.attributionNotes: Ælfric's authorship of Genesis (and the preface) is certain; the other books are by an anonymous contemporary.

works.title: Old English Martyrology
works.description: An anonymous ninth-century calendar of saints, the earliest substantial martyrology in any European vernacular: entries for each day of the year recording the feasts, passions, and wonders of the saints, compiled from Latin sources and full of exotic geographical and zoological lore.
works.plot: The martyrology proceeds day by day through the calendar year, each entry briefly narrating the saint's life or passion — apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins of east and west — with digressions on the places and creatures mentioned (the phoenix, the whale, the peoples of India).
works.significance: The earliest vernacular martyrology of Europe and a major source for Anglo-Saxon hagiography and geography.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Compiled in Mercia in the ninth century, probably before the Viking wars; survives in six fragmentary manuscripts, none complete.
works.characters: the saints of the universal church
works.structure: A calendar-ordered compendium of short hagiographical notices.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Old English Orosius
altTitles: The Old English History of the World
works.form: translation (universal history) in Old English prose
works.description: The Alfredian translation of Orosius's Seven Books of History against the Pagans, the standard ancient universal history, expanded with original accounts of the geography of northern Europe and the voyages of the Norwegian Ohthere and the Dane Wulfstan — the first travel literature in English.
works.plot: Orosius's history narrates the calamities of the world from creation to his own day (c. 417) to prove that the pagan past was more wretched than the Christian present; the translator condenses and adapts the narrative, and prefaces it with a geographical survey of the world that includes the famous reports of Ohthere's voyage around the North Cape into the White Sea and Wulfstan's voyage into the Baltic, told to King Alfred by the travellers themselves.
works.significance: The first universal history in English and the earliest English travel narrative (the Ohthere and Wulfstan passages).
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Translated in Alfred's circle c. 890-899; the principal manuscript is British Library, Additional MS 47967 (the Lauderdale or Tollemache Orosius, early tenth century).
works.characters: Ohthere; Wulfstan; Alfred (as recipient of the voyage accounts); the rulers of world history
works.structure: Seven books of world history, preceded by the translator's original geographical preface.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation of the Alfredian circle.
sources: The King's Reformation: Henry VIII and the Remaking of the English Church

works.title: Old English Pastoral Care (with Alfred's Preface)
altTitles: Gregory's Pastoral Care in Old English
works.form: translation (didactic treatise) in Old English prose
works.description: King Alfred's translation of Gregory the Great's Regula pastoralis, the handbook of episcopal duties, prefaced by Alfred's own letter on the decay of learning and his program of translation — the founding document of English prose. Copies were sent to every bishopric, and the surviving manuscripts are the earliest extensive works of Old English prose.
works.plot: Gregory's treatise instructs the pastor in the office of the soul's physician — how the teacher must adapt his speech to each condition of his flock, the virtues required of rulers of souls, and the discipline of preaching; Alfred's Preface recounts how learning had decayed in England ('so clean fallen away'), and how he therefore resolved to translate into English the books most needful for all men to know.
works.significance: The cornerstone of the Alfredian program and of the entire Old English prose tradition.
works.meter: Old English prose of the early Alfredian style.
works.context: Translated c. 890-899 with the help of Plegmund, Asser, Grimbald, and John; the earliest manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Hatton 20, c. 890-897) was sent to Bishop Werferth of Worcester.
works.characters: Alfred (preface); Gregory the Great (text)
works.structure: Preface (prose letter) followed by the four books of the translation, with Alfred's characteristic expansions of Gregory's images.
works.attributionNotes: The Preface is Alfred's own; the translation was executed by his circle under his direction.
sources: Sir Thomas Wyatt: The Complete Poems

works.title: Old English Soliloquies
altTitles: The Old English Soliloquies of Augustine
works.form: translation (philosophical dialogue) in Old English prose
works.description: The Alfredian translation of Augustine's Soliloquies — a dialogue between Augustine and his Reason on God and the immortality of the soul — with additions from Augustine's other works and the translator's own reflections, including the famous image of gathering timber in the forest to build a fair dwelling (the book as a house of wisdom).
works.plot: Reason leads Augustine (the translator's 'Mind') through the argument for the soul's immortality: from the desire for knowledge to the certainty of one's own existence ('I know that I am'), the nature of truth, and the vision of God after death; the work closes with the image of the king's woodcutters gathering timber for the house of the mind, where each man may rest and live.
works.significance: The first English rendering of Augustine and a central text of the Alfredian philosophic program.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Translated in Alfred's circle c. 890-899; the unique manuscript is British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv, fols. 4-59 (mid-twelfth century), copied with the same manuscript tradition as Beowulf.
works.characters: the Mind (Augustine/Alfred); Reason
works.structure: A question-and-answer dialogue in the Boethian manner, with the translator's expansions (the ship and anchor, the lord's favourite, the timber image) added to Augustine's text.
works.attributionNotes: Traditionally attributed to Alfred; the attribution rests on the Preface of the work and the conventions of the Alfredian canon.
sources: Tudor Drama before Shakespeare, 1485–1590: New Directions for Research, Criticism, and Pedagogy

works.title: On the Properties of Things
works.description: John Trevisa's English translation of Bartholomaeus Anglicus's De proprietatibus rerum (On the Properties of Things), the great medieval encyclopedia of nature, man, and the cosmos, completed c. 1398–99: nineteen books from God and the angels through the elements, animals, and plants to the human body and soul. Printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1495, it was the standard English encyclopedia for two centuries.
works.plot: The work proceeds systematically through the orders of creation — God, angels, the soul, the elements, the heavens, birds, beasts, herbs, and the arts and sciences — describing each thing's properties and their moral and medical meanings, in a summa of medieval natural knowledge.
works.significance: The great English encyclopedia of the Middle Ages and the principal channel by which medieval natural science entered English prose.
works.meter: Prose: Trevisa's learned yet idiomatic English, rich in technical vocabulary.
works.context: Completed in 1398–99 at Berkeley, dedicated to Thomas, Lord Berkeley; printed by Wynkyn de Worde (c. 1495), when it served the medical and scientific reading of the Tudor period; Shakespeare drew on it.
works.characters: none (encyclopedia)
works.structure: Nineteen books of encyclopedic description, each subdivided by topic, in the tradition of Isidore and the thirteenth-century encyclopedists.
works.attributionNotes: Trevisa's authorship of the translation secure (named in the text).

works.title: Opus Maius
works.description: Roger Bacon's encyclopedic proposal for the reform of learning, written c. 1267 at the request of Pope Clement IV and sent to him with the Opus Minus and Opus Tertium; its seventh part on moral philosophy and its treatment of optics, experimental science, and the applications of mathematics to theology make it a landmark of thirteenth-century thought.
works.summary: Bacon surveys the causes of error, the relation of philosophy to scripture, the utility of grammar and of the learned languages (Hebrew, Greek, Arabic), mathematics and its uses (including calendar reform and geography), the science of perspective, experimental science, and moral philosophy — arguing throughout that the sciences are necessary instruments for the understanding and defence of the faith.
works.significance: The fullest medieval statement of an experimental and mathematically grounded program of learning; a foundation text for the later reputation of Bacon and a principal witness to thirteenth-century optics and natural philosophy.

works.title: Ordinatio
works.description: Duns Scotus's great revision of his Oxford lectures on the Sentences of Peter Lombard, left unfinished at his death; the Ordinatio sets out the subtle doctor's metaphysics of univocity, his formal distinction, his defence of the Immaculate Conception, and his voluntarist ethics, and became the authoritative alternative to Thomism in late medieval theology.
works.summary: In four books following the structure of the Sentences, Scotus develops a systematic theology distinguished by its precise use of logic: the univocal concept of being, the formal distinction, the primacy of the will, the demonstration of God's existence through the concept of infinite being, and the case for Mary's immaculate conception — arguments that set the agenda for fourteenth-century scholasticism.
works.significance: One of the most demanding and influential works of medieval philosophy and theology; the foundation of the Scotist school, taught in the universities into the seventeenth century and beyond.

works.title: Orpheus and Eurydice
works.description: Robert Henryson's retelling of the Orpheus myth (c. 1480, 633 lines): the harper-king's descent to the underworld to reclaim Eurydice, his fatal backward look, and — in Henryson's distinctive addition — a long moralitas allegorizing Orpheus as the intellect, Eurydice as the appetite, and the harrowing journey as the soul's quest for its lost harmony. The most learned of the makars' classical poems.
works.plot: Orpheus, whose harping masters the beasts and the spheres, loses Eurydice to the serpent's bite and follows her to the underworld, where his music wins her release on the one condition; his backward look loses her forever, and the poet's moralitas expounds the fable as the story of reason seeking the soul's lost good.
works.significance: The classic Scottish treatment of the Orpheus myth and a landmark in the allegorical reading of classical poetry that runs from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas, with the moralitas in Henryson's plainest expository verse.
works.context: Composed c. 1480, drawing on Boethius's Consolation (the standard medieval source for the myth) and the commentary tradition; printed by Chepman and Myllar (1508), the first printed Scots poem.
works.characters: Orpheus; Eurydice; Pluto; Proserpina; the Furies; the narrator
works.structure: A bipartite poem: the classical narrative (with its celebrated catalogue of the underworld's inhabitants) followed by the allegorical moralitas.
works.attributionNotes: Henryson's authorship secure.

works.title: Passio Sancti Eadmundi
altTitles: Life of St Edmund, King and Martyr
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Tiberius B.ii; also transmitted through Ælfric's Old English adaptation
works.description: The earliest Latin life of Edmund, king of East Anglia, killed by the Viking Great Army in 869 and venerated as a martyr at Bury St Edmunds. Abbo of Fleury wrote it at Ramsey Abbey (985-987) from the eyewitness testimony of the aged Dunstan, who had heard the story from Edmund's own sword-bearer, and dedicated the work to Dunstan.
works.plot: The Danish army of Ingwar and Ubba invades East Anglia and demands Edmund's submission; the king, a model Christian ruler, refuses to deny Christ or rule as a viking's vassal, and is beaten, shot with arrows, and beheaded. A wolf guards the severed head until the faithful find it; the head rejoins the body, and Edmund is buried and venerated as a martyr whose body remains incorrupt.
works.significance: The founding text of the cult of St Edmund, England's royal patron saint, and the direct source of Ælfric's Old English life; an important link between continental hagiography and the English Benedictine Reform.
works.context: Written in the 980s when England again faced Danish attacks and when the cults of royal martyrs were being cultivated by the reformers; Abbo's Ramsey sojourn made the text a channel of continental learning into the English reform, and its story became the foundation of Bury St Edmunds' great cult.
works.characters: Edmund of East Anglia, Ingwar, Ubba, Bishop Theodred, Dunstan (as source)
works.structure: A classic passio in three movements: the invasion and the tyrant's demands, the martyrdom itself with its arrow-martyrdom patterned on St Sebastian, and the discovery and incorruption of the body, framed by Abbo's prefatory letter to Dunstan.
works.attributionNotes: Securely attributed to Abbo of Fleury, who dedicates the work to Dunstan and describes its composition at Ramsey.

works.title: Paston Letters
works.description: The correspondence and papers of the Paston family of Norfolk, spanning 1422–1509: over a thousand letters, wills, and memoranda recording the family's rise from yeoman stock to gentry status, their lawsuits (above all the struggle for Caister Castle), their marriages, and the texture of fifteenth-century provincial life. The richest surviving archive of medieval English family letters.
works.plot: The letters move among the three generations of Pastons — the judge William, his sons John I and John II, their wives Margaret and Margery — and their circle: the siege of Caister, John II's life at court, Margery's secret marriage, the boys' schooling, and the daily business of land, law, and loyalty in East Anglia.
works.significance: The first great English family letter collection: a unique window on the language, law, and life of fifteenth-century England, and the ancestor of the English epistolary tradition.
works.meter: Prose: the varied, idiomatic English of a literate gentry family, from Margaret's dictated letters to John II's courtier prose.
works.context: Written 1422–1509 by the Norfolk Pastons, whose archive passed to the Earl of Yarmouth and was edited by John Fenn (1787); it documents the Wars of the Roses from the perspective of a gentry family and is a primary source for the period's social history.
works.characters: William Paston; Margaret Paston; John Paston I; John Paston II; Margery Paston; the family's servants and opponents
works.structure: An epistolary archive, not a composed work: its order is chronological and documentary, spanning the reigns of Henry VI, Edward IV, and Henry VII.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative (many family members and correspondents); authorship_status reflects the archive's collective character.

editions.title: Paston Letters and Papers of the Fifteenth Century

works.title: Patience
works.description: The Gawain-poet's homiletic poem of 531 lines on the prophet Jonah, expounding the beatitude 'blessed are the patient' through the comic drama of the reluctant prophet, the storm, the whale, and the withered woodbine. Patience, the poem argues, is the virtue God himself practises with sinners — and the one Jonah must learn.
works.plot: Jonah, fleeing God's command to preach at Nineveh, boards ship for Tarshish; the storm God raises forces the sailors to cast him overboard, and he is swallowed by the whale, in whose belly he prays his psalm of thanksgiving; delivered, he preaches at Nineveh, whose repentance God accepts — to Jonah's fury, which the parable of the woodbine answers: if Jonah pities a plant, shall not God pity a city of a hundred and twenty thousand?
works.significance: The liveliest biblical poem of the alliterative revival and the most sustained Middle English treatment of patience; its comic sympathy with the reluctant prophet is without parallel in the period.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line, handled with colloquial vigour.
works.context: Composed c. 1375–1400 by the Gawain-poet; preserved uniquely in Cotton Nero A.x. The Jonah story had a special medieval resonance through its typological link to the Resurrection.
works.characters: Jonah; God; the sailors; the Ninevites
works.structure: A homiletic prologue on the eight beatitudes, then a three-movement biblical narrative (flight and storm; whale and prayer; Nineveh and the woodbine), with the parable as the poem's doctrinal climax.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; assigned to the Gawain-poet on grounds of style and shared manuscript.

works.title: Pearl
works.description: The great elegiac dream vision of the Gawain-poet: 1,212 lines in 101 twelve-line stanzas linked by concatenation, in which a grieving father, mourning a lost 'pearl' (his infant daughter), dreams of her transfigured among the blessed, debates with her the theology of grace, and glimpses the heavenly Jerusalem. The most perfectly wrought poem of the Alliterative Revival.
works.plot: In an arbour where his pearl slipped from his hand, the dreamer falls asleep and finds himself by a crystal stream; across it stands a maiden crowned with pearls, whom he recognizes as his lost child grown in heaven. Their dialogue unfolds the parable of the vineyard — the justice of the penny's wage, the grace that admits the innocent and the repentant alike — and culminates in his vision of the New Jerusalem and the Lamb, before his waking returns him to the earth where the pearl is buried.
works.significance: The greatest English religious elegy and the most technically brilliant poem of the Middle English period; its theology of grace and its jewelled art have made it the centre of a vast critical literature.
works.meter: Twelve-line alliterative stanzas rhyming ababababbcbc, with concatenatio linking stanza to stanza.
works.context: Composed c. 1375–1400 by the Gawain-poet in the north-west Midlands, in the Ricardian flowering of the dream vision; preserved uniquely in Cotton Nero A.x with Sir Gawain, Patience, and Cleanness.
works.characters: the Dreamer (father); the Pearl-maiden; the Lamb; St John
works.structure: Twenty sections of five stanzas each, the last line of each stanza echoed by the first of the next, and the poem's final line repeating its first; the stream divides the poem into the two worlds of earth and heaven.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; assigned to the Gawain-poet on grounds of style and shared manuscript.

works.title: Pharaoh
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.form: religious narrative fragment in alliterative verse
works.description: An eight-line fragment on the drowning of Pharaoh's host in the Red Sea, dramatizing the moment when the returning waters destroy the pursuing Egyptians. Probably a fragment of a longer Exodus poem or a brief independent composition.
works.plot: Pharaoh's army, pursuing the Israelites across the sea-bed, is engulfed when the waters return; the poem emphasizes the totality of the destruction and the might of the God who saved his people.
works.significance: A witness to the popularity of the Exodus story in Old English verse beyond the Junius manuscript, and to the heroic idiom's capacity to render scriptural battle scenes.
works.meter: Eight alliterative long lines of heroic density; the diction of battle and the sea is that of the heroic tradition applied to scriptural warfare.
works.context: The Exodus was the type of baptism and of the Church's deliverance throughout Anglo-Saxon literature, most elaborately in the Junius manuscript Exodus.
works.characters: Pharaoh
works.structure: A single dramatic scene in eight lines, culminating in the overwhelming of the Egyptian host.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The fragment's relationship to the Junius Exodus is uncertain.

works.title: Philip Sparrow
works.description: A mock-elegy of some 1,400 Skeltonic lines in which Jane Scrope, a young gentlewoman of the household at Carrow Abbey, laments her pet sparrow Philip, killed by the cat Gib — the lament swelling into a virtuoso parody of the Latin Office of the Dead, with a commendation of Jane and a digressive defense of women.
works.plot: Jane Scrope mourns her sparrow; the poem moves from tender elegy through liturgical parody (Placebo, Dirige) to the praise of Jane's beauty and virtue, ending with an envoy sending the book to her.
works.significance: The classic of the English mock-elegy and a touchstone of Skelton's art; its play with the liturgy and its defense of women made it one of the most read poems of the century.
works.meter: The Skeltonic at its most supple: short lines of two or three stresses, tumbling rhymes, and Latin tags woven into English.
works.context: Written for the household of Sir Philip Calthorpe's widow at Carrow; the text's allusions to Jane Scrope's family place it about 1505.
works.characters: Jane Scrope; Philip (the sparrow); Gib (the cat)
works.structure: A single-voiced lament that repeatedly breaks its frame: elegy, liturgical parody, blazon, and envoy succeed one another by association.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: John Skelton: The Complete English Poems

works.title: Philobiblon
works.description: Richard de Bury's treatise in praise of books and of the love of learning, completed on his birthday, 24 January 1345 (i.e., 1344 by modern reckoning), while he was bishop of Durham; the work draws on his experience assembling one of the great private libraries of medieval England.
works.summary: In twenty chapters the Philobiblon celebrates the wisdom preserved in books, argues that they should be shared with scholars rather than hoarded, defends the clergy against the charge of neglecting their books, and prescribes the care, repair, and circulation of manuscripts; it closes with provisions for the dispersal of the author's own library to the scholars of Oxford.
works.significance: The most famous medieval book about books, a primary witness to the book culture of fourteenth-century England, and a key document for the history of libraries and of Oxford scholarship.

works.title: Piers Plowman
works.form: allegorical dream vision in alliterative verse
works.description: William Langland's visionary masterpiece, surviving in three authorial versions (the A-text c. 1367–70, B-text c. 1377–79, C-text c. 1386–88): a sequence of ten dream visions in which the dreamer Will searches for Truth, Dowel, Dobet, and Dobest through the estates of fourteenth-century England — the fair field full of folk, the pilgrimage of the seven deadly sins, the Tree of Charity, and the harrowing of hell. The greatest English poem of social and spiritual reform.
works.plot: Will falls asleep on the Malvern Hills and sees a field full of folk between the Tower of Truth and the Dungeon of Wrong; the quest for St Truth becomes the ploughing of the half-acre under Piers the Plowman; the later visions pursue Dowel, Dobet, and Dobest through the confession of the sins, the feast of Patience, the Tree of Charity, the Passion and harrowing of hell, and the founding of Holy Church, which the final vision shows besieged from within by Antichrist and the friars.
works.significance: With the Canterbury Tales and Sir Gawain, one of the three summits of Ricardian literature: its blend of estates satire, theological vision, and vernacular prophecy made it the rallying text of reform for two centuries, from the rebels of 1381 to the Tudor reformers who printed it.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line, ranging from colloquial satire to liturgical sublimity.
works.context: Composed and revised c. 1367–88, probably in London, against the background of plague, labour legislation, the Peasants' Revolt (1381), and Wycliffite controversy — all refracted in the poem's satire; preserved in over fifty manuscripts, more than any English poem except the Prick of Conscience.
works.characters: Will (the dreamer); Piers the Plowman; Holy Church; Lady Meed; Conscience; Patience; the Seven Deadly Sins; the Samaritan; Christ; Antichrist
works.structure: A series of ten (or eight) dream visions within dreams, progressing from social satire through theological allegory to apocalyptic vision, with Will's own spiritual biography as the connective thread; the B-text adds the great inner dreams of the C-text's revisions.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to William Langland by manuscript evidence and internal acrostic signatures; the three texts represent the author's own revisions.

editions.title: Piers Plowman: The B Version
editions.editor: George Kane and E. Talbot Donaldson (eds.)

works.title: Piers the Plowman's Creed
works.description: A Lollard-leaning alliterative satire of some 850 lines in imitation of Piers Plowman: a simple man, seeking to learn his creed, questions the four orders of friars in turn and finds only greed, sophistry, and pride — until the ploughman Piers teaches him the creed in the plain words of charity and labour. The fiercest of the Piers Plowman imitations.
works.plot: The narrator, who cannot say his creed, applies to the friars; each order's answer is a satiric portrait — their fine houses, their begging, their hatred of the ploughman's tithes — until Piers and his family, labouring in poverty, recite the creed and denounce the friars with apocalyptic anger.
works.significance: The most important literary offspring of Piers Plowman and the principal verse monument of Lollard satire; its Tudor printing made 'Piers Plowman' a name for English reform.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line with rhyme incorporated in places.
works.context: Composed c. 1395 in the orbit of the Lollard movement, satirizing the friars' wealth in the spirit of FitzRalph and Wyclif; preserved in BL Royal MS 18 B.xvii and printed by the Tudor reformers (1553).
works.characters: the narrator; the four friars; Piers the Plowman; his wife and children
works.structure: A quest-satire in the Piers tradition: four failed consultations with the friars, resolved by the ploughman's plain teaching.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; formerly attributed to the author of the Plowman's Tale.

works.title: Poema Morale
works.description: A sermon in verse of some 400 lines on the conduct of life and the last things, often called the earliest Middle English poem of any consequence: the aged speaker meditates on a misspent youth, the brevity of life, and the terrors and joys of judgement, urging repentance before death.
works.plot: The speaker reviews the stages of life, the certainty of death and judgement, the pains of hell and the bliss of heaven, and counsels amendment of life while time remains.
works.significance: A touchstone of early Middle English: its popularity (seven manuscripts) and its homiletic style anticipate the great penitential literature of the thirteenth century.
works.meter: The loose fourteener (septenarius) couplet of the earliest Middle English homiletic verse.
works.context: Composed in the south of England c. 1170, in the Kentish or south-western dialect; preserved in seven manuscripts, the earliest in the Lambeth and Trinity homily collections of c. 1200.
works.characters: the aged speaker
works.structure: A monologic homily moving from personal confession through doctrinal exposition (death, judgement, heaven, hell) to exhortation.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the speaker's self-description as old is a homiletic persona.

works.title: Policraticus
altTitles: Policraticus: Of the Frivolities of Courtiers and the Footprints of Philosophers
works.description: John of Salisbury's treatise on politics, court life, and philosophy in eight books, completed in 1159 and dedicated to Thomas Becket; the first full work of medieval political theory, famous for its organic metaphor of the body politic and its defence of tyrannicide.
works.summary: The Policraticus satirizes the frivolities of courtiers, expounds the duties of prince and magistrate under the image of the body politic (the prince as head, the clergy as soul), argues that the tyrant is a public enemy whose killing may be lawful, and ends with a survey of ancient philosophy and the true happiness of the contemplative life.
works.significance: The most important political treatise written in twelfth-century Europe, a conduit of classical political thought into the Middle Ages, and a standard authority cited into the seventeenth century.

works.title: Polychronicon (Trevisa's translation)
works.description: John Trevisa's English translation of Ranulf Higden's Polychronicon, the universal history that dominated English historical reading: the world's geography, the history of Britain from the Britons to the fourteenth century, and the wonders of the world, in Trevisa's fluent, expansive prose, completed in 1387 for Thomas, Lord Berkeley. Printed by Caxton in 1482, it is the great English prose chronicle of the period.
works.plot: Following Higden's seven books, the work describes the world and Britain, then narrates English history from the Britons and Saxons through the Norman kings to the reign of Edward III, with its famous prefatory Dialogue on Translation in which Trevisa defends the rendering of Latin learning into English.
works.significance: The principal English universal history of the later Middle Ages and, with its Dialogue on Translation, a classic text of vernacular self-consciousness.
works.meter: Prose: fluent, idiomatic, and expansive — a landmark of fourteenth-century English prose style.
works.context: Completed in 1387 by Trevisa, chaplain of Thomas, Lord Berkeley, at Berkeley Castle; printed by Caxton (1482, with his continuation to 1460) and read into the sixteenth century.
works.characters: the kings and peoples of British history
works.structure: Seven books of world and British history, with Trevisa's Dialogue and the Berkeley continuations as its frame and sequel.
works.attributionNotes: Trevisa's authorship of the translation secure (named in the Berkeley manuscripts).

works.title: Prayers or Meditations
altTitles: Prayers Stirring the Mind unto Heavenly Meditations
works.description: Catherine Parr's book of devotional prayers and meditations, published in 1545; the first book published by an English queen under her own name, which ran through nineteen editions by 1600.
works.plot: The book adapts the third book of Thomas à Kempis's Imitation of Christ into a sequence of prayers, meditations on the passion, and exhortations to penitence, faith, and the amendment of life, addressed to the reader in the queen's own voice as a fellow sinner seeking grace.
works.significance: The first printed book by an English queen and a landmark in the history of women's devotional writing; its combination of à Kempis's piety with Reformation emphasis on faith made it the century's most popular royal book.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1545 by Thomas Berthelet with the queen's name on the title page, in the months when Parr's evangelical household (including Askew's associates) was under suspicion; the book's success established the royal devotional voice that Elizabeth I and others would imitate.
works.structure: A devotional manual of prayers and meditations arranged by spiritual states — contrition, faith, thanksgiving — with scriptural centos and personal application.

editions.title: Katherine Parr: Complete Works and Correspondence

works.title: Precepts
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A wisdom poem of 94 lines in which a wise father addresses ten counsels to his son, one by one: to avoid anger and envy, choose wise companions, keep faith, practise generosity, and fear God. Each counsel is introduced by a repeated formula of address.
works.plot: The father, speaking 'many winters' of experience, delivers ten distinct precepts to his son on the conduct of a good life — on anger, friendship, wisdom, speech, generosity, and the fear of the Lord — closing with an exhortation to remember the counsels always.
works.significance: The most elaborate surviving Old English example of the father-to-son instruction genre, valuable for its picture of the ethical ideals taught to the young Anglo-Saxon elite.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with the gnomic compression of the Exeter wisdom tradition; the anaphoric frame gives the poem its ceremonial regularity.
works.context: The father-son instruction poem has biblical and classical roots (Proverbs, the Disticha Catonis) and was a recognized genre in Anglo-Saxon England, as the Old English translation of the Distichs shows.
works.characters: the wise father, his son
works.structure: A decalogue structure: ten formally parallel counsels, each marked by the repeated address 'the wise father said to his son', framed by an introduction and a concluding admonition.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Ralph Roister Doister
works.description: Nicholas Udall's five-act comedy of the braggart Ralph Roister Doister, written c. 1552–54 and printed c. 1566–67; generally regarded as the first English comedy.
works.plot: Ralph Roister Doister, a vainglorious suitor encouraged by the parasite Merrygreek, woos Dame Christian Custance, who is betrothed to the merchant Gawin Goodluck; his letters and verses are read to her as insults, and his siege of her house ends in a comic battle with her maids, the braggart routed by a broom; the play closes with the lovers reunited and Roister Doister invited to dinner — folly corrected without malice.
works.significance: The first English comedy: it transplants the Roman braggart soldier and parasite into a London setting, joins classical form to native farce, and inaugurates the line that runs through Gammer Gurton's Needle to Shakespeare and Jonson.
works.meter: Irregular rhyming couplets ('rhyming fourteeners'), with songs
works.context: Written c. 1552–54, probably for performance by the boys of Westminster School (Udall was headmaster there from 1555, earlier at Eton); drawing on Plautus's Miles Gloriosus and Terence's Eunuchus, it belongs to the academic revival of Roman comedy that would produce Gammer Gurton's Needle and the school drama of the 1560s.
works.characters: Ralph Roister Doister; Matthew Merrygreek; Dame Christian Custance; Gawin Goodluck; Tristram Trusty; Madge Mumblecrust; Tibet Talkapace; Annot Alyface
works.structure: Five acts modelled on the Roman comedy of Plautus and Terence, with a braggart soldier, a parasite, and a reunion plot; the action is domestic and the verse a rollicking doggerel.

works.title: Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye
altTitles: The Recuyell of the Histories of Troy
works.description: William Caxton's translation of Raoul Lefèvre's French Recueil des histoires de Troyes, begun in Bruges in 1468 and completed in Cologne in 1471, and printed by Caxton at Bruges in 1473–74 as the first book printed in English. A courtly Troy compilation made for the Burgundian duchess Margaret of York, it inaugurated both Caxton's career and the English printed book.
works.plot: The compilation recounts the deeds of Hercules and the first destruction of Troy, then the rebuilding of the city under Priam and the second war — the rape of Helen, the battles before Troy, the deaths of Hector and Achilles, and the fall of the city through the wooden horse.
works.significance: The first book printed in English and the founding text of the English print tradition; its Troy matter carried the medieval romance of antiquity into the print era.
works.meter: Prose: Caxton's early style, French-inflected and courtly, before his London plainness matured.
works.context: Begun in Bruges in 1468 for Margaret of York, sister of Edward IV, and printed at Bruges c. 1473–74 — the first English printed book; Caxton's famous prologue records his despair over the labour of translation and the duchess's command to finish.
works.characters: Hercules; Jason; Priam; Hector; Achilles; Paris; Helen; Ulysses
works.structure: Three books in Lefèvre's arrangement, translated in full, with Caxton's prologue and epilogue recording the circumstances of its making.
works.attributionNotes: Caxton's authorship of the translation and printing is documented in his own prologue and epilogue.

editions.title: The Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye

works.title: Regularis Concordia
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Tiberius A.iii (mid-eleventh century) and Cotton Faustina B.iii
works.description: The customary drawn up at the Council of Winchester (c. 970) under Æthelwold of Winchester to unify the observance of all English monasteries: a national supplement to the Rule of St Benedict, adapting continental customaries from Fleury and Ghent to English conditions and binding the reformed houses together under royal protection.
works.plot: The Concordia sets out the daily, weekly, and yearly round of the monastic life — the hours of prayer, the psalms and canticles, the ceremonies of the great feasts, the commemoration of the king and queen, and the dramatic rites of Holy Week, including the earliest recorded Visitatio Sepulchri (the 'Quem quaeritis' dialogue) in England.
works.significance: The founding document of the unified English monasticism of the late tenth century, and the source of the earliest English dramatic text (the Visitatio Sepulchri), making it a landmark in the history of English theatre as well as of monasticism.
works.context: Produced at the high point of the Benedictine Reform under King Edgar (959-975), the Concordia institutionalized the alliance of crown and monastery: the king and queen are commemorated in the daily office, and the text was issued with royal authority for all houses.
works.structure: A prologue addressed to King Edgar, followed by a systematic customary organized by the liturgical day and year; the prescriptions culminate in the elaborated rites of the Triduum, with the dialogue of the three Marys and the angel at the Easter sepulchre.
works.attributionNotes: Written by Æthelwold of Winchester, who names himself as the compiler; the text is securely attributed.

works.title: Resignation
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A first-person penitential prayer in which the speaker, an exile and outcast from his lord's favour, submits himself wholly to God's will and prays for guidance through the storms of life. The poem fuses the secular conventions of the exile's lament with Christian devotion.
works.plot: The speaker, alienated from his earthly lord and wandering in misery, turns to God as his true protector, acknowledging that he has suffered for his sins, and prays for wisdom, steadfastness, and a safe passage through life's sea of troubles to the heavenly home.
works.significance: A major example of the Old English religious lyric's absorption of elegiac conventions, and a witness to the penitential spirituality of late Anglo-Saxon England.
works.meter: Standard alliterative long line with the formulaic diction of the elegiac tradition; the poem is textually imperfect, with apparent lacunae.
works.context: The poem belongs to the late Old English religious lyric, where the conventions of heroic exile poetry were appropriated for penitential devotion; comparable to The Wife's Lament in its fusion of personal loss and landscape imagery.
works.structure: A sustained first-person prayer in which the imagery of exile, sea-voyage, and homelessness is progressively reinterpreted as the soul's spiritual condition; some editors detect a break in the middle of the text suggesting an incomplete or composite poem.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The title 'Resignation' is an editorial convenience, not in the manuscript.

works.title: Respublica
works.description: An anonymous Protestant morality play of the commonwealth, written for performance at Christmas 1553 during the first months of Mary I's reign; a sophisticated political allegory of the misgovernment of the 1540s.
works.plot: Respublica, the widowed commonwealth, is robbed by Avarice and his crew — Oppression, Adulation, and Insolence (disguised as Policy, Honesty, and Authority) — who plunder her goods and divide them among themselves; the four sisters People, Verity, Peace, and Justice return, strip the thieves of their disguises, and restore the commonwealth, with Mercy pronouncing judgement and the audience promised amendment under the new queen.
works.significance: The most politically sophisticated of the sixteenth-century moralities: its allegory of the commonwealth, its disguised Vices, and its address to the monarch anticipate the political drama of the Elizabethan stage, and it documents the mid-Tudor crisis of counsel and plunder.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic speeches
works.context: Performed at Christmas 1553, evidently by a company of boys, in the first months of Mary's reign; the play's allegory of the plunder of the commonwealth under Edward VI's ministers (Somerset and Northumberland) and its restoration under the Catholic queen marks a rare moment when the morality tradition served immediate dynastic politics.
works.characters: Respublica; Avarice; Adulation; Oppression; Insolence; People; Verity; Peace; Justice; Mercy; Nemesis
works.structure: Five acts of morality allegory applied to contemporary politics, with the Vice Avarice doubling his disguises and a final scene of restoration and loyal address to Mary I.
works.attributionNotes: No author is named in the manuscript; Nicholas Udall has been proposed by some scholars, but the attribution remains unproven, and the work is treated as anonymous.

works.title: Revelations of Divine Love
works.description: Julian of Norwich's account of the sixteen revelations ('showings') she received during a grave illness on 8 May 1373, in two versions — the Short Text written soon after, and the Long Text, the fruit of some twenty years of meditation, completed c. 1393. Its theology of divine love — 'all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well' — and of Jesus as mother makes it the greatest work of English mysticism and the first book in English known to be by a woman.
works.plot: At the point of death, the thirty-year-old Julian receives a series of visions of Christ's Passion, the Virgin, the world's littleness (the hazelnut), and the Lord's meaning: that love is his meaning; the Long Text unfolds these showings into a theology of sin, suffering, divine motherhood, and the 'great deed' by which all shall be made well.
works.significance: The summit of the English mystical tradition: the first major theological work by an English woman, and a text of the first importance for the history of women's writing and of Christian theology.
works.meter: Plain, meditative prose of extraordinary depth; homely images (the hazelnut) carrying speculative theology.
works.context: The showings occurred in Norwich on 8 May 1373; Julian became an anchoress at St Julian's church and wrote the Short Text shortly after and the Long Text c. 1393; Margery Kempe visited her c. 1413; the Long Text circulated in manuscript and in the printed editions of Serenus Cressy (1670).
works.characters: Julian (visionary); Christ; the Virgin Mary; the fiend
works.structure: Eighty-six (or more) chapters of vision, exposition, and prayer, organized by the order of the showings and the decades of their meditation.
works.attributionNotes: The author is known only as Julian of Norwich (from her church); her name in the world is unknown.

editions.title: The Writings of Julian of Norwich

works.title: Reynard the Fox
altTitles: The History of Reynard the Fox
The Historye of Reynart the Foxe
works.description: William Caxton's translation of the Dutch prose Reinaert de Vos, printed at Westminster in 1481: the beast epic of the fox Reynard, whose crimes are arraigned at the court of King Noble the lion, and whose cunning turns every accusation — and his own execution — into the ruin of his accusers. Caxton's print brought the European Reynard tradition to English readers and printers alike.
works.plot: Summoned to the lion's court to answer the complaints of the wolf Isengrim, the bear Bruin, and the other beasts, Reynard tricks each accuser in turn, confesses to save his neck, and is sent on pilgrimage only to murder his escort; his enemies' heads decorate his house, and the lion makes him his counsellor — the trickster triumphant.
works.significance: The classic English Reynard and the ancestor of the beast satire that runs through Spenser's Mother Hubberds Tale to the seventeenth-century Reynard reprints; a landmark of Caxton's publishing program.
works.meter: Prose: Caxton's plain, lively narrative style at its best.
works.context: Translated by Caxton from the Dutch and printed in 1481, in the same year as his Godfrey of Boulogne; it fed a long English print tradition of Reynard editions and the beast satire of the sixteenth century.
works.characters: Reynard the Fox; King Noble the Lion; Isengrim the Wolf; Bruin the Bear; Tibert the Cat; Chanticleer the Cock
works.structure: A beast epic in episodic form: arraignment, defence, confession, and triumph, in the framework of the animals' court.
works.attributionNotes: Caxton's translation documented in his own colophon.

editions.title: The History of Reynard the Fox

works.title: Robert Mannyng's Chronicle
works.description: Robert Mannyng of Brunne's verse history of England from Noah and the Trojan Brutus to the death of Edward I (1307), completed in 1338: the first part translates Wace's Roman de Brut, the second Peter Langtoft's French chronicle. It is the principal vernacular chronicle in English verse between Layamon and the fifteenth century.
works.plot: The poem narrates British and English history in sequence — Brutus, Arthur, the Saxon kings, the Norman Conquest, and the Plantagenet reigns — with particular fullness on the baronial wars of the thirteenth century.
works.significance: The chief English verse chronicle of the fourteenth century and a key witness to the national, vernacular historical consciousness of the period.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets in the first part, six-line tail-rhyme stanzas in the second.
works.context: Completed in 1338 by Mannyng, Gilbertine canon of Sempringham, at Sixhills, for the instruction of lay readers in English history; preserved in two manuscripts, BL Harley MS 1317 and Lambeth Palace MS 131.
works.characters: Arthur; the English kings from William I to Edward I; Simon de Montfort
works.structure: A two-part regnal chronicle (Brut section; Langtoft section) with patriotic and didactic digressions.
works.attributionNotes: Securely attributed to Mannyng in the poem's own colophon.

works.title: Sawles Warde
works.description: An allegorical homily in AB-language prose on the custody of the soul: the house of the body is governed by Wit and Will, guarded by the five senses, threatened by the devil, and comforted by the virtues and the joys of heaven. It adapts Hugh of St Victor's De Anima and is the earliest extended allegory of the inner life in English prose.
works.plot: Wit (reason), with his wife Will, rules the soul's house; the messenger Fear of Death warns of the devil's assaults; the virtues — Prudence, Strength, Moderation, Righteousness — and the vision of the heavenly bliss fortify the household against temptation.
works.significance: A foundation stone of English allegory: its personified psychology anticipates the moralities (The Castle of Perseverance) and the dream allegories of the fourteenth century.
works.meter: Rhythmical alliterative AB-language prose.
works.context: Composed in the early thirteenth-century West Midlands, adapting Hugh of St Victor; preserved in Bodleian MS Bodley 34, BL Cotton MS Titus D.xviii, and Royal MS 17 A.xxvii.
works.characters: Wit; Will; Fear of Death; the Virtues; the Devil
works.structure: A continuous allegorical narrative built on the house/castle metaphor, with set-piece descriptions of the pains of hell and the joys of heaven.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Seasons for Fasting
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Additional MS 43703 (a sixteenth-century transcript by Laurence Nowell of the lost Cotton Otho B.xi)
works.description: A poem of some 230 lines on the proper observance of the Ember fasts, defending the English custom of four seasonal fasts against the laxity of those who fast only once a year, and citing biblical and canonical authority for the practice. The text breaks off imperfectly.
works.plot: The poet rebukes priests who observe the Ember days wrongly, argues from scripture (Moses, Elijah, the Ninevites, Christ's forty days) that fasting is commanded, sets out the correct times of the four seasonal fasts, and attacks drunken priests; the poem ends incomplete amid a catalogue of fasts.
works.significance: A rare Old English poem on a live question of ecclesiastical discipline, valuable for its picture of eleventh-century religious controversy and its fusion of homiletic and satirical verse.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with the homiletic urgency of Wulfstan's prose; the text is incomplete, and some lines are metrically irregular.
works.context: The poem belongs to the late Old English period's debates over ecclesiastical discipline, contemporary with Wulfstan's legislation on fasting and the reform of the clergy; its strictures on drunken priests echo the reformers' campaigns.
works.structure: An argumentative structure: rebuke, biblical proof-texts, prescription of the fasts, and invective against clerical abuses, in the manner of Wulfstanian homiletic verse.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The poem's Wulfstanian manner has suggested to some scholars an origin in his circle, but no attribution is established.

works.title: Sermo Lupi ad Anglos
altTitles: The Sermon of the Wolf to the English
works.description: Wulfstan's most famous sermon, preached in the crisis year 1014 as the Danish conquest of England was completed: an impassioned jeremiad interpreting the Viking devastation as God's punishment for the nation's sins, culminating in the vision of the enslaved nation — 'an Englishman is not worth more to a Dane than a dog'. The masterpiece of Old English pulpit rhetoric.
works.plot: The sermon catalogues the nation's sins — betrayal of lords, perjury, oppression of the poor, the violation of churches — and reads the tribulations of Æthelred's reign (the treachery of Eadric Streona, the burning, plundering, and enslavement of the people) as the biblical pattern of divine wrath; it calls the nation to repentance before the last things overtake it, in a crescendo of Wulfstan's two-stress rhythms.
works.significance: The greatest Old English sermon and the classic statement of the period's theology of national sin.
works.meter: Wulfstan's rhythmical prose: two-stress phrases, alliteration, anaphora, and word-pairs ('byman and bærnan' — burn and ravage).
works.context: Preached in 1014, after the expulsion of Æthelred and before Cnut's final conquest (1016); preserved in five manuscripts, including British Library, Cotton MS Nero A.i.
works.characters: Wulfstan (preacher, as 'Lupus'); the English nation
works.structure: A single continuous exhortation built on the antithesis of sin and punishment, with the historical crisis framed as the fulfilment of prophecy.
works.attributionNotes: Wulfstan's authorship is certain ('Lupus' is his Latin signature).

works.title: Sermon of the Plough
works.description: Hugh Latimer's most famous sermon, preached at Paul's Cross on 18 January 1548 and printed the same year; the classic Protestant sermon of social criticism, built on the text of the sower.
works.plot: Taking the gospel of the sower, Latimer expounds the 'plough' of preaching, the 'seed' of God's word, and the spiritual husbandry required of clergy and laity alike; he attacks the idleness of prelates ('unpreaching prelates'), the rack-renting of landlords, and the neglect of the poor, calling the realm to the work of the spiritual plough — a sustained sermon of estates satire turned to gospel ends.
works.significance: The most celebrated English sermon of the Reformation: its homely agricultural allegory and its fearless attack on clerical and landlord abuses made it the model of the Protestant pulpit's social criticism from the sixteenth century to the nineteenth.
works.meter: Prose
