works.context: Preached at Paul's Cross on 18 January 1548, in the first months of Edward VI's reign, as part of the reform campaign against images and non-residence; printed by John Day in 1548 and reprinted through the century, the sermon made Latimer the voice of the Edwardian Reformation's social conscience.
works.structure: A single sermon structured by the parable's allegory — the plough, the seed, the soil — with digressions into the abuses of church and commonwealth.

works.title: Sir Degaré
works.description: A Breton lay of the foundling knight: Degaré, son of a fairy knight who ravished his mother, is exposed at birth, raised by a hermit, and wins his spurs through combat with a dragon; his search for his father ends in recognition, reunion, and the marriage of his widowed mother to her long-lost lover. Preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript.
works.plot: Degaré, given his father's broken sword at birth, defeats the dragon, unhorses the knights of Arthur's court, and proves himself; seeking his father, he jousts with the fairy knight himself, and the two recognize each other; the poem ends with the father's return and the family's reunion.
works.significance: A representative minor lai valuable for the incest-anxieties and recognition patterns of the genre, and a staple of romance anthologies.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets, plain and rapid.
works.context: Composed c. 1325, probably in the south-east; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript (c. 1330) and later copies including the Percy Folio.
works.characters: Degaré; the fairy knight (his father); his mother; the hermit
works.structure: A foundling-quest in the lai manner, with the father-son combat as its climactic recognition scene.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
works.description: The supreme masterpiece of the Alliterative Revival and one of the greatest poems of the English Middle Ages: 2,530 lines in alliterative stanzas with the 'bob and wheel' close, recounting Gawain's beheading-game with the Green Knight and his testing in the castle of Sir Bertilak. A romance of courtesy, chastity, and shame, in which the pentangle and the green girdle measure the hero against an ideal he cannot perfectly keep.
works.plot: At Arthur's Christmas court, the Green Knight offers his axe-blow for a return stroke a year hence; Gawain beheads him, and the knight rides off alive. The following winter Gawain journeys to the Green Chapel, is entertained for three days at Hautdesert — where his host's wife tests his chastity with escalating temptations while the host hunts deer, boar, and fox in parallel scenes — and, having accepted the protective green girdle and concealed it, receives at the Chapel a nick on the neck: the girdle's shame is revealed as the whole adventure was Bertilak's design, set on him by Morgan le Fay.
works.significance: The most admired English romance ever written: its fusion of alliterative craft, courtly ideals, and moral seriousness — and its unmatched winter landscapes and temptation scenes — have made it a touchstone of English literature (translated by Tolkien, Armitage, and many others).
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line in stanzas of varying length, each closed by the five-line rhymed 'bob and wheel'.
works.context: Composed c. 1375–1400 by an unknown north-west Midlands poet (the 'Gawain-poet'), probably in the household circle of the Cheshire/Staffordshire gentry; preserved uniquely in BL Cotton MS Nero A.x, with Pearl, Patience, and Cleanness.
works.characters: Gawain; the Green Knight (Sir Bertilak); Lady Bertilak; Arthur; Guinevere; Morgan le Fay; the guide
works.structure: A two-part structure (the beheading game at Camelot; the journey, temptations, and exchange of winnings at Hautdesert), interlaced by the three parallel hunts and the three bedroom temptations, and closed by Gawain's return and Arthur's court's adoption of the girdle.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; attributed with Pearl, Patience, and Cleanness to the single 'Gawain-poet' on grounds of style, dialect, and shared manuscript.

editions.title: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
editions.editor: J. R. R. Tolkien and E. V. Gordon (eds.); rev. Norman Davis

works.title: Sir Launfal
works.description: Thomas Chestre's late fourteenth-century Breton lay of the fairy mistress: the knight Launfal, impoverished and slighted at Arthur's court, receives boundless wealth and the love of the fairy lady Tryamour on condition of secrecy, and is saved from death by her at his trial. The most accomplished English version of Marie de France's Lanval.
works.plot: Launfal, neglected by Arthur, rides out in despair and meets Tryamour, whose gifts restore his magnificence; his boast of her beauty at court — provoked by the queen's advances — brings trial for treason, but Tryamour appears at the judgement, vindicates him, and carries him to the fairy isle of Olyroun.
works.significance: The finest English fairy-mistress lay and the standard version of the Lanval story in English; a key text for the romance's treatment of women and power.
works.meter: Twelve-line tail-rhyme stanzas of the popular romance kind.
works.context: Composed c. 1390 by Thomas Chestre (who names himself in the poem), reworking the earlier Sir Landevale and Marie de France; preserved in BL Cotton MS Caligula A.ii.
works.characters: Launfal; Tryamour; Arthur; Guinevere (unnamed queen); the mayor of Caerleon
works.structure: The classic lai structure: courtly exclusion, otherworld encounter, transgression, trial, and translation to the otherworld.
works.attributionNotes: The author names himself 'Thomas Chestre' in the poem's opening lines.

works.title: Sir Orfeo
works.description: The masterpiece of the English Breton lay: the classical myth of Orpheus and Eurydice retold as a Celtic fairy romance, in which King Orfeo, harper of Winchester, loses his queen Heurodis to the fairy king and wins her back through the power of his music. Some 600 lines of haunting narrative, preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript.
works.plot: Heurodis is taken by the fairy king from under the ympe-tree; Orfeo abandons his throne to live as a harper in the wilderness, sees his queen among the fairy riders, follows them into their castle, and recovers her by his harping; the poem ends with the steward's loyalty tested and the kingdom restored.
works.significance: Universally regarded as the finest of the Middle English Breton lays and one of the great short narratives of the period; the classical myth's medieval transformation is a touchstone of romance criticism.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with lyrical set-pieces; economical and evocative.
works.context: Composed c. 1300, perhaps in the London area, reworking the Orpheus myth through Celtic fairy-lore and the Breton lai tradition; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript (c. 1330) and two fifteenth-century copies.
works.characters: Orfeo; Heurodis; the fairy king; the steward
works.structure: A lai of loss, wilderness exile, and recovery, framed by the steward episode; the Otherworld journey is its centre.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Solomon and Saturn I and II
altTitles: The Dialogue of Solomon and Saturn
works.description: Two wisdom dialogues in which Solomon, the biblical master of wisdom, contends with Saturn, the legendary Chaldean sage, over questions of fate, prayer, and the powers of the Pater Noster — its letters imagined as armed warriors assailing the devil. The poems are the most extravagant of the Old English wisdom tradition.
works.plot: In Solomon and Saturn II, the sages debate the powers of the Pater Noster: each letter becomes a warrior with a specific weapon against the fiend ('P has a golden rod and fights the devil...'); the poem surveys the poem's battles against evil in a fantasia of personified letters. Solomon and Saturn I concerns the praise of the Pater Noster and the books it governs, with a runic passage on the letter R.
works.significance: The wildest flights of the Old English wisdom tradition; central to the study of Anglo-Saxon learned imagination.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; dense, sometimes eccentric diction.
works.context: Preserved in Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MSS 41 and 422; the dialogues draw on apocryphal Solomonic and computistical lore.
works.characters: Solomon; Saturn; the personified letters of the Pater Noster
works.structure: Question-and-answer dialogue in the wisdom-contest tradition, elaborated with the allegorical letter-warfare of the Pater Noster passages.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Soul and Body I and II
altTitles: The Soul's Address to the Body
works.form: religious debate poem in alliterative verse
works.description: A pair of related poems (Vercelli Book I, 166 lines; Exeter Book II, 121 lines) in which the soul, revisiting its decaying body once a week, reproaches it for the sins of the flesh and foretells the torments of judgment. The earliest English body-and-soul debate, ancestor of a long medieval tradition.
works.plot: The damned soul, forced to revisit its corpse, addresses the silent body: 'Where are the riches you gathered? The hall you feasted in?' — enumerating the body's pleasures and their price in hell, the worms and the fire; the Exeter version closes with a brief address to the blessed soul by contrast. The debate's later fortunes run through the Middle English 'Desputisoun bitwen the Bodi and the Soule' to the danse macabre.
works.significance: Inaugurates the body-and-soul debate tradition that runs through Middle English literature.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 101v-103v) and the Exeter Book (fols. 98a-100a); the genre derives from Latin and homiletic sources.
works.characters: the Soul; the Body; (in II) the blessed soul
works.structure: A monologue of reproach and warning, spoken by the soul to the body at the grave; the two versions differ in length and ending.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Speke Parrot
works.form: verse satire in Skeltonics with macaronic Latin
works.description: The first of Skelton's great anti-Wolsey satires: a parrot — polyglot, learned, and fearless — speaks the court's dangerous truths in a torrent of macaronic verse, attacking the Cardinal's pride, his monopoly of the king's ear, and the corruption of the church, all under the parrot's traditional licence of the fool.
works.plot: The Parrot complains of his cage and his mistress's neglect, then turns to the abuses of the age: Wolsey's supremacy, clerical greed, and the decay of learning; the poem closes with a prayer for amendment.
works.significance: The founding text of the English tradition of political satire under censorship; its speaking-bird device recurs through the century to Spenser and beyond.
works.meter: Skeltonic lines studded with Latin, Greek, and school tags; the parrot's 'speaking' is a display of learned polyglot wit.
works.context: Written in 1521 as Wolsey's power peaked; the parrot's cage is the poet's own position under surveillance, and the poem circulates the satirical truths the court could not speak.
works.characters: the Parrot; (implicitly) Cardinal Wolsey
works.structure: A monologue of the speaking bird in the complaint tradition, shifting between personal grievance and public satire without fixed argument.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: St Erkenwald
works.description: An alliterative miracle-legend of 352 lines on the discovery, during the rebuilding of St Paul's, of a pagan judge's incorrupt tomb: the bishop Erkenwald's tearful prayer draws from the corpse the story of his just life and the baptism that, in the moment of his speech, admits the just pagan to heaven. The finest short alliterative poem of the period.
works.plot: Workmen excavating at St Paul's find a tomb whose body lies uncorrupted as in life; none can identify it, until Bishop Erkenwald, summoned to the mystery, speaks to the dead man, who reveals himself as a judge of heathen London, just in all his dealings; at the bishop's words of baptism, the corpse — denied heaven's sight so long — sighs, and crumbles to dust as its soul ascends.
works.significance: The classic Middle English treatment of the salvation of the just pagan (the problem Dante faced with Trajan and Virgil), and one of the most moving poems of the alliterative tradition.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line, restrained and solemn.
works.context: Composed c. 1386–1400 in the north-west Midlands, in the circle of the Gawain-poet (many scholars assign it to him), perhaps occasioned by work on St Paul's; preserved uniquely in BL Harley MS 2250 (dated 1477).
works.characters: Erkenwald; the pagan judge; the London crowd
works.structure: A single dramatic episode: discovery, wonder, dialogue, and resolution, in the manner of the alliterative miracle-legend.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; attributed by many scholars to the Gawain-poet.

works.title: Summa Logicae
works.description: William of Ockham's systematic treatise on logic, written c. 1323 before his summons to Avignon; in three parts it expounds terms, propositions, and the theory of argument, developing the nominalist ontology — the rejection of universals as real entities — for which Ockham is chiefly remembered.
works.summary: Part I analyses terms and the problem of universals, arguing that only individuals exist and that universal concepts are signs in the mind; Part II treats propositions and the properties of terms; Part III examines syllogistic, demonstrative, and probable argument, including the analysis of fallacies. The work is the vehicle of Ockham's razor in its methodological form: entities are not to be multiplied without necessity.
works.significance: The most influential logic textbook of the later Middle Ages; its nominalism reshaped fourteenth-century philosophy and theology and remains a principal point of reference in the history of logic.

editions.title: Guillelmi de Ockham Summa Logicae
editions.editor: Philotheus Boehner, Gedeon Gál, and Stephen F. Brown (eds.)

works.title: Surrey's Poems
altTitles: Sonnets and Lyrics of Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey
works.description: The collected shorter poems of the Earl of Surrey — sonnets in the new 'English' form he devised (three quatrains and a couplet), elegies, and lyrics such as 'The soote season', 'Alas, so all things now do hold their peace', and the elegy on Wyatt — printed posthumously in Tottel's Miscellany (1557).
works.plot: A courtier's lyric record: love's complaints, the seasons' changes, the deaths of friends, and the poet's imprisonment at Windsor, all in a grave, musical decasyllabic line.
works.significance: With Wyatt, the founder of the English sonnet; Surrey's smoother line and his rhyme scheme became the Elizabethan standard, and Tottel's printing of his verse made him the model of the English courtly poet.
works.meter: The regular iambic pentameter and the English sonnet rhyme scheme (abab cdcd efef gg) that Surrey perfected and Shakespeare inherited; smooth alternation of the accents.
works.context: Written in the last decade of Surrey's life, under the factional warfare that ended in his execution in 1547; the elegy on Wyatt makes the dead poet a mirror of his own fate.
works.characters: the speaker; the beloved ('Geraldine', Elizabeth Fitzgerald); the court
works.structure: Miscellany of sonnets and lyrics without narrative frame; Tottel's printed canon of forty poems is the principal witness.
works.attributionNotes: The Tottel canon of forty poems is accepted in the main; a few attributions are contested.

editions.title: Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey: Poems

works.title: Testament of Love
works.description: Thomas Usk's allegorical prose apologia, written in the Tower of London before his execution in 1388: the imprisoned author, in Boethian dialogue with Love and her company, defends his political career, expounds free will and grace, and seeks the 'Margaret' of his devotion. For three centuries it was printed and read as Chaucer's.
works.plot: The narrator, cast down by fortune and imprisoned, laments until the lady Love appears with her sisters; in three books she teaches him the nature of love and virtue, vindicates his service and his betrayals, and leads him through the doctrine of predestination and free will to the vision of the pearl of perfect bliss.
works.significance: The first major prose work in the Chaucerian line and a unique document of the political prisoner's consolation; its false attribution shaped the early reception of Chaucer himself.
works.meter: Prose, richly Chaucerian in vocabulary and cadence.
works.context: Composed 1384–88 in prison, in the factional struggles of Richard II's London (Usk had betrayed John of Northampton to Nicholas Brembre); the author's identity was recovered from the acrostic, overturning the Chaucerian attribution, only in the nineteenth century.
works.characters: the Narrator (Usk); Love; Margaret (the pearl); Fortune; the Virtues
works.structure: Three books of Boethian consolation, with the acrostic of the opening chapters spelling the author's name and his lady's — 'MARGARETE OF VIRTW HAVE MERCI ON THIN USK'.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to Usk secure from the acrostic and the records of his trial; previously attributed to Chaucer.

works.title: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
works.form: history and chronicle (prose with verse insertions)
works.description: A set of interrelated vernacular annals recording English history from the arrival of Julius Caesar to 1154, begun c. 892 (the 'Common Stock') in the circle of King Alfred and continued in centres across England for over two and a half centuries. The earliest continuous vernacular history of any European people and the backbone of the period's historiography.
works.plot: The annals record year by year the wars of the kings of Wessex and England, the Viking invasions, ecclesiastical events, and natural portents; they incorporate poems (The Battle of Brunanburh, The Capture of the Five Boroughs, the deaths of Edgar and Edward), documents, and, in the Peterborough continuation (to 1154), the last original Old English prose composed in England.
works.significance: The foundation of English historical prose; a continuous vernacular record unmatched elsewhere in early medieval Europe.
works.meter: Prose, with alliterative verse poems incorporated at several annal years.
works.context: The Common Stock was compiled c. 892, probably under Alfred's direction, from earlier annals, Bede, and oral tradition; continuations were kept at Winchester, Abingdon, Worcester, Peterborough, and Canterbury.
works.characters: Alfred; Æthelstan; Edgar; Æthelred; Cnut; Edward the Confessor; William the Conqueror; Peterborough continuator
works.structure: Annalistic: brief yearly entries of varying fullness, from single sentences to extended narrative set-pieces; the seven manuscripts (A-G) diverge into regional continuations.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous, corporate authorship; traditionally associated with Alfred's court for the Common Stock.

editions.title: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle: A Revised Translation

sources: Middle English Dictionary

works.title: The Awntyrs off Arthure
altTitles: The Anturs of Arther at the Tarnewathelan
works.description: An alliterative Arthurian poem of some 700 lines in two adventures: the ghost of Guinevere's mother, risen from a lake in Tarn Wadling to warn of pride and the fall of the Round Table, and the duel in which Gawain and Galeron contest disputed lands before Arthur's judgement. Its spectral first episode is among the most powerful scenes in the alliterative corpus.
works.plot: While hunting at Tarn Wadling, Guinevere and Gawain meet a ghost who prophesies the ruin of Arthur's court and shows the torments of the dead; in the second adventure, Gawain fights the knight Galeron for the lands Arthur has granted him, and Arthur's equitable judgement restores them — with the ghost's warning shadowing the court's splendour.
works.significance: The finest of the northern Gawain romances after Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, and the classic statement of the ghost-warning topos in Arthurian verse.
works.meter: Thirteen-line alliterative stanzas with rhyme and wheel.
works.context: Composed c. 1400 in the north of England, perhaps for a northern gentry audience with an interest in its Cumberland setting; preserved in four manuscripts and printed in the sixteenth century.
works.characters: Gawain; Guinevere; the ghost of Guinevere's mother; Galeron; Arthur
works.structure: A two-part romance (ghostly warning; judicial combat) linked by the theme of land, justice, and mortality.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Ayenbite of Inwyt
works.description: The Kentish translation, completed in 1340 by Dan Michel of Northgate, monk of St Augustine's, Canterbury, of the Somme le Roi of Frère Lorens: a comprehensive prose manual of the vices, virtues, commandments, and the art of holy dying. Its title — 'remorse of conscience' — gives the work its penitential keynote.
works.plot: The treatise anatomizes the deadly sins and their remedies, the Ten Commandments, the Lord's Prayer, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the preparation for death, in a systematic scheme of moral and catechetical instruction.
works.significance: The most extensive Kentish text in Middle English, invaluable to historical linguistics, and a principal document of lay catechesis in the age of the Somme le Roi tradition.
works.meter: Prose; a famously conservative Kentish dialect with heavy French-derived vocabulary.
works.context: Completed in 1340 at St Augustine's Abbey, Canterbury, on the eve of the Black Death; preserved in a single autograph manuscript, BL Arundel MS 57.
works.characters: none (doctrinal treatise)
works.structure: A systematic doctrinal handbook following the structure of the French Somme le Roi, with illustrative exempla.
works.attributionNotes: The translator names himself in the colophon: Dan Michel of Northgate.

works.title: The Babees Book
works.description: The classic late medieval courtesy book: a poem of instruction for young boys ('babees') entering noble households, teaching them how to stand, dress, serve at table, and speak to their betters, with the companion courtesy poems and John Russell's Boke of Nurture that accompany it in the manuscripts. The standard English manual of the civility that defined the late medieval and early modern gentleman.
works.plot: The poem addresses the boy entering service, prescribing his conduct from rising to bedtime — cleanliness, table manners, deference of speech and gesture — and moralizing the discipline of courtesy as the school of virtue, in the tradition of the medieval courtesy literature descended from the classical 'nurture' of the young.
works.significance: The classic English courtesy book and the ancestor of the early modern conduct tradition (Erasmus, Castiglione's English imitators); its rules of table and speech chart the history of English civility.
works.meter: Couplets and seven-line stanzas, plain and mnemonic.
works.context: Composed c. 1475, when the great households' demand for trained service and the school curriculum of manners converged; preserved in BL Harley MS 5086 and related manuscripts; edited by F. J. Furnivall (1868) in the volumes that founded the study of English manners literature.
works.characters: the 'babee' (addressee); the master
works.structure: A single didactic poem in the courtesy tradition, with the companion poems (Urbanitatis, Stans Puer ad Mensam, Russell's Boke of Nurture) forming a curriculum in the manuscripts.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Battle of Brunanburh
works.form: battle poetry (chronicle poem) in alliterative verse
works.description: A panegyric of 73 lines, entered in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for the year 937, celebrating the crushing victory of King Æthelstan and his brother Edmund over a coalition of Scots, Strathclyde Britons, and Dublin Norsemen led by Constantine and Anlaf (Olaf) Guthfrithson. The greatest of the Chronicle's poems, composed in the full heroic manner.
works.plot: The poem exults in the day-long battle — 'never was greater slaughter in this island' — as the West Saxons and Mercians pursue the fleeing allies; Constantine, his son slain, and Anlaf flee to their ships, and the victors return to Wessex leaving the battlefield to the carrion beasts, the raven, eagle, and wolf.
works.significance: The masterpiece of late heroic panegyric; Tennyson's translation (1880) is a landmark of Victorian medievalism.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; dense use of kennings and the beasts-of-battle formula.
works.context: The battle of Brunanburh (937), the greatest English victory of the tenth century, secured Æthelstan's supremacy in Britain; the poem is preserved in four manuscripts of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.
works.characters: Æthelstan; Edmund; Constantine of Scotland; Anlaf Guthfrithson
works.structure: A compact celebration in the heroic mode: the boast of victory, the pursuit, the flight of the kings, and the 'beasts of battle' topos, with a closing return to the annalistic frame.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife

editions.title: The Battle of Brunanburh: A Casebook

sources: British Library Digitised Manuscripts

works.title: The Battle of Maldon
works.description: A fragmentary poem of 325 lines commemorating the battle of Maldon (10 or 11 August 991), in which Ealdorman Byrhtnoth of Essex and his retinue fought a Viking army at the causeway of the Blackwater and were destroyed; the poem is the last great expression of the heroic code, celebrating loyalty unto death.
works.plot: Byrhtnoth arrays his levies against the Vikings on the tidal causeway of the Pante; he refuses tribute, and when the Vikings ask passage he grants it 'for his ofermod' (overconfidence) — the poem's great crux — drawing up for battle on the shore. After Byrhtnoth falls, a series of retainers make speeches vowing to avenge him or die beside him, and the poem breaks off in the midst of the last stand.
works.significance: The fullest poetic statement of the comitatus ethic of loyalty unto death; Byrhtwold's speech is among the most quoted passages of Old English verse.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of the classical kind, with sustained martial diction.
works.context: The battle is recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle s.a. 991 and in the Vita Oswaldi; the poem survives only in an early eighteenth-century transcript of Cotton MS Otho A.xii, destroyed in the Cotton fire of 1731. The tribute of 10,000 pounds paid after the battle began the Danegeld payments.
works.characters: Byrhtnoth; Wulfstan; Ælfhere; Maccus; Offa; Ælfwine; Leofsunu; Dunnere; Byrhtwold; Godric (the betrayer)
works.structure: A single continuous battle-narrative built from speeches: the Viking messenger's demand, Byrhtnoth's reply, the combat, and the laddered sequence of retainers' vows (Ælfwine, Offa, Leofsunu, Dunnere, Byrhtwold — 'will shall be the harder, heart the keener').
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the opening and closing of the poem are lost with the manuscript.
sources: Dictionary of Old English: A to I online

works.title: The Bestiary
works.description: A Middle English bestiary of 802 lines, probably of East Anglian origin, describing the nature of the lion, eagle, serpent, stag, whale, and other creatures and drawing from each a moral and allegorical lesson, in the tradition of the Physiologus. It is the earliest English bestiary to survive in the vernacular.
works.plot: Each animal's natural history — the lion's sleep with open eyes, the whale luring sailors, the phoenix's rebirth — is expounded as a figure of Christ, the devil, or the Christian soul.
works.significance: The link between the Old English Physiologus poems and the later English bestiary tradition, and a vivid example of medieval allegorical natural history in the vernacular.
works.meter: Irregular rhyming couplets of varying length, with some alliterative ornament.
works.context: Composed c. 1250, translated from the Latin Physiologus of Theobaldus; preserved uniquely in BL Arundel MS 292, with Norwich connections.
works.characters: the animals (lion, eagle, serpent, stag, fox, spider, whale, siren, elephant, turtle-dove, panther, dove)
works.structure: A sequence of discrete animal exempla, each divided between natural description (natura) and moralization (significacio).
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Boke Named the Governour
works.description: Elyot's treatise on the education and conduct of the English ruling class, the first major work of English political and educational theory written in the vernacular rather than Latin.
works.plot: The first book prescribes the upbringing of a future governor from infancy — nurses, tutors, the curriculum of classical authors, music, painting, and physical exercise. The second book treats the virtues proper to a ruler: justice, fortitude, temperance, wisdom, and the golden mean. The third discusses the cardinal virtues and their application in counsel and judgement.
works.significance: A founding text of English humanism in the vernacular: it established the ideal of the educated magistrate, coined or first recorded many English words ('education', 'encyclopaedia'), and remained an authority on gentlemanly conduct for two centuries.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written c. 1530–31 while Elyot, a diplomat and clerk, was out of royal favour after Wolsey's fall; dedicated to Henry VIII, it drew on Castiglione's Il Cortegiano and Patrizi's De regno, and shaped the humanist programme of gentlemanly education institutionalized in the grammar schools.
works.structure: Three books of systematic exposition, dense with citation of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, and Plutarch, and illustrated with exemplary stories of classical princes.

works.title: The Book of Common Prayer (1549)
altTitles: The First Prayer Book of Edward VI
The Booke of the Common Prayer and Administracion of the Sacramentes
works.description: The first Book of Common Prayer, compiled chiefly by Thomas Cranmer and imposed by the Act of Uniformity of 1549 as the single liturgy of the English church; the foundational text of Anglican worship.
works.plot: The book replaces the medieval service books (missal, breviary, manual, pontifical) with one English liturgy: Morning and Evening Prayer, the collects, the order for Holy Communion, baptism, confirmation, matrimony, visitation of the sick, burial, and the ordination rites, with the psalter and lectionary — retaining much medieval devotion while recasting the eucharist as a communion of all the people in both kinds.
works.significance: The greatest single achievement of English liturgical prose: Cranmer's collects ('whose service is perfect freedom', 'read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest') entered the language itself, and the book's cadences shaped English prose from Hooker to the Authorized Version and beyond.
works.meter: Prose with psalmody
works.context: Drafted in 1548–49 by Cranmer with a committee of bishops and divines, authorized by the first Act of Uniformity (January 1549), and introduced at Whitsun 1549, provoking the Prayer Book Rebellion in Devon and Cornwall; the book was revised in 1552 (the Second Prayer Book), restored by Elizabeth in 1559, and its language survives in the 1662 book used for four centuries.
works.structure: A complete liturgical manual arranged by rite, with rubrics, calendar, and lectionary; the prose is Cranmer's — sonorous, cadenced, and scriptural.
works.attributionNotes: The book is the work of Cranmer and his committee; the title page names no author, and the record attributes the compilation to Cranmer as chief author, following universal scholarly usage.

editions.title: The Book of Common Prayer: The Texts of 1549, 1559, and 1662

works.title: The Book of Faith
works.description: Reginald Pecock's vernacular treatise of 1456 on the nature of faith and its relation to reason, written in the last years before his condemnation: faith, he argues, is a species of knowledge grounded in evidence and reason, not mere belief on authority — the doctrine that brought him to trial and abjuration. It survives in the author's own manuscript.
works.plot: Pecock analyzes faith as intellectual assent produced by the 'doom of reason' on credible testimony, distinguishes it from opinion and knowledge, answers the objections of the 'unbilevers', and defends the lay person's right and duty to understand what he believes.
works.significance: The boldest medieval English statement of the rationality of faith, and the terminus of vernacular theology before the Reformation.
works.meter: Argumentative English prose, technical and precise.
works.context: Completed in 1456, a year before Pecock's trial; its rationalism was among the charges against him, and the work survives only in the Trinity College, Cambridge, autograph manuscript (MS B.14.45).
works.characters: none (theological treatise)
works.structure: Two books of philosophical-theological analysis, in the scholastic quaestio manner adapted to English.
works.attributionNotes: Pecock's authorship secure.

works.title: The Book of Homilies
altTitles: Certain Sermons or Homilies Appointed by the King's Majesty to Be Declared and Read
works.description: The first official book of sermons of the Church of England, issued in 1547 under the direction of Thomas Cranmer (who wrote several of the homilies himself) to be read in parish churches; a principal vehicle of Reformation doctrine for the laity.
works.plot: Twelve homilies expound the Protestant faith in plain English: on scripture, the misery of mankind, salvation by faith alone, good works, Christian love, against swearing and perjury, against strife, obedience to rulers, and against whoredom and adultery — each designed to be read from the pulpit by clergy who could not preach.
works.significance: The official voice of the English Reformation for ordinary congregations: the homilies translated Protestant doctrine into a national plain style and remained binding on the church for three centuries, feeding directly into the religious language of the Elizabethans.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Issued in 1547, the first year of Edward VI, as part of the royal Injunctions requiring the homilies' use; the homily 'Of Good Works' and others are Cranmer's own, and the second book (with the famous homily 'Against Disobedience and Wilful Rebellion') followed in 1571, making the two books the official theology of the Elizabethan church.
works.structure: Twelve self-contained sermons, each with a scriptural text, exposition, and application, written for oral delivery by non-preaching clergy.
works.attributionNotes: The book is a collaborative production of Cranmer, Thomas Becon, and other reformers; the record attributes it to Cranmer as the supervising compiler, following standard scholarship, while noting the collaboration.

works.title: The Book of Margery Kempe
works.description: The dictated spiritual autobiography of Margery Kempe of King's Lynn (c. 1436–38), commonly called the first autobiography in English: her conversion after childbirth, her marriage and vow of chastity, her uncontrollable weeping at the thought of the Passion, her pilgrimages to Jerusalem, Rome, and Santiago, and her examinations for heresy before the archbishops of Canterbury and York. A unique document of female lay piety and of fifteenth-century English life.
works.plot: Margery recounts her visionary conversations with Christ, her struggle with her husband for chastity, her travels through Europe and the Holy Land, her clashes with hostile clergy and her vindications, her visit to Julian of Norwich, and her old age caring for her ailing husband — the whole narrated in the third person through her scribes.
works.significance: The first autobiography in English and the earliest extended account of a laywoman's religious life; its frankness about body, marriage, and authority has made it a founding text of women's literary history.
works.meter: Direct, colloquial prose, vivid in dialogue and detail, mediated by her scribes.
works.context: Dictated c. 1436–38, with a second book of the 1430s–40s, in the East Anglian culture of orthodox lay devotion shadowed by the Lollard trials; the complete text was lost until the discovery of the manuscript in 1934 (BL Additional MS 61823), and first published in 1936.
works.characters: Margery Kempe; John Kempe (her husband); Julian of Norwich; Christ (in dialogue); the archbishops
works.structure: Two books of episodic autobiography, moving between mystical colloquy and the social world of East Anglian towns, courts, and pilgrim routes.
works.attributionNotes: Margery Kempe's authorship (by dictation to scribes) is recorded within the book itself.

editions.title: The Book of Margery Kempe
editions.editor: Sanford Brown Meech and Hope Emily Allen (eds.)

works.title: The Book of St Albans
altTitles: The Book of Hawking, Hunting, and Heraldry
works.form: courtesy book and household manual (verse and prose)
works.description: The gentleman's handbook printed at St Albans in 1486: treatises in verse and prose on hawking, hunting, and heraldry, together with the terms of venery and the 'companies of beasts', traditionally attributed to Dame Juliana Berners, prioress of Sopwell. It is the classic English manual of the gentleman's arts, reprinted and expanded into the seventeenth century.
works.plot: The book instructs the reader in the falconer's and hunter's crafts — the mews, the lure, the chase of the hart, the terms of the hunt — and in the blazoning of arms, closing with the famous catalogues of collective nouns ('a parliament of rooks', 'a murmuration of starlings') that fixed the English vocabulary of the field.
works.significance: The foundational English manual of the gentleman's arts: its venery terms entered the language and its heraldry shaped Tudor and Stuart practice.
works.meter: Mixed: the hawking and hunting treatises in rhyme royal and couplets, the heraldry in prose.
works.context: Printed at the schoolmaster press of St Albans in 1486 (a colophon names 'the schoolmaster of St Albans'), in the post-Caxton provincial print boom; the attribution to Juliana Berners appears in the 1496 de Worde reprint.
works.characters: none (manual)
works.structure: A compilation of distinct treatises (hawking; hunting; arms; blazoning) in the practical-manual tradition.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dame Juliana Berners (prioress of Sopwell) in the 1496 reprint; the attribution is traditional and doubted. authorship_status reflects this traditional attribution.

works.title: The Book of the Duchess
altTitles: The Deth of Blaunche the Duchesse
works.description: Chaucer's earliest major poem (1,334 lines in octosyllabic couplets), a dream vision elegy for Blanche, Duchess of Lancaster, who died in 1368: the insomniac dreamer overhears a grieving knight in black, whose lament for his lost lady — 'White' — unfolds the ideal of courtly love into a meditation on death and consolation. The poem that founded the English dream-vision tradition.
works.plot: The dreamer, sleepless from an eight-year love-sickness, reads Ovid's tale of Ceyx and Alcyone and falls asleep; in his dream he meets the Man in Black, who tells of his long service to Fortune and of the peerless lady White whom he won and has now lost; only the dreamer's blunt question — 'she is dead?' — breaks the elegy's obliqueness, and the dream ends with the hunting of the hart and the poem's closure on the word 'king'.
works.significance: The first great English dream poem and the foundation of Chaucer's mature art; its fusion of consolation, allegory, and courtly elegy shaped the entire English dream-vision tradition.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets of courtly grace, adapted from Machaut and the Roman de la Rose.
works.context: Composed c. 1368–72, commemorating Blanche of Lancaster (d. 12 September 1368), first wife of John of Gaunt, Chaucer's patron; the poem's courtly audience would have recognized the dead duchess in the knight's 'White'.
works.characters: the Dreamer; the Man in Black; Lady White; Fortune
works.structure: A double frame (reading; dream) enclosing the knight's elegiac autobiography, in the French dit manner; the wordplay on 'White', 'hart/heart', and 'king' ties consolation to allegory.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure; the occasional reference to Blanche is universally accepted.

works.title: The Bowge of Courte
works.description: Skelton's first major poem, a dream satire in rhyme royal: the dreamer Drede boards the ship Bowge of Courte, where the personified vices of the court — Flattery, Suspicion, Harvy Hafter, Disdain, Riot, Deceit — successively menace and betray him, until he leaps overboard. It is the founding text of the Tudor court-satire tradition.
works.plot: Drede, standing at the shore, is invited aboard the Bowge of Courte; each passenger woos him and then turns on him, and the poem breaks off as he prepares to leap from the ship to save his life.
works.significance: The first sustained court satire of the English Renaissance, combining the dream vision of Chaucer with the estates satire of the Middle Ages and setting the pattern for the complaint literature of the sixteenth century.
works.meter: Seven-line rhyme royal stanzas, handled with Chaucerian fluency but a distinctly satirical edge.
works.context: Written at the turn of the century, when Skelton was moving from court service to the country living at Diss; its portrait of court corruption anticipates his later anti-Wolsey satires.
works.characters: Drede (the dreamer); Flattery; Suspicion; Harvy Hafter; Disdain; Riot; Deceit
works.structure: Dream vision with prologue; an allegorical sea voyage in which successive encounters with the courtly vices build to a single climactic decision to abandon the court.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; printed by Wynkyn de Worde about 1499.

editions.title: John Skelton: The Complete English Poems

works.title: The Brus
works.description: John Barbour's verse chronicle of Robert Bruce and the Scottish wars of independence, completed c. 1375 in some 14,000 octosyllabic lines: the murder of the Red Comyn, the crowning at Scone, the years of guerrilla warfare, and the great victory at Bannockburn (1314), with James Douglas as the poem's second hero. The first great work of Scottish literature and the fountainhead of the nation's heroic self-image.
works.plot: The poem follows Bruce from the killing of Comyn and his coronation through defeat, exile, and the legendary perseverance of the spider episode to the recovery of the kingdom castle by castle, the battle of Bannockburn, the raids of Douglas into England, and the king's death — all framed by the poem's great theme, that 'fredome is a noble thing'.
works.significance: The first great poem in Scots and the founding text of Scottish national literature; Burns's 'Scots Wha Hae' and the whole Bruce tradition descend from it.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets of energy and speed, in Older Scots.
works.context: Completed in 1375 by the archdeacon of Aberdeen, in the court of Robert II (Bruce's grandson), when the Stewart dynasty needed a heroic past; preserved in two manuscripts (1487, 1489) and printed in 1571.
works.characters: Robert Bruce; James Douglas; Edward II; Edward Bruce; the Scottish and English armies
works.structure: Twenty books of continuous narrative in the romance-chronicle manner, with set-piece battles and speeches, closed by the king's death and the poet's envoy.
works.attributionNotes: Barbour's authorship secure (named in the text and the royal records).

editions.title: Barbour's Bruce
editions.editor: Matthew P. McDiarmid and James A. C. Stevenson (eds.)

works.title: The Brut Chronicle
works.description: The Middle English prose Brut, the most popular secular text in late medieval England: a chronicle of Britain from the Trojan Brutus through the Arthurian kings to the fourteenth century, with continuations carrying the story through the Wars of the Roses. Over 180 manuscripts survive in English — more than any other secular work — and Caxton's print (1480) made it the standard popular history of England.
works.plot: The chronicle narrates the legendary British history of the Brut tradition — Brutus, Lear, Arthur — then the Saxon, Norman, and Plantagenet reigns, with the continuations adding the Lancastrian and Yorkist wars; its plain, annalistic prose made it the layman's history of England.
works.significance: The bestselling secular book of the English Middle Ages: its diffusion defines the popular historical culture out of which Tudor history writing grew.
works.meter: Plain, formulaic prose of the chronicle tradition.
works.context: The earliest version was made in the later fourteenth century, probably in London, from French and Latin sources; it was expanded continuously through the fifteenth century (the 'common version' to 1419, continuations to 1461 and later) and printed by Caxton in 1480.
works.characters: Brutus; Arthur; the kings of England to Edward IV
works.structure: A regnal chronicle in the Brut tradition, open-ended and continuously continued by successive compilers.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous and compilational.

works.title: The Buke of the Howlat
works.description: Richard Holland's Scottish alliterative beast-allegory of some 1,000 lines, composed c. 1448 for the Douglas family: the owl, ashamed of his ugliness, appeals through the assembly of birds to the pope and the emperor, each bird vying in flattery, until Dame Nature restores him to his proper worth. A satire of pride, courts, and flattery, and the last major alliterative poem of the tradition.
works.plot: The howlat, complaining of his feathers, is counselled by the peacock to seek redress; the birds assemble in parliament before the pope and emperor, but the debate degenerates into mutual slander and sycophancy, until Nature intervenes, clothes the owl in dignity, and the poem ends with the Douglas heraldry and the family's praise.
works.significance: The last major alliterative poem in the British tradition and a key document of Douglas politics, heraldry, and the Scottish reception of the Alliterative Revival.
works.meter: Thirteen-line alliterative stanzas with rhyme and wheel, in Older Scots.
works.context: Composed c. 1448 by Richard Holland, secretary to Archibald Douglas, Earl of Moray, for the Douglas family at a moment of their power; preserved in the Asloan and Bannatyne manuscripts (c. 1515, 1568).
works.characters: the Howlat; the Peacock; the Pope; the Emperor; Dame Nature; the birds of the parliament
works.structure: A beast-parliament in the Chaucerian manner, framed by the owl's complaint and closed by the heraldic celebration of the Douglases.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Richard Holland on the evidence of the poem's colophon and Douglas records.

works.title: The Canterbury Tales
works.description: Chaucer's unfinished masterpiece and the supreme achievement of Middle English literature: a frame-tale collection in which some thirty pilgrims journeying from the Tabard Inn to Canterbury agree to a storytelling contest, the tales ranging from the Knight's romance and the Miller's fabliau to the Wife of Bath's prologue, the Pardoner's sermon, and the Parson's treatise. Begun c. 1387 and left unfinished at Chaucer's death in 1400.
works.plot: In the General Prologue the narrator joins a company of pilgrims — knight, miller, reeve, wife of Bath, pardoner, summoner, nun's priest, and the rest — each vividly portrayed; Harry Bailly, the Host, proposes the tale-telling game, and the tales that follow answer and quarrel with one another across the whole range of medieval genres, from courtly romance (Knight, Squire, Franklin) through fabliau (Miller, Reeve, Shipman, Merchant) and saint's life (Second Nun, Prioress) to sermon (Pardoner), beast fable (Nun's Priest), and the closing penitential treatise of the Parson.
works.significance: The most influential single work of English literature: its pilgrims, its tales, and its frame established the English tradition of comic realism, dramatic monologue, and narrative irony that runs through Shakespeare to the novel.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of unprecedented flexibility, with rhyme royal, tail-rhyme, and prose for special effects; the decasyllabic line perfected.
works.context: Composed c. 1387–1400 in London, drawing on Boccaccio, Ovid, Boethius, and the estates tradition; the pilgrimage to Becket's shrine at Canterbury supplied the frame; circulated in some eighty manuscripts and printed by Caxton (1476–78) and his successors, making it the foundation of the English printed canon.
works.characters: the Narrator; the Host (Harry Bailly); the Knight; the Miller; the Reeve; the Wife of Bath; the Pardoner; the Friar; the Summoner; the Nun's Priest; the Parson; and the other pilgrims
works.structure: A frame narrative (the pilgrimage, the Host's game) enclosing twenty-four tales grouped into ten fragments; the links between tales stage the pilgrims' quarrels and judgments, and the work's unfinished state is part of its design.
works.attributionNotes: Uniquely well attested: Chaucer's authorship of the Tales is not in doubt, though the ordering of the fragments and some links are editorial.

works.title: The Castle of Health
works.description: Elyot's vernacular treatise on diet and regimen, the first substantial English medical handbook written by a layman for lay readers.
works.plot: The book surveys the four humours and complexions, the properties of foods and drinks, sleep, exercise, and the regimen proper to each age and season, advising the reader how to preserve health through moderation and self-knowledge.
works.significance: A landmark in the vernacularization of medicine and natural knowledge in Tudor England, influential on later dietary literature and a document of humanist attitudes to the body.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in the mid-1530s and printed by Thomas Berthelet in 1539 (with editions to 1610); Elyot's attempt to bring learned medicine into English paralleled his linguistic programme in The Governour.
works.structure: Four books of systematic exposition, compiled from Galen, Hippocrates, and the medieval regimen literature.

works.title: The Castle of Perseverance
works.description: The earliest complete English morality play (c. 1400–25, 3,649 lines): the life of Mankind (Humanum Genus) from birth to judgement, staged on the famous circular 'place' with its central castle and five scaffolds, as the virtues and vices battle for his soul through the Seven Ages. The most ambitious play of the English medieval stage.
works.plot: Mankind, born in sin, is led by his Bad Angel through World, Flesh, and the Devil to the seven deadly sins; rescued by Confession, he is garrisoned in the Castle of Perseverance with the virtues; the sins' siege fails, but Covetousness wins him in old age, until Death strikes and the debate of the four daughters of God — Mercy, Peace, Righteousness, Truth — yields his salvation.
works.significance: The foundational English morality: its stage diagram, its allegorical cast, and its theology of mercy set the pattern for the genre through Everyman to the Elizabethan stage.
works.meter: Thirteen-line stanzas (rime couée with wheel), with stage directions prescribing the elaborate fixed staging.
works.context: Composed c. 1400–25 in East Anglia (the manuscript's language is Norfolk), in the milieu of the great fifteenth-century moralities; preserved uniquely in the Macro manuscript (Folger Shakespeare Library, MS V.a.354, c. 1440) with Mankind and Wisdom.
works.characters: Mankind (Humanum Genus); the Bad and Good Angels; World, Flesh, and the Devil; the Seven Deadly Sins; the Seven Virtues; Confession; Death; God; the Four Daughters of God
works.structure: A four-scaffold cosmic drama (God; World; Flesh; Devil) around the central castle, with the banns, the siege, the death scene, and the parliament of heaven as its great movements.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Chief Promises of God unto Man
altTitles: A Tragedy or Interlude Manifesting the Chief Promises of God unto Man
works.description: John Bale's interlude of the covenants of God from Adam to Christ, composed c. 1538 and printed at Wesel in 1547; a dramatic sermon on the promises fulfilled in the gospel.
works.plot: God the Father, in seven acts, makes his successive promises to man — to Adam of the woman's seed, to Noah of the rainbow covenant, to Abraham of the blessing of nations, to Moses of the law, to David of the everlasting throne, to Isaiah of the virgin's son, and to John the Baptist of the Lamb of God — each act closing with a prayer or antiphon, the whole demonstrating that the Old Testament is fulfilled in Christ.
works.significance: The most accomplished of Bale's biblical interludes and a model of Reformation dramaturgy: its covenant structure turned the mystery-cycle tradition to doctrinal ends and influenced the biblical drama of the Elizabethan church.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic passages with antiphons
works.context: Written c. 1538 during Bale's service as a Protestant dramatist under Cromwell, and printed at Wesel in 1547 in the collection of Bale's biblical plays; the play embodies the Protestant programme of replacing the old mysteries with doctrinal drama drawn from scripture alone.
works.characters: God the Father (Pater Coelestis); Adam; Noah; Abraham; Moses; David; Isaiah; John the Baptist; Baleus Prolocutor
works.structure: Seven acts, each a dialogue between God the Father (as Pater Coelestis) and a biblical figure, framed by a prologue (Bale as Prolocutor) and an epilogue; the play is a doctrinal pageant of the covenants.

editions.title: The Complete Plays of John Bale, vol. 2

works.title: The Cloud of Unknowing
works.description: The classic English treatise of apophatic contemplation, written in the late fourteenth century by an anonymous master (perhaps a Carthusian or secular priest) for a young disciple: the soul seeking God must enter the 'cloud of unknowing' between itself and God, striking down every thought with the dart of longing love and the 'naked intent' of the single word. The most intellectually rigorous work of the English mystical canon.
works.plot: The author teaches his disciple the work of contemplation: the forgetting of all creatures, the rejection of discursive meditation, the piercing of the darkness with love — and warns throughout against the false mysticism of physical fervour and deluded visions, prescribing the discipline of the single word ('God' or 'love') repeated in the heart.
works.significance: The supreme English expression of the negative way and a work of the first rank in the European contemplative tradition; its psychology of attention and intention has given it a continuing modern readership.
works.meter: Precise, sinewy prose, paradoxically articulate about the ineffable; vivid negative imagery (clouds, darts, nakedness).
works.context: Composed c. 1375–1400, probably in the north-east Midlands, in the orbit of the Carthusian order; it circulated with the author's other works (The Book of Privy Counselling, the translation of pseudo-Dionysius's Mystical Theology) and was read by the English Benedictine revival and by modern contemplatives (Thomas Merton).
works.characters: the author (spiritual director); the young disciple (addressee)
works.structure: Seventy-five short chapters of graduated instruction, in the apophatic tradition of pseudo-Dionysius, with the 'cloud' as its organizing image.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the author is often identified as a Carthusian on grounds of the work's transmission, but the identification is conjectural.

works.title: The Coverdale Bible
altTitles: Biblia: The Bible Faithfully Translated into English
works.description: Miles Coverdale's translation of the whole Bible into English, printed in 1535 (probably at Antwerp); the first complete printed Bible in English.
works.plot: A complete Bible — Old Testament, Apocrypha, and New Testament — translated 'out of Douche and Latyn' (German and Latin versions) as Coverdale's title page honestly states, with Tyndale's New Testament and Pentateuch incorporated; dedicated to Henry VIII, with a preface defending vernacular scripture.
works.significance: The first complete English Bible in print and the bridge from Tyndale to the authorized versions: its psalter became the Prayer Book psalter of 1662, still sung in Anglican worship, and its title page initiated the tradition of the English Bible as a national book.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Printed in 1535, probably at Antwerp (the colophon of some copies points to Cologne); Anne Boleyn's patronage and Cromwell's diplomacy won it royal acceptance, and in 1537 it was licensed for sale in England, making the English Bible legal for the first time.
works.structure: The full biblical canon with prologues, chapter summaries, and a dedication to the king.

works.title: The Creed
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.form: religious lyric (creedal paraphrase) in alliterative verse
works.description: A versification of the Apostles' Creed in 57 lines, expanding each article of the faith — the creation, the Incarnation, the Passion, the harrowing of hell, the Ascension, and the last judgment — into alliterative verse of notable doctrinal clarity.
works.plot: The poem follows the articles of the Creed in order: God the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth; Christ's conception, birth, suffering, death, descent into hell, resurrection, and ascension; and the coming judgment of the living and the dead.
works.significance: The only surviving Old English verse rendering of the Apostles' Creed, valuable for its formulation of Christology and eschatology in the native idiom.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the poem's compact clauses follow the Creed article by article.
works.context: The Creed was taught to all Christians as the summary of the faith and recited in the daily offices; its versification belongs to the same vernacular devotional project as the Lord's Prayer poems.
works.structure: A sequential paraphrase of the Creed's articles, each expanded with traditional doctrinal imagery (the descent into hell, the trumpet of judgment).
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Descent into Hell
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.form: religious narrative poem in alliterative verse
works.description: A narrative poem on Christ's descent into hell between the Crucifixion and the Resurrection, his release of the patriarchs and prophets, and the Resurrection itself. It draws on the Gospel of Nicodemus tradition and dramatizes the harrowing as a triumphant act of liberation.
works.plot: Christ descends to hell, breaks its gates, and frees the captive righteous — Adam, the patriarchs, and the prophets — who greet him as their long-awaited redeemer. The poem closes with the women's discovery of the empty tomb and the angel's announcement of the Resurrection.
works.significance: The only surviving Old English poem devoted wholly to the harrowing of hell, and an important witness to the devotional imagination that also produced The Dream of the Rood and Christ III.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with formulaic phrasing; the speeches of the patriarchs are given rhetorical weight through balanced alliterative clauses.
works.context: The harrowing of hell was a central motif of early medieval devotion, represented in art and liturgy as well as poetry; the poem is contemporary with the flourishing of the theme in Anglo-Saxon stone sculpture and homiletic prose.
works.characters: Christ, Adam, the patriarchs and prophets, the women at the tomb
works.structure: A compact narrative in two movements: the harrowing itself (the descent, the breaking of the gates, the speeches of the patriarchs) and the Resurrection morning at the tomb, with typological echoes of the Exodus throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. No attribution has been proposed.

works.title: The Destruction of Troy
altTitles: The Gest Hystoriale of the Destruction of Troy
works.description: The longest alliterative poem of the revival (over 14,000 lines), translating Guido delle Colonne's Latin Historia destructionis Troiae: the full Trojan story from Jason and the golden fleece to the fall of the city and the homecomings of the Greeks. A work of encyclopedic narrative scope, prized for its battles, storms, and sieges, preserved in a single manuscript.
works.plot: The poem recounts the causes and course of the Trojan war — the Argonauts, the first destruction of Troy, the judgement of Paris and rape of Helen, the ten years' siege with its councils, battles, and single combats, the treachery of the wooden horse, the burning of the city, and the fates of the returning heroes.
works.significance: The fullest Middle English Troy narrative and the summit of alliterative translation; its matter links the revival to Lydgate's Troy Book and the Tudor Troy tradition.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line sustained over an unprecedented length.
works.context: Composed c. 1385–1400 in the north-west Midlands, translating Guido delle Colonne (1287) with additions; preserved uniquely in Glasgow, Hunterian MS V.2.8 (mid-sixteenth century).
works.characters: Hector; Achilles; Priam; Paris; Helen; Agamemnon; Ulysses; Troilus
works.structure: A continuous chronicle-romance in the Guido tradition, organized by the war's causes, course, and aftermath, with elaborate set-piece descriptions.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Dictionary
altTitles: The Dictionary of Syr Thomas Eliot Knyght
works.description: Elyot's Latin–English dictionary, the first classical dictionary of the English language and the basis of the later English lexicographical tradition.
works.plot: A reference work with no argument: Latin headwords with English definitions, drawing on Calepino's Dictionarium and enriched by Elyot's own scholarship, published in a revised edition as Bibliotheca Eliotae in 1542 (revised and enlarged by Thomas Cooper, 1548).
works.significance: The founding work of English lexicography: it made classical learning accessible in the vernacular, standardized English equivalents for Latin terms, and served as the model for all subsequent Latin–English dictionaries.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Compiled 1536–38 for Thomas Berthelet, with a dedication to Henry VIII; it was the first Latin–English dictionary intended for the study of classical authors rather than the medieval vocabularies, and Cooper's revisions made it the foundation of Renaissance lexicography in England.
works.structure: Alphabetical dictionary entries.

works.title: The Distichs of Cato (Old English)
altTitles: The Old English Dicts of Cato
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Trinity College MS R.9.17 (c. 1100); also London, British Library, Cotton Julius A.ii and Cotton Vespasian D.xiv
works.description: An Old English prose translation of the Disticha Catonis, the late-antique collection of moral distichs that was the standard first reader of the medieval schoolroom. The translation renders Cato's maxims — on wisdom, speech, friendship, thrift, and the conduct of life — into plain vernacular prose for readers without Latin.
works.plot: The text translates the four books of Cato's moral couplets and the prefatory matter: exhortations to wisdom, prudence in speech, care in friendship, moderation in all things, and the fear of God, each maxim expanded into a clear Old English sentence with occasional explanatory glosses.
works.significance: The first English version of the most influential moral textbook of the Middle Ages, linking the Old English wisdom tradition to the classical curriculum inherited by later English literature.
works.context: The Disticha Catonis was the most widely read school text of the Middle Ages; its translation into Old English shows the vernacular classroom tradition of the reform era extending the standard curriculum to those learning through English, in the same spirit as Ælfric's Grammar and Colloquy.
works.structure: A book-by-book, maxim-by-maxim prose translation following the order of the Latin distichs, with each couplet rendered as one or two vernacular sentences.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.

works.title: The Dream of the Rood
works.description: The greatest religious poem of the Old English period (156 lines): a dream vision in which the Cross itself speaks, recounting the Crucifixion as a heroic battle in which Christ, the young warrior-king, mounts the cross of his own will. Related texts survive on the eighth-century Ruthwell Cross runic inscription and the Brussels Cross.
works.plot: The dreamer sees a wondrous tree shining with gold and gems, stained with blood, and the Rood tells its story: cut down in the forest, it was made the gallows of the young hero who climbed it willingly; it trembled, dared not bow, and with Christ it was pierced with nails and mocked, then buried and later raised up as the honoured sign of salvation. The poem ends with the dreamer's hope of the heavenly homeland and the injunction to seek the tree of victory.
works.significance: The supreme fusion of Germanic heroic form with Christian content in the period; one of the great medieval dream poems.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre, richly figured; the poem's end has been thought to show hypermetric lines.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (Vercelli, Biblioteca Capitolare CXVII, fols. 104v-106r); the Ruthwell Cross (Dumfriesshire, early eighth century) carries an inscribed extract in runes, and the Brussels Cross (c. 1000) a related couplet, evidence of the poem's early circulation.
works.characters: the Dreamer; the Rood (Cross); Christ (the young hero)
works.structure: A frame vision enclosing the Cross's first-person narrative, followed by the dreamer's response and a homiletic conclusion; the Cross is the earliest sustained prosopopoeia in English poetry.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; early attributions to Cædmon or Cynewulf are not accepted.

works.title: The Dreme
altTitles: The Dreme of Schir David Lindsay
works.form: dream vision in couplets and stanzas
works.description: Lindsay's dream vision addressed to the young James V: the poet, transported in sleep to hell, purgatory, and paradise, meets the spirit of the king's ancestors and returns to instruct the king in the duties of rule — an epistle to the sovereign that founds Lindsay's career as the conscience of the Scottish crown.
works.plot: The poet dreams he travels with Dame Remembrance through the three realms, hears the lament of the dead Scots kings over the realm's decay, and wakes to write the 'Exhortation to the King' that closes the poem.
works.significance: The classic Scots poem of princely counsel and the seed of the Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis; its vision of national decay set the tone of the Scottish Reformation's literature.
works.meter: Scots couplets and stanzaic passages in the Makar tradition; plain, forceful didactic verse.
works.context: Written in 1528 as James V escaped the Douglas faction and took personal rule; Lindsay, his childhood companion, speaks as the king's tutor and conscience.
works.characters: the poet; Dame Remembrance; James V (addressed); the dead kings
works.structure: Dream vision with epilogue; the three-realm journey frames the political exhortation, which is the poem's true centre.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Durham Proverbs
works.description: A collection of forty-six Old English proverbs, each paired with a Latin version, written into a Durham cathedral manuscript of Ælfric's Grammar. The proverbs are earthy and practical — about friendship, speech, household management, and the follies of men — and descend from a common European proverb tradition.
works.plot: The proverbs counsel prudence in speech and friendship ('a friend in need is a friend indeed'), household thrift, and wariness of fair words, pairing each English saying with its Latin equivalent in the manner of a bilingual schoolbook.
works.significance: The only substantial surviving Old English proverb collection outside the poetic corpus, and evidence of the international proverb lore that fed later English wisdom literature.
works.meter: The Old English proverbs are rhythmical prose, often with alliterative patterning; they are not verse in the strict metrical sense.
works.context: Copied into a manuscript associated with the reform's school curriculum, the collection shows the continuity between vernacular wisdom literature (Maxims, Precepts) and the bilingual classroom tradition of the eleventh century; several proverbs have parallels in Wulfstan's homilies.
works.structure: A numbered list of proverb pairs (Old English with Latin), without framing narrative; the sayings range from two to six lines.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The proverbs are drawn from common tradition; the compiler is unknown.

works.title: The Dyetary of Health
altTitles: A Compendyous Regyment or a Dyetary of Helth
works.description: Andrew Boorde's vernacular regimen of health, first printed in 1542; a popular handbook of diet, dwelling, and daily conduct for the English householder.
works.plot: The book advises on diet (meats, drinks, bread, and their digestions), on choosing a healthy dwelling site, on sleep and clothing, and on the management of the body's humours, in a plain and often earthy prose salted with proverbs and personal opinion.
works.significance: One of the most popular health manuals of the sixteenth century and a rich source for Tudor domestic life, diet, and popular medicine; Boorde's colloquial style anticipates the plain-speaking of later popular medical writing.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written by Boorde after his return from his European travels and printed in 1542 (with many later editions to 1630); it belongs to the same vernacular medical movement as Elyot's Castle of Health, aimed at readers without Latin.
works.structure: A systematic handbook in short chapters, arranged by topic from dwelling-place to foodstuffs to regimen.

works.title: The Eclogues (Barclay)
works.description: Barclay's five eclogues, the first English pastoral poetry: three adapted from Mantuan and two from Aeneas Sylvius's De Curialium Miseriis, in which shepherds debate the miseries of courts and the corruption of the clergy, and the city's poverty is set against the country's sufficiency.
works.plot: Shepherds — Coridon, Cornix, Faustus, Amyntas — meet and debate in turn: the woes of courtiers, the pride of churchmen, the pleasures of the country life, and the duties of the rich toward the poor.
works.significance: The first English pastoral, founding the tradition that runs through Spenser's Shepheardes Calender to the great pastoral of the 1590s.
works.meter: Rhyme royal for the pastoral dialogue; the smooth didactic verse of the early Tudor humanists.
works.context: Written in the decade when the court satire was becoming the period's dominant mode; the eclogues import the Mantuan model that every Elizabethan grammar school would memorize.
works.characters: Coridon; Cornix; Faustus; Amyntas; Codrus; Minalcas
works.structure: Five discrete eclogues in the Virgilian-Mantuan manner, each a debate between named shepherds with its moral explicit.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the eclogues are adaptations of Mantuan and Aeneas Sylvius.

works.title: The Examinations of Anne Askew
altTitles: The First Examination of Anne Askew
The Latter Examination of Anne Askew
works.description: Anne Askew's first-person accounts of her two examinations for heresy before the ecclesiastical authorities, printed in 1546 and 1547 with prefaces by John Bale; the most important English text written by a woman in the first half of the sixteenth century.
works.plot: Askew narrates her arrest and first examination before the bishop's chancellor (March 1545) and the second, harsher examination before Bishop Bonner, Bishop Gardiner, Wriothesley, and the privy council (1545–46), recording her scriptural answers on the eucharist, her refusal to name her fellow evangelicals, and her racking in the Tower — 'I answered that I would not deny my master and my God'; the account ends with her condemnation, the burning following on 16 July 1546.
works.significance: The first sustained autobiographical narrative by an English woman in print and the founding text of the English martyr tradition; Askew's scriptural self-defence under torture made her a model of the speaking female subject for later centuries.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in prison in 1545–46, smuggled out, and printed by Bale at Wesel in 1546 (first examination) and 1547 (latter examination) as Protestant propaganda against the Henrician church; John Foxe incorporated the Examinations into the Book of Martyrs, making Askew the most famous of the Henrician women martyrs.
works.characters: Anne Askew (narrator); Bishop Edmund Bonner; Bishop Stephen Gardiner; Thomas Wriothesley; Christopher Dare; John Bale (editor)
works.structure: A first-person testimonial narrative in two parts, with Bale's framing prefaces and his 'elucidations' printed alongside; the latter examination includes the exchange with the council and the account of the rack.
works.attributionNotes: The text is Askew's own account, edited (and heavily framed) by John Bale; the record attributes authorship to Askew, with Bale's role as editor noted.

editions.title: The Examinations of Anne Askew
editions.publisher: Oxford University Press (Women Writers in English 1350–1850)

works.title: The Example of Virtue
works.description: Hawes's first major poem, an allegory of the soul's life: Youth, guided by Discretion, journeys through the world and learns virtue's lessons from Lady Sapience, marries Cleanness, and passes through Age to the vision of Eternity. Printed by Wynkyn de Worde about 1504.
works.plot: Youth, counselled by Discretion, crosses the sea of the world, defeats the dragon of vice, and is led by Sapience and Fortune's lessons to the marriage with Cleanness; Age overtakes him, and the soul enters Eternity.
works.significance: A minor but characteristic example of the late medieval moral allegory, showing the tradition Spenser was to transform.
works.meter: Rhyme royal in the Lydgatian manner, with aureate vocabulary.
works.context: Written early in the reign of Henry VII, when the court still sustained the allegorical tradition of the fifteenth century.
works.characters: Youth; Discretion; Lady Sapience; Cleanness; Fortune; Age; Eternity
works.structure: A moral allegory in the pilgrimage form, moving from instruction through trial to the vision of eternity.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Exeter Book Riddles
works.description: A collection of some ninety-five riddles in the Exeter Book, ranging from the majestic (the swan, the iceberg, the storm, the bookworm) to the bawdy double entendres (the onion, the key, the churn), all spoken in the first person by their subjects — the largest surviving body of riddles in any early medieval vernacular.
works.plot: Each riddle presents an oblique first-person self-description — 'I am a wonderful creature...' — inviting the reader to name the hidden subject; subjects include weapons, tools, animals, natural forces, writing, and domestic objects, with several deliberately suggestive 'obscene' solutions masking innocent ones.
works.significance: The cornerstone of the English riddle tradition; a unique window onto the everyday and the marvellous in Anglo-Saxon imagination.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the riddles vary from four lines to over a hundred.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 101a-115a and elsewhere); the genre descends from the Latin enigmata of Symphosius and Aldhelm.
works.characters: the speaking objects (swan, iceberg, bookworm, onion, key, etc.)
works.structure: A sequence of independent enigmas, likely arranged by the compiler in thematic groups; the collection ends with a famous series of double-entendre riddles.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the collection may include compositions by several poets over centuries.

editions.title: The Old English Riddles of the Exeter Book

works.title: The Fates of the Apostles
works.form: religious catalogue poem in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 122 lines cataloguing the deaths and missionary fields of the twelve apostles, signed by Cynewulf in a runic acrostic that spells his name. The catalogue frame encloses a meditation on the poet's own need for grace, the best-known of the four Cynewulfian signatures.
works.plot: The poet, speaking as a weary traveller, enumerates the apostles in order — where each preached and how each died (Peter crucified, Paul beheaded, Andrew in Achaia, John at Ephesus, and so on) — then turns to himself: begging the prayers of the reader, weaving the runes of his name into a meditation on the gifts of God and the terror of judgment.
works.significance: The earliest signature of an English poet in his own verse; a key document for the Cynewulf canon.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the runic acrostic spells CYNEWULF.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 52v-54r) and in the same collection as Andreas and the homilies.
works.characters: the twelve apostles; the poet (Cynewulf)
works.structure: A thula-like catalogue of the apostles followed by the runic signature passage, which modulates from report to prayer.
works.attributionNotes: Signed by Cynewulf in runes; accepted as authentic.

works.title: The Finnsburh Fragment
works.manuscriptDate: lost; preserved in an early eighteenth-century transcript
works.description: A fragment of about 48 lines of an older heroic lay describing the night attack on the hall of Finn, king of the Frisians, in which the Danish prince Hnæf and his men defend the doors for five days. The story — later told allusively in Beowulf's 'Finnsburg episode' — is one of the great Germanic tales of feud and loyalty.
works.plot: A watchman sees the gleam of weapons as Finn's men attack the hall by night; Hnæf's Danes hold the doors, and the fight lasts five days without a man falling, until the fragment breaks off. The fuller story, reconstructed from Beowulf and other sources, involves the peace-pledge of Hildeburh, the death of Hnæf and Finn's son, and Finn's eventual slaying by the Danes.
works.significance: The sole surviving example, alongside Beowulf, of the heroic hall-fight; indispensable for reconstructing the legend and the older lay tradition.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of an archaic, compressed kind.
works.context: The story belongs to the fifth-century Germanic migrations; the text survives only in the transcript made by George Hickes for his Thesaurus (1705) of a manuscript leaf (Lambeth Palace MS 487) now lost.
works.characters: Hnæf; Finn; Hildeburh; Hengest; Sigeferth; Garulf; Guðlaf; Ordlaf
