works.structure: A single vivid scene of hall-fighting, extended by speeches (the door-defenders Garulf and Guðere, the veteran Sigeferth); the poem's brevity and compression suggest the style of the older lays behind Beowulf.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: The Form of Living
works.description: Richard Rolle's English epistle of spiritual guidance, written c. 1348 for Margaret Kirkby, the anchoress of Ainderby, and the most influential of his English works: a rule of the devout life in twelve chapters, from the love of God and the practice of prayer through the discernment of true contemplation to the joy of the heavenly song. It became the classic handbook of English anchoresses after Ancrene Wisse.
works.plot: Addressed to Margaret 'in the form of living', the epistle teaches the love of God above all things, the exercise of prayer and meditation on the Passion, the temptations and consolations of the solitary life, and the discernment of the true 'song' of contemplation from delusion.
works.significance: The bridge between Ancrene Wisse and the fifteenth-century devotional manuals, and the classic of the Rolle tradition in English.
works.meter: Rhythmical alliterative prose of the Rolle school.
works.context: Written c. 1348 for Margaret Kirkby, recluse of Ainderby, in the last year of Rolle's life; the most widely copied of his English writings, it circulated into the fifteenth century and was printed by Wynkyn de Worde.
works.characters: Rolle (writer); Margaret Kirkby (addressee)
works.structure: Twelve short chapters of practical and mystical instruction, in the epistle form of the Rolle canon.
works.attributionNotes: Rolle's authorship secure.

works.title: The Forme of Cury
works.description: The earliest English cookery collection: some 200 recipes compiled c. 1390 by the master cooks of King Richard II, from potages and roasted meats to the subtleties and spiced dishes of the royal table, including the first English recipe for pasta ('macrows') and dishes with olive oil. It is the foundation document of English culinary literature.
works.plot: The collection proceeds from the 'furmenty' and potages through flesh and fish days to the elaborate final courses, with the spices of the East (saffron, cloves, mace) and the French culinary vocabulary of the court marking the recipes' royal provenance.
works.significance: The first English cookbook and the classic document of medieval English courtly cuisine; its recipes are still cooked by food historians today.
works.meter: Prose: terse, practical recipe English with French technical terms.
works.context: Compiled c. 1390 by the chief master cooks of Richard II, and preserved in the manuscript BL Additional MS 5016 (with the closely related manuscripts of the Curye on Inglysch group); first printed by Samuel Pegge (1780).
works.characters: none (recipe collection)
works.structure: A recipe collection in the medieval cookbook tradition, organized by course and occasion, with the royal headnote claiming its authority.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous (compiled by the king's cooks).

works.title: The Fortunes of Men
works.description: A poem of 98 lines cataloguing the fates that befall men — one dies young, one by the sword, one from a fall, one on the gallows; the hawk dies, the wolf mourns, the singer is praised — closing with the assurance that God apportions all gifts. A companion to The Gifts of Men.
works.plot: The poem surveys the deaths and destinies of men (and, in an admired passage, of a hawk), then turns to the arts — one man learns song, one harp, one the law — and concludes that the Measurer shapes each man's lot, bestowing craft, wealth, and wisdom as he will.
works.significance: A finely crafted example of the catalogue poem and of the period's providential view of human diversity.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 87a-88b), following Widsith.
works.characters: none
works.structure: A double catalogue (fates, then gifts) closed by a doxological gnome on divine providence.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Four Elements
altTitles: A New Interlude and a Mery, of the Nature of the Four Elements
works.description: John Rastell's pedagogical interlude on the four elements and the new geography, printed by the author c. 1520; the first English play designed to teach natural science.
works.plot: Humanity, instructed by Nature and Studious Desire, is taught the four elements, the roundness of the earth, and the new-found lands of America; he is then tempted by Sensual Appetite into the tavern, where he wastes his learning in drinking, and the fragment (the play survives incomplete) breaks off with Experience promising his restoration.
works.significance: The first English play to teach science and geography, and a pioneering attempt to harness the stage to the new learning; it documents the arrival of the Age of Discovery in English popular culture.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic songs
works.context: Printed c. 1520 by Rastell, More's brother-in-law, who had himself attempted a voyage to the New World in 1517; the play's geography lesson celebrates the discovery of America, and its music survives in the unique fragment (British Library).
works.characters: Nature; Humanity; Studious Desire; Sensual Appetite; Experience; Ignorance; The Taverner
works.structure: A morality framework used for instruction: a series of lectures on cosmology and geography alternating with scenes of temptation and fall, with songs (including one with music) and a dance.

works.title: The Four PP
altTitles: The Play Called the Four PP
works.description: John Heywood's best-known farce, a lying contest among a Palmer, a Pardoner, a Pothecary, and a Pedlar; the earliest surviving edition is that of William Middleton, c. 1544.
works.plot: A Palmer, Pardoner, and Pothecary each boast of his trade and its profits, and the Pedlar proposes a contest: whoever tells the greatest lie wins the wager. The Pothecary's tale of a marvellous cure and the Pardoner's account of a soul released from hell's pains — capped by the Palmer's claim that he has met a woman patient and uncomplaining — end the contest, the Palmer winning the palm and the company concluding in good fellowship.
works.significance: The most famous of the Tudor interludes and the classic English stage farce before Shakespeare; its tale of the woman patient in all things circulated into later jest-books and remains the play by which Heywood is chiefly remembered.
works.meter: Couplets
works.context: Composed c. 1520–30 in Heywood's period as a court entertainer and virginal player to Henry VIII; the lying contest reworks the fabliau tradition (the tale of the patient wife appears in Boccaccio) and the satire of pardons and relics reflects pre-Reformation criticism of popular piety.
works.characters: The Palmer; The Pardoner; The Pothecary; The Pedlar
works.structure: A single-scene farce built of successive set-piece tales, with the Pedlar as proposer and judge of the wager.

works.title: The Fox and the Wolf
works.description: The earliest English beast fable, a comic tale of some 300 lines in which the fox, trapped in a bucket down a well, persuades the gullible wolf that he is in paradise, and escapes by the wolf's folly. It inaugurates the English Reynardian tradition that runs to Caxton's Reynard the Fox.
works.plot: The thirsty fox climbs into one well-bucket and is stranded; when the wolf asks what he does there, the fox claims the well is paradise, induces the wolf to descend in the other bucket, and is drawn up as the wolf goes down.
works.significance: The beginning of the English Reynard tradition and the earliest English fabliau-fable; an essential witness to the continental debts of early Middle English narrative.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with lively dialogue.
works.context: Composed c. 1250–75, adapted from the French Roman de Renart; preserved in the late thirteenth-century Digby MS 86 (Bodleian Library).
works.characters: the Fox; the Wolf
works.structure: A single comic episode built on the trickster's persuasive lie and the dupe's comeuppance.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Garland of Laurel
works.form: dream vision in rhyme royal and Skeltonics
works.description: Skelton's self-crowning dream vision: the poet, wandering in a forest, is brought before Queen Fame and the assembled court of the Countess of Surrey at Sheriff Hutton, where Pallas and the ladies of the court intercede for him and Fame grants him the laurel — the poem including a catalogue of his own works that is the first English poet's bibliography.
works.plot: The dreamer debates with Occupation and Fame whether he deserves the laurel; the ladies of the court, led by the Countess of Surrey, petition on his behalf; Fame crowns him, and the poet wakes to compose the envoy of praise.
works.significance: The first English poem to canonize its own author, with a bibliography of his works; a unique document of the poet's self-understanding at the Tudor court.
works.meter: Mixed rhyme royal and Skeltonic passages; the courtly and the demotic styles deliberately alternated.
works.context: Written at Sheriff Hutton in Yorkshire, in the household of the Countess of Surrey, in 1523, when Skelton's laureate claims needed the court's support against Wolsey.
works.characters: the poet; Queen Fame; Pallas; the Countess of Surrey; Occupation
works.structure: Dream vision with debate and pageant; the catalogue of the poet's works embedded in the intercession of the court ladies.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Gifts of Men
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A catalogue poem of 113 lines celebrating the diversity of human talents as gifts of God: one man is strong, another wise, another skilled in song, hunting, navigation, smithing, or counsel. The poem's theme is that every gift comes from the Lord and none should be despised.
works.plot: The poet enumerates the many endowments distributed among mankind — physical strength, beauty, eloquence, song, learning, craftsmanship, skill in the hunt, the sea, the harp, and the council — and concludes that God, the giver of all gifts, has so ordered the world that no one possesses everything and each talent has its place.
works.significance: A major statement of the Old English wisdom tradition's social vision, and a companion piece to The Fortunes of Men; both poems treat the same theme of distributed human destiny.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the catalogue form is carried by parallel clauses of the 'sum... sum...' (one... another...) type characteristic of Old English gnomic verse.
works.context: The poem belongs to the Exeter Book wisdom tradition alongside Maxims I and II and The Fortunes of Men, with which it is often compared; it reflects the Anglo-Saxon conviction that society is knit together by complementary gifts under divine providence.
works.structure: A sustained catalogue organized by successive human activities and skills, framed by an opening assertion of God's generosity and a closing meditation on the ordered distribution of gifts.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Golden Legend
works.description: William Caxton's translation of Jacobus de Voragine's Legenda Aurea, printed at Westminster in 1483: the great medieval collection of saints' lives and feasts of the church year, in nearly 450 leaves and the first English printing of the work. It became the standard English legendary for a century, reprinted repeatedly into the 1520s.
works.plot: Following the church year, the collection narrates the lives and martyrdoms of the saints — from St Andrew through the apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins — with the great feasts (Advent, Christmas, Passiontide) expounded and the legends moralized for the reader's instruction.
works.significance: The great bestseller of Caxton's press and the principal English channel of the Legenda Aurea; its saints' lives nourished English devotional reading into the sixteenth century.
works.meter: Prose: Caxton's mature plain style at its most ample.
works.context: Translated by Caxton from French and Latin sources and printed at Westminster in 1483, in the orthodox devotional market of pre-Reformation England; nine editions appeared by 1527, before the Reformation ended the cult of the saints it served.
works.characters: the saints of the calendar
works.structure: A calendrical legendary in the Voragine tradition, with Caxton's additions (including lives of English saints) and his prologue explaining the work's purpose.
works.attributionNotes: Caxton's translation is documented in his own prologue.

editions.title: Caxton's Golden Legend
editions.editor: Mayumi Taguchi, John Scahill, and Satoko Katsumata (eds.)

works.title: The Great Bible
works.description: The first authorized English Bible, a revision of Matthew's Bible (itself based on Tyndale and Coverdale) carried out by Miles Coverdale and printed in Paris and London in 1539 under Thomas Cromwell's patronage; the Bible ordered to be set up in every parish church.
works.plot: A complete Bible in large folio format, with the title page by Hans Holbein showing Henry VIII handing the Word to Cranmer and Cromwell; the text revises the Matthew Bible's Old Testament against the Hebrew and Latin, and its 1540 second edition carried Cranmer's preface, giving the book its later name.
works.significance: The Bible that made the English Bible a public institution: chained in the churches, read aloud to the people, it established the vernacular scriptures at the centre of English religious life and supplied the psalter of the Prayer Book.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Commissioned by Cromwell and begun in Paris (the French printing was seized by the Inquisition, and the presses moved to London), the Great Bible of 1539 was ordered by the injunctions of 1538 to be placed in every parish church; its psalter entered the Prayer Book tradition, and it remained the standard English Bible until the Bishops' Bible of 1568.
works.structure: The full biblical canon with prologues, summaries, and the famous illustrated title page.
works.attributionNotes: The revision is Coverdale's, on the basis of the Matthew Bible (edited by John Rogers from Tyndale and Coverdale); the record attributes the work to Coverdale as revising editor, following standard usage.

works.title: The Harley Lyrics
works.description: A collection of some forty secular and religious lyrics preserved in the Ludlow scribe's anthology, BL Harley MS 2253 (c. 1340), the richest single manuscript of early Middle English lyric: love songs, laments, satires, and devotional poems in French, Latin, and English, including such masterpieces as 'Alysoun', 'Wynter wakeneth al my care', and 'Blow, northerne wynd'.
works.plot: The poems range across the lyric repertoire: the lover's springtime longing and complaint, the satire of corrupt clergy and unjust lords, the meditation on death and the Passion, and the praise of the Virgin.
works.significance: The indispensable witness to the early Middle English lyric tradition at its best, and the principal source of the poems that bridge early and Ricardian poetry.
works.meter: A remarkable variety: tail-rhyme stanzas, alliterative long lines, and French-derived stanza forms, often with refrains.
works.context: Copied c. 1340 by a professional scribe working near Ludlow, Herefordshire, for a gentry household, from materials of the later thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries.
works.characters: the lovers and speakers of the lyrics
works.structure: An anthology, not a sequence: the manuscript's trilingual arrangement (with English poems often paired with their French and Latin analogues) supplies the order.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the poems are the work of many hands, assembled by the scribe.

works.title: The History of King Richard III
altTitles: History of King Richard the Third
works.description: More's unfinished prose history of the rise and fall of Richard III, composed in parallel English and Latin versions; the English text was first printed in a corrupt form in Hardyng's Chronicle (1543) and the definitive version appeared in Rastell's edition of More's English Works (1557).
works.plot: The narrative traces Richard's path to the throne: the death of Edward IV, Richard's seizure of power as Protector, the removal of the princes, Buckingham's rebellion, and Richard's coronation and brief reign, breaking off during Morton's embassy to France. It portrays Richard as a dissembling tyrant whose deformity mirrors his moral deformity.
works.significance: The first great work of English prose history and the fountainhead of the Tudor myth of Richard III; its psychological portraiture and dramatic irony made it a major source for Shakespeare and for sixteenth-century historiography.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written during More's second period of public service, probably 1513–1518, drawing on oral testimony from Morton's household where More was raised; the work circulated in manuscript and shaped the Tudor 'black legend' of Richard III long before Shakespeare used Hall's chronicle (which incorporated More's account) for his play.
works.characters: Richard III; Edward IV; Elizabeth Woodville; Henry Stafford, Duke of Buckingham; John Morton; Lord Hastings; Edward V; Richard, Duke of York
works.structure: Unfinished chronicle in five books, driven by dramatic set-piece speeches (Buckingham's oration, Elizabeth Woodville's lament) and a Tacitean focus on character and motive rather than providential design.

editions.title: The History of King Richard III (The Yale Edition of the Complete Works of St. Thomas More, vol. 2)

works.title: The House of Fame
works.description: Chaucer's comic dream vision of fame and rumour (2,158 lines in octosyllabic couplets, unfinished): the dreamer is carried by a talkative eagle through the heavens to the House of Fame, where the goddess dispenses reputation with sublime arbitrariness, and on to the whirling House of Rumour where every report, true and false, takes wing. A poem about poetry, authority, and the instability of language itself.
works.plot: The dreamer, pondering the causes of dreams and the nature of fame, finds himself in a temple of Venus adorned with the story of the Aeneid; an eagle (comically garrulous, in the Dantean manner) snatches him up and lectures him on sound, air, and the physics of speech; before the House of Fame he sees the petitioners — great and small — receive arbitrary reward or oblivion; and in the twig-built, whirling House of Rumour every tiding breeds and flies; the poem breaks off as 'a man of gret auctorite' appears.
works.significance: The most brilliant medieval English poem about poetry, fame, and the circulation of language; its self-reflexive comedy anticipates the metacritical concerns of modern literature.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with colloquial verve; the eagle's lecture burlesques the didactic mode.
works.context: Composed c. 1378–80, during Chaucer's Italian-inspired middle period, drawing on Dante, Virgil, Ovid, and Boethius; the invocation promises tidings 'of love or such thinges glade' — a tease never fulfilled.
works.characters: the Dreamer (Geffrey); the Eagle; Fame; Aeolus; the suitors of Fame; the 'man of great authority'
works.structure: Three movements (the temple of Venus; the eagle's flight and lecture; the houses of Fame and Rumour), with the Aeneid and the physics of sound as its digressive armature.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure.

works.title: The Husband's Message
works.description: An elegiac poem of 54 lines in which a wooden rune-stave, carved with a message, speaks on behalf of an exiled lord to the woman he loves, recalling their former vows and summoning her to join him across the sea.
works.plot: The stave tells how its lord was forced into exile by a feud, how he longs for his lady, and how he now sends word that he has wealth and a hall prepared for her; the poem closes with a runic passage (often solved as 'sige', 'rad', and other rune-names) promising their reunion and the renewal of their vows.
works.significance: An early and sophisticated use of the speaking-object device and of runic writing as poetic material.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book, following the riddles; often paired with The Wife's Lament as complementary perspectives on exile and separated love.
works.characters: the rune-stave (speaker); the lord; the lady
works.structure: A speaking object (prosopopoeia) delivers the lord's message; the closing runic riddle has prompted attempts to read the poem as part of a composite sequence with the riddles that follow it in the manuscript.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
movements: The AB Language Group (West Midlands Devotional Prose)
sources: English Historical Documents, Volume I: c. 500–1042

works.title: The Introduction of Knowledge
altTitles: The Fyrst Boke of the Introduction of Knowledge
works.description: Andrew Boorde's popular geography and travel book of 1547, the first English printed book to describe the nations of Europe in verse and prose for the general reader.
works.plot: The book presents each nation of Europe (and beyond) through a woodcut portrait of a native in national dress, a verse dialogue spoken by the figure, and a prose description of the country's customs, currency, and distances — a compendium of travel knowledge for merchants and pilgrims.
works.significance: The first printed English survey of European nations and an early document of English ethnographic description; its woodcut national portraits founded a visual tradition that lasted into the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Prose with verse interludes
works.context: Compiled from Boorde's European travels of the 1530s and printed in 1547 by William Copland; Boorde, physician and Carthusian, had been licensed to travel by Thomas Cromwell, and the book reflects the expansion of English geographical curiosity in the mid-Tudor period.
works.structure: Thirty-nine chapters, one per nation, each combining woodcut, verse self-description, and prose itinerary.

works.title: The Itinerary
works.description: John Leland's topographical survey of England and Wales, the record of his itineraries undertaken with a royal commission from Henry VIII to search the libraries of the monasteries, compiled c. 1535–43 and first printed by Thomas Hearne in 1710–12.
works.plot: The Itinerary is a county-by-county record of Leland's travels: towns, rivers, bridges, castles, churches, and the antiquities of each place, noted in terse first-person entries that document the landscape of England on the eve of the dissolution of the monasteries.
works.significance: The founding text of English antiquarianism and topography; it inaugurated the tradition of the county survey that runs through Camden, Aubrey, and the eighteenth-century antiquaries, and its value as an eyewitness record of pre-dissolution England is irreplaceable.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Leland held a commission from Henry VIII (1533) to search the monastic and collegiate libraries; his itineraries of c. 1535–43 covered most of England and Wales, and his notes preserve records of books, inscriptions, and buildings later destroyed in the dissolution and after.
works.structure: Topographical notes arranged by county, preserved in autograph notebooks; the printed text of 1710–12 follows Hearne's edition of the surviving manuscripts.

works.title: The Judgement Day I and II
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990 (Judgement Day I); Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201 (Judgement Day II)
works.description: Two independent eschatological poems on the last judgment. Judgement Day I (119 lines) describes the cosmic terrors of doomsday and the soul's reckoning; Judgement Day II (306 lines), based on Bede's De die iudicii, is a sustained meditation on sin, penance, and the judgment, addressed to the individual soul.
works.plot: Judgement Day I depicts the universal conflagration, the trumpets, and the assembly of all souls before the judge, contrasting the fate of the blessed and the damned. Judgement Day II urges the penitent soul to recall its sins now, while confession is still possible, painting the terrors of judgment in images of fire, darkness, and weeping, and closes with hope for those who repent.
works.significance: The fullest Old English verse treatments of the last judgment, and (in Judgement Day II) an important vernacular witness to the reception of Bede's Latin eschatological poetry.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; Judgement Day II's sustained length and homiletic urgency make it the most ambitious of the Exeter/CCCC 201 eschatological poems.
works.context: The judgment was the master-image of Anglo-Saxon homiletics, from the Blickling and Vercelli homilies to Wulfstan's Sermo Lupi; the poems belong to that culture of penitential fear and are the verse counterpart of the homilists' doomsday rhetoric.
works.structure: Both poems move from description of the cosmic catastrophe to exhortation; Judgement Day II is organized as a sequence of meditations on sin, the hour of death, the judgment, and the possibility of mercy through penance.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The two poems are independent compositions; Judgement Day II is an adaptation of Bede's De die iudicii, not by Bede himself.

works.title: The Katherine Group
altTitles: The Lives of St Katherine, St Margaret, and St Juliana
works.description: Three prose lives of virgin martyrs — St Katherine of Alexandria, St Margaret of Antioch, and St Juliana of Nicomedia — written in the same West Midlands 'AB language' as Ancrene Wisse for a female religious audience. They are the classic Middle English saints' lives: rhetorically elaborate, vivid in their debates and torments, and fervent in their celebration of virginity.
works.plot: Each saint refuses a pagan suitor and judge, defeats her learned or demonic adversaries in debate, endures spectacular torments, and wins a martyr's crown, with Christ or angels as her comforters.
works.significance: The founding texts of the AB language group and the model for Middle English hagiography in the thirteenth century and after.
works.meter: Rhythmical alliterative prose with the characteristic AB-language vocabulary and spelling.
works.context: Composed c. 1190–1225 in the same Herefordshire milieu as Ancrene Wisse; preserved in Bodleian MS Bodley 34 and BL Royal MS 17 A.xxvii.
works.characters: St Katherine; St Margaret; St Juliana; the tyrant-judges (Maxentius, Olibrius, Eleusius); the demons
works.structure: Conventional martyr-act structure (arraignment, debate, torture, death) enriched by long speeches and prayers; Juliana includes the saint's dialogue with a demon.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; grouped with Ancrene Wisse and the Wooing Group by dialect and manuscript kinship.

works.title: The Kentish Hymn
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Vespasian D.vi, fol. 69 (tenth century)
works.form: religious lyric (liturgical paraphrase) in alliterative verse
works.description: A 43-line paraphrase of the Gloria in excelsis in the Kentish dialect, the only substantial Old English poem preserved in that dialect. It praises the Trinity, Christ the Lamb, and the Holy Spirit, and prays for the mercy of the Lord.
works.plot: The poem renders the Greater Doxology clause by clause: praise of God the Father, the Lamb of God who takes away sin, the Holy Spirit with Father and Son, and a closing petition for the Lord's mercy and protection.
works.significance: A rare dialectal witness to Old English religious verse and an early example of the Gloria rendered in English verse.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the Kentish forms of the text are among the few dialectally marked verse survivals outside West Saxon.
works.context: The hymn was added to a manuscript otherwise containing Kentish glosses and documents; it attests the spread of vernacular liturgical paraphrase beyond the West Saxon heartland of the literary standard.
works.structure: A direct liturgical paraphrase following the order of the Gloria; the doxological clauses are expanded with brief devotional glosses.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Kingis Quair
works.description: The dream vision traditionally attributed to James I of Scotland, written c. 1424 after his eighteen years of captivity in England: the imprisoned narrator, sleepless with love, reads Boethius, sees his lady from the tower window, and is taught by the goddesses of Love, Fortune, and Wisdom in a vision that reconciles him to his fate. The fountainhead of the Scottish Chaucerian tradition.
works.plot: The sleepless captive, turning the pages of Boethius, hears the bell of matins and falls into a dream; guided by the goddesses, he ascends to the sphere of Venus, where his love for the lady seen from the tower is confirmed and fortune's wheel is explained; waking, a dove brings him the message of hope, and he ends his book in praise of love and his lady.
works.significance: The fountainhead of the makars' tradition: the first great poem in the Scottish Chaucerian line and the model for the royal and courtly poetry of the Stewart century.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas of Chaucerian fluency, in Older Scots.
works.context: Composed c. 1424, on the eve of James's release, celebrating his love for Joan Beaufort, whom he married in February 1424; preserved uniquely in the Selden manuscript (Bodleian Arch. Selden. B.24, c. 1488).
works.characters: the captive narrator (James I); the lady (Joan Beaufort); Venus; Minerva; Fortune; the dove
works.structure: A single dream vision in the Chaucerian-Boethian manner: reading, waking complaint, dream ascent, counsel of the goddesses, and waking resolution.
works.attributionNotes: The attribution to James I rests on the poem's autobiographical frame and manuscript tradition; it is widely but not universally accepted.

editions.title: The Kingis Quair and Other Prison Poems
editions.editor: Linne R. Mooney and Mary-Jo Arn (eds.)

works.title: The Lamentation of a Sinner
works.description: Catherine Parr's spiritual autobiography and treatise on justification by faith, published posthumously in 1547; the fullest statement of the queen's evangelical faith.
works.plot: Parr confesses her former life 'in superstition and ignorance', recounts her awakening to the doctrine of justification by faith through the reading of scripture, and expounds the gospel of free grace against the reliance on works, ending with a meditation on the passion and an exhortation to trust wholly in Christ's merits.
works.significance: The first spiritual autobiography by an English queen and an important document of the Reformation's inward turn; it shows the queen — the only woman whose books were printed in her lifetime in Tudor England — articulating the doctrine of faith in her own voice.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in the last years of Henry VIII's reign, when Parr's evangelical circle faced persecution (Askew was burned in July 1546), and published by William Cecil (later Lord Burghley) in 1547 after the king's death; the book became a manual of Edwardian Protestant piety.
works.characters: Catherine Parr (narrator)
works.structure: A two-part work: a first-person confession and conversion narrative, followed by a doctrinal exposition of faith, grace, and the law.

editions.title: Katherine Parr: Complete Works and Correspondence

works.title: The Land of Cokaygne
works.description: A rollicking satire of some 190 lines on the fantasy land of Cokaygne, a paradise of food, sleep, and license reached by a week in a sow's belly, whose abbey of gluttonous monks is described with anti-monastic glee. It is the earliest English example of the European Cockaigne tradition and a masterpiece of clerical self-satire.
works.plot: The poet describes the geography of Cokaygne — roast geese flying, rivers of oil and wine, the fountain of youth — and dwells lovingly on the abbey where the monks, fattened without labour, fly about at their pleasure with the abbess.
works.significance: The first English Cockaigne poem and the liveliest anti-clerical satire before Langland; a favourite of modern anthologies for its comic invention.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets of comic energy, in an Irish-influenced Middle English.
works.context: Composed c. 1300, perhaps in Ireland (the sole manuscript is the Kildare miscellany, BL Harley MS 913, c. 1330), where the Cockaigne tradition flourished among the friars.
works.characters: the monks of Cokaygne; the abbess
works.structure: A catalogue-description of the dream land, closing with the burlesque of the monastic abbey.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Laws of Cnut
works.form: law code in Old English prose
works.description: The comprehensive law code of King Cnut (r. 1016-1035), drafted by Archbishop Wulfstan: the most elaborate legislation of the Anglo-Saxon period, combining royal law, ecclesiastical regulation, and Wulfstan's characteristic moral exhortation into a grand statement of a Christian commonwealth.
works.plot: The two parts of the code regulate the church (tithes, sanctuary, feast days, the clergy's conduct), the king's peace, legal procedure (ordeals, oaths, hundred courts), the ranks and dues of society, theft, homicide, and the punishment of the faithless; framed by Wulfstan's homiletic prologues exhorting all men to love God and keep the law.
works.significance: The summit of Anglo-Saxon legislation and the last great royal code in English before the Norman period.
works.meter: Old English prose with Wulfstan's rhythmical cadences.
works.context: Promulgated in the councils of 1020-1023 after Cnut's accession; preserved in later eleventh- and twelfth-century legal manuscripts.
works.characters: Cnut (legislator); Wulfstan (draftsman)
works.structure: A systematic code in two parts, with homiletic prologues and perorations.
works.attributionNotes: Drafted by Wulfstan for Cnut; Wulfstan's authorship is established on stylistic grounds.

works.title: The Laws of Ine
works.form: law code in Old English prose
works.description: The law code of King Ine of Wessex (688-726), preserved as an appendix to Alfred's law book: the earliest West Saxon legislation, covering church dues, theft, the status of the Welsh, land law, and the mutual obligations of lords and men.
works.plot: The code's seventy-six clauses regulate church dues and oaths, theft and its pursuit, the wer and wergild of each rank (including the Welsh), land tenure and the duties of gesiths and ceorls, and the penalties for harbouring fugitives.
works.significance: The earliest surviving West Saxon law and a major source for early English social structure.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Issued c. 688-694; preserved in the earliest manuscript of Alfred's laws (Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 173), to which Alfred appended it.
works.characters: Ine (legislator); his counsellors (the prologue names his father Cenred and bishops Hædde and Eorcenwald)
works.structure: A clause-by-clause royal code.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ine in the code's prologue.

works.title: The Laws of Æthelberht
works.form: law code in Old English prose
works.description: The law code of King Æthelberht of Kent, the earliest written English law and the oldest surviving document in the English language: a tariff of compensations for injuries, from homicide through wounding to the loss of a toe or a fingernail, with provisions protecting the Church and its property.
works.plot: The code opens with compensations for offences against the Church's property and peace, then proceeds by descending tariff through the body — head, hair, ear, eye, nose, teeth, fingers, nails, feet — assigning a fixed bot (compensation) for each injury according to the victim's rank.
works.significance: The earliest English law and the first extended document in the English language.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Issued by Æthelberht of Kent c. 602/3, shortly after the arrival of Augustine's mission (597); preserved only in the Textus Roffensis (Rochester, Cathedral Library, MS A.3.5, c. 1120).
works.characters: Æthelberht (legislator)
works.structure: A list of ninety clauses in the Germanic tariff style.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Æthelberht by Bede (Historia II.5) and by the manuscript's rubric.

works.title: The Legend of Good Women
works.description: Chaucer's unfinished collection of exemplary women's legends (some 2,700 lines), framed by the Prologue in which the god of Love arraigns the poet for slandering women and his queen Alceste assigns him the penance of commemorating good women betrayed by men. Its nine completed legends — Cleopatra, Thisbe, Dido, Hypsipyle and Medea, Lucrece, Ariadne, Philomela, Phyllis, and Hypermnestra — are the seedbed of the English legendary tradition.
works.plot: The Prologue stages the daisy-worship of the poet and his dream trial before the god of Love, who condemns him for the Troilus and the Romaunt; Alceste's intercession wins him the commission to write of faithful women and false men. The legends that follow retell the classical stories of love and betrayal in rhyme royal, until the collection breaks off, unfinished, in the legend of Hypermnestra.
works.significance: The founding text of the English 'good women' tradition (Bokenham's Legends, the Tudor mirrors) and a key witness to Chaucer's negotiation with the courtly politics of gender.
works.meter: Rhyme royal, with the prologue in heroic couplets in the G version.
works.context: Composed c. 1386–88, partly at the queen's (Anne of Bohemia's) request, during the period of the Canterbury Tales' beginnings; its Prologue is the richest single document of Chaucer's self-presentation as poet.
works.characters: the Narrator; the god of Love; Alceste; Cleopatra; Thisbe; Dido; Medea; Lucrece; Ariadne; Philomela; Phyllis; Hypermnestra
works.structure: A dream-vision prologue (two versions, F and G) framing a series of Ovidian legends, each structured as betrayal narrative with moral close.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure; the relationship of the two prologues is editorial.

works.title: The Legend of the Seven Sleepers
altTitles: The Old English Legend of the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Julius E.vii (c. 1100)
works.description: An Old English translation of the legend of the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus: seven Christian youths who fled the persecution of the emperor Decius, were walled up in a cave, and awoke after some two hundred years to find a Christian empire. The legend was read as a proof of the resurrection of the body and was one of the most widespread stories of the Middle Ages.
works.plot: Seven young Christian nobles of Ephesus hide from Decius's persecution in a cave and fall into a miraculous sleep. Two centuries later they wake to find the world changed: the persecutor is dead and the emperor is Christian. One of them, Malchus, ventures into the city to buy bread with old coins and is taken for a treasure-finder; the emperor Theodosius comes to the cave, and the sleepers, after testifying to the resurrection, die in peace.
works.significance: The earliest English version of a legend that became proverbial across medieval Europe, and a document of the Anglo-Saxon church's teaching on resurrection.
works.context: The legend circulated in both eastern and western Christianity as a demonstration of bodily resurrection, and was known in England from at least the time of Aldhelm; this late Old English translation belongs to the vernacular hagiographic wave of the later eleventh century, and the story later reappears in Middle English and in the Anglo-Norman and continental traditions.
works.characters: Malchus and the six sleepers, the emperor Decius, the emperor Theodosius
works.structure: A single narrative arc in three movements — the persecution and concealment, the awakening and the bewildered visit to the city, and the public vindication before the emperor — framed by the theological point that God can raise the dead as easily as he woke the sleepers.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.

works.title: The Leiden Riddle
works.manuscriptDate: Leiden, Universiteitsbibliotheek, Voss. Lat. Q. 106, fol. 25v (c. 800, Northumbrian)
works.description: A fourteen-line Old English riddle translating Aldhelm's Latin Enigma 33 on the mail-coat (lorica): the garment made of many small iron rings, woven by no woman's hands, that guards the warrior's breast. It is the earliest surviving English riddle, preserved in a Northumbrian dialect.
works.plot: The riddle-speaker describes itself: a garment whose countless rings are joined without thread, forged of iron by smiths' skill, protecting the breast of the warrior who wears it in battle. The solution is the mail-coat (lorica).
works.significance: The earliest surviving English riddle and the earliest evidence of the Anglo-Latin riddle tradition's translation into the vernacular, bridging Aldhelm and the Exeter Book.
works.meter: Fourteen alliterative long lines translating Aldhelm's hexameters; the poem keeps the riddle's obliquity while adapting it to vernacular alliterative technique.
works.context: Written into the last leaf of a Leiden manuscript of the Latin riddles, the poem documents the translation of Aldhelmian learning into Northumbrian vernacular verse in the age of Bede; it is the direct ancestor of the Exeter Book riddle tradition.
works.structure: A classic first-person riddle in the Aldhelmian manner, moving from the material of the object to its making to its use in war.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation of Aldhelm's Enigma 33 ('Lorica'); the translator is unknown.

works.title: The Letter of Alexander to Aristotle
works.form: travel and wonders literature in Old English prose
works.description: The Old English translation of the apocryphal letter in which Alexander the Great writes to his teacher Aristotle of the wonders of India — monsters, beasts, and marvels encountered on his campaign — preserved in the Nowell Codex beside Beowulf. A key text of the Alexander legend's early reception in England.
works.plot: Alexander recounts to Aristotle his march into India: the battle with Porus, the encounter with the monstrous beasts (the beast with three horns, the giant crabs, the white lions, the two-headed serpents), the night of terrors in the wilderness, and the wonders of the trees of the sun and moon, concluding with the oracles of his death.
works.significance: The earliest English text of the Alexander legend and a major source for the monstrous imagination of the period.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Translated from the Latin Epistola Alexandri in the late tenth or early eleventh century; preserved in the Nowell Codex (British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv, fols. 107v-131v).
works.characters: Alexander the Great; Aristotle (addressee); Porus
works.structure: An epistolary travel narrative in the first person, framed by the dedication to Aristotle.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Life and Death of Cardinal Wolsey
works.description: George Cavendish's memoir of Cardinal Wolsey, composed in the 1550s from the author's service in Wolsey's household; the first major English biography written by a layman and household servant.
works.plot: Cavendish recounts Wolsey's rise from butcher's son to cardinal and lord chancellor, his magnificence and building, the divorce crisis and the legatine court, his fall from favour, his death at Leicester Abbey in 1530, and the moral of Fortune's wheel; the narrative is thick with eyewitness detail of the cardinal's household, progresses, and final days.
works.significance: A masterpiece of Tudor biographical prose and the great contemporary portrait of Wolsey; its sympathetic account of the cardinal's fall and its influence on Shakespeare's Henry VIII make it a central document of early English biography.
works.meter: Prose with verse interludes
works.context: Written c. 1554–58, partly to vindicate Wolsey against the Protestant chroniclers Hall and Foxe; circulated in manuscript for decades and used by Stow, Holinshed, and Shakespeare, before its first printing in 1641 as The Negotiations of Thomas Wolsey.
works.characters: Cardinal Thomas Wolsey; George Cavendish (narrator); Henry VIII; Anne Boleyn; Thomas Cromwell (in the final scenes)
works.structure: A first-person memoir in chronological order, framed by a prologue on Fortune and divided by the rise, greatness, and fall of its subject; interludes of verse mark the turns of fortune.

editions.title: Two Early Tudor Lives
editions.editor: Richard S. Sylvester and Davis P. Harding

works.title: The Life of Sir Thomas More
altTitles: The Lyfe of Sir Thomas Moore, Knighte
works.description: William Roper's intimate biography of his father-in-law Sir Thomas More, written in the 1550s but not printed until 1626; the first biography in English of a private subject written by a close contemporary.
works.plot: Roper recounts More's household and public career from his own memory and family tradition: More's early marriage and life at Chelsea, his rise under Henry VIII, the succession crisis, his resignation of the chancellorship, his imprisonment, trial, and execution, with the celebrated dialogues between More and his wife and daughters and More's reported words to his son-in-law on the king's favour.
works.significance: The founding text of English biographical writing and the principal source for the domestic life of More; its vivid remembered dialogue made it one of the most influential portraits of a Tudor statesman ever written.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written c. 1553–58, probably during Mary's reign, by More's son-in-law who had lived in More's household for sixteen years; circulated in manuscript (the 'Harpsfield' manuscript) and first printed at Saint-Omer in 1626, with the first English printing in 1726.
works.characters: Sir Thomas More; William Roper (narrator); Margaret Roper (More's daughter); Alice More; Henry VIII
works.structure: A continuous first-person memoir in chronological order, emphasizing the domestic and moral More, with set-piece conversations and the famous 'King's servant but God's first' speech.

editions.title: Two Early Tudor Lives
editions.editor: Richard S. Sylvester and Davis P. Harding

works.title: The Life of St Katharine
altTitles: Capgrave's Life of Saint Katharine of Alexandria
works.description: John Capgrave's verse life of St Katharine of Alexandria, composed c. 1445: the learned virgin's conversion, her debate with the fifty philosophers, her refusal of the emperor Maxentius, the wheels of her torture, and her mystical marriage to Christ. The most polished saint's life of the fifteenth century, in rhyme royal with an elaborate prologue.
works.plot: Katharine, the learned princess of Alexandria, is converted by a hermit's vision of the Virgin and wedded to Christ; she confounds the emperor's philosophers in public debate, converts them and the empress, endures the wheels and the prison's angelic visits, and is beheaded — her body borne by angels to Sinai, where the milk, not blood, flows from her severed neck.
works.significance: The most accomplished Middle English life of St Katharine — the patron saint of learning — and the summit of fifteenth-century learned hagiography in verse.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas of Lydgatean polish, with aureate diction and classical allusion.
works.context: Composed c. 1445 by the Augustinian friar John Capgrave of Lynn, in the learned East Anglian tradition of Lydgate and Bokenham; the prologue places the poem in the line of Chaucer's Legend of Good Women; preserved in Bodleian Rawlinson Poet. 118 and Arundel MS 396.
works.characters: St Katharine; the Emperor Maxentius; the fifty philosophers; the Virgin Mary; the hermit Adrian
works.structure: Five books of hagiographical narrative, from birth and conversion through debate and passion to translation, in the classical five-book scheme.
works.attributionNotes: Capgrave's authorship secure (he names himself in the prologue).

works.title: The Lord's Prayer I, II, and III
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990 (versions I and II); Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201 (version III)
works.form: religious lyric (prayer paraphrase) in alliterative verse
works.description: Three independent Old English versifications of the Lord's Prayer. The first (123 lines with its doxology) expands each petition into doctrinal and devotional verse; the second (19 lines) is a close rendering; the third, in a Mercian dialect, survives in Corpus Christi College MS 201.
works.plot: Each poem paraphrases the petitions of the Pater Noster — the hallowing of God's name, the coming of the kingdom, daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance from evil — expanding them with commentary on the soul's needs, the devil's snares, and the last judgment.
works.significance: The fullest surviving Old English treatment of the central Christian prayer, showing how poets turned liturgical texts into vernacular verse of considerable doctrinal ambition.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the first version's expansions use formulaic homiletic diction familiar from the Exeter Book religious poems.
works.context: The Lord's Prayer was among the first texts every Christian learned, and Alfred's preface to the Pastoral Care singles out prayer as a duty of the learned; vernacular versifications made the prayer available for devotion and meditation in the native idiom.
works.structure: The first version works petition by petition through the prayer, ending with an elaborated doxology; the shorter versions render the prayer more directly with brief homiletic expansions.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The three versions are independent texts by different poets, grouped here for convenience as in the standard editions.

works.title: The Menologium
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Tiberius B.i (Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201), eleventh century
works.description: A metrical calendar of the church year in 231 lines, versifying the fixed feasts and saints' days from Christmas through the year to Advent, with careful attention to the intervals of days between festivals. It is prefixed to the C-text of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle in Corpus Christi College MS 201.
works.plot: The poem proceeds through the liturgical year — Christmas, Epiphany, the spring feasts, Easter's movable cycle, the summer and autumn saints' days, and the return of Advent — computing the days between the major festivals and naming the saints honoured in the English church.
works.significance: The only surviving Old English metrical calendar, and a document of the English church's festal year at the height of the Benedictine Reform.
works.meter: Alliterative long line disciplined to the calendar's enumerative demands; the poet's art lies in varying formulaic phrasing within a rigid frame.
works.context: The poem reflects the English church's calendar as reformed in the tenth century, and its position beside the Chronicle shows the integration of liturgical and historical time in Benedictine Reform culture.
works.structure: A strictly sequential calendar, each feast introduced with its date and interval from the last; the structure is numerical and liturgical rather than narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Metrical Charms
works.description: A group of verse charms against illness, theft, and misfortune, preserved mainly in eleventh-century medical manuscripts (the Lacnunga and related collections). The charms blend Christian prayer with pre-Christian incantation — most famously the Nine Herbs Charm, invoking Woden as the healer of herbs, and Wið færstice, against a sudden stabbing pain caused by a 'mighty woman's' riding.
works.plot: Each charm prescribes words and actions for a specific ill: the Nine Herbs Charm enumerates the nine sacred herbs and their powers against poison and infection, invoking Woden's victory with nine glory-twigs; Wið færstice fights the elf-shot with a spear-image and a boiled herbal drink; others protect bees from swarming, fields from blight, and travellers from harm.
works.significance: The richest vernacular evidence for Anglo-Saxon folk medicine and for the survival of Germanic ritual in a Christian culture.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre, often irregular; incantatory repetition.
works.context: Preserved in London, British Library, Harley MS 585 (the Lacnunga), the Old English Herbarium manuscripts, and other medical compilations; the pre-Christian elements survived within Christian manuscripts.
works.characters: Woden (in the Nine Herbs Charm); the healer; the malevolent powers
works.structure: Prescriptive lyric sequences: invocation, narrative of the ill or its cure, and ritual instruction, often in verse alternating with prose directions.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Metrical Psalms of the Paris Psalter
works.description: A verse translation of Psalms 51-150 preserved in the Paris Psalter (Bibliothèque nationale de France, lat. 8824), accompanying the prose translation of Psalms 1-50. Once attributed to King Alfred, the verse psalms are now regarded as anonymous tenth- or eleventh-century work; they constitute the largest single body of Old English psalmody.
works.plot: The psalms are rendered in fluent alliterative verse, expanding the biblical text with traditional poetic diction; the collection provides the fullest surviving example of Old English liturgical translation in verse.
works.significance: The fullest English verse psalter before the late Middle Ages; important for the study of vernacular liturgy.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of a relatively plain, expository kind.
works.context: Preserved in the Paris Psalter (Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, MS lat. 8824), a mid-eleventh-century manuscript with Latin text and Old English translation in parallel columns; the first fifty psalms are in Alfredian prose.
works.characters: David (as psalmist); God
works.structure: A continuous psalter translation, psalm by psalm, in the versified mode.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the older attribution to Alfred is not now accepted, though the prose portion may be Alfredian.

works.title: The Middle English Lyric
works.description: The corpus of short Middle English lyric poems, secular and religious, composed and copied between c. 1200 and 1500: spring songs, love complaints, carols, lullabies, Passion meditations, and Marian praises, preserved in manuscripts and early printed collections. The most widely practised and most elusive of medieval English genres.
works.plot: The corpus's subjects are love and spring, mortality and judgement, the joys and sorrows of the Virgin, and the Passion; many poems are songs, with refrains and burdens, meant for performance.
works.significance: The lyric is the most continuous English poetic tradition of the period, feeding the courtly song of the Ricardians, the carol, and the Tudor songbooks.
works.meter: Every available stanza form, from the tail-rhyme romance stanza to carol form, rhyme royal, and the macaronic hymn.
works.context: Preserved in preaching manuscripts, commonplace books (Harley 2253; the Vernon manuscript), and, at the end of the period, in the printed collections of Wynkyn de Worde and Richard Pynson; the carol flourishes in the fifteenth century.
works.characters: the lovers, mourners, and devotees who speak the lyrics
works.structure: A corpus rather than a single work; individual lyrics are typically stanzaic, with refrain patterns.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous as a corpus; individual poems occasionally attributable (e.g., to Rolle's circle or to Lydgate).

works.title: The Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ
works.description: Nicholas Love's English translation and adaptation of the pseudo-Bonaventuran Meditationes Vitae Christi, completed c. 1410: a life of Christ from the Annunciation to Pentecost, written for the 'simple' reader to make the humanity of Jesus present to the imagination, with meditations, prayers, and passages against Lollard positions. The most widely circulated devotional work of fifteenth-century England.
works.plot: Following the gospel narrative day by day, the Mirror unfolds the life, ministry, Passion, and resurrection of Christ in vivid meditative episodes — the nativity, the sermons, the agony, the crucifixion as witnessed by Mary — each closed with moral application, and supplemented by Love's own anti-Wycliffite 'treatise on the sacrament'.
works.significance: The great bestseller of late medieval English devotion: it fixed the affective image of Christ's humanity for a century of English readers and is the key exhibit in the politics of vernacular theology after Arundel's Constitutions.
works.meter: Plain, warm prose of the Carthusian devotional school.
works.context: Completed c. 1410 by Nicholas Love, Carthusian prior of Mount Grace, with the explicit approval of Archbishop Arundel as an orthodox counter to Lollard vernacular scripture; preserved in more manuscripts than any other Middle English devotional text and printed by Caxton (1484) and his successors.
works.characters: Christ; the Virgin Mary; the disciples
works.structure: A day-by-day meditation on the life of Christ in the Meditationes tradition, with the Passion as its affective centre and devotional prayers appended.
works.attributionNotes: Love's authorship secure (named in the work's memorial note).

editions.title: The Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ: A Reading Text

works.title: The Morall Fabillis of Esope the Phrygian
works.description: Robert Henryson's cycle of thirteen beast fables (c. 1480s), translating and transforming Aesopian material into the great vernacular fable collection of the British Middle Ages: the cock and the jasper, the two mice, the lion and the mouse, the fox and the wolf, and the parliament of beasts before King Lion. Its moralitates raise the fable to satiric and philosophical art, with a marked sympathy for the poor and the small.
works.plot: The fables move from the country mouse's visit to the town and back, through the fox's adventures with the wolf and the cock's with the fox, to the lion's parliament, where the beasts' complaints against their rulers and their own natures are heard and judged; each fable closes with its moralitas applying the tale to the estates of men.
works.significance: The summit of the medieval European fable tradition in any vernacular: its moralitates are among the finest medieval poems on justice, poverty, and power.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas of supple, colloquial power in Older Scots.
works.context: Composed c. 1480s by the Dunfermline schoolmaster Robert Henryson, in the European fable revival of the fifteenth century (Steinhöwel, Caxton's Aesop of 1484); printed in 1570–71, and preserved in the Bannatyne and other manuscripts.
works.characters: the Cock and the Fox; the Town and Country Mice; the Lion; the Wolf; the Sheep; the Swallow; the Toad
works.structure: A prologue and thirteen fables, each bipartite (taill and moralitas), in the medieval Aesopic tradition raised to a coherent cycle.
works.attributionNotes: Henryson's authorship secure (named in the manuscripts).

works.title: The New Chronicles of England and France
works.description: Robert Fabyan's chronicle of England and France from Brutus to the reign of Henry VII, compiled from the London chronicles and printed by Richard Pynson in 1516 as The New Chronicles of England and France; the first city chronicle of London to reach print.
works.plot: The chronicle narrates the kings of England (with a parallel account of France) reign by reign, drawn from the Brut, the London chronicles, and the work of the French chroniclers, and closes with the accession of Henry VIII; the appended 'Concordance of Histories' aligns the chronicles of England and France.
works.significance: The first printed London chronicle and a major conduit of the English historical tradition from the medieval Brut to the Tudor chroniclers; Shakespeare knew its material (including the story of Lear) through Holinshed and the chronicle tradition.
works.meter: Prose with verse envoys
works.context: Compiled by Fabyan, a London draper and alderman, from the 1490s to c. 1504, with continuations to 1516; printed by Pynson in 1516 and again by William Rastell in 1533, it supplied material to Hall, Holinshed, and the Elizabethan playwrights.
works.structure: Annalistic chronicle in seven parts, each divided by reign; Fabyan's additions include the civic history of London and verse 'Lenvoyes' moralizing each reign.

works.title: The New Testament (Tyndale's translation)
altTitles: The New Testament Translated by William Tyndale
works.description: William Tyndale's translation of the New Testament from the Greek, the first English New Testament translated directly from the original language and the foundation of all later English Bibles, including the King James Version.
works.plot: A complete translation of the Greek New Testament with prefaces and marginal notes; the Cologne fragment (Matthew 1–22) was interrupted by the authorities in 1525, and the first complete edition appeared at Worms in 1526, followed by Tyndale's thorough revisions of 1534 and 1535.
works.significance: The fountainhead of English Bible translation: Tyndale's phrasing survives in as much as 80–90 per cent of the King James New Testament, and his English — 'the powers that be', 'a law unto themselves', 'the spirit is willing' — permanently shaped the language's biblical register.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Tyndale, denied episcopal support in England (the famous rebuke attributed to a Gloucestershire divine — 'we were better to be without God's law than the Pope's'), went to the continent in 1524; the Cologne printing (Quentel, 1525) was raided, and the Worms octavo of 1526 was smuggled into England, where Bishop Tunstall bought up copies for burning. Tyndale's 1534 revision is the text behind the later English versions.
works.structure: Biblical text in the order of the Greek canon, with prologues to the books and expository marginal glosses.

works.title: The Obedience of a Christian Man
altTitles: The Obedience of a Christen Man and How Christen Rulers Ought to Governe
works.description: Tyndale's treatise on the obedience owed by Christians to rulers and on the reading of scripture, printed at Antwerp in 1528; the book that, shown to Henry VIII, drew the king's reported remark that 'this is the book for me and all kings to read'.
works.plot: The book argues that every Christian — ploughman, weaver, or king — must obey his temporal rulers, whom God has ordained; it attacks the pope's claim to absolve subjects of allegiance, defends vernacular scripture against the charge that it breeds heresy, and expounds the duties of fathers, husbands, masters, and kings from the New Testament.
works.significance: The most politically consequential English book of the early Reformation: its doctrine of obedience made the English Reformation conceivable as an act of state, and its defence of vernacular scripture became the platform of the English Bible.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Printed at Antwerp in 1528 (by Hans Luft's press or its associates); Anne Boleyn's copy reached Henry VIII, and the book's doctrine of royal supremacy over the church made it a cornerstone of Henrician propaganda, feeding directly into the Reformation statutes of the 1530s.
works.structure: A continuous treatise divided into topical sections on the estates and their duties, with a famous preface on the reading of scripture.

editions.title: The Obedience of a Christian Man

works.title: The Old English Gospel of Nicodemus
altTitles: The Old English Version of the Gospel of Nicodemus
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, University Library Ii.2.11 (c. 1075); also London, British Library, Cotton Vitellius A.xv (twelfth century)
works.form: apocryphal gospel narrative (Old English prose translation)
works.description: An Old English translation of the apocryphal Gospel of Nicodemus, comprising the Acts of Pilate and the Harrowing of Hell: the trial, crucifixion, and burial of Christ as recorded by Nicodemus, followed by the testimony of the two sons of Simeon, raised from the dead, on Christ's descent into hell and his liberation of the patriarchs. It is the fullest Old English apocryphal gospel narrative.
works.plot: The first part recounts the trial before Pilate, the miracles that testified for Christ, the crucifixion and burial; the second part is the report of Charinus and Lenthius, the sons of Simeon, who describe how Christ broke the gates of hell, bound Satan, and led Adam and the patriarchs into paradise.
works.significance: The earliest English version of the most influential apocryphal gospel of the Middle Ages, and a principal channel by which the harrowing of hell became a central theme of later English literature.
works.context: The Latin Gospel of Nicodemus was one of the most widely read religious texts of the Middle Ages; its Old English translation belongs to the later eleventh century and stands behind the great Middle English prose and verse versions of the harrowing that culminate in Piers Plowman and the mystery plays.
works.characters: Pilate, Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathea, Christ, Satan, Adam, Charinus and Lenthius
works.structure: A two-part apocryphon: the Acts of Pilate (a trial narrative dense with dialogue) and the Descensus (a first-person testimony of the harrowing), the second part giving the work its enduring doctrinal importance.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.

works.title: The Old English Herbarium
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Vitellius C.iii (c. 1050), with two further copies (Harley 585; Harley 6258B)
works.description: An Old English translation of the enlarged Herbarium of Pseudo-Apuleius together with the Medicina de quadrupedibus, the standard late-antique herbal handbook of 185 plants and their medicinal uses. The translation is illustrated with painted plant portraits, making it the earliest illustrated English medical book.
works.plot: The herbal proceeds plant by plant, describing each herb's appearance and habitat and prescribing its preparations and cures — for snakebite, fever, wounds, stomach complaints, and the ailments of women — followed by the quadruped remedies drawn from badger, hare, and other animals.
works.significance: The first illustrated herbal in the English vernacular and a key witness to the transmission of classical pharmacology into early England and thence into the Middle English medical tradition.
works.context: Translated in the late tenth or early eleventh century as part of the vernacular medical programme that produced the Leechbook and Lacnunga; the illustrated Cotton copy shows the book's use in a wealthy late Anglo-Saxon medical household.
works.structure: An alphabetical-sequential catalogue of 185 chapters, each a self-contained plant monograph; the accompanying illustrations follow the antique pictorial tradition transmitted through continental exemplars.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation of the Latin Herbarium of Pseudo-Apuleius; the translator is unknown.

works.title: The Old English Life of St Christopher (fragment)
altTitles: The Passion of St Christopher (Old English fragment)
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Vitellius A.xv, fol. 94 (the Nowell Codex, c. 1000)
works.description: A fragmentary Old English prose passion of St Christopher, the giant cynocephalus (dog-headed) saint of the eastern church, preserved on a single damaged leaf of the Nowell Codex, the manuscript of Beowulf. It is the earliest surviving English version of the Christopher legend.
works.plot: The surviving text narrates Christopher's origin among the man-eating cynocephali and his conversion: granted human speech by divine grace, he receives baptism and the name Christopher ('Christ-bearer') and is sent by the king Dagnus to Alexandria, where he preaches; the fragment breaks off before the martyrdom itself.
works.significance: The earliest English witness to the Christopher legend, and part of the 'marvels' programme of the Beowulf manuscript, illuminating the reception of eastern hagiography in late Anglo-Saxon England.
works.context: The text's position in the Nowell Codex, between the prose Wonders of the East and the Letter of Alexander, shows the manuscript's compiler grouping marvels and monsters of the East; the Christopher legend's eastern marvels made it a natural member of that collection.
works.characters: Christopher, King Dagnus
works.structure: A continuous passio narrative of which only the opening survives; the preserved portion stresses the wonder of Christopher's monstrous nature transformed by grace — a thematically apt companion to the Beowulf manuscript's interest in monstrous beings.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.

works.title: The Old English Life of St Euphrosyne
altTitles: The Old English Legend of St Euphrosyne
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Julius E.vii (c. 1100)
works.description: An Old English translation of the life of St Euphrosyne, the Alexandrian maiden who fled her father's marriage plans and lived disguised as the monk Smaragdus for thirty-eight years, unrecognized by the father who mourned her. The life is the classic transvestite-saint legend of the eastern church.
works.plot: Euphrosyne, the only daughter of the wealthy Paphnutius of Alexandria, secretly takes monastic vows and enters a men's monastery disguised as the eunuch Smaragdus, where her holiness is recognized by the abbot. Her grieving father, visiting the monastery, is consoled by the unknown monk, and only on her deathbed does Euphrosyne reveal herself to him before dying in his arms.
works.significance: The only Old English witness to the transvestite-saint legend, and an early English example of the motif of the disguised woman that recurs through medieval literature.
works.context: Translated in the later eleventh century as part of the wave of vernacular hagiography for monastic and lay readers; the transvestite-saint motif, rooted in eastern monastic legend, held a lasting fascination for medieval English religious writing, reappearing in later legends and romances.
works.characters: Euphrosyne (Smaragdus), Paphnutius, the abbot
works.structure: A single sustained plot unusual in hagiography: disguise, concealment, and deferred recognition generate dramatic irony throughout, culminating in the deathbed revelation scene between father and daughter.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.

works.title: The Old English Life of St Giles
altTitles: The Old English Legend of St Giles
works.description: An Old English translation of the life of St Giles (Aegidius), the hermit of Provence nourished by a hind and wounded by a king's hunting arrow, whose abbey became a famous pilgrimage shrine. The life combines the eremitical ideal with the romance of the royal hunt.
works.plot: Giles, a Greek nobleman who gives his inheritance to the poor, becomes a hermit in the Provençal wilderness, fed by the milk of a tame hind. When the king's huntsmen wound him with an arrow meant for the hind, the repentant king builds the monastery of Saint-Gilles; Giles heals a possessed man, and his sanctity is confirmed by miracles, including his appearance before Charlemagne to absolve the emperor's secret sin.
works.significance: The earliest English witness to the cult of one of the most popular saints of the medieval West, and a representative of the late Old English eremitic legend.
works.context: Translated in the later eleventh century, when Giles's cult was spreading through England (over 160 English churches were dedicated to him); the life belongs to the same wave of vernacular hagiography as the lives of Margaret and Nicholas in CCCC 303.
works.characters: Giles, the hind, the king (Flavius), Charlemagne
works.structure: A conventional confessor's vita: renunciation, hermitage, the arrow episode, the foundation of the monastery, and a series of healing miracles, climaxing in the Charlemagne episode that made Giles the patron invoked for secret sins.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.

works.title: The Old English Life of St Margaret
altTitles: The Old English Legend of St Margaret of Antioch
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 303 (c. 1100); also London, British Library, Cotton Tiberius A.iii
works.description: An Old English prose life of St Margaret of Antioch, the virgin martyr swallowed by a dragon: the most popular female saint's life of the Middle Ages, here translated from the Latin passio of the Mombritius type. The text combines the romance of the dragon-fight with the passio's scenes of torture, making it a favourite of female devotional reading.
works.plot: Margaret, a shepherd's daughter of Antioch, rejects the prefect Olibrius and is tortured for her faith; in prison she overcomes a dragon that swallows her (bursting it from within by the sign of the cross) and a demon in the form of a black man; her final prayer asks that women in childbirth who invoke her be delivered, and she is beheaded, promising her intercession to all who read her passion.
works.significance: The earliest English version of the most influential female saint's legend of the Middle Ages, and a bridge between the Old English hagiographic tradition and the Middle English legendaries.
works.context: Translated in the later eleventh century when vernacular saints' lives multiplied for lay and female audiences; Margaret's cult, with its promise of protection in childbirth, spread through England in the twelfth century and her life became the most copied Middle English saint's legend.
works.characters: Margaret of Antioch, the prefect Olibrius, the dragon, the demon
works.structure: A classic virgin-martyr passio in the Mombritius tradition: courtship-refusal, tortures, the dragon and demon combats in prison, the trial's climax, and a death-scene culminating in the prayer for women in labour that made Margaret the patroness of childbirth.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.

works.title: The Old English Life of St Mary of Egypt
altTitles: The Old English Legend of Mary of Egypt
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Julius E.vii (fragmentary) and a Gloucester fragment
works.description: An Old English translation of the life of Mary of Egypt, the penitent harlot of the desert: the story of the sinner who fled to the wilderness and, after forty-seven years of solitary penance, was discovered by the monk Zosimas and found to have attained holiness. One of the great penitential legends of the Middle Ages.
works.plot: Mary, a prostitute of Alexandria, joins a pilgrimage to Jerusalem for wicked ends but is barred from the church by an invisible force; repenting before an icon of the Virgin, she crosses the Jordan and lives as a naked hermit for forty-seven years. The monk Zosimas finds her, hears her confession, gives her communion, and returns a year later to find her dead, with a lion helping him to bury her.
works.significance: The earliest English version of one of the most influential penitential legends of the Middle Ages, notable for its sympathetic treatment of female sin and sanctity.
works.context: Translated in the later eleventh century from the Latin vita, the life circulated among the vernacular devotional texts that multiplied after the Conquest; its themes of sexual sin, penance, and solitary holiness made it a staple of medieval penitential literature, later retold in Middle English.
works.characters: Mary of Egypt, Zosimas, the Virgin Mary (in the icon), the lion
works.structure: A frame narrative: Zosimas's search for a holy man greater than himself encloses Mary's first-person confession of her sins and penance, followed by her death and burial, the whole punctuated by the miracle of the lion and the testimony of the monastery.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.

works.title: The Old English Life of St Nicholas
altTitles: The Old English Legend of St Nicholas of Myra
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 303 (c. 1100); also London, British Library, Cotton Caligula A.xiv
works.description: An Old English translation of the life and miracles of St Nicholas, the fourth-century bishop of Myra, patron of sailors, children, and the unjustly condemned: the most popular male saint of the later Middle Ages. The text is the earliest English life of Nicholas and the ancestor of the great Middle English legends of the saint.
works.plot: The life recounts Nicholas's precocious sanctity and election as bishop of Myra; among his miracles are the secret dowering of three impoverished maidens (the origin of his gift-giving legend), the rescue of sailors from a storm, the restoration to life of three murdered scholars, and the deliverance of three unjustly condemned men, together with his death and the translation of his relics to Bari in 1087.
works.significance: The first English life of St Nicholas, source of the medieval English Nicholas legend tradition and of the gift-giving saint's enduring popular image.
works.context: Nicholas's cult swept western Europe after the translation of his relics to Bari in 1087, and this late Old English life shows the cult's arrival in England; the text's miracle stories became the staple of the Middle English Nicholas legends and of the saint's later folklore.
works.characters: Nicholas of Myra, the three maidens, the sailors, the three scholars, the emperor Constantine
works.structure: A conventional episcopal vita followed by a miracle collection, each miracle self-contained; the translation of the relics to Bari is narrated as the crowning vindication of the saint's cult.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.

works.title: The Old English Rule of Chrodegang
altTitles: The Old English Version of the Enlarged Rule of Chrodegang
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 191 (eleventh century)
works.form: translation of a canonical rule (Old English prose)
works.description: An Old English translation of the enlarged Rule of Chrodegang of Metz, the eighth-century rule for communities of secular canons, adapted with English material. Made in the Benedictine Reform period, it regulated the communal life of the canons who served the great minsters, prescribing their common meals, dormitory, chapter, and penitential discipline.
works.plot: The rule legislates the canonical life in chapters: the bishop as head of the community, the common refectory and dormitory, the daily chapter and the reading of scripture, confession and penance for faults, and the duties of the canons in the liturgy and the care of the minster.
