works.significance: A major document of the reform's extension beyond the monasteries to the secular church, and evidence of the vernacular's role in enforcing ecclesiastical discipline.
works.context: The Benedictine Reform's expulsion of secular clerics from Winchester's minsters in 964 created the need to reform the remaining communities of canons along quasi-monastic lines; the translated rule, together with Æthelwold's Regularis Concordia, extended the reform's discipline to the canonical clergy.
works.structure: A chapter-by-chapter translation of the enlarged rule, with the English material added to the Carolingian original; the text is a working legislative document rather than a narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.

works.title: The Old English Rule of St Benedict
altTitles: Æthelwold's Translation of the Rule of St Benedict
works.manuscriptDate: Five manuscripts including Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 178 and the Wells Cathedral copy (eleventh to thirteenth centuries)
works.description: A complete Old English translation of the Rule of St Benedict, traditionally attributed to Bishop Æthelwold of Winchester, made for the use of reformed monks and nuns whose Latin was limited. The translation is close, clear, and enriched with explanations of difficult terms.
works.plot: The text renders Benedict's rule for monastic life chapter by chapter: the abbot's office, obedience and humility, the daily round of prayer and work, food, sleep, and clothing, the reception of guests, and the discipline of faults, in continuous Old English prose.
works.significance: The first vernacular version of the most influential document of western monasticism, and a foundation text of the reform's vernacular programme of which Ælfric's writings are the culmination.
works.context: The translation belongs to the first years of the Benedictine Reform, when Æthelwold expelled the clerics of Winchester's minsters and replaced them with monks needing vernacular instruction in the rule they were to live by; it is the earliest translation of Benedict's rule into any European vernacular.
works.structure: A chapter-by-chapter translation following the order of the Latin rule, with occasional double glosses (Latin term plus English explanation) for technical vocabulary.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Æthelwold by tradition and by the evidence of his known translation activity; the attribution is widely but not universally accepted. Æthelwold's own preface and the translation are preserved together.

works.title: The Order of the World
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A wisdom poem of some 102 lines in which the poet urges his hearer to contemplate the created order — the sun's course, the stars, the seasons, and the harmony of the world — and to praise the Creator who sustains it all. The poem is an exercise in natural contemplation leading to worship.
works.plot: The poet calls on his audience to observe the wonders of creation: the journey of the sun, the movement of the heavens, the alternation of day and night, the order of the seasons. From the beauty and regularity of the world he turns to its maker, whom all creation serves, and urges man to praise God while he lives.
works.significance: One of the finest Old English poems of natural contemplation, notable for its integration of cosmology and devotion.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the descriptive passages on the heavens and seasons use the formulaic resources of the wisdom tradition with unusual lyrical polish.
works.context: The poem belongs to the Exeter Book wisdom corpus and shares its cosmological interests with the metrical version of Psalm 18 and the creation passages of the Cædmonian poems; it reflects the monastic ideal of contemplating God through his works.
works.structure: An exhortation framed as direct address to a 'wise one', moving from the observation of nature through reflection on the Creator to a closing call to praise; the poem is built of successive contemplations of the cosmic order.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Ormulum
works.description: A vast collection of verse homilies on the gospels read in the mass throughout the year, composed by the Augustinian canon Orm c. 1180, of which about a fifth survives (some 10,000 short lines). Its unique, meticulously consistent spelling system makes it a document of the first importance for the history of English.
works.plot: Each homily paraphrases the day's gospel text and expounds it allegorically and morally, with explanations of names and doctrine for the instruction of the English laity.
works.significance: The most ambitious vernacular religious work of the twelfth century and a uniquely valuable witness to early Middle English phonology, orthography, and East Midland dialect.
works.meter: An unrhymed fifteen-syllable septenarius in short couplet lines, strictly syllabic; the spelling system (double consonants after short vowels) is unique and systematic.
works.context: Composed c. 1180 by Orm, an Augustinian canon, probably of Elsham Priory, Lincolnshire, for his brother Walter; preserved in a single authorial or near-authorial manuscript, Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Junius 1.
works.characters: Christ; the evangelists' figures (none dramatically developed)
works.structure: A sequential homiliary following the liturgical year, with each sermon divided between gospel paraphrase, allegorical exposition, and moral application.
works.attributionNotes: Named in the dedication: 'þiss boc iss nemmnedd Orrmulum forrþi þatt Orrm itt wrohhte'.

editions.title: The Ormulum
editions.editor: Robert Meadows White (ed.); rev. Robert Holt

works.title: The Owl and the Nightingale
works.description: A debate poem of 1,794 lines in octosyllabic couplets in which the Owl and the Nightingale dispute which of them is the more useful and virtuous bird, arguing before a judge (Master Nicholas of Guildford) on matters of song, morality, marriage, and the religious life. It is the masterpiece of early Middle English poetry, combining French courtly wit with native English proverb and invective.
works.plot: The Nightingale accuses the Owl of ugliness and gloom, the Owl the Nightingale of frivolity and seduction; their quarrel ranges over theology, sex, and music, and both appeal to Master Nicholas of Guildford to render judgement — a judgement the poem never records.
works.significance: The outstanding literary achievement of early Middle English and the fountainhead of the English debate tradition that runs through Winner and Waster and the Parliament of Fowls to the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with enjambment and proverbial density; a sophisticated blend of French debate form and native English idiom.
works.context: Probably composed in Dorset or the south-west around 1200 (the text names King Henry as dead, dating it after 1189); preserved in two manuscripts of the mid-thirteenth century (BL Cotton Caligula A.ix and Jesus College, Oxford, MS 29).
works.characters: the Owl; the Nightingale; Master Nicholas of Guildford (named as judge)
works.structure: A continuous debate with prologue and framing judgment scene; the two birds' alternating speeches develop antithetical cases without resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous, but the poem names Master Nicholas of Guildford as its hoped-for judge; the authorship_status reflects scholarly practice in referring the work to its internal speaker.

editions.title: The Owl and the Nightingale: Text and Translation

works.title: The Palice of Honour
works.description: Douglas's first major poem, a courtly dream vision of prodigious learning: the dreamer, in a wilderness, sees a procession of the courts of Venus, Diana, and Minerva, faints before Venus's pageant, and is led to the Palace of Honour, where he learns the true source of fame and virtue. An answer to Chaucer's House of Fame and the foundation of Douglas's poetic career.
works.plot: The dreamer journeys with a guide from the garden of desire through the courts of Venus and Diana to the Palace of Honour, where the great of all ages sit enthroned; waking, he commits himself to the pursuit of honour through virtue.
works.significance: The most learned poem of the Scottish Renaissance and a central text of the Chaucerians; its allegorical courts prefigure The Faerie Queene.
works.meter: The nine-line stanza (ababbcbcC) inherited from Chaucer; aureate diction and encyclopaedic allusion.
works.context: Written about 1501, when Douglas was provost of St Giles; the poem's learning advertises the Scottish court's claim to the European Renaissance.
works.characters: the dreamer; Venus; Diana; Minerva; Calliope (guide)
works.structure: A dream vision in three movements — desire, instruction, and the vision of honour — modelled on Chaucer's House of Fame.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Panther
works.description: A poem of 74 lines from the Old English Physiologus group: the panther, fairest of beasts with its dappled coat, sleeps for three days and then calls with a sweet breath that draws all animals except the dragon. The poem allegorizes the panther as Christ, whose death, descent, and resurrection draw all souls — and the dragon as the devil who flees his fragrance.
works.plot: The poem describes the panther's beauty and gentleness, its three-day sleep and awakening, and the sweet breath that gathers the beasts; the interpretation identifies the panther with Christ, the dappled coat with his many virtues, and the sweet breath with the call of the gospel, which the old serpent, the devil, cannot endure.
works.significance: Part of the earliest English bestiary and of the allegorical natural-history tradition that culminates in the medieval bestiaries.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book with The Whale and The Partridge; the Physiologus tradition reached England via Latin intermediaries and remained productive through the Middle Ages.
works.characters: the Panther (Christ); the Dragon (the devil)
works.structure: Description followed by explicit allegorical interpretation, the standard Physiologus pattern.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Parable of the Wicked Mammon
altTitles: The Parable of the Wycked Mammon
works.description: Tyndale's exposition of the parable of the unjust steward (Luke 16), printed in 1528; his first published work and the classic statement of the Reformation doctrine of justification by faith alone.
works.plot: The treatise expounds the parable to teach that works do not justify but follow justification: the faithful are justified by faith in Christ's blood, and good works are the fruit of that faith, performed to one's neighbour without thought of merit; Tyndale defends the doctrine against the charge of encouraging licence and attacks the theology of merits, purgatory, and the intercession of saints.
works.significance: The first full English statement of justification by faith and the opening salvo of the English print war between Tyndale and More; its doctrine and its plain style set the terms of the English Reformation debate.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Printed in 1528 (STC 24454), the year of the Obedience, during Tyndale's exile in the Low Countries; it was among the first English books to state the Lutheran doctrine of justification, and it made Tyndale the prime target of More's Dialogue Concerning Heresies.
works.structure: A continuous doctrinal exposition with a preface 'To the Reader', arguing from scripture in Tyndale's plainest homiletic style.

works.title: The Pardoner and the Friar
works.description: John Heywood's anti-clerical farce of a pardoner and a friar who compete for the offerings of a parish church and come to blows in the pulpit; printed by William Rastell in 1533.
works.plot: A pardoner and a friar each claim the right to preach and collect money in a church; each denounces the other's hypocrisy and greed before the parish priest and his neighbour, until the contest descends into a brawl, the parson attempts to expel them, and both are dragged off toward the secular courts — with the parting promise that the devil will decide between them.
works.significance: The most anticlerical of Heywood's plays and a bridge between medieval estates satire and Reformation polemic; it shows the interlude absorbing the controversies of its moment without ceasing to be entertainment.
works.meter: Couplets
works.context: Written c. 1519–33 in the climate of lay criticism of clerical abuses that preceded the Reformation; the play draws on Chaucer's Pardoner and the long anticlerical tradition of estates satire, and its printing in 1533 coincided with the height of the campaign against church wealth.
works.characters: The Pardoner; The Friar; The Parson; The Neighbour
works.structure: A single-scene farce of rival harangues escalating into violence, framed by the parson's and neighbour's comments.

works.title: The Parliament of Fowls
works.description: Chaucer's St Valentine's Day dream vision (699 lines in rhyme royal): guided by Scipio's dream and the gate's ambiguous inscription, the dreamer enters the garden of love, where Nature presides over the parliament of birds choosing their mates on the feast of Venus. The debate between the noble eagles and the commons of birds is the great medieval comedy of class, desire, and natural law.
works.plot: After reading Cicero's Somnium Scipionis, the dreamer is led by Africanus through the gate ('through me men go to that blessed place' / 'through me the way to sorrow') into Nature's park, where the goddess holds the parliament of fowls; three aristocratic eagles court the formel on her wrist, their courtly pleas answered by the lower birds' impatient cry 'have done, and let us wende!' — and the formel's request for a year's delay leaves the parliament, and the poem, in unresolved suspension.
works.significance: The classic English poem of Valentine's Day and the finest medieval treatment of the bird parliament; its satire of courtly and common 'commune profyt' is a touchstone of Chaucer's political art.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas, with the lyric roundel ('Now welcom somer') inset.
works.context: Composed c. 1380–82, traditionally read against the marriage negotiations of Richard II (to Anne of Bohemia, 1382); the Valentine convention and the bird parliament derive from French and Italian love vision.
works.characters: the Dreamer; Africanus; Nature; the three eagles; the formel; the goose, cuckoo, turtledove, and other birds
works.structure: A tripartite vision (reading and gate; the garden and temple; the parliament and debate), with the roundel of summer as its lyric centre.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure.

works.title: The Parliament of the Three Ages
altTitles: The Parlement of the Thre Ages
works.description: An alliterative debate vision of the three ages of man: a dreamer watching a deer hunt overhears Youth, Middle Age, and Old Age dispute the values of their lives, in a poem that grafts the morality of the ages onto the romance glamour of the hunt and the nine worthies. Its hunt scene is among the finest descriptive passages of the revival.
works.plot: The dreamer, concealed in the woods, follows the elaborate ritual of the hunt — the harbouring, the chase, the breaking of the deer — and then overhears three debaters: Youth, vaunting love and tournament; Middle Age, priding himself on wealth; and Old Age, who answers with the ubi sunt catalogue of the nine worthies and the lesson of Death the leveller.
works.significance: The most accomplished of the alliterative debate visions after Winner and Waster, and a principal vernacular statement of the ages-of-man topos.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line with stanzaic variation.
works.context: Composed c. 1370–90 in the north or north-west Midlands, drawing on the tradition of the ages of man and the nine worthies; preserved uniquely in BL Additional MS 31042 and (in part) Additional MS 33942.
works.characters: the Dreamer; Youth; Middle Age; Old Age; Death
works.structure: A frame vision enclosing the hunt and the three speeches, in the debate-vision convention.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Partridge
works.description: A poem of 16 lines, the third of the Exeter Book Physiologus group: the partridge, which steals and broods the eggs of other birds, sees its stolen brood desert it when they hatch and hear their true mother's call. The allegory (imperfectly preserved) contrasts the devil's stolen brood with those who hear the true voice of Christ.
works.plot: The partridge hatches eggs not its own; when the chicks hear their real mother they leave the deceiver. The brief application praises those who turn to their true parent — the text breaks off where the interpretation of the fable is developed.
works.significance: Completes the earliest English bestiary group.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book, immediately after The Whale.
works.characters: the Partridge; the stolen brood
works.structure: Fable followed by a broken-off allegorical application.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Pastime of People
altTitles: The Pastyme of People: The Cronycles of Dyuers Realmys
works.description: John Rastell's chronicle of the kings of England, printed by the author c. 1529 and known principally through the celebrated woodcut portraits of the kings that illustrate it.
works.plot: The chronicle surveys the kings of Britain from the legendary line (Brutus, Arthur) through the Saxon, Norman, and Plantagenet reigns to the author's own day, each reign summarized with a woodcut portrait, the whole prefaced by a prologue on the use of history.
works.significance: A pioneering illustrated chronicle whose woodcut royal portraits influenced the visual tradition of the English kings for centuries; it documents the early Tudor printing industry's combination of history and spectacle.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Printed c. 1529 by Rastell, More's brother-in-law, printer, and playwright, at his own press; only three copies survive, and the king-portraits became a standard visual source for the Tudor image of English kingship.
works.structure: A compressed annalistic chronicle with full-page woodcut portraits of the kings, arranged by reign.

works.title: The Pastime of Pleasure
altTitles: The Historie of Graunde Amoure and La Bell Pucell
works.form: allegorical romance in rhyme royal and couplets
works.description: Hawes's allegorical romance of the education of the knight Graunde Amoure: his instruction by Lady Fame and the seven liberal arts in the Tower of Doctrine, his courtship of La Belle Pucelle, his combat with a giant, their marriage, and his death, with Time and Eternity closing the poem. Printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1509, it is the last great allegory of the medieval English tradition.
works.plot: Graunde Amoure, guided by Governance and instructed in the Tower of Doctrine, wins La Belle Pucelle through the arts and arms, marries her, and rules until Age and Death take him; Fame memorializes the lovers.
works.significance: The bridge between the medieval allegorical romance and Tudor poetry; its catalogue of the arts and its ideal of the learned knight were formative for Spenser's Faerie Queene.
works.meter: Rhyme royal handled in the Lydgatian manner, with couplet passages; aureate diction over a clear narrative line.
works.context: Written at the court of Henry VII, to whom the ideal of the educated knight was addressed; printed in 1509, the year of Henry VIII's accession.
works.characters: Graunde Amoure; La Belle Pucelle; Lady Fame; Governance; Godfrey Gobelive (the giant); Time; Eternity
works.structure: An allegorical romance in three movements — instruction, quest, and the fall of the hero — framed by a dream prologue and an epilogue on fame and time.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Penitential Psalms
works.form: psalm paraphrase in terza rima (prologue) and various stanzas
works.description: Wyatt's paraphrase of the seven penitential psalms (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143), framed by a prologue in which David, the royal lover of Bathsheba, is made the type of the penitent courtier. Based on Aretino's I Sette Salmi, the work turns the psalmist's repentance into a sustained meditation on the dangers of the court and the sovereignty of God.
works.plot: The frame narrative follows David from his sin with Bathsheba through the prophet Nathan's parable to his repentance; each psalm is then paraphrased as David's own speech, with Wyatt's added commentary.
works.significance: The major English religious poem of the Reformation's first generation and the ancestor of Sidney's and Milton's psalm paraphrases; its David is the first great self-portrait of the Tudor courtier in verse.
works.meter: Terza rima in the prologue — the first sustained English use of Dante's metre — and ottava rima in the psalm paraphrases.
works.context: Written after Wyatt's imprisonment of 1536, during the fall of Anne Boleyn; the psalmist's court becomes a mirror of Henry VIII's, and repentance the courtier's only safety.
works.characters: David; Bathsheba; Nathan
works.structure: Prologue narrative (in terza rima) followed by seven paraphrases; each psalm introduced by a stanza of commentary.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Pentateuch (Tyndale's translation)
works.description: Tyndale's translation of the first five books of the Old Testament from the Hebrew, printed at Antwerp in 1530; the first English translation of any part of the Hebrew Bible from the original language.
works.plot: A complete translation of Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, with prefaces to each book explaining its sense and typological bearing, and a prologue to the whole ('W. T. to the Reader') setting out Tyndale's principles of translation from the Hebrew.
works.significance: The first English translation from the Hebrew and the origin of the English Old Testament's distinctive phrasing ('let there be light', 'the Lord bless thee and keep thee'); it established the principle that the Bible must be rendered from the original tongues.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Tyndale learned Hebrew on the continent (probably from Jewish scholars), and the Pentateuch of 1530 was printed by Hans Luft at Antwerp (or Marburg) and smuggled into England; it supplied the Old Testament basis for the Matthew Bible (1537) and, through it, for the Great Bible and the King James Version.
works.structure: Biblical text in the Hebrew order, with per-book prefaces and glosses; Genesis and Numbers were printed separately with their own title pages.

works.title: The Phoenix
works.form: allegorical religious narrative in alliterative verse
works.description: An allegorical poem of 677 lines on the legend of the phoenix, which burns itself on its nest of spices and rises renewed: a figure, the poem explains, of the resurrection of the body and the Christian's hope of the heavenly homeland. Based on the Carmen de ave phoenice attributed to Lactantius, it contains one of the finest paradise descriptions in Old English.
works.plot: The poem describes the earthly paradise in the east where the phoenix dwells; after a thousand years the bird flies to Syria, builds a nest of spices, is consumed by fire, and after three days revives from the ashes. The second half interprets the legend allegorically: the phoenix is Christ and the blessed soul, the nest the good works, and the renewal the resurrection at the Last Judgment.
works.significance: The fullest Old English allegory of resurrection and the richest nature-description in the corpus.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the poem is notable for its extended descriptive set-pieces.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; the Latin source (fourth century, attributed to Lactantius) circulated widely in Anglo-Saxon England.
works.characters: the Phoenix (as bird and as allegorical figure)
works.structure: A bipartite structure of literal legend followed by sustained allegorical exposition (the latter an original expansion of the Latin source).
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Play of the Weather
altTitles: A New and a Very Mery Enterlude of All Maner Wethers
works.description: John Heywood's interlude in which Jupiter receives petitions for every kind of weather and reconciles them all by leaving the weather as it is; printed by William Rastell in 1533.
works.plot: Jupiter, wishing to settle the world's complaints about the weather, summons the estates of the realm: a gentleman wants fair weather for hunting, a merchant wind for his ships, a ranger frost, a water-miller rain, a laundress sun, a boy snow; each pleads his case, and Jupiter's final decree — that the weather shall continue as it has been — demonstrates the impossibility of pleasing all parties and the wisdom of accepting the established order.
works.significance: The best known of Heywood's interludes and a classic of early Tudor political satire: its survey of competing interests remains the liveliest dramatic picture of the Tudor commonwealth, and Mery Report is a landmark in the development of the stage Vice.
works.meter: Couplets and doggerel, with prose in Mery Report's asides
works.context: Printed by William Rastell in 1533, the year of Henry VIII's divorce crisis and the statute in restraint of appeals; the play's debate on sovereignty and the impossibility of pleasing all suitors has been read as a commentary on royal counsel and the conflicts of the Reformation Parliament.
works.characters: Jupiter; Mery Report (the Vice); The Gentleman; The Merchant; The Ranger; The Water-Miller; The Wind-Miller; The Laundress; The Boy
works.structure: A single continuous action of successive petitions before Jupiter's throne, ending with a report of Jupiter's decree; the comic petitions build a survey of the commonwealth by estates.

works.title: The Practice of Prelates
works.description: Tyndale's polemic against the English bishops and Cardinal Wolsey, published in 1530, arguing that the prelates' craft had corrupted both church and state and broken the king's marriage.
works.plot: The book traces the 'practice' (craft) of the prelates through English history, attacks Wolsey's legatine power and the annulment proceedings, defends the king's cause against the pope's usurped jurisdiction, and argues from scripture that no man may set himself over kings; it closes with the charge that the bishops oppose the vernacular scripture because it exposes their greed.
works.significance: The most aggressive of Tyndale's political works and a landmark in the English tradition of anti-prelatical polemic that runs to Milton; it documents the convergence of Reformation doctrine and Tudor statecraft.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1530 at the height of the king's 'great matter', while Wolsey's fall was fresh (November 1529); Tyndale's attack on the annulment as the prelates' contrivance, and his denial of the pope's dispensing power, aligned him with the Henrician propaganda campaign while going further than the king would allow.
works.structure: A continuous polemic in three movements — historical narrative, political argument, and scriptural proof — addressed to the king, lords, and commons.

works.title: The Prick of Conscience
works.description: A northern poem of some 9,600 lines on the last things — the wretchedness of life, death, purgatory, the pains of hell and joys of heaven, and the day of doom — traditionally attributed to Richard Rolle but now generally denied to him. It was the most widely copied Middle English poem of all, surviving in more manuscripts than any other verse of the period, including Piers Plowman and the Canterbury Tales.
works.plot: In seven parts the poem moves from the misery of human life through the certainty and terror of death to the topography of the afterlife — purgatory's cleansing fire, hell's torments, heaven's bliss — and the signs and terrors of the last judgement, closing with the exhortation to live so as to die well.
works.significance: The most widely read Middle English poem of its century and the great vernacular encyclopedia of the afterlife; its manuscript diffusion is a central fact of late medieval English literary culture.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets in the northern dialect, plain and insistent.
works.context: Composed c. 1350 in the north of England, in the pastoral tradition of the fourth Lateran council's emphasis on penance; preserved in over 120 manuscripts and translated into Latin (Stimulus Conscientiae); its popularity made it the period's standard popular eschatology.
works.characters: the preacher-narrator
works.structure: A seven-part didactic sequence on the four last things, in the memento mori tradition, with the 'prick' of conscience as its titular image.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Richard Rolle in many manuscripts, but modern scholarship rejects the attribution (Ralph Hanna and others); authorship_status reflects the dispute.

works.title: The Proverbs of Alfred
altTitles: The Proverbs of Alfred of Wessex
works.description: A collection of proverbial wisdom in verse, cast as the sayings of King Alfred assembled 'at Seaford' before a gathered folk, on kingship, wealth, wisdom, women, and the conduct of life. It is the principal early Middle English example of the native gnomic tradition continuing under the name of the great West Saxon king.
works.plot: Alfred, enthroned at Seaford, delivers counsel in a series of proverb-laden sections — on wisdom and wealth, on choosing a wife, on old age — punctuated by the poet's own commentary.
works.significance: The chief witness to the survival of the Old English wisdom tradition into Middle English, and a favourite anthology text of the early period.
works.meter: Loose alliterative and rhyming couplets in the transitional early Middle English manner.
works.context: Composed c. 1150–80, perhaps in Sussex, in the south; preserved in Jesus College, Oxford, MS 29 (c. 1275) with The Owl and the Nightingale, and fragmentarily elsewhere.
works.characters: Alfred (speaker); the assembled folk
works.structure: A framing scene of the king's council enclosing discrete gnomic sections with connective commentary.
works.attributionNotes: The attribution to Alfred is traditional and pseudonymous; the poem is the product of the twelfth-century cult of the king.

works.title: The Regiment of Princes
works.form: mirror for princes in rhyme royal
works.description: Thomas Hoccleve's mirror for princes of 5,463 lines in rhyme royal, addressed to the future Henry V and completed in 1411: an adaptation of the pseudo-Aristotelian Secretum Secretorum, Egidius Romanus's De Regimine Principum, and Jacobus de Cessolis's chess moralities, framed by the poet's famous dialogue with a beggar on poverty, patronage, and the life of the London clerk. The classic Lancastrian poem of good governance.
works.plot: The sleepless poet, walking the fields of Westminster, meets an old beggar who catechizes him on the vanity of court service and the miseries of poverty; the dialogue then opens into the treatise proper — justice, mercy, patience, chastity, liberality, and the duties of the prince — closing with the counsel to the young Henry of Monmouth, prince of Wales.
works.significance: The principal English mirror-for-princes of the fifteenth century and a landmark of autobiographical poetry; its beggar dialogue inaugurates the tradition of the poor poet's complaint.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas of plain correctness, in Hoccleve's characteristic conversational register.
works.context: Completed in 1411 by the Privy Seal clerk Hoccleve for the prince of Wales, on the eve of Agincourt; its portrait of the poor clerk's London is the most vivid account of bureaucratic life in the period; preserved in forty-three manuscripts.
works.characters: Hoccleve; the Beggar; Henry, Prince of Wales (addressee)
works.structure: A mirror-for-princes in the frame of the poet's own autobiographical dialogue, the first English poem to make the writer's economic anxieties its prologue.
works.attributionNotes: Hoccleve's authorship secure; he names himself throughout.

works.title: The Repressor of Over Much Blaming of the Clergy
works.description: Reginald Pecock's great vernacular apologia (c. 1449–55), answering the Lollards' eleven 'blamings' of the clergy — against images, pilgrimages, clerical endowments, the pope, and the religious orders — not by authority but by the 'doom of reason'. The most original work of English theology between Wyclif and the Reformation, and the cause of its author's own condemnation.
works.plot: Pecock restates the Lollard objections with scrupulous fairness and answers each by rational argument: faith is grounded in reason, images and pilgrimages serve the memory and the affections, clerical endowment is lawful when used rightly, and the church's hierarchy is the ordinance of God — while insisting, to his ruin, that the clergy must be judged by scripture and reason rather than by bare authority.
works.significance: The supreme monument of fifteenth-century English rational theology and a tragic witness to the church's fear of its own vernacular defenders.
works.meter: Plain English of argument, with an invented philosophical vocabulary ('unbileve', 'moral philosophi').
works.context: Composed c. 1449–55 by the bishop of Chichester, in the controversy over vernacular theology after Arundel's Constitutions; Pecock's reliance on reason over authority led to his trial (1457), his abjuration at Paul's Cross, and the burning of his books.
works.characters: Pecock (as reasoner); the Lollard interlocutors (implied)
works.structure: Five parts answering the successive Lollard conclusions, in the dialectical form of objection and response.
works.attributionNotes: Pecock's authorship secure.

editions.title: The Repressor of Over Much Blaming of the Clergy

works.title: The Rhyming Poem
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A unique experiment in Old English prosody: an elegiac meditation on the fall of a once-powerful lord, written in rhyming couplets with end-rhyme sustained line after line, a technique otherwise foreign to alliterative verse. The speaker remembers his former glory as a generous ruler surrounded by retainers, and contrasts it with his present misery and loss.
works.plot: The speaker recalls his past prosperity as a lord who distributed treasure and ruled a loyal comitatus, then laments the reversal of fortune that has stripped him of wealth, retainers, and honour. The poem moves from remembered joy to the recognition that all earthly glory decays, and closes with reflection on the grave and the soul's fate.
works.significance: The earliest extended rhyming poem in English; evidence that Old English poets could adapt the alliterative line to rhyme, anticipating the rhyming experiments of later medieval English verse.
works.meter: Rhymed couplets with pervasive end-rhyme and internal rhyme over an alliterative base; the poet sustains rhyme through some 87 lines, a virtuoso performance in a language whose native metre is alliterative.
works.context: Composed in the later Old English period, when the heroic conventions of the hall and the comitatus were already literary memory rather than living institutions; the poem shares the vocabulary of exile and transience with The Wanderer and The Seafarer.
works.structure: A single first-person meditation organized around the contrast between past splendour and present ruin, framed by ubi sunt reflection; the paired rhymes and internal rhymes bind short clauses into couplets.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. No attribution has ever been proposed.

works.title: The Romaunt of the Rose
works.description: A Middle English translation of the Roman de la Rose, surviving in a single manuscript and divided by scholarship into three fragments (A, B, and C), of which only Fragment A is now widely accepted as Chaucer's — and even that attribution is debated. The work is the great conduit by which the French allegory of love entered English, and its early attribution to Chaucer long shaped the poet's canon.
works.plot: The dreamer enters the garden of Mirth, where the god of Love shoots him and he pledges service; the narrative then follows the lover's quest for the Rose through the allegorical figures of the garden — Fair Welcome, Danger, Reason, Shame, Jealousy — in the French poem's anatomy of courtly love.
works.significance: The principal English version of the poem that dominated late medieval literary culture; the attribution question remains a central problem of Chaucerian scholarship.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets.
works.context: Composed in the 1360s–70s (Fragment A possibly c. 1360s), translating Guillaume de Lorris and Jean de Meun; preserved uniquely in the Hunterian manuscript (Glasgow, Hunter 409); the attribution to Chaucer rests on his own mention of a Romaunt translation in the Legend of Good Women prologue and on Thynne's 1532 edition.
works.characters: the Dreamer-Lover; the Rose; the god of Love; Fair Welcome; Danger; Reason; Jealousy; the Old Woman
works.structure: A continuous allegorical dream vision following the French original's sequence of episodes, surviving here in three discontinuous fragments.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship disputed: Fragment A is often accepted as Chaucer's; Fragments B and C are generally rejected; modern editors treat the whole as doubtful. authorship_status reflects this uncertainty.

works.title: The Ruin
works.description: A fragmentary elegy (about 49 lines, damaged by burning of the manuscript leaf) describing the ruins of a great stone city — hot springs, halls, and baths that are almost certainly Roman Bath — and meditating on the fall of its builders.
works.plot: The speaker marvels at 'enta geweorc' (the work of giants): broken walls, fallen roofs, and the hot baths where once many men bathed in comfort; the city's warriors are dead, its halls decayed, and the poem closes with the reflection that a hundred generations have passed since its glory.
works.significance: The earliest ruin-poem in English, anticipating the ruin tradition of the eighteenth century; a haunting witness to Anglo-Saxon wonder at Roman remains.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the text is incomplete through fire damage.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; the identification with Roman Bath is standard.
works.characters: none (descriptive speaker)
works.structure: A description of ruins moving from sensory observation to historical meditation, in the ubi sunt mode.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle: A Revised Translation

works.title: The Rune Poem
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Otho B.x, fol. 165 (destroyed in the Cotton fire of 1731; survives in the transcript printed by George Hickes, 1705)
works.form: runic wisdom poem in alliterative verse
works.description: A wisdom poem of 94 lines in which each of the 29 runes of the Anglo-Saxon futhorc is given a stanza beginning with the rune's name and elaborating its traditional meanings: feoh (wealth), ur (aurochs), thorn, the gods, the horse, the sun, and the rest. The poem fuses native Germanic rune-lore with Christian wisdom.
works.plot: Stanza by stanza, the poem unfolds the lore of each rune — wealth's mutability, the aurochs' ferocity, thorn's sharpness, the sun's blessing to seafarers, the grave's coldness — building a gnomic encyclopaedia of the natural and social world as encoded in the runic alphabet.
works.significance: The principal source for the names and meanings of the Anglo-Saxon runes, and a bridge between Germanic pagan lore and Christian Old English poetry; its loss in the 1731 fire makes Hickes's transcript the only witness.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; each stanza opens with the rune's name, and the verses carry the gnomic compression of the Exeter wisdom tradition.
works.context: The poem is the fullest surviving statement of the Anglo-Saxon runic tradition, composed when runes were still written for inscriptions and magic while the script's pagan associations were being absorbed into Christian learning; it descends from the same tradition as the Old Norwegian and Old Icelandic rune poems.
works.structure: A catalogue of 29 stanzas, one per rune, in the fixed order of the Anglo-Saxon futhorc; each stanza is a self-contained gnomic meditation introduced by the rune-name.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The prose and verse traditions around the runes descend from a common Germanic inheritance; the Old English poem is an independent composition.

editions.title: The Old English Rune Poem: A Critical Edition

works.title: The Scale of Perfection
works.description: Walter Hilton's masterpiece, in two books: the first (c. 1380s) addresses an anchoress on the reformation of the soul in faith and the destruction of the image of sin; the second (c. 1390s), on the reformation of the soul in feeling, expounds the contemplative life and the discernment of true spiritual experience. The most systematic and influential English treatise on contemplation.
works.plot: Book I anatomizes the soul's sinfulness and its reformation through faith, humility, and the practice of prayer, with the famous analysis of the image of sin to be broken down; Book II teaches the higher work of contemplation — the entry into the 'darkness' of unknowing, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the tests by which true spiritual experience may be known from false.
works.significance: The classic systematic treatise of English mysticism: its discrimination of true and false spiritual experience and its doctrine of the image of God shaped English devotional thought for three centuries.
works.meter: Measured, precise prose, plainer than Rolle's and theologically more careful.
works.context: Composed c. 1380–96 by the Augustinian canon Walter Hilton, for a woman recluse and for the devout laity; printed by Wynkyn de Worde (1494) and read by the English Benedictine revival of the seventeenth century.
works.characters: Hilton (teacher); the anchoress (addressee)
works.structure: Two books of graduated instruction (the 'scale'), moving from the active to the contemplative life, in the tradition of the spiritual ladder.
works.attributionNotes: Hilton's authorship secure.

works.title: The Schoolmaster
works.description: Ascham's posthumously published treatise on the education of children, especially the teaching of Latin by double translation, with an autobiographical preface on the occasion of its writing.
works.plot: Book I, framed by the preface recalling a 1563 dinner conversation at Windsor on the flogging of schoolboys, advocates gentleness in teaching, criticizes the harsh grammar-school regime, and sketches the ideal education of a gentleman's son. Book II offers a practical method — the 'double translation' of Latin — by which the student imitates classical models, with detailed advice on style, imitation, and the choice of authors.
works.significance: The classic statement of Elizabethan humanist pedagogy; its doctrine of imitation and its advocacy of the vernacular prose style influenced Sidney, Spenser, and the school curriculum for generations.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Begun c. 1563 after the Windsor dinner with Cecil and Sackville (the latter of whom prompted the book), and left unfinished at Ascham's death in December 1568; published in 1570 by his widow Margaret with a dedication to Cecil. Its composition and publication bridge the early Tudor and Elizabethan periods.
works.characters: Roger Ascham (narrator); Sir William Cecil; Sir Richard Sackville
works.structure: Two books; the first is anecdotal and hortatory, the second a systematic method with specimen exercises.

editions.title: The Schoolmaster (1570)
editions.publisher: Cornell University Press (for the Folger Shakespeare Library)

works.title: The Seafarer
works.description: An elegy of 124 lines spoken by a veteran seafarer who describes the hardship and the irresistible pull of the sea voyage, then allegorizes it as the soul's pilgrimage away from the world toward its heavenly home.
works.plot: The speaker recounts winters of cold watch on the ice-cold sea, hunger, and isolation, yet declares that the sea calls him again; earthly joys, lords, and kingdoms all pass, and the wise man sets his hope on the eternal home where all things endure — the journey of the seafarer becoming a figure for the Christian's exile in the world.
works.significance: Alongside The Wanderer, the great poem of Old English exile; its seascape and spiritual allegory influenced Pound's 'The Seafarer' and much modern poetry.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; vivid winter seascape imagery rare in the corpus.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; influenced by the penitential and pilgrimage traditions (the phrase 'dryhtnes dreamas' has suggested the peregrinus ideal of Irish and Anglo-Saxon monasticism).
works.characters: the Seafarer (speaker)
works.structure: Two movements: a first-person account of seafaring hardship and longing, and a homiletic second half that interprets the voyage allegorically (peregrinatio pro amore Dei); the transition between them is a crux of interpretation.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: A Guide to Old English, 8th edition

works.title: The Series
works.description: Thomas Hoccleve's linked sequence of poems (c. 1419–21), beginning with the Complaint and the Dialogue with a Friend — the first extended account of mental illness in English poetry, describing his 'wylde infirmity' of 1416 — and continuing with the tale of the emperor Jereslaus's wife and the Learn to Die, translated from the Gesta Romanorum and Suso. The founding text of English confessional poetry.
works.plot: The poet, unable to persuade the world of his recovered wits, complains of his illness and its social stigma; a Friend counsels and cajoles him back to writing; the sequence then proceeds through the exemplary tale of the empress and the treatise on dying, the poet's own voice threading the whole.
works.significance: The first extended English poem of mental illness and recovery, and the first secular autobiography in English verse; its frankness has made it a touchstone of disability and confessional studies.
works.meter: Rhyme royal throughout, with the prosimetric flourishes of the translated treatises.
works.context: Composed c. 1419–21, after Hoccleve's breakdown of 1416, for Humphrey Duke of Gloucester among others; preserved in the holograph manuscripts (Durham, Cosin V.iii.9; BL Harley 4866) — the earliest English authorial manuscripts after Orm.
works.characters: Hoccleve; the Friend; the Emperor Jereslaus and his wife (tale)
works.structure: A self-consciously linked series — complaint, dialogue, tale, and treatise — in which the frame of the poet's illness governs the exemplary matter.
works.attributionNotes: Hoccleve's authorship secure; parts survive in his own hand.

works.title: The Sermons before King Edward VI
altTitles: The Seven Sermons before Edward VI
works.description: Hugh Latimer's seven Lenten sermons preached before King Edward VI in the privy garden at Westminster in 1549 and printed the same year; the fullest surviving example of Latimer's court preaching.
works.plot: Preached weekly in Lent 1549, the sermons press the young king and his court with the duties of the magistrate: Latimer denounces the greed of landlords and enclosers, the plunder of church goods, the oppression of the poor, and the corruption of officials, urging the king to be the father of the commonwealth and warning that England's plagues are God's judgement on its sins.
works.significance: The classic example of court preaching in English and a prime source for the social history of Edwardian England; Latimer's plainspoken rebukes of the powerful made him the archetype of the prophetic preacher.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Preached at Westminster in Lent 1549, the year of the First Prayer Book, the rebellions of 1549, and the fall of Protector Somerset; printed by John Day in 1549, the sermons document the preaching office at the summit of the state and the social crisis of the mid-Tudor years.
works.characters: King Edward VI (addressee)
works.structure: Seven self-contained sermons, each on a set text, in Latimer's direct, colloquial, and anecdotal style, with running rebukes of his courtly audience.

works.title: The Seven Penitential Psalms (Fisher's exposition)
altTitles: This treatise concerninge the fruytfull saynges of Davyd the kynge and prophete in the seven penytencyall psalmes
works.description: John Fisher's devotional exposition of the seven penitential psalms, preached as sermons to Margaret Beaufort and published by Wynkyn de Worde in 1508; the first work of the English Catholic humanist reform tradition.
works.plot: The treatise expounds Psalms 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, and 143 as a programme of penitence — contrition, confession, and satisfaction — applying each psalm to the life of the Christian penitent and to the passion of Christ as the ground of forgiveness.
works.significance: The finest English devotional prose before the Reformation controversy and a witness to the scriptural piety of the pre-Reformation English Church; its emphasis on preaching and scripture anticipates the reform movements on both sides of the sixteenth-century divide.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Preached as a Lenten course to the household of Lady Margaret Beaufort, the king's mother, whose confessor Fisher was; printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1508 and reprinted in 1509 and 1525, it belongs to the devotional revival associated with the Charterhouse and the early humanist circle.
works.characters: David (as penitent)
works.structure: Seven sermon-treatises, one per psalm, each structured by the threefold division of the penitential process, with a preface to Margaret Beaufort.

works.title: The Ship of Fools
altTitles: The Shyp of Folys of the Worlde
works.description: Barclay's Englishing of Sebastian Brant's Narrenschiff through Locher's Latin version: a fleet of fools — the bookish fool, the covetous, the gluttonous, the lecherous clergy, the negligent bishops — each shipped aboard the vessel of folly in a comprehensive satire of the estates, printed by Richard Pynson in 1509.
works.plot: The narrator gathers the fools of every estate aboard the Ship of Fools; chapter by chapter, each folly is exhibited and moralized, from the pride of scholars to the corruption of Rome.
works.significance: The channel by which the great European estates satire reached England; its catalogue form and its moralizing woodcuts shaped a century of English satirical writing.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas of fluent competence; the moralized catalogue form of the continental Renaissance satire.
works.context: Translated in the years before the Reformation, when anticlerical satire was already a licensed genre; printed by Pynson in December 1509.
works.characters: the narrator; the fools (by estate and vice)
works.structure: A catalogue satire in over a hundred sections, each an emblem of a folly with its moral appended; the ship provides the unifying frame.
works.attributionNotes: Barclay's adaptation of Brant (via Locher) is freely made with English additions; recorded as translation-adaptation.

works.title: The Siege of Jerusalem
works.description: An alliterative poem of some 1,300 lines on the Roman destruction of Jerusalem by Vespasian and Titus, cast as vengeance for the crucifixion: the siege, the famine, the fall of the city, and the punishment of the Jews who bought and tortured Christ. A poem of notorious violence whose anti-Judaism reflects the worst of its age, and a major witness to the romance of Christian vengeance.
works.plot: Titus, healed by the vernicle, vows vengeance on the Jews; the poem narrates the siege and its horrors — the famine, the mother who eats her child, the crucifixions and selling of Jews — and the city's destruction, framed throughout as the working out of Christ's blood-debt.
works.significance: The most widely copied alliterative poem of its theme and a text of central importance — and difficulty — for the study of medieval Christian anti-Judaism in literature.
works.meter: Alliterative long lines in couplets and stanzaic clusters.
works.context: Composed c. 1390 in the north-west Midlands, from the French Vengeance de Nostre Seigneur and related sources; preserved in nine manuscripts, including the Thornton manuscript and Bodleian Laud Misc. 656.
works.characters: Vespasian; Titus; Pilate; Josephus; Caiaphas
works.structure: A single-movement siege narrative built from the French Vengeance tradition, with the torments of the Jews as its repeated set-pieces.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Siege of Thebes
works.form: verse narrative in couplets (framed as Canterbury tale)
works.description: John Lydgate's continuation of the Canterbury Tales (c. 1420–22), presented as the monk of Bury's own tale on the return journey from Canterbury: the story of Thebes from the founding of the city by Cadmus through the tragedy of Oedipus, the war of the Seven, and the deaths of the Theban and Argive heroes. Its frame makes it the first great poem of the Chaucerian succession.
works.plot: Joining the pilgrims at Canterbury, Lydgate's monk tells the Theban story: Oedipus's parricide and incest, the quarrel of his sons Eteocles and Polynices, the expedition of the Seven against Thebes, the duel of the brothers, and the funeral of the heroes — a chain of fortune's falls moralized throughout.
works.significance: The first great act of Chaucerian imitation: by writing himself into the pilgrimage, Lydgate claimed Chaucer's mantle and set the pattern for the fifteenth-century canon of English poetry.
works.meter: Decasyllabic couplets in the Lydgate manner.
works.context: Composed c. 1420–22, in direct response to Chaucer's Knight's Tale (the Theban matter of its background), and copied with the Canterbury Tales in many manuscripts; printed by Wynkyn de Worde (1497).
works.characters: the Monk of Bury (narrator); Oedipus; Eteocles; Polynices; Tydeus; Adrastus; Creon
works.structure: A Chaucerian frame (the return-journey tale) enclosing the three-part Theban narrative, with the 'tragedy' of Fortune as its moral armature.
works.attributionNotes: Lydgate's authorship secure.

works.title: The South English Legendary
works.description: The earliest great collection of verse saints' lives in Middle English, compiled in the south-west (probably Gloucestershire) c. 1270–85: a cycle of some 300 poems following the church year, from St Michael through the apostles and martyrs to All Souls. Its rollicking couplets and marvel-filled narratives made it the most popular legendary in medieval England.
works.plot: Each entry narrates a saint's life, martyrdom, or feast — with dragons, tortures, and miracles — and draws the moral for the hearers; the collection includes the famous account of St Brendan's voyage and lives of English saints such as Thomas Becket.
works.significance: The foundational text of popular English hagiography and a principal source for Mirk's Festial and the later legendary tradition.
works.meter: Septenary (fourteener) couplets, loose and lively, designed for public reading.
works.context: Compiled in the 1270s–1280s in the diocese of Worcester or Hereford, for parish and household reading; copied and expanded in some sixty manuscripts into the fifteenth century.
works.characters: the saints of the calendar (Thomas Becket, Brendan, Edmund, Cecilia, and many others)
works.structure: A calendrical cycle of independent verse legends, ordered by the liturgical year, in a frame of prologue and epilogue.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; compilational authorship by one or more clerical redactors.

works.title: The Supplication of Souls
works.description: More's defence of purgatory, written as the answer of the souls in purgatory to Simon Fish's Supplication for the Beggars (1529), which had demanded the dissolution of the monasteries and denounced purgatory as a clerical fiction.
works.plot: The souls of the dead speak in their own persons, showing from scripture and reason that purgatory exists, that prayers and masses for the dead avail them, and that those who deny purgatory rob both the dead and the living poor who depend on clerical charity.
works.significance: The most rhetorically inventive of More's early controversial works — using the fiction of the speaking dead — and a key document of the pre-Reformation debate on purgatory and monastic wealth.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Printed late in 1529 as a direct reply to Fish's Supplication for the Beggars, which Henry VIII is said to have shown to More; the exchange belongs to the parliamentary debates of the Reformation Parliament and the campaign against church wealth.
works.characters: The Souls in Purgatory
works.structure: A continuous oration in two books, framed as a supplication addressed to the king, lords, and commons, with the dead themselves as the petitioners.

works.title: The Temple of Glas
works.description: John Lydgate's early dream vision (1,403 lines in rhyme royal, c. 1400–05): the dreamer, enclosed in a glass temple of Venus, overhears the complaint of a lady bound by an unwanted marriage and the answering lament of her true lover, until the goddess unites them. The most accomplished of Lydgate's courtly poems and the first printed by Caxton.
works.plot: The dreamer finds himself before a temple of glass whose walls depict famous lovers; within, the lady laments her forced betrothal and the knight his despair; Venus, appealed to by both, grants them one another, and the dreamer wakes to write his vision for his own lady.
works.significance: The finest of Lydgate's courtly visions and a key text of the early Chaucerian tradition; its printing history marks the beginning of the English poetry market.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas with the early Lydgate line's characteristic fluency.
works.context: Composed c. 1400–05, early in Lydgate's career, perhaps for a marriage occasion; widely copied and printed — it was among the first poems Caxton printed at Westminster (1477).
works.characters: the Dreamer; the Lady; her Lover; Venus
works.structure: A courtly dream vision in the Chaucerian manner (House of Fame, Parliament of Fowls), with the double complaint as its centre.
works.attributionNotes: Lydgate's authorship secure (named in the envoy).

works.title: The Testament of Cresseid
works.description: Robert Henryson's great continuation of Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde (616 lines, c. 1475–90): the abandoned Cresseid, stricken with leprosy as judgement on her blasphemy against Venus and Cupid, meets the leper troop at the roadside and is recognized, too late, by Troilus, who cannot name her but casts her alms; she dies repentant, her testament a warning against the falsehood of love and fortune. The most powerful 'continuation' in English literature.
works.plot: The narrator, taking up 'ane uther quair' on the fate of Cresseid, tells how Diomede abandoned her; in her complaint she blasphemes Venus and Cupid, and the planetary court, convened by Saturn and Cynthia, condemns her to leprosy; in the lazar house she meets Troilus, who pities the unknown leper; learning the truth from the leper woman, she makes her testament, dies, and is buried under a tomb inscribed with her tragedy.
works.significance: Universally ranked among the great short tragedies of English literature; its compassion for Cresseid and its cosmic judgement scene make it the supreme Scottish response to Chaucer.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas of austere, compassionate power in Older Scots.
works.context: Composed c. 1475–90 in the Chaucerian tradition of the Scottish makars, answering Chaucer's Troilus with a Scottish judgement on its heroine; printed with Chaucer's works by Thynne (1532), where it long passed as Chaucer's own.
works.characters: Cresseid; Troilus; Diomede; Saturn; Cynthia; Venus; Cupid; the leper woman
works.structure: A five-movement tragedy (abandonment; blasphemy and judgement; leprosy; the roadside meeting; testament and death), closed by the narrator's warning to the women of the audience.
works.attributionNotes: Henryson's authorship secure (named in the manuscripts).

works.title: The Testament of the Papyngo
altTitles: The Testament and Complaynt of Our Soverane Lordis Papyngo
works.form: verse satire in the testament tradition
works.description: Lindsay's satire of court and church: the king's parrot, dying after a fall from the palace wall, makes her testament — leaving her heart to the king, her body to the courtiers, and her counsel to the clergy — and delivers a dying bird's-eye satire of the bishops, the court, and the vices of the age.
works.plot: The Papyngo, perched high on the palace wall, falls and dies; before death she disposes of her estate in a testament that satirizes each legatee in turn, closing with an epistle to the bishops on their duties.
works.significance: The wittiest of Lindsay's satires and a classic of the Scots complaint; its parrot looks back to Skelton's Speke Parrot and forward to the beast satires of the later century.
works.meter: Scots couplets and stanzas; the mock-legal diction of the testament handled with satirical point.
works.context: Written in 1530 as the Scottish church's wealth and the court's corruption became the subjects of Reformation debate; the parrot speaks with the licence of the dying.
works.characters: the Papyngo; James V (legatee); the courtiers; the bishops
works.structure: The testament form — the dying bird's will and last counsel — used as a vehicle for estates satire; mock-legal framework, satirical legacies, and a closing sermon.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Tretis of the Tua Mariit Wemen and the Wedo
altTitles: The Treatise of the Two Married Women and the Widow
works.description: William Dunbar's scandalous Midsummer Eve debate (c. 1500–07, 530 lines): the eavesdropping poet overhears three women — two wives and a widow — exchanging frank confidences on marriage, their husbands' inadequacies, and the arts of deceiving them, in the most sustained exhibition of female licence (and male ventriloquism) in medieval English verse. The most brilliant of Dunbar's alliterative poems.
works.plot: Hidden in the hedge on a June night, the narrator hears the first wife anatomize her husband's age, impotence, and jealousy, the second mock hers as a coward and braggart, and the widow — dismissing both as amateurs — advise on choosing, managing, and surviving husbands, until the dawn and the lark's song end the colloquy.
works.significance: The supreme comic-satiric poem of the Scottish tradition: its frankness and metrical brilliance made it a scandal in its own day and a touchstone of medieval misogyny debate in ours.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line in Dunbar's hands — colloquial, obscene, and metrically audacious.
works.context: Composed c. 1500–07 at the court of James IV, in the makars' revival of alliterative verse; printed by Chepman and Myllar (1508) and preserved in the Bannatyne manuscript.
works.characters: the narrator (Dunbar); the two married women; the widow
works.structure: A debate-frame of three long monologues, each more outrageous than the last, in the tradition of the débat and the Wife of Bath's prologue.
works.attributionNotes: Dunbar's authorship secure.

works.title: The Tunning of Elinour Rumming
works.description: Skelton's carnivalesque masterpiece: a Skeltonic account of the alewife Elinour Rumming of Leatherhead and the procession of women who come to drink her noxious ale, a low-life gallery from drunken Alice to the beggarly Maud Ruggy — ugliness, appetite, and disorder rendered with gleeful verbal energy.
works.plot: The poem describes Elinour's brewing and her customers in turn — their poverty, their lechery, their brawling — as the alehouse degenerates into a riot of appetite without plot or moral.
works.significance: The most vivid low-life poem in English before the eighteenth century; its catalogue form and demotic energy made it a model for later satire.
works.meter: The Skeltonic at its most anarchic — breathless rhymes, macaronic puns, and tavern speech.
works.context: Set at Leatherhead in Surrey; the poem belongs to the alehouse satire of the early sixteenth century and reflects the moralists' anxieties about disorderly women.
works.characters: Elinour Rumming; her customers (drunken Alice, Maud Ruggy, and others)
works.structure: A catalogue or procession of drinkers, framed by the description of the brewing; no plot, but a mounting carnival intensity.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: John Skelton: The Complete English Poems

works.title: The Two Ways
altTitles: The Boke of the Two Ways
works.description: Sir John Clanvowe's devotional prose tract on the two ways of life and death — the narrow way of virtue and the broad way of the world — a Lollard-leaning meditation written in the circle of the 'Lollard knights' of Richard II's court, probably in 1391. It is the earliest prose work of the English reforming tradition by a lay courtier.
works.plot: The tract expounds Christ's teaching of the two ways, contrasts the few who walk the narrow path with the many on the broad road to perdition, and anatomizes the sins of the world — pride, avarice, gluttony — with a particular Lollard sharpness against clerical wealth and display.
works.significance: A principal document of the Lollard sensibility among the courtly elite and the earliest lay devotional prose of the Ricardian court.
works.meter: Plain, earnest prose with scriptural quotation.
works.context: Composed c. 1391 by the courtier-knight Clanvowe (d. October 1391), in the company of the Lollard knights at the court of Richard II; preserved in Bodleian MS Eng. th. c. 39 and later copies.
works.characters: the writer (as penitent teacher)
works.structure: A single homiletic meditation organized by the scriptural image of the two ways, with catalogue of sins and exhortation.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Clanvowe in the manuscripts.

editions.title: The Works of Sir John Clanvowe

works.title: The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York
altTitles: The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancastre and Yorke
works.description: Edward Hall's chronicle of the Wars of the Roses and the triumph of the house of Tudor, from the deposition of Richard II to the death of Henry VIII; printed posthumously by Richard Grafton in 1548 and continued by Grafton in later editions.
works.plot: Hall narrates the dynastic strife between Lancaster and York as a providential drama culminating in the union of the two houses in Henry VIII, with long set-piece speeches and a moralizing emphasis on the ruin brought by ambition, faction, and rebellion; the reign of Henry VIII occupies the final section ('The Triumphant Reign of King Henry the VIII').
works.significance: The principal source of Shakespeare's English history plays (the second tetralogy follows Hall closely) and the classic statement of the Tudor myth of union and providential kingship; its dramatic speeches made it the most literary of the Tudor chronicles.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Compiled over the 1530s and 1540s by Hall, a lawyer and MP, drawing on More's Richard III, Polydore Vergil, and Fabyan; the 1548 edition was supervised by Grafton, who added continuations in the editions of 1550.
works.characters: Henry IV; Henry V; Henry VI; Edward IV; Richard III; Henry VII; Henry VIII; Cardinal Wolsey
works.structure: Chronicle divided by reigns, from Richard II through Henry VIII, framed by a preface on the theme of union and enriched with speeches invented in the manner of classical historiography.

works.title: The Vision of Leofric
altTitles: The Old English Vision of Leofric, Earl of Mercia
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 367, part II (eleventh century)
works.description: An Old English account of four visions granted to Leofric, earl of Mercia (d. 1057), written soon after his death: a vision of the cross and the hand of God during a mass at St Mary's, a miraculous vision through the mist at Wednesbury, a visit to the shrine of St Peter in Rome, and a vision of the soul's judgment at Christ Church, Canterbury. It is the earliest vernacular prose vision narrative in English.
works.plot: The text narrates Leofric's visionary experiences in order: at mass he sees the cross of light and God's hand blessing the congregation; at Wednesbury the mist parts to reveal the church as God sees it, with Leofric guided by a mysterious companion; in Rome he kneels before St Peter; and at Canterbury he witnesses a dying man's soul weighed in judgment and rescued by the saints through Leofric's intercession.
works.significance: The earliest surviving prose vision narrative in English, anticipating the great medieval genre of Piers Plowman and the Pearl-poet, and a precious first-person witness to eleventh-century English devotional practice.
works.context: Written in the Confessor's reign by a writer close to Leofric's household, the text documents the piety of the last great Old English earl and the penitential spirituality of the eleventh-century church on the eve of the Conquest; it is contemporary with the earliest continental prose visions that shaped later medieval vision literature.
works.characters: Earl Leofric, the mysterious guide, St Peter
works.structure: Four discrete vision episodes in chronological order, each grounded in named places and dates and framed by Leofric's devout response; the Wednesbury and Canterbury visions are developed at length, the others briefly.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the author writes from within Leofric's circle and is otherwise unknown.

works.title: The Wallace
altTitles: The Acts and Deeds of Sir William Wallace
works.description: Blind Hary's epic life of William Wallace, composed c. 1477 in some 11,800 lines: the hero's outlawry after the killing of Selkirk's sheriff, his battles against the English — Stirling Bridge, the invasion of England, Falkirk — his betrayal and execution at London (1305), and his posthumous vindication. For four centuries it was, after the Bible, the most read book in Scotland, and it fixed Wallace in the national memory.
works.plot: Wallace, driven to outlawry by English oppression, gathers his men, defeats the English at Stirling Bridge, harries England as far as York, and is named guardian of Scotland; betrayed at Falkirk and by the treachery of Menteith, he is taken to London, tried as a traitor to a king he never acknowledged, and executed — his dismembered body displayed, his fame immortal.
works.significance: The great popular epic of Scotland: its Wallace shaped the national hero for five centuries, and its influence on Burns and the romantic revival of Scottish identity is incalculable.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in Older Scots, declamatory and rapid.
works.context: Composed c. 1477 by Blind Hary, who recited it before James IV for payment, drawing on John Blair's lost Latin life and oral tradition; printed by Chepman and Myllar (c. 1508) and endlessly reprinted — Burns acknowledged it as his first poetic inspiration.
works.characters: William Wallace; Edward I; Menteith; Graham; Bruce (epilogue)
works.structure: Twelve books of epic narrative, from outlawry through triumph to martyrdom, in the minstrel chronicle manner, with the poet's appeals to his audience throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Blind Hary (Henry the Minstrel) by the poem and the treasurer's accounts.

works.title: The Wanderer
works.description: An elegy of 115 lines in which a solitary exile, deprived of lord and hall, meditates on the transience of earthly joy and arrives at a hard-won Christian consolation. One of the most admired poems in the Exeter Book and the supreme statement of the Old English ubi sunt theme.
works.plot: The speaker, an 'eardstapa' (earth-stepper) wandering the frozen seas since the death of his lord, remembers the lost joys of the hall and laments the ruin of the world's splendour ('Where is the horse? Where is the young warrior?'); the poem closes with the famous gnomic consolation that a wise man keeps faith and seeks mercy from the Father in heaven, where all stability dwells.
works.significance: The classic Old English elegy; a locus classicus for the ubi sunt topos and for the Christian reframing of the heroic ethos.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre with the formulaic diction of the heroic tradition, turned to meditative ends.
works.context: Preserved only in the Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 76v-78r), a late tenth-century anthology; the poem's heroic nostalgia is often read against the upheavals of the Viking age, though its date of composition is unknown.
works.characters: the Wanderer (speaker); the lost lord
works.structure: A movement from personal lament through the ubi sunt catalogue of vanished glories to a generalizing wisdom passage and a prayerful conclusion; framed by the figure of the wise man who speaks little and reflects much.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
movements: Early Anglo-Latin Learning and the Northumbrian Golden Age
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Old English Literature, 2nd edition

works.title: The Wedding of Sir Gawain and Dame Ragnelle
altTitles: The Weddynge of Sir Gawen and Dame Ragnell
works.description: A fifteenth-century Arthurian romance on the loathly lady theme: to save Arthur's life, Gawain marries the hideous Dame Ragnelle, who holds the answer to the riddle 'what women most desire' — sovereignty — and his courtesy at the wedding night transforms her into a beauty. The wittiest of the Gawain romances and the source of the Wife of Bath's Tale's plot.
works.plot: Arthur, challenged by Sir Gromer Somer Joure, must learn what women most desire; Ragnelle supplies the answer (sovereignty) in exchange for Gawain's hand; Gawain's free gift of choice on the wedding night breaks the enchantment, making Ragnelle fair by day and night, and the two live happily until her death.
works.significance: The most entertaining of the late Gawain romances and the fullest English statement of the 'sovereignty' motif central to late medieval debates on marriage.
works.meter: Six-line tail-rhyme stanzas with comic energy.
works.context: Composed c. 1450 in the East Midlands; preserved uniquely in Bodleian Library, Rawlinson MS C.86 (c. 1500); the loathly lady plot derives from Irish and English folk tradition (and parallels Chaucer's Wife of Bath's Tale).
works.characters: Gawain; Dame Ragnelle; Arthur; Sir Gromer Somer Joure
works.structure: A riddle-romance in two movements (the quest for the answer; the marriage and its testing), resolved by the courtesy test.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The West-Saxon Gospels
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, University Library Ii.2.11 (c. 1075) and five other copies including Oxford, Bodleian Library, Bodley 441 and Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 140
works.description: An anonymous translation of the four gospels into late West Saxon, made in the last decade of the tenth century, probably in the south-west of England. It is the first complete translation of the gospels into English and circulated widely, with six surviving manuscripts and copies reaching into the twelfth century.
works.plot: The translation renders Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John continuously, in a plain, literal but idiomatic Old English prose that follows the Vulgate closely while producing natural vernacular sentences.
works.significance: The first complete English translation of the gospels, the ancestor of the Wycliffite and later English bibles, and a cornerstone of the Old English prose corpus studied by every student of the language.
works.context: Produced in the aftermath of the Benedictine Reform, when vernacular preaching and reading were encouraged; Ælfric's biblical translations belong to the same movement, and the gospels' circulation shows the demand for scripture in English among clergy and laity alike.
works.characters: Christ, the apostles, Mary, John the Baptist, Pilate
works.structure: Four continuous gospel narratives in traditional order, with chapter divisions supplied in the manuscripts; the translation is a continuous prose version without glossing apparatus.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. No convincing attribution has been proposed; the language is late West Saxon with south-western features.

editions.title: The Old English Version of the Gospels
editions.publisher: Early English Text Society (Oxford University Press)

works.title: The Whale
works.description: A poem of 89 lines on the legend of the whale (Fastitocalon) that lies like an island: sailors moor to it, light fires, and are dragged down when the beast dives. The poem reads it as an allegory of the devil, who lures sinners with the appearance of safety and plunges them into hell.
works.plot: Mariners mistake the whale's back for an island, anchor and kindle fires; when the creature senses the heat it dives, drowning the crew. The allegory applies the story to the devil, whose deceptive promises — the sweet sins that seem secure ground — drag the unwary soul into the abyss.
works.significance: The earliest English version of the whale-island legend, later famous in the Navigatio Sancti Brendani and Mandeville; a vivid allegory of temptation.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book with The Panther and The Partridge.
works.characters: the Whale (Fastitocalon; the devil); the mariners (sinners)
works.structure: Narrative exemplum followed by allegorical application, in the Physiologus manner.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Wife's Lament
works.description: An elegy of 53 lines, unique in the corpus for its sustained female voice: a woman separated from her lord laments her exile in an earth-cave beneath an oak tree and curses the man responsible for her misery.
works.plot: The speaker tells how her lord departed over the sea, how his kin plotted against them, and how she was banished to a desolate dwelling in the wilderness, where she sits weeping through the long days; she ends by wishing upon her beloved the sorrow of one who sits apart, remembering a happier home.
works.significance: The first sustained female voice in English poetry and a key text for feminist criticism of the period.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; unusually personal and passionate diction.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; the poem has been read as autobiography, as allegory (the Church or the soul lamenting Christ), and as a riddle-like exercise — a famous crux of Old English scholarship.
works.characters: the Wife (speaker); the absent lord
works.structure: A first-person lament moving from past happiness through separation and exile to a bitter wish against the absent beloved; the obscurity of the situation (which lord, which feud) is itself part of the poem's design.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
