themes: The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
sources: The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition

works.title: The Wonders of the East
works.form: travel and wonders literature in Old English prose
works.description: The Old English catalogue of the marvels of the East, preserved in the Nowell Codex beside Beowulf and illustrated with vivid drawings: dog-headed men, giants, serpents, the phoenix's nest, the hens that burn men, and the gold-guarding ants of Gorgoneus — the fantastic geography of the age compiled for an English audience.
works.plot: The text proceeds place by place through the wonders of Egypt and the East — the two-headed beasts, the monoculi, the cynocephali, the generous king of the Hostes, the locusts and dragons of the desert — describing each marvel's appearance and habits, with the famous closing account of the gold-digging ants as large as dogs.
works.significance: The fullest English witness to the medieval geography of marvels and to the monstrous races that haunted the period's imagination.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Translated from a Latin original (itself from the Epistola Alexandri tradition) in the late tenth or early eleventh century; preserved in the Nowell Codex (British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv), the Beowulf manuscript, and in Cotton MS Tiberius B.v.
works.characters: the monstrous races and beasts of the East
works.structure: A catalogue of marvels organized by region, each entry a short description.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: The Wooing of Our Lord
altTitles: On Wel Swuðe God Ureisun of God Almihti
works.description: A group of lyrical prose meditations on the love of Christ, in the AB language: the Wooing of Our Lord, On Ureisun of Ure Louerde, On Lofsong of Ure Louerde, and related prayers. Addressed to a female recluse, they figure Christ as a knightly wooer whose love and Passion the anchoress must return, in prose of extraordinary affective intensity.
works.plot: The speaker addresses Christ as lover and spouse, meditating on his beauty, his suffering on the cross, and the soul's answering love, weaving prayer, praise, and erotic-spiritual longing into a single meditation.
works.significance: The earliest English expression of the bride-mysticism and Passion devotion that culminate in Rolle, Julian, and the lyrics; a landmark of affective prose.
works.meter: Rhythmical, alliterative, incantatory prose with lyric repetitions and refrains.
works.context: Composed in the early thirteenth-century West Midlands for a woman recluse, in the same milieu as Ancrene Wisse; preserved in BL Cotton MS Nero A.xiv and Titus D.xviii.
works.characters: Christ as wooer; the anchoress speaker
works.structure: A sequence of meditative addresses, each moving from invocation through Passion meditation to petition.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Tottel's Miscellany
altTitles: Songes and Sonettes, written by the ryght honorable Lorde Henry Haward late Earle of Surrey, and other
works.form: anthology of sonnets, lyrics, and epigrams
works.description: The first great printed anthology of English poetry: 271 poems by Surrey, Wyatt, Nicholas Grimald, and other courtly poets, published by Richard Tottel on 5 June 1557 under the title Songes and Sonettes. It fixed the public canon of the Henrician lyric and went through nine editions by 1587.
works.plot: An anthology without narrative frame: sonnets, songs, elegies, and epigrams arranged by author, beginning with Surrey, whose name gave the volume its selling title.
works.significance: The founding anthology of English poetry: it created the reading public for the lyric, fixed the reputations of Wyatt and Surrey, and supplied the Elizabethan poets with their metre and manner.
works.meter: The full range of the early Tudor lyric: sonnets, poulter's measure, short-line songs; the anthology standardized the decasyllabic line for a public audience.
works.context: Printed two years after the Marian restoration began; the miscellany carried the Henrician court's poetry into the Elizabethan age and made the court lyric a national possession.
works.characters: the courtly poets (Surrey, Wyatt, Grimald, and others)
works.structure: Miscellany organized by poet, with the Earl of Surrey's poems first; the arrangement itself constitutes the first printed history of the English lyric.
works.attributionNotes: Compiled by Richard Tottel (publisher); the authorship of the 'uncertain authors' poems remains largely unknown. Recorded as collaborative with no author links, per the validator's anonymity rule.

works.title: Towneley Plays
works.description: The Towneley (Wakefield) cycle of thirty-two plays, from the Creation to the Last Judgement, preserved in the Towneley manuscript (c. 1500) and long associated with Wakefield: famous above all for the six plays in the nine-line 'Wakefield stanza' attributed to the Wakefield Master — including the Second Shepherds' Play, the comic masterpiece of the English cycles, with its sheep-stealing Mak and its nativity of the stolen lamb.
works.plot: The cycle retells salvation history from Lucifer's fall through the patriarchs to Christ's Passion and the Judgement; the Master's plays — Noah and his scolding wife, the two Shepherds' plays, Herod, and the Buffeting — transform the biblical matter with a vernacular comedy of Yorkshire shepherds, shrews, and ranting tyrants unmatched in the other cycles.
works.significance: The Second Shepherds' Play is the most famous English medieval drama: the cycle's blend of farce and nativity embodies the mystery tradition at its theatrical summit.
works.meter: The unique nine-line 'Wakefield stanza' (aabcccbddb with internal rhyme) in the Master's plays; thirteen-line stanza and couplets elsewhere.
works.context: Composed and compiled c. 1400–1500, probably at Wakefield, where the plays were performed on Corpus Christi day; the manuscript (Huntington Library, MS HM 1) belonged to the Towneley family of Lancashire, from which the cycle takes its name.
works.characters: Mak the sheep-stealer; Gill; the shepherds (Coll, Gib, Daw); Noah and his wife; Herod; Christ; Pilate
works.structure: A pageant cycle of thirty-two plays, partially dependent on York but transformed by the Wakefield Master's comic and homiletic genius.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative; the 'Wakefield Master' is a scholarly construct for the author of the six stanza-linked plays.

editions.title: The Towneley Plays
editions.editor: Martin Stevens and A. C. Cawley (eds.)

works.title: Toxophilus
works.description: Ascham's dialogue on the art of archery, presented to Henry VIII as both a practical treatise and a model of English prose style — the first book on a sport written in the English language.
works.plot: Two speakers, Toxophilus ('lover of the bow') and Philologus ('lover of learning'), debate whether study or shooting better befits a gentleman; Toxophilus vindicates archery as recreation, describes the bow, its parts, and the craft of shooting, and argues for the health and military value of the sport, while the dialogue itself demonstrates the eloquence the English tongue can achieve.
works.significance: The first English treatise on a sport and a deliberate demonstration of the capacities of English prose for learned subjects; together with The Schoolmaster it established Ascham's reputation as a stylist and educational theorist.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written 1544–45 when Ascham was reader in Greek at St John's College, Cambridge, and presented to Henry VIII in 1545 in the royal library at Westminster, for which Ascham received a pension; archery's military role had been reaffirmed by statute in 1541.
works.characters: Toxophilus; Philologus
works.structure: Two-book dialogue framed by a preface to 'all gentle men and yeomen of England', with a systematic technical exposition embedded in the conversational form.

works.title: Treatise on the Astrolabe
works.description: Chaucer's prose treatise on the construction and use of the astrolabe, written in 1391 for his ten-year-old son Lewis: the first technical treatise in English prose, and the earliest English work on a scientific instrument. Its precision, clarity, and fatherly address make it unique in the medieval English canon.
works.plot: In five planned parts — of which the first two and a supplement survive — the treatise describes the astrolabe and its parts, teaches the child to take altitudes and tell the time, and promises the tables and theories that would complete the work; the famous prologue addresses 'Lyte Lowys my sone' with pedagogical tenderness.
works.significance: The first scientific prose in English and the classic of its kind: the treatise's plain style is a landmark in the development of English as a language of learning.
works.meter: Prose: plain, exact, and carefully ordered, in the tradition of the practical manual.
works.context: Dated 1391 in the prologue, written for Lewis Chaucer, then about ten years old, in London; it draws on the Latin tradition of Messahala and the practical astronomy of the universities; preserved in some thirty manuscripts.
works.characters: the author (as father-teacher); Lewis (addressee)
works.structure: A didactic treatise of definitions, propositions, and conclusions, each numbered for the child's use, with worked examples from the Oxford latitude.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure (named in the prologue).

editions.title: A Treatise on the Astrolabe (A Variorum Edition of the Works of Geoffrey Chaucer, vol. VI)

works.title: Troilus and Criseyde
works.description: Chaucer's great poem of love and loss, some 8,200 lines in rhyme royal, translating and transforming Boccaccio's Il Filostrato: the Trojan prince Troilus, aided by Pandarus, wins the love of Criseyde, loses her to the Greek camp in an exchange of prisoners, and learns of her betrayal with Diomede before his death in battle — all concluded by the narrator's Boethian repudiation of worldly love. The greatest love poem in Middle English.
works.plot: Troilus, scorning love, is struck by Criseyde's beauty in the temple; his friend and uncle Pandarus engineers their union through letters and stratagems, and the lovers enjoy a secret happiness — until Criseyde is exchanged for the prisoner Antenor and sent to the Greek camp, where Diomede courts her and she yields; Troilus, after ominous dreams and the sight of the brooch he gave her on Diomede's armour, seeks death in battle, and his soul ascends to the eighth sphere, laughing at the woe of the world below.
works.significance: The greatest narrative poem of the English Middle Ages after the Canterbury Tales; its psychological depth and tragic irony made it the model for Henryson's Testament of Cresseid and the ancestor of Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas (seven-line, ababbcc) handled with supreme flexibility; the first sustained masterpiece of the English decasyllabic line.
works.context: Composed c. 1382–86 in London, after Chaucer's Italian journeys, adapting Boccaccio's Filostrato with additions from Boethius, Dante, and the Trojan romances; dedicated to 'moral Gower and philosophical Strode'; preserved in sixteen manuscripts and printed by Caxton (c. 1483).
works.characters: Troilus; Criseyde; Pandarus; Diomede; Hector; the Narrator
works.structure: Five books moving from courtship through consummation to betrayal and death, framed by the narrator's ironic service to the servants of love and closed by the palinode commending the love of God.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure; the work is the first he names in the Retraction.

editions.title: Troilus and Criseyde: A New Edition of 'The Book of Troilus'

works.title: Troy Book
works.description: John Lydgate's vast verse translation (over 30,000 lines) of Guido delle Colonne's Historia destructionis Troiae, commissioned by Henry V in 1412 and completed in 1420: the full Trojan story retold as a mirror of chivalry, kingship, and tragedy. The most ambitious poem of the fifteenth century and the foundation of Lydgate's fame.
works.plot: From Jason and the golden fleece through the rape of Helen and the ten years' war to the fall of Troy and the wanderings of the Greeks, the poem recounts the Trojan matter at length, moralizing throughout on pride, treason, and the fickleness of fortune, with Hector as its pattern of knighthood.
works.significance: The fullest English Troy narrative and the great monument of Lancastrian literary patronage; it made Lydgate the laureate of the fifteenth century and fed the Tudor cult of Troy.
works.meter: Decasyllabic couplets in the 'Lydgate line', frequently headless, with aureate diction.
works.context: Commissioned by Henry, Prince of Wales, in 1412, completed in 1420, and dedicated to the king after Agincourt; its Troy matter spoke to Lancastrian imperial ambition; printed by Pynson (1513) and widely read into the sixteenth century.
works.characters: Hector; Achilles; Priam; Paris; Helen; Troilus; Ulysses; Agamemnon
works.structure: Five books following Guido's divisions, with prologue and envoy to Henry V; set-piece descriptions, speeches, and moral digressions throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Lydgate's authorship secure.

works.title: Twelve Conclusions of the Lollards
works.description: The Lollard manifesto of 1395, presented to parliament and nailed to the doors of Westminster Hall and St Paul's during its session: twelve conclusions denouncing the church's temporal lordship, clerical celibacy, transubstantiation, blessing of material things, clerical exemption, and the wars, crafts, and oaths by which the clergy sustain their power. The most famous document of English medieval dissent.
works.plot: The conclusions move from the church's worldly dominion and the clergy's unworthy estate through the 'false miracle of the sacrament' to the 'unnecessary trades' (goldsmiths, armourers) that serve the church's pride, closing with the demand for a poor, preaching clergy and the renunciation of war and oaths.
works.significance: The founding manifesto of English religious dissent: its arguments against images, pilgrimage, and transubstantiation anticipate the Reformation by a century and a quarter.
works.meter: Plain, forceful English with Latin tags, in the Lollard plain style.
works.context: Presented to parliament and posted at Westminster and St Paul's in 1395, in the political crisis of Richard II's reign; it provoked the orthodox counter-writings of Roger Dymmok and others and fixed the public image of Lollardy.
works.characters: none (collective manifesto)
works.structure: Twelve numbered propositions, each with its brief scriptural and logical support, in the petitionary form of a parliamentary bill.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous (collective authorship in the Wycliffite movement).

works.title: Utopia
altTitles: Libellus vere aureus, nec minus salutaris quam festivus, de optimo rei publicae statu deque nova insula Utopia
works.description: A humanist dialogue in two books describing the imaginary island commonwealth of Utopia, where property is held in common, religious toleration prevails, and the social and economic abuses of early sixteenth-century Europe are criticized by contrast.
works.plot: Book I frames the work as a report of a conversation in Antwerp among More himself, his friend Peter Giles, and the fictional traveller Raphael Hythlodaeus, who denounces the social evils of Europe — enclosure, penal severity, court flattery — and debates whether a philosopher should serve princes. Book II contains Hythlodaeus's full description of Utopia: its geography, magistrates, working day, communal property, marriage customs, education, religion, and warfare.
works.significance: The founding text of the utopian genre and one of the masterpieces of northern humanism; its punning title (ou-topia 'no place' / eu-topia 'good place') and its fusion of satire, political theory, and fiction made it the most influential secular prose work of the English Renaissance, directly shaping works from Bacon's New Atlantis to modern dystopian fiction.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Composed in 1515–16 during More's embassy to the Netherlands for the wool trade negotiations, at the height of his humanist circle's activities; printed at Louvain by Thierry Martens under the supervision of Erasmus, Giles, and others, and translated into English by Ralph Robinson in 1551.
works.characters: Thomas More; Peter Giles; Raphael Hythlodaeus; Cardinal John Morton (recalled in the dialogue)
works.structure: Two-part dialogue framed by a prefatory letter to Peter Giles and paratexts (maps, Utopian alphabet and quatrain); Book I is a debate on counsel, Book II a systematic description of the island, with the whole enclosed in the fiction of Hythlodaeus's eyewitness report.

editions.title: Utopia (The Yale Edition of the Complete Works of St. Thomas More, vol. 4)
editions.editor: Edward Surtz, S.J., and J. H. Hexter

works.title: Vainglory
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A moralizing poem of 84 lines contrasting the boastful man, puffed up with wine and pride in the hall, with the wise man who walks humbly before God. The poem analyses the psychology of vainglory and warns that pride corrupts the soul and courts the devil.
works.plot: The poet describes the vainglorious man at the feast, eloquent in self-praise but hollow within, deceived by the devil's arrows of pride; against him is set the wise man of measured speech and right counsel, whom God rewards. The poem closes with the warning that the proud man's fall is certain.
works.significance: A penetrating psychological study of pride that fuses the wisdom and homiletic traditions, and a vivid picture of the moral dangers of the Anglo-Saxon feast-hall.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with the homiletic diction of the Exeter religious poems; the hall setting is evoked in the heroic vocabulary of feasting and treasure.
works.context: Pride was the sin of the heroic hall culture, and the poem turns the imagery of the feast and the boast against its own social setting, in the manner of the homilists' attacks on drunkenness and vainglory.
works.structure: A diptych structure: parallel portraits of the proud man and the wise man, developed through antithesis, followed by a homiletic conclusion on the wages of pride.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Vercelli Homilies
works.description: A collection of twenty-three anonymous Old English homilies and six poems (including The Dream of the Rood, Andreas, Elene) preserved in the Vercelli Book: the largest body of anonymous late tenth-century vernacular preaching, notable for its intense eschatological themes, penitential fervour, and vivid accounts of judgment and the afterlife.
works.plot: The homilies treat repentance, judgment, and the last things — the coming of Antichrist, the signs before doomsday, the fate of the soul, the joys of heaven and the torments of hell — together with Rogationtide sermons, expositions of the Creed and Lord's Prayer, and saints' day pieces, several drawing on the same apocryphal sources as the Blickling collection.
works.significance: A central witness to the anonymous homiletic tradition of the Benedictine Reform era.
works.meter: Old English prose of the late tenth-century homiletic register.
works.context: Copied in the late tenth century, probably in the south-east; the manuscript's presence at Vercelli (northern Italy) is usually attributed to pilgrims on the Rome road.
works.characters: Christ the Judge; the penitent; the blessed and the damned
works.structure: Twenty-three independent homilies of varying length, interspersed with the six poems of the manuscript.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Humanist education and the ideal commonwealth

works.title: Vita Sancti Cuthberti (metrical and prose lives)
works.form: hagiography (saint's life) in Latin verse and prose
works.description: Bede's two lives of St Cuthbert: a metrical life (c. 705) and a prose life (c. 721), the latter revised and expanded from the earlier anonymous Life by a monk of Lindisfarne. They are the fullest early accounts of the great Northumbrian hermit-bishop of Lindisfarne and a classic of insular hagiography.
works.plot: The lives trace Cuthbert's youth, his vision of the soul of Aidan, his years as prior of Melrose and Lindisfarne, his eremitic retreat on Farne, and his reluctant episcopate, with the famous miracle stories (the otters who warmed his feet, the sea that served him food) and the account of his incorrupt body at the translation of 698.
works.significance: The canonical life of the Northumbrian church's greatest saint; a model for later insular hagiography.
works.meter: The metrical life is in Latin hexameters; the prose life in Bede's clear narrative Latin.
works.context: Composed at Wearmouth-Jarrow for the community of Lindisfarne; the prose life was written after the translation of Cuthbert's relics in 698.
works.characters: Cuthbert; Aidan; Boisil; Æthelthryth; King Ecgfrith; the monks of Lindisfarne
works.structure: Biographical narrative ordered by the saint's successive vocations, with miracle collections attached to each phase; the prose life adds chapters on posthumous miracles at the shrine.
works.attributionNotes: Bede's authorship is certain.
sources: English Historical Documents, Volume III: 1189–1327

works.title: Vita Sancti Gregorii
altTitles: The Earliest Life of St Gregory the Great
The Whitby Life of Gregory the Great
works.description: The earliest life of Pope Gregory the Great, written at Whitby in the early eighth century by an anonymous monk of the double house, and a principal source for the story of Gregory's encounter with the Anglian slave-boys in the Roman market — 'not Angles but angels' — that led to the mission of Augustine to England in 597.
works.plot: The Life recounts Gregory's Roman background, his election to the papacy against his will, the providential encounter with the English boys that inspired the English mission, the sending of Augustine and his companions, and the miracles that confirmed the mission's success; it closes with Gregory's death and the vindication of his authority.
works.significance: The earliest biography of the pope who sent the mission that converted the English, the source of the 'non Angli sed angeli' story that became part of English national legend, and a witness to the piety of the Whitby community of the early eighth century.
works.context: Written at Whitby under Abbess Ælfflæd, the text defends the Roman and Gregorian foundations of the English church at a time when the authority of Rome was disputed in Northumbria; it preserves traditions of the conversion not found in Bede's Historia ecclesiastica.
works.characters: Gregory the Great, the Anglian slave-boys, Augustine of Canterbury, King Edwin of Northumbria
works.structure: A loosely organized collection of episodes rather than a strictly chronological biography, mingling Roman history, English conversion narrative, and edifying miracles, written in the unpolished Latin of a remote Northumbrian house.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the author is conventionally called the Anonymous of Whitby. No author record is created for this work, per the database's policy that anonymous works carry no author links.

editions.title: The Earliest Life of Gregory the Great

works.title: Vita Sancti Guthlaci
works.description: Felix of Crowland's prose life of Guthlac, the Mercian warrior turned hermit of the fens, composed at the request of King Ælfwald of East Anglia. The first Latin saint's life written in England for an English saint, and the source of the Old English poems Guthlac A and B and of the later vernacular lives.
works.plot: The life narrates Guthlac's youth in the Mercian warband, his conversion after nine years of warfare, his two years at Repton, and his retreat to the island of Crowland in the fens, where he fought with demons, was consoled by the apostle Bartholomew, and died in 714; the second book records posthumous miracles, including the healing of King Æthelbald.
works.significance: The foundational text of the Guthlac tradition and a major witness to eighth-century monastic culture.
works.meter: Latin prose.
works.context: Written c. 730-740, within a generation of Guthlac's death (714), for the East Anglian court; the cult centred on Crowland Abbey, refounded in the tenth century.
works.characters: Guthlac; Bartholomew; Æthelbald; Ælfwald; Beccel; Pega; the fen demons
works.structure: Two books — the saint's life and his posthumous miracles — in the pattern of the Antonine and Martinian lives.
works.attributionNotes: Felix's authorship is stated in the prologue.
sources: The Cambridge History of Early Modern English Literature

works.title: Vita Sancti Wilfridi
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Vespasian D.vi (ninth century, with later additions)
works.description: The earliest surviving biography written in England of a contemporary English churchman: a partisan life of Bishop Wilfrid of York (c. 634-709) by Stephen of Ripon, a priest of Wilfrid's household, written at the request of Acca of Hexham and Tatberht of Ripon. It defends Wilfrid's career — his appeals to Rome, his quarrels with kings and bishops, and his missionary work — against his detractors.
works.plot: The Life follows Wilfrid from his education at Lindisfarne and his journeys to Rome and Gaul, through his consecration and his building of the stone churches of Ripon and Hexham, to his repeated exiles, his missionary work among the South Saxons and Frisians, his vindication at Rome, and his death at Oundle in 709, with posthumous miracles at Ripon.
works.significance: A principal source for the seventh-century Northumbrian church and for the career of its most controversial bishop; with the anonymous life of Cuthbert it inaugurates the English tradition of the contemporary saint's life that culminates in Bede's hagiography.
works.context: Written within a decade of Wilfrid's death amid continuing controversy over his legacy; the Life is a contribution to that controversy, answering the charges of Wilfrid's enemies and presenting him as a persecuted saint in the manner of the confessors of the early church.
works.characters: Wilfrid of York, King Ecgfrith, King Aldfrith, Archbishop Theodore, Acca of Hexham
works.structure: A chronological vita in the hagiographic manner, interweaving documented events (the synods, the appeals to Rome) with miracle stories; the narrative is punctuated by set-piece scenes — the shipwreck of Wilfrid's party on the Sussex coast, his baptisms, and his deathbed settlement of his affairs.
works.attributionNotes: Securely attributed to Stephen of Ripon (Eddius Stephanus), who names himself; his identification with Bede's 'Æddi' is traditional but unproven.

editions.title: The Life of Bishop Wilfrid by Eddius Stephanus

works.title: Vox Clamantis
works.description: John Gower's Latin poem of some 10,000 elegiac couplets: an estates satire and dream vision in which the poet, during the Peasants' Revolt of 1381, sees the commons transformed into beasts and the social order inverted, then hears the estates — clergy, knights, peasants, merchants, lawyers — arraigned for their corruption. The great Latin poem of Ricardian England.
works.plot: The first book (the Visio) allegorizes the 1381 rising as a bestial horde under Wat Tyler and Jack Straw ravaging the land; the remaining books survey each estate in turn, condemning clerical greed, knightly violence, peasant envy, and mercantile fraud, and close with a vision of the king (Richard II) as the realm's hope.
works.significance: The most substantial Latin poem of fourteenth-century England and the classic estates satire of the Ricardian period; its account of the revolt is the age's defining literary image of 1381.
works.meter: Ovidian elegiac couplets, sustained with remarkable facility.
works.context: Composed 1377–81, with the Visio added after the revolt of June 1381 (which Gower probably witnessed in London); revised in the 1390s; preserved in ten manuscripts, several with Gower's own annotations.
works.characters: the Poet; the rebels (as beasts); the estates of society; Richard II
works.structure: Seven books: a dream-vision prologue on the revolt, then a systematic estates satire with the poet's own voice as its moral centre.
works.attributionNotes: Gower's authorship secure.

editions.title: The Complete Works of John Gower, vol. IV: The Latin Works

works.title: Vulgaria
works.description: Robert Whittington's collection of everyday sentences in English with their Latin renderings, printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1520; the most celebrated of the Tudor vulgaria used to teach Latin composition by translation.
works.plot: The book presents model English sentences — the talk of the schoolroom, the market, and the household — each with its idiomatic Latin equivalent, arranged to drill the schoolboy in the idiom of daily speech turned into classical Latin.
works.significance: The finest surviving example of the Tudor vulgarium and a vivid record of early sixteenth-century English speech and schoolroom practice; it documents the humanist method of teaching Latin through the vernacular.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Printed in 1520 at the height of the grammar-school humanist reform; Whittington, a prolific grammarian and laureate of Oxford, was among the schoolmasters who replaced the medieval grammars with humanist vulgaria, and his book was reprinted through the 1520s.
works.structure: A collection of sentence-pairs grouped by topic, prefaced by Whittington's remarks on teaching method.

works.title: Waldere
works.description: Two fragments (about 63 lines) of an Old English heroic poem on Walter of Aquitaine, the legend known fully from the tenth-century Latin Waltharius: the hostage Walter, escaped with his beloved Hildegyth, is overtaken by the Burgundian king Guthhere (Gunther) and refuses to surrender his treasure and his bride.
works.plot: In the first fragment, Hildegyth urges Walter to fight, praising his sword Mimming and the treasures of the world's kings; in the second, a warrior (perhaps Guthhere or Hagen) taunts Walter over the shield and byrnie taken from Weland's workshop, and Walter answers boastfully that the man who comes for the gold shall have battle. The fragments preserve the defiant speech-exchange before the single combats of the fuller legend.
works.significance: The English witness to one of the great heroic legends of the Middle Ages, bridging the worlds of Beowulf and the continental epics.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: The legend of Walter of Aquitaine, rooted in fifth-century events, circulated across the Germanic world (Waltharius, the Nibelung tradition); the English fragments were discovered in 1860 in the Royal Library, Copenhagen, used as binding material.
works.characters: Waldere (Walter); Hildegyth; Guthhere; Hagen (in the underlying legend); Weland (as maker of the arms)
works.structure: A dialogue of challenge and defiance between two (or three) warriors, in the heroic flyting mode.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Medieval English Literature 1100–1500

works.title: Why Come Ye Nat to Courte?
works.description: Skelton's most direct assault on Cardinal Wolsey: taking up the courtiers' question of the title, the poet answers that the court is barred to all but Wolsey's creatures, and proceeds to a full-scale attack on the Cardinal's arrogance, his building, his rule of the king, and the degradation of the realm under his hand.
works.plot: The poem opens with the question of why honest men shun the court, answers that Wolsey has shut the king away from his subjects, and develops into a sustained invective against the Cardinal's person and policy, closing with a warning to the king.
works.significance: The most fearless political satire of the early Tudor period and the classic of the English anti-court diatribe.
works.meter: Skeltonics of unusual venom and speed; the metre's rattle becomes a weapon.
works.context: Written when Wolsey's power was absolute and Skelton had taken sanctuary at Westminster (1523) to escape the Cardinal's anger; the poem circulated in manuscript before printing.
works.characters: the poet (speaker); Cardinal Wolsey
works.structure: A satirical diatribe organized as an answer to a question; cumulative invective rising to direct warning.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Widsith
works.description: A catalogue-poem of 143 lines spoken by the scop Widsith, who boasts of the lands, kings, and tribes he has visited — a thula (name-list) that preserves the oldest stratum of Germanic heroic legend in English, from Eormanric the Goth to Hrothgar of the Danes.
works.plot: Widsith introduces himself as a poet of the Myrgings, recounts the lords he has served (Eormanric, Eadgils, Ælfwine, Hrothgar and Hrothwulf among dozens), and ends with a professional credo on the value of the scop, who wanders among peoples earning praise and treasure with his songs.
works.significance: The earliest map of Germanic heroic geography in English; a key text for the prehistory of Beowulf's world.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of the older, stichic kind.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; its name-lists reach back to the fourth-century Gothic world and have been central to reconstructing Germanic heroic legend.
works.characters: Widsith (speaker); Eormanric; Hrothgar; Hrothwulf; Eadgils; Ælfwine; Offa; Ealhhild
works.structure: Three thulas (catalogues of kings, tribes, and personal patrons) framed by first-person narrative and a gnomic coda on the poet's craft.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: Beowulf: A Verse Translation

works.title: Winner and Waster
works.description: The earliest datable poem of the Alliterative Revival (c. 1352): a debate dream vision in which Winner (the thrifty, hoarding merchant) and Waster (the lavish, spending lord) plead their cases before the king, who assigns each his proper sphere. Its satire of Edward III's economic policies — and its superb description of the armies — make it a key document of mid-century social thought.
works.plot: The dreamer sees two armies drawn up in a land divided between wealth and want; Winner and Waster, their champions, dispute before the king: Winner attacks Waster's reckless feasting and ruinous retinues, Waster defends liberality as the lifeblood of the realm; the king's judgement — sending Winner to the papal court and the friars, Waster to London and the magnates — restores each to his proper economy.
works.significance: The earliest witness to the alliterative revival's social satire and the direct ancestor of Piers Plowman's field of folk; its economic debate has made it a touchstone for medieval political thought.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line, early and vigorous.
works.context: Composed c. 1352, referencing the Order of the Garter (1348), the Statute of Treasons (1352), and the king's household; preserved uniquely in BL Additional MS 31042 (mid-fifteenth century), with a line lost to damage.
works.characters: the Dreamer; Winner; Waster; the king (Edward III)
works.structure: A debate vision framed by the arming of the two hosts, in the tradition of the altercatio; the poem breaks off, unfinished, in the king's judgement.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Wisdom
works.description: The most learned and musical of the English moralities (c. 1460–70): the play of the soul — Mind, Will, and Understanding — wedded to Wisdom (Christ), corrupted by Lucifer into a life of lechery and law, and reclaimed through penance. Its elaborate costumes, dances, and liturgical music suggest performance by a learned monastic or clerical household.
works.plot: Wisdom (Christ) espouses the soul with her powers Mind, Will, and Understanding; Lucifer tempts them to abandon contemplation for the world, and the soul falls into lechery, maintenance of law, and perjury; Wisdom returns, and the powers, moved by his speeches, do penance and are restored to grace.
works.significance: The most theologically sophisticated English morality: its fusion of mystical doctrine, music, and dance makes it a summit of the genre's learned tradition.
works.meter: Stanza forms with Latin liturgical texts and music cues, the most literate of the moralities.
works.context: Composed c. 1460–70, probably for an East Anglian monastic or noble household with trained singers; preserved in the Macro manuscript (Folger MS V.a.354) and Bodleian Digby MS 133.
works.characters: Wisdom (Christ); Anima (the Soul); Mind; Will; Understanding; Lucifer; the Seven Deadly Sins
works.structure: A two-movement morality (union with Wisdom; fall and restoration), with the masque-like dances and the court of Lucifer as its theatrical centre.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Wit and Science
altTitles: The Play of Wit and Science
works.description: John Redford's morality play of the courtship of Wit and Science, the masterpiece of the educational interludes written for the choirboys of St Paul's; surviving in a single manuscript and first printed in 1848.
works.plot: Wit, son of Nature, sets out to win the lady Science, daughter of Reason; beguiled by Idleness he falls asleep and is transformed by the enchantment of Ignorance into the fool Ingenio; Shame and Reason restore him, Instruction and Study arm him anew, and he defeats the giant Tediousness, winning Science in a dance of reconciliation. The play celebrates the humanist programme of learning through labour.
works.significance: The finest of the school interludes and the purest dramatic expression of Tudor humanist pedagogy; its allegory of the arduous courtship of learning shaped the later academic plays and the tradition of the children's companies.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic songs
works.context: Composed c. 1530–47 by Redford, choirmaster of St Paul's, for performance by the cathedral choirboys; the play belongs to the humanist transformation of the morality tradition into a vehicle for the new learning, and its songs survive with music by Redford himself.
works.characters: Wit; Science; Reason; Nature; Idleness; Ignorance; Shame; Instruction; Study; Diligence; Tediousness; Honest Recreation
works.structure: A two-part morality play of quest, fall, and restoration, with songs, dances, and stage spectacle; the action alternates between Wit's education and the comic threats of Tediousness and Idleness.

editions.title: The Moral Play of Wit and Science

works.title: Witty and Witless
altTitles: A Dialogue on Wit and Folly
works.description: John Heywood's debate dialogue on the relative happiness of the witty man and the witless, surviving in a single manuscript; first printed in 1846 by the Percy Society.
works.plot: James and John dispute whether it is better to be witty or witless: James argues that wit brings care and envy, John that witlessness is mere animal contentment; each supports his case with proverbs, exempla, and the testimony of fools, until the conclusion grants each condition its proper happiness.
works.significance: A minor but revealing document of the Erasmian debate on wisdom and folly in the English household; its survival in manuscript shows the interlude circulating beyond print.
works.meter: Couplets with proverb-dense argument
works.context: Written c. 1525–33, probably for a household audience; the debate on wit and folly belongs to the Erasmian praise-of-folly tradition, and the play's proverb lore links it to Heywood's collection of proverbs and epigrams.
works.characters: James; John
works.structure: A continuous debate in alternating speeches, without action, in the manner of the scholastic disputation turned to moral entertainment.
works.attributionNotes: The manuscript ascribes the work to John Heywood; the attribution is accepted in modern scholarship.

works.title: Wulf and Eadwacer
works.form: elegiac dramatic monologue in alliterative verse
works.description: A famously enigmatic poem of 19 lines in which a woman cries out against the separation of 'Wulf' from herself and 'Eadwacer', their child; its refrain — 'Ungelice is us' ('It is different for us') — and its riddling situation have made it the most debated short poem in Old English.
works.plot: The speaker laments that her people will take Wulf if he comes to them ('they will receive him if he comes in a band'), that their child is being carried off to the woods, and that the embrace she once knew is gone; the poem closes on the refrain and the image of Wulf carrying their whelp to the wood.
works.significance: The most mysterious and most modern-sounding of the Exeter Book poems; a touchstone for theories of the Old English lyric.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre with a refrain; the irregular lineation has suggested an underlying strophic form.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; interpretations range from heroic legend to riddle to Christian allegory.
works.characters: the speaker; Wulf; Eadwacer (their child)
works.structure: A compressed dramatic monologue of seven half-stanzas bound by a refrain, preserving an otherwise lost story (perhaps from the cycle of Wulf and Eadwacer, or a riddle, or an allegory).
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: The Blackwell Encyclopaedia of Anglo-Saxon England, 2nd edition

works.title: Wulfstan's Eschatological Homilies (De Antichristo, De falsis deis, and related sermons)
altTitles: Wulfstan's Homilies on the Last Things
works.description: Wulfstan's corpus of sermons on the end times and the faith: the coming of Antichrist and the signs of the end, the true God and the false gods (De falsis deis), baptism and the duties of Christians. These homilies, saturated with the belief that the world was in its last age, formed the moral engine of Wulfstan's preaching and lawgiving.
works.plot: De Antichristo narrates the rise of the deceiver in the last days, the persecution of the faithful, and the judgment; De falsis deis traces the history of idolatry from the pagan gods of the classical pantheon (Saturn, Jove, Mercury — euhemerized as wicked men) to the Danish idols, and urges the English to hold to the one God; the related sermons expound the Creed and the duties of the baptized.
works.significance: The classic vernacular statement of early medieval eschatology and the theology of the one true God against the gods.
works.meter: Wulfstan's rhythmical two-stress prose.
works.context: Composed c. 1000-1023, in the atmosphere of millennial expectation surrounding the year 1000 and the Danish conquest; preserved in manuscripts of Wulfstan's 'commonplace book' (e.g. British Library, Cotton MS Nero A.i).
works.characters: Antichrist; the false gods; the faithful
works.structure: Independent homilies on eschatological and catechetical themes, each a self-contained exhortation.
works.attributionNotes: Wulfstan's authorship is established on stylistic grounds.
themes: The education of princes and magistrates

works.title: Wyatt's Poems
altTitles: Sonnets and Lyrics of Sir Thomas Wyatt
works.description: The collected shorter poems of Sir Thomas Wyatt — sonnets translated and imitated from Petrarch, rondeaux, epigrams, and songs — including the masterpieces 'Whoso list to hunt', 'They flee from me', 'My galley charged with forgetfulness', and 'Blame not my lute'. They circulated in court manuscript during his life; ninety-six were printed posthumously in Tottel's Miscellany (1557).
works.plot: A lyric sequence without narrative frame: the poems trace the courtly lover's service, betrayal, and disenchantment, and the courtier's peril under the prince's eye.
works.significance: The foundation of the English lyric: Wyatt brought the Petrarchan sonnet and the courtly song into English, and his 'difficult' style set the standard of authenticity the Elizabethans imitated.
works.meter: The first English sonnets, in deliberately rough iambic pentameter with enjambment against rhyme; songs in short lines built for music.
works.context: Written across Wyatt's diplomatic career and his two imprisonments (1536, 1541); the poems encode the dangers of Henrician court life in the idiom of Petrarchan love.
works.characters: the speaker; the beloved (variously identified); the court
works.structure: Manuscript miscellany; the Egerton MS (with Wyatt's own revisions) is the principal witness, supplemented by Tottel's printed text.
works.attributionNotes: The canon rests on the Egerton MS and Tottel; a few poems printed under Wyatt's name in 1557 are of uncertain authorship.

editions.title: Sir Thomas Wyatt: The Complete Poems

works.title: Wyatt's Satires
works.description: Three verse epistles — 'Mine own John Poins', 'My mother's maids', and 'A spending hand' — written from Wyatt's Kentish retirement after his 1536 imprisonment: adaptations of Horace and Alamanni in which the speaker rejects the court's falseness and the town's corruption for the honest poverty of the country life.
works.plot: Each epistle weighs the court against the country: to Poins, the speaker explains why he cannot flatter; to the courtiers, why he will not hunt with them into the wind; to Bryan, why honesty is the only policy he can keep.
works.significance: The first English satires in the classical manner and the models for the Elizabethan verse epistle and satire (Donne, Hall, Marston); their country-house ideal anticipates the seventeenth-century poems of retirement.
works.meter: Terza rima throughout — the metre of the Penitential Psalms prologue — giving the epistles a grave, conversational movement.
works.context: Written at Allington after Wyatt's release from the Tower in 1536; the satires voice the disillusion of the courtier who has survived the fall of Anne Boleyn.
works.characters: the speaker; John Poins; Francis Bryan
works.structure: Three independent verse epistles in the Horatian manner, linked by their common theme of withdrawal from the court.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Wycliffite Bible
works.description: The first complete translation of the Bible into English, produced in the circle of John Wyclif at Oxford and Lutterworth: the literal Early Version (c. 1382), associated with Nicholas of Hereford, and the idiomatic Later Version (c. 1388–95), associated with John Purvey. Banned by Archbishop Arundel's Constitutions (1409) but copied throughout the fifteenth century, it is the greatest monument of Lollard vernacular theology.
works.plot: The translation renders the whole Vulgate — Old and New Testaments, with the apocrypha — into English, the Early Version word-for-word after the Latin, the Later Version in fluent, idiomatic prose, with prologues defending vernacular scripture and a general prologue expounding the Lollard program of 'poor priests' and scriptural preaching.
works.significance: The foundational text of the English Bible: its phrasing passed into the sixteenth-century translations and into the common language of English devotion, and its very existence redefined the politics of vernacular religion.
works.meter: Prose: the Later Version in particular is a landmark of plain, idiomatic English style.
works.context: Made c. 1382–95 in Wyclif's circle, condemned by the Blackfriars council (1382) and by Arundel's Constitutions (1409), which forbade unlicensed vernacular scripture; despite the ban, some 250 manuscripts survive, and the translation fed the English biblical tradition through Tyndale to the King James Version.
works.characters: none (scriptural translation)
works.structure: The complete biblical canon in translation, with the characteristic Lollard prologues and glosses (in some manuscripts) as its apparatus.
works.attributionNotes: Traditionally called the 'Wycliffe Bible', but modern scholarship dissents from Wyclif's personal authorship; the translation is the work of his circle (Hereford, Purvey, and others). authorship_status reflects this traditional attribution.

editions.title: The Holy Bible ... in the Earliest English Versions Made from the Latin Vulgate by John Wycliffe and His Followers

works.title: York Play
works.description: The York Corpus Christi cycle: forty-eight (originally more) pageants dramatizing sacred history from the fall of Lucifer to the Last Judgement, performed annually by the city's craft guilds on wagons through the streets of York from the late fourteenth century to 1569. The longest and most complete surviving mystery cycle, registered in the great civic manuscript of 1463–77.
works.plot: The cycle moves from the creation and fall of the angels, through the Old Testament pageants (Adam and Eve, Noah, Abraham, Moses), to the life of Christ — the Annunciation, Nativity, ministry, the great Passion sequence (the Crucifixion and the death of Christ are its summit), the Harrowing of Hell, and the Resurrection — and closes with the Last Judgement.
works.significance: The greatest surviving English mystery cycle: its Passion sequence is among the most powerful religious writing of the Middle Ages, and its civic organization is the fullest expression of medieval urban piety.
works.meter: Thirteen-line stanza and couplet forms, with the alliterative 'York realism' of the Passion pageants.
works.context: The play is first mentioned in 1376, and the surviving register (BL Additional MS 35290) was compiled 1463–77; performances continued until suppressed in 1569, the cycle's long life making York the best-documented of the English civic dramas.
works.characters: God; Lucifer; Adam and Eve; Noah; Abraham; the Virgin Mary; Christ; Pilate; Herod; the soldiers of the Crucifixion
works.structure: A sequential pageant cycle performed on Corpus Christi day, each play assigned to a guild (the Shipwrights' Noah, the Pinners' Crucifixion), the whole forming a civic salvation history.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative (many guild poets, revised over generations); authorship_status reflects the cycle's collective making.

works.title: Ywain and Gawain
works.description: The northern English adaptation of Chrétien de Troyes's Yvain: the knight Ywain wins Laudine by slaying her husband at the magic fountain, loses her by overstaying his leave, and regains her through madness, penance, and a career of championing the oppressed, with his lion as companion. The most accomplished English Arthurian romance after Sir Gawain and the Green Knight.
works.plot: Ywain kills the fountain's defender and marries the widow Laudine through her maid Lunet's advocacy; forgetting his year's leave, he is rejected, goes mad, and is healed; as the Knight of the Lion he rights a succession of wrongs (the giant Harpin, the sisters' inheritance), and by keeping faith at last wins back Laudine.
works.significance: The chief English witness to the French Arthurian romance's central themes of love, honour, and self-knowledge, and a bridge between continental romance and Malory.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets in the northern dialect.
works.context: Composed c. 1325–50 in the north of England from Chrétien's Yvain (with an intermediary version); preserved uniquely in BL Cotton MS Galba E.ix (c. 1400).
works.characters: Ywain; Laudine; Lunet; Gawain; the lion; the giant Harpin
works.structure: A quest-sequence of episodes bound by the fountain, the lion, and the promises made and broken, in the interlaced manner of French romance simplified for English taste.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
